reference_book.title: The Book of the Unnamed Midwife (The Road to Nowhere, #1)
reference_book.review_text:
It took me a while to get into this book - these old eyes didn't deal well with the change of font. But thank goodness for Kindles and the ability to change the size of the fonts! This is an excellent apocalyptic/PA book about a virus that kills most of the people in the world - and even more women than men, and ALL the babies at birth. How can we have hope and keep trudging on in a changed world without the hope of a future with children? 
 The "unnamed" person is a midwife on the coast of California when the disease hits. She struggles with losing both babies and mothers. Then, she too gets sick with the mysterious fever. But...she wakes up eventually and sets off to find a place to make a life. The trek is hard and cruel, and she meets a few real crazies along the way. 
 I loved this book!

book_a.title: Article 5 (Article 5, #1)
book_a.user_review: I liked this book okay - enough that I will continue on with the series. BUT - I had a hard time with about the first 1/3 - it was just TOO YA. There are flashbacks to her first kiss, first love...and it goes on a bit too much for this old broad. After that the mushy flashbacks end, she seems to grow up a bit, and the action gets...more active?

sample_reviews.review_text:
I thought that this was really great! I have been wanting to read this for a while, and then my sister finally got it for Easter and of course she instantly hid it away from me, but I have at last gotten my hands on it. I love the premise of the book. And I know that sometimes the post apocalyptic world is a bit overdone and everyone's just dying and there's no hope, but I never get tired of it. I love the end of the world books. And I love Chase and Ember's relationship. Their relationship is so complex and there is so much going on between them, but at the same time, the reader is never confused. They can relate because everyone has had someone in their life who they were close with and then they dramatically changed and you're just left so confused about what happened. That's how Ember feels, and probably Chase too. And they just don't know how to get back to where they were after so much has happened. I thought it was so good, and I am getting the next one, Breaking Point as soon as I can. 
 If you liked Legend, I would recommend this book.

the fuck...the girl is so stupid plus annoying plus idk whatever happened to those intelligent, daring, irresistibly admirable old fashioned heroines...i want to read a book about them, instead of all these craps :( 
 unbearable road trip theme..seriously, dystopian society and road trip just doesn't go along, unless ofcourse there are zombies lol and once again..what the fuck is wrong with this girl? first she tries to take on the arresting officers, then she tries to plan an escape, she has no regards for anyone else, she thinks she is going to break out save her mother bla bla i mean she acts like she has a superpower or something..one girl against the world...lol, seriously, saving the world? she is more likely to slip off a banana peel and die...seeing how much brain and common sense this girl poses. 
 also the flashbacks could have explained so much better about the why and hows...but they were simply boring and repetitive...thank god it ended as soon as girl meets boy again and then some more repetitive boring driving, talking and stuff 
 okay i think its not really the protagonist but the writer i'm annoyed at :( i really dont have any decent new book ( john green anyone?) and books like these is making me mad...thus the rant :(

I think I may have read too many Dystopian books in a row. I found Ember to be a very realistic teen girl throw into a horrible world and stumbling her way along. She doesn't wallow in self pity but tries to find a way to fight and get out and survive. 
 But, even though she was a great main character, I just didn't connect to her. I think that had a lot to do with the fact that I just couldn't buy this dystopian world. If we destroy all and go to rebuild, I just can't imagine this is how it will be. And since I had tough time with the world, I had a tough time with the book 
 But, I did like Ember and Chase. I liked the underground world they ended up trudging through, their shot at trying to survive in cold weather with little food and not enough sleeping bags and the strange love/hate/hurt/struggle thing they had going on. Chase and Ember (and some of the supporting characters) are reason alone to read this book.

I found this book to be rather problematic; while the concept intrigued me in its comparison to Nazi Germany, the forced romantic tension between the main character and her ex/love interest was so ridiculous that I was rolling my eyes more often than feeling any type of feeling towards the main characters. I really just wanted to yell at Ember to tell her to stop whining and say what she was thinking rather than just whining about her issues. I will not read any sequels to this books since the character development was so lacking that I really do not care what happens to the characters.

I didn't finish this book and know that I won't. I tried, I really did. The heroine was annoying and the book was just so easy to put down and not pick up again. After I checked GoodReads, I realised that it wasn't going to improve so I decided not to waste my time. To say it wasn't a page turner is an understatement.

I enjoyed this book immensely! It's a great dystopian novel and the story sucked me in and wouldn't let me go! It's got the angsty feeling, the harsh environment, the rush to save someone, the need to save each other...I really liked it! 
 Full review here: 
 http://mystmusician.wordpress.com/201...
Why???? This was the question I asked the entire book. And not in a good way. Sigh.

This was an okay book...I was looking for a good dystopian adventure and, although it started out well, went downhill from there. I realize the protagonist was a teenager, but her back-and-forth deliberations and decisions seemed more those of a 14-year old, not an almost-18 year old. And the way that Chase and Ember didn't talk to each other - with the history they had - was incredibility unbelievable to me. Do I want to know what happens in book two? Sort of....

I've had this on my list for a while, but haven't read it yet because of the mixed reviews. Now getting into it, I see why (and I was right to wait). 
 Article 5 is about a girl named Ember who gets arrested early on in the book because of Article 5, one of the mandates now in the United States. Don't ask me why a War (you always know if it's in capital letters, it's IMPORTANT-- no, not being sarcastic AT ALL) would create this mandate, or why people would think it was the way to stop wars, but whatever. So she loves this boy, Chase, who of course is a soldier that helps enforce these rules. 
 I admit that I could only get through 45% of this book before giving up. And there was at least 10% that I was skimming, hoping to make it to the end, just so I could see if there were any redeeming twists. But I was so fed up with the lack of world building, the vagueness of the whole situation, and the really annoying and unlikeable protagonist, Ember. I was hoping the whining and bad attitude would get better, but she basically just blames everyone else for her problems. I know life is bad, but eventually, you have to move on and try to get through the awfulness that is going on. Otherwise, you might as well just give up. In real life, this chick wouldn't have made it past the first few chapters. After scratching that guard, she would have been killed. Her relationship with her mother is completely unhealthy, and focusing on that as the big emotional connection in the book felt very false. Not to mention Chase-- if I were him, I would have dumped her on the side of the road a long time ago. 
 Overall, a huge disappointment, and I couldn't even finish it.

book_b.title: Where She Went (If I Stay, #2)
book_b.user_review: I loved If I Stay, and this 2nd book is a very satisfying follow up. Just what happened in the 3 years between when Mia left for Julliard, and when Adam attended her concert in NYC? This book tells the story, from Adam's point of view. It alternates between present day and the past, to fill us in on what they have been doing the past 3 years. It made me cry at points, it also made me smile. It left me hopeful. I highly recommend that anyone who read the 1st book read this follow up.

sample_reviews.review_text: I absolutely loved IF I STAY, so when I heard there would be a sequel from Adam's POV I was thrilled! Gayle Forman does NOT disappoint. Just read it.

I think that Adam Wilde might be the most unlikeable character I've read in a very, very long while. 
 I did not read this book for his diatribey, paranoid, privileged, whiney, misogynistic male tears. I read this book for Mia. Unfortunately, Mia is only present in half of the book, and even for that half we have to slog through Adams bullshit hangups as narration about their past. I seriously hate Adam Wilde. 
 Although, I didn't hate the ending. It seemed right because it was a very young adult literature way to tie up the story. I would have, however, LOVED if the ending were different. I would have loved to see more of Mia's process and agency and seen her make a different decision and force Wahdum to deal with it. But it still gave me a warm feeling to see things tied up the way they did.
It was a good book, liked the first one better though :)

Wow! Aunque de una manera u otra sabia como terminaria la historia no me parecio un cliche. Adam logro enamorarme en la forma que cuenta su historia. De lo que a sentido y pasado en esos tres anos que pasaron separados, lo que sufrio y lo que no lograba comprender
I love it when authors can write the same story in different perspectives and still suck me in. Such a lovely story :) quick read

People always say that the first book/movie isn't better than the first, but that is absolutely not true about this particular mini series. Reading it from Adam's view changed my whole prospective and was even more heart wrenching than the first. I am so in love with Adam and Mia, more so than I was in the first book. You truly feel that you are right beside them through it all and the imagery is perfect.
Not bad, but not as good as the first,
Love the idea of the book and would have given it more stars if the swearing wasn't so offensive. It just isn't necessary.

Wow, I am speechless. What an amazingly beautiful book! Adam is a hot, hot mess and such a compelling and complex character. Gayle Forman has outdone herself, and I'm sure I'll be thinking about these characters for a long time.
Read my full review on: https://fridayread.wordpress.com/2016...

reference_book.title: Vanished (Nick Heller, #1)
reference_book.review_text: I've always enjoyed Finder's coporate thrillers and this one is no exception...Nick Heller is a former special forces operative who now works as an investigator...he becomes involved in the intrigue when his own brother is kidnapped...while figuring out the maze of clues and "Red herrings" Nick's "smart aleck" asides are a fun addditions to the faced pace plotting and action...I look forward to the 2nd Nick Heller!!!

book_a.title: Nothing to Lose (Jack Reacher, #12)
book_a.user_review: My least favorite in the Reacher series. Preachy and my 1st disappointment of the series!

sample_reviews.review_text: Another solid thriller

Lee Child starts "Nothing to Lose" with a guy wandering in the desert. He's delirious, dehydrated and a perfect foreshadow for what's to come. Jack Reacher, our hero, is heading southwest across the country. He comes to a couple of towns about 20 miles apart. One is called Hope, the other goes by Despair. And of course that catches Reacher's fancy. He's got to know more. Since he left his only real job as a military cop, he's been wandering around wearing clothes until they stink too much and throwing them out for another new set. No luggage, no identification, no purpose other than to see what's over the next ridge. What Reacher finds in Despair takes him nearly the entire novel to figure out. What he discovers immediately is that the cops in Despair don't like him. In fact, one of them sends four "deputies" to keep him from drinking a cup of his beloved coffee in the only diner in town. Reacher's mantra is "you leave me alone and I leave you alone." Despair starts like a Children of the Corn scenario. The town is nuts and they all want Reacher out. So he hightails it to Hope where he meets Officer Vaughn. He also stumbles across a dead body. Mysteries abound. And while "Nothing to Lose" is a slow build, the stakes are probably the highest Child's had his character face. I read one review that gave the book one or two stars out of five. And I thought about it as I plowed through the pages. All I can think of is that the bad guy really isn't so terrible. At least at first. Then it makes sense. But the real conflict here is with the whole town. Very intense.

I found this story to be way to plodding. It's told solely from the main charactor's point of view, Jack Reacher, and he doesn't say anything until he has to. 531 pages of boring slowly moving story. If I hadn't been bored with nothing else to read, I've have never finished this one.

Ho hum, same old, same old. Not much new in storyline of this Reacher novel. . Town in middle of nowhere, ingenious Reacher, lone woman cop, quick bedroom caper, town problem solved, time to move on. Ho, hum.

I listened to the audio version which kept me entertained on the two-day drive to Denver. The speaker's voice is very good / easy to listen to. The story is much like the last Lee Child novel I read, but I enjoy the main character, Jack Reacher, and am getting to know him. Lee Child's descriptions of minute details may drag a bit, but it really brings you into that world and gives good insight into Reacher. If I had been reading the printed version, I would have skipped over some of the detail, but I would have missed some of the clues the author sprinkled throughout the chapters, but which sharp-eyed Reacher spotted. Good mindless fun.

Waiting for departure at Midway. No book for the flight. People who know I like crime novels and mysteries have recommended Lee Child. A well-known, and respected author also cited Lee Child as a guilty pleasure. Despite the fact that this "stranger from out of town" seems never to have lost a fight, I finished the book in 36 hours. And bought another (the first) in the series. Let's see if Jack Reacher wears thin.
Not the best of his that I've read.
I didn't like it

** spoiler alert ** 
 Gave the three stars because it's good in the fact that it has all the aspects that makes Jack Reacher a guilty pleasure - still a loner, slept with the girl and beat up a boat load of people. And while he found himself in the usual scenario only he can find, this one was beyond far fetched. There were multiple reasons why this town was so bizarre. At first it was OK because as we found out more it kept the pages turning but the conclusion was not to satisfying, almost on the boring side.

One of the worst novels from the author. The only interesting part was the name of the towns- Hope and Despair. Other than that a run of the mill stuff. The hero goes into a mysterious town and is forcibly removed. A woman cop from the other city helps him fight his battle against a preacher. Religion and the futility of war is touched upon in such a haphazard way that it seems like a novice attempt. Avoid!

book_b.title: Killing Kennedy: The End of Camelot
book_b.user_review: Decent telling of events leading up to and after November 22...realistic presentation of Camelot...great reminiscence!!!

sample_reviews.review_text: Whether you like O'Reily's politics or not, he has presented what appears to be a non-biased account of the events leading to and following the assassination of JFK. Does he have all the facts? I don't think anyone will ever know for sure.
An excellent read that makes me have a whole new respect for JFK and Jackie.
The book its is great. I learned a ton of history I had not known before. I listed to the audiobook and did notice some quality issues with the recording. I highly recommend this book.
Absolutely amazing! I thoroughly enjoyed this book!!

Easy Read. Not much learned for a person who already knows a bit about this history. A few fun interesting facts but over all could have been a bit more entertaining. More build up on the conspiracy theories would have been interesting. Less on the history before the assassination and more on the aftermath would have been better.

Having known the 'overall' story behind JFK's assassination as well as the various conspiracy theories since childhood, I was very interested to read up on facts compiled by somebody who appears to be - at least on the fringe - involved in the case. As it turns out, Bill O'Reilly was a reporter 'after the fact' turned political commentator and anchor of 'The O'Reilly Factor' on TV. Of course that does not mean that he infallible and knows all the facts surrounding this very important and sad for the entire world event, but judging by his account, he did grave research on everybody involved and arrived at his conclusions with the information and details gathered. Will we ever know exactly what happened and why? Will the conspiracy theories ever stop? Probably now. But that is something we have to live with every day.
I guess my main question is WTF is O'Reilly doing? This is so full of fiction, I guess you could say it is a Romance Novel for Teabaggers.
Book Club- July 2013

While I try to separate the reader of this audio book from the author, I don't like either one. The tone was irreverent and disrespectful. The things reported seem to take the fiction side of the road.

After reading Killing Lincoln I was really looking forward to reading this book when it came out. I like the way Bill O' Reilly and Martin Dugard write a book. Little snippets of historical information leading up to the assassination gave me enough information and are almost as shocking as the assassination is. They give the reader just enough information to keep you page turning until the end. I suggest to those who are looking for more from this book to read books on those events that capture your interest. I think the authors gave us one side of a story that is true. Do I believe there is more to the assassination? You bet I do. Keep reading there is plenty of books on this assassination to keep you questioning for a long time to come.

reference_book.title: Beautiful Creatures (Caster Chronicles, #1)
reference_book.review_text:
An extremely average YA novel with paranormal overtones that are drowned out by the teenage angst. 
 The idea of Casters is new but we barely get to explore that because the authors are all obsessed with the frustrated relationship between Lena (something bad is going to happen on her 16th birthday)and Ethan (big fish in a small pond). 
 This book could have done with some serious editing. It's far too long and whole scenes drag by with nothing happening. Overall, it was a disappointment.

book_a.title: The Knife of Never Letting Go (Chaos Walking, #1)
book_a.user_review:
I liked this book, but I didn't love it. My problem was the running. 
 The set up is great -- a colony has established itself on a new world where everyone can hear what everyone else is thinking and all the women are dead. Todd is the last child in Prentistown, a month away from reaching adulthood. The authorities come for him at his foster parent's home and he has to run into the swamp where he meets a girl, Viola, who's just crash landed there in a spaceship. 
 This is all great, but then the characters start running. They run across a bridge and burn it down. "No problems," Hildy the kind lady on the other side tells them, "it'll take 2 days for the men to cross the river and we know how to defend ourselves here." 
 But they don't and soon Todd, Todd's dog and Viola are on the move again. Ness does a good job of describing what it's like for two kids moving across a countryside they don't understand recording hunger, bruises and falls but the effect is rather ruined when the bad guys come riding in on horseback all neat and pressed. 
 Todd gets a work out in this book. At one point he contracts a lung infection and spends 5 days in a coma. Upon waking, Viola feeds him breakfast and then off they go, running again. Sorry, but that's just not possible. You don't wake up from a 5 day coma and run to the bathroom let alone the next town. 
 I really wanted to like this book but reading it exhausted me. I don't think I'll be buying the sequel.

sample_reviews.review_text: I got off to a shaky start with this one. The narration of Todd in the first few chapters was extremely jarring, with all of the bad spelling and grammar but I understand why he's written this way, this barely literate farm boy. Once I got used to it, I didn't put the book down until the end. And yes, I cried. In fact this is the first book in years to ever make me cry. So fantastic book and have the sequel queued up t oreads as soon as I finish work tonight :)

Okay. It took me a.) a really long time to get around to reading this, since it seems to be such a classic YA dystopian and b.) it also took me a lengthy time to get through reading this. I think the premise is good. It was gripping, it moved quickly, and I liked Viola and Todd as main characters. I wasn't bothered by the occasional incorrect spelling or grammar. My first problem with this was that there is a certain death 3/4th of the way through the book that broke me in half. I had to put the book down for literally 2 weeks because I was so upset over the death that occurred. And I know, this should actually lend itself to me giving the book a super high rating because I was so emotionally impacted by something that happened. BUT I just found that scene to be the only thing that sticks out in my mind as emotionally gripping. Every other plot piece going on throughout the novel was uninteresting to me. I expected a huge plot twist (like Aaron being some sort of robot and everyone in Prentisstown being turned into a cyborg at age 13... yes, this was honestly where I was hoping things were going), but instead, it just made me upset and confused me. I didn't see the motivations for the characters to do what they did. I don't think I'll continue on with the trilogy, even though the end of this was such a massive cliffhanger.

OK, so anybody reading this please bear in mind I was listening to it ass an audiobook. 
 The first thing that grabbed me was how much it sounded like Richard Burton narrating 'Under Milkwood'. There was a poetic flavour to the text, and the lyrical note to the narrator. 
 Unfortunately, that's not my scene. I like the books I read to be 'clean' in a grammatical and syntactical sense, but I am not a fan of stuff that goes out of its way to be 'literary'. There were times as I listened to this that I felt I was back at school reading 'Kes', or 'Cider with Rosie'. 
 And there's my problem. I'm not qualified to judge this book, simply because I avoid this style (normally) and thus have nothing to compare it against. The concept itself was fascinating, and a part of me was disappointed that I would probably never get to find out what happened, but after I realised I had screamed 'get ON with it' at my iPod for the third time in one trip home, I guessed it was time for me to part company with this novel :) 
 Please, if you have a literary bent, or want to explore that sort of material, read Patrick Ness. I'm sure you will enjoy it. Sadly, perhaps, just not for me.

I pushed through this book, but it didn't really do it for me. 
 My favourite character was the dog, who could talk, but even he became a bit annoying as all he seemed to say was that he needed to poo. I didn't connect with the characters and found the phonetic spelling of some words distracting. The fact that two 13 year old kids spent days on end running without food or sleep wasn't believable. Disaster after disaster, then some more running.

I'm a massive Patrick Ness fame and this book just made me love him more. The pacing was spot on, throughout the entire 500 pages I was gripped and just waiting to find out what's around each corner. It's a brilliant book and I can't recommend it enough. Ness really is an incredible writer.
No me engancho como pense que lo haria. No se si continuare con la saga.. . (Seguramente no).
Trainspotting for virgins.

Well, I finally finished it. A few months ago I began this book, got halfway through, and then life happened so I put it down. Thanks to some airplane time this weekend, I have finished. I wish I had been able to finish it when I had planned, but it was east enough to pick back up. It has been a long time since I have began a YA distopian society that really frightened me, and alternately intrigued and horrified. This is a well done, well planned first in a series. It managed to set up a tale and only begin to unpack it, and leave me begging for book two with one hell of a cliffhanger. In this world of men, yep women are not a thing, at least until Viola shows up (not something to be weary of at all), and poor young Todd has one heck of an adventure to lead. This book contains it's own language (a well done one at that, which is difficult to pull off), talking animals, crazy overly religious men, and seriously grisly violence. I look forward yo finding out how the rest of this series unfolds.
10 out of 5 stars!!!!

This was a weird book. I liked it in the beginning, then it seemed to drag too much for the next 300-400 pages. I was just trying to finish it, thinking I would not read the second book (or third). Then the ending came and it leaves you so totally hanging. I think I might want to read the second book now to figure out what happens.

book_b.title: The Girl Who Played with Fire (Millennium, #2)
book_b.user_review:
I liked this second in the Larsson series, probably because the Swedish to English translation was handled much better here. 
 The story is very readable and keeps you engrossed even though Larsson has an annoying habit of describing everything Lisbeth Salander is doing. (I should have kept a running tally of how many times she went into a convenience store to buy smokes and how many times she ate pizza). I've always had a good opinion of the Swedes but, after reading these books, the whole country seems to be teaming with serial killers and sexual perverts all of whom have a magnetic attraction to Salander, the book's heroine. 
 That being said, the story does move well and keeps you up at night, desperate to find out what happens after Salander finishes her cigarette.

sample_reviews.review_text: Great book. I love this trilogy.

I had to stop reading this book because Larsson's prose style is too reminiscent of my ex-roommate's ex-boyfriend's mind numbing hour long detailed monologue on an utterly unremarkable and featureless five minute trip to the corner store to buy D cell batteries. By the time he got to the point, I had utterly ceased to care. I think the tipping point was the completely mind numbing description of Lisbeth's boob job. I completely and utterly don't get why people like this. All of the characters lack humanity and any sort of appeal.

The first book was for the most part plot-driven. The 40-year old mystery took a while to unfold, but was interesting when it did. So was Lisbeth, although she wasn't the main focus. Enter, The Girl Who Played With Fire. The story has now turned character-driven with Lisbeth as the protagonist. But instead of having much of a plot of any character revelations about her early on, we read about her buying a new apartment, grocery shopping, and what furniture she picked out at IKEA in *great* detail. Seriously, you could go down to the store and decorate the same way if you wanted, that's the level of description he gave. I was bored out of my mind. This goes on for a staggering 172 pages. 
 Mystery thriller? Surely you jest! This book wasn't a mystery whatsoever for me. The fact that the police and everyone else working to solve the case chose to ignore it was pitiful. 
 The turning point didn't happen until page 172, which was about 100 pages too late to hold the interest of any reader who's not a masochist. The quick pace and interest it generates rapidly disappears until 375.Really. It was more bloated than a rotting whale. 
 The Girl With the Dragon Tattoo was a better book. I wanted to throw this one against the wall a few times.

Relectura febrero 2014. La agrego nada mas para que figure en el reading challenge, pero estoy maquinando la review de la trilogia entera porque LISBETH, TE AMO. Y creo que me enamore de Mikael Blomkvist. No tengo remedio.

Hold on tight. We left off the last book with just a hint of sexual mischievousness and now the author has chosen to go all out soft porn. I'm sure it added something to the novel, I just can't imagine what.

This is the second book in the Millennium series and just as good as the first one. It's the kind of book, for which one wouldn't mind giving up some sleep to get to its last page. The mystery surrounding Lisbeth Salander's past is solved and we get an insight into her tragic and unjust childhood. A lot of new characters with very difficult names are introduced, while the author continues to write passionately about causes he believes in by blending them well into the story. 
 The Girl Who Played with Fire, begins with Salander holidaying on a Caribbean island and passing her time solving math equations while a plot is being hatched against her, back home in Sweden. The story switches locations from Grenada to Sweden, until finally Salander decides to return home after being away for over a year. She gets into trouble as soon as she's back and is wanted for triple murder. Blomkvist, the "naive do-gooder", is the only one who believes she is innocent from the start and begins his own investigation to prove it. What follows is a lot of action, a big revelation, and the putting together of different puzzle pieces to get the real picture. 
 Too bad the third and final book in the trilogy won't be out until the middle of next year!! :(

i read the first in this series in a quick pace, it was an interesting read - however that wasn't really the case here (no pun intended). The book is a fast read, no doubt, but the plot was slow and so much of it was just keeping the reader in the dark - very frustrating. When the mystery was revealed, it was a good twist but i just couldn't believe that Lisbeth seemed to encounter every bad thing in the world, not one good person in her life for so long and yet the sister somehow survives??? 
 i also don't get why everyone in this book seems to be sleeping with everyone else, is there no one in Stockholm who believes in fidelity?? And why are there so many jerks in the police force, in the security company, everywhere in Lisbeth's life?? She seems to have a propensity for finding the world's worst people. 
 Also heavy scenes of lesbian sex, so be forewarned. 
 Recommend for a long airplane flight, maybe for a book but it didn't hold my interest enough to want to invest the time to pick up the last book in the series (I just went onto the internet to find out what happens),
Loved the intrigue, suspense and character insight. Finished in a few days.
Lisbeth Salander is one hell of a fictional character. She's definitely one of my top-ten-most-kick-ass-fictional-characters-list.
Salander isn't as vulnerable in this. I miss that

reference_book.title: The Green Mile
reference_book.review_text: Another great story for those of us who enjoy a great stories.

book_a.title: The Hum and the Shiver (Tufa, #1)
book_a.user_review:
Unispired: This is a total beach book. Read... or not. 
 It reminds me of a romance author (not disparaging) first attempt at a full novel without gratuitous sex scenes. 
 No original concepts and two dimensional characters... blagh 
 Painful

sample_reviews.review_text: I was really pleasantly surprised by this book. Love it when that happens.

The premise is awfully intriguing, but the writing is pretty bad. Many of the plot twists led nowhere. The author is clearly a dudelike dude and doesn't do well with his female protagonist's viewpoint. None of the characters are well fleshed out. Feels drafty, in the sense that given this as a draft, it seems possible to make it into a pretty amazing novel. Unfortunately it was published too soon. I loved most things about the Tufa and the setting, etc., so I didn't hate the book. I will probably hang onto it and not recycle - read it another time or two first at least.
So far not sure I want to finish this book...I'm having trouble with the main character, Bronwyn. She's about as interesting as grass growing.

3.5 stars. 
 *hardcore spoilers ahead!* 
 This story was a solid work of contemporary fantasy. The Tufa people, long ago descendents of the Tuatha or fairies from Ireland, reside in Cloud County, Tennessee. Bronwyn Hyatt is a returning war hero (though we never find out quite what happened other than hearsay), who has to come to grips with the fact that she is being haunted by a haint and she thinks her mother might die. She also can't remember how to play her mandolin or any of the songs the Tufa people seem to inherently know (which area HUGE part of their culture). 
 I thought this story was very imaginative. The hidden ancestry of the Tufa was interesting and the way they always danced around the answer to any questions was artful. The characters were pretty vivid and although there wasn't a HUGE amount of character development, I enjoyed reading about all of them (especially Don Swayback, his story was neat). The writing was decent, and I was left wanting to know more about the Tufa community and what happens next. 
 However, upon further investigation, I found out the next two books are about different people, which doesn't really thrill me. I can't exactly pinpoint why I don't want to read the rest of the trilogy, but the burning desire I usually have to read a next book just isn't there. Plus, since this story seems to be technically over, I'm happy with just treating it like a standalone novel and leaving it at that.

This was an odd book. I liked the interesting world-building he did with the Tufa culture and how much music was involved in their culture and life. But the book got very sexual and while I don't have any specific problem with that, it felt very awkward and it tended to pull me out of the story. It just had nothing to do with the characterization and I kept waiting for a reason for it all, but no.

I overall enjoyed the storyline and writing. The book reminded me a little bit of Charles de Lint, but I ultimately think I enjoyed de Lint a bit more. Nonetheless, this was creative, if a bit stiff and slow plotwise.

Sword and Laser June book of month. Here is another one that started out a little slow for me, but picked up rather quickly. I really want to know more about the history of the Tufa. This seems to be a running theme with a lot of the books I've been reading of late. I'm introduced to a universe but not given a history of it. I'm all about knowing the little nuances of what has come before and how we got to where the story currently is. I've added the four other books in the Tufa series to my queue to see if that will be given to me.

Disappointing. I won't be continuing with this series. I much prefer his sword fantasy series. This went off the rails because Bronwyn Hyatt makes no sense to me. She is a very strange character, starting with her killer instincts, her pride and love for family and they return the affection, yet she takes pleasure in the masochism of giving blow jobs to every man, literally, in town. She is First Daughter, pure blood, raised with respect, but she's a damaged teenaged soul giving blow jobs to whoever wants one. She's so rebellious, she will not obey her community's expectations or responsibilities, despite the damage that will cause. She would rather go to war and kill because despite her masochism and lack of self-respect for herself and her community, somehow she's also aggressive and patriotic, then when she comes back horribly damaged by war drama and trauma, she's powerful and strong enough to go to war to defend her brother from a local criminal, but too weak and scared and destroyed by war to defend her mother, who she loves as much as her brother. But maybe that's so because she came home and walked in on her parents making love on the couch after a date, and her mother sees her but continues on maliciously to have an orgasm while staring at her daughter. Otherwise they all adore and respect each other, and would kill for each other. Really? This make sense to you?

To me, Alex Bledsoe wrote a perfect book. It's subtle, but not dull in any way. It's got great characters without resorting to cliche. It's got a fresh concept, but still feels familiar. I didn't think I was going to like this book, but I ended up loving it from cover to cover. 
 Bledsoe's continued work in the Tufa realm shows that he's created a rich, deep world worth mining.

This book wasn't for me. Where to start? 
 Let's start with Bron -- 
 It's actually a case study of why I hate to read books with female leads by male authors. His characterization of Bron was much like Heinlein. As in, all she really wanted was sex-sex-sex. Actually, her whole character was based around sex. That was pretty much the only thing that made her a 'wild child', so to speak. 
 Her sexual exploits were talked about over and over and over again. At one point, even her own mother said (and I swear I'm being honest here) that sometimes she hated her daughter because she knew she was sleeping with every boy in town and that made her SO jealous. 
 Truly. I shit you not. Of course, this was said after she walked into her house and caught her parents screwing on the couch (and her mother staring at her without stopping, etc.) 
 Yeah, no thanks. 
 World Building -- 
 This is a big issue too because the author doesn't spend any time explaining anything. We get tiny snippets throughout but it's not done cleverly or deftly. It's really poorly doled out, almost like an afterthought. So you spend most of the book completely confused by everything. 
 I guess their magic is songs and weird hand gestures? And only the full blooded get to learn them because it's 'the way it's always been done'? (Yeah, love the cope out excuse too.) 
 Plot -- 
 Very slow with very little action. She sees a ghost. She lusts after every man (including her father.) She learns a bit of music. She complains and thinks about how bad she was and sex. Then she thinks about more sex. 
 Occasionally she goes outside to think about sex. 
 Death -- 
 The death in this book was so stupid and pointless. The author was trying to be clever but, yeah, no.

book_b.title: The Moon is a Harsh Mistress
book_b.user_review: Interesting concept but not enough to keep me going the whole way. Lemmed it half way :(

sample_reviews.review_text: This here is my favorite book. I suppose The Road meant more to me, but when I'm taking my entrance test for heaven, and they ask me what my favorite book was and why, I'll say this one. And it'll be because of the amazing world Heinlein created, and the amazing characters he had populate it, and the ideas, which aren't always new -- in fact, certain of them are awfully old, and crusty from disuse -- those characters have, and the story, oh!, the amazing story of the liberation of the moon. I have a tattoo with a brass cannon over a field or stars with a red bar sinister and the acronym TANSTAAFL on my left arm. This is my favorite book.

This is from Heinlein's later production when he had gotten more chatty. And in the first three hundred pages there was plenty of "talk-talk" as the narrator would have said. Being a computer technologist he finds this trying. I don't know if Heinlein himself found it trying or if it was his subconscious telling him to move along. I found it trying. 
 I enjoyed the fact that the moon being a destination for convict transportation from all the nations on earth there was some language variation. Calling one another "gospodin", for example - when not calling one another "cobber". Language otherwise spare for taste. Pronouns in short-supply on moon. Narrator talk-talk easy understand, but unimproved reading pleasure. 
 I like Heinlein's take on race. The narrator's name is Manuel Garcia O'Kelly. He may be mostly Hispanic, but nobody cares. Other people may be black, may be white, not important. 
 But with a title like this one, I would expect a little more bounding across the surface, falling down craters, being scorched by radiation or frozen by shadow. Here people hang out in tunnels all the time. Well, they do get outside on occasion, but briefly and without any real danger. I suppose it is earth who finds her a harsh mistress when their grain supply world starts throwing rocks. 
 Heinlein has cogent ideas on revolution, rather far-out ideas on government and pretty wild ideas on family but with less lecturing they would have been more fun. 
 But being Heinlein, brighter and more far-seeing than most he hits the mark on more than one occasion. As, for example, on the current situation in Syria: "Correctly organized and properly timed it (revolution) is a bloodless coup. Done clumsily or prematurely and the result is civil war, mob violence, purges, terror." 
 There is too little humor, but now and again he throws us a bone... "Wyoh recruited Sidris; Sidris started own cell by recruiting her other assistant and Bon Ton Beaute Shoppe became hotbed of subversion." 
 There are some other good bits, prophetic? "Wyoh" is named after "Wyoming" where she was born. The chatty AI "Mike" fills her in on her birth place: "It is a region of high plains and of mountains, having limited fertility but esteemed for natural beauty. Its population was sparse until augmented through the relocation subplan of the Great New York Urban Renewal Program, A.D. twenty-twenty-five through twenty-thirty". Hmmm. Brooklyn-West south of Ten Sleep? Lost Springs swelling from a population of four to forty? Interesting times await.

A classic to be sure but this thing just isn't my bag baby. What's most unrealistic about this book where people live on the moon and send water and wheat back to Earth by magnetically propelled canisters? The ideas he has about some kind of crazy inbreeding family where everyone sleeps with everyone else.
9th Reading

Definitely one of the most impressive and unforgettable sf novel I've ever read. This is an amazing story about typical Heinleinian revolution & Heinleinian libertarian (and in some sense, the limitation of the latter. After all, TANSTAAFL).

**Hugo/Nebula Awards Reading Challenge - 38 of 93** 
 Without a doubt, this was one of the best books I've ever had the pleasure of reading. Five stars seem insufficient to do it justice. A wonderful mash up of an early stage sci fi lunar penal colony (with laughably old-school but cool tech) and an important treatise on how to conduct a revolution and the necessity of human freedom from over-government. 
 The matriarchal, polygamous, anarchist/communist colony, where debts seem to be best written off by gambling and badly behaved individuals make discreet trips outside airlocks without wearing a pressure suit, is the very best and most realistic of the utopias I've discovered. I'm impressed that a sci fi written back in '66 still stands impressive over 50 years later, where so many of its cohort seem so awfully outdated. The sexism apparent in the earlier Heinlein books I've read (Stranger in Strange Land and Starship Troopers) was a little toned down in this one, and certainly made me appreciate the value of the novel more without sparking my righteous feminist indignation with every unnecessary bottom slap. 
 As an Australian, and descendant of a harsh a penal colony I feel a special connection with the characters sent to the moon to work themselves to death, or survive and thrive. This novel reminds me of another favourite, The Dispossessed, although I imagine it should be the other way around, as The Dispossessed was written some eights years later. 
 The highest possible praise I can give a novel - this one should be required reading for all. Go forth and spread the love!

I have to admit I have struggled with this book for a long time, and not to be disrespectful to an acknowledged master in the SF genre or to his many devoted fans, I am inclined to bestow on it what noted SF writer and critic Thomas M. Disch might call a St. Bradbury. 
 The feast of St. Bradbury, Disch says, is when critics, readers, and reviewers gather up all the books they've been "unable, despite their best intentions and firmest resolves, to read all the way to the end," and ceremoniously dispose of them. Disch puts it a bit more caustically, but like I said I don't want to be disrespectful, since, despite what for me is a difficult roadblock on the Heinlein highway, I acknowledge there must be something good to account for Heinlein's amassed critical and popular following. 
 So what's my problem? Let's just say that with The Moon Is a Harsh Mistress, considered by most critics and many readers to be Heinlein's finest, the gender issue once again raises its ugly head. Not half a dozen pages can pass in this avowedly political novel, without the male characters' lengthy verbal and visual ogling of the female characters, and the female characters then simpering, giggling, and cooing their appreciation of the men's appreciation. And this is generally DURING any of said political and philosophical conversations, although fortunately not so much during the action sequences, comprised so far in my reading of political rallies meeting with government reprisal, strongly flavored by the novel's 1960's origins. 
 All of this "he looked her up and down, and whistled"--followed by four or five paragraphs of extraneous flirtation--wouldn't be so bad if Heinlein didn't seem so bent on generalizing about what women think (and, believe me, Heinlein has NO problem writing with paranormal authority on what women think) and how women are different-which so far in my reading mostly seems to involve a propensity for intuition and girlish gossip, occasional short-lived and inexplicable (yet adorable) flirtatious huffs, and an abiding love of compliments. 
 Now, don't mistake me, Heinlein may be a product of his times, but he is no misogynist. To quote Disch once again, Heinlein is more than eager to grant women "equal wages and equal fun" and a certain naive amount of mental acuity. To cite another of Heinlein's well-loved novels, Stranger in a Strange Land presents a passel of female character, all of them nurses and secretaries, but at least he gives a few of them eidetic memories, plenty of smarts, and great job skills. Conveniently, as we are at length informed, they are also extremely attractive. But then, as Heinlein says in Moon, there are no ugly women. 
 The Moon Is a Harsh Mistress is the story of political dissent and government rebellion at a former penal colony on the moon; it is also the story of a computer achieving consciousness. Is the computer "Mike" really a Michelle? Heinlein's characters must, of course, dicker about this, since they have crystal clear ideas about gender differences, even when talking about banks of electronic controls. For myself, I will continue to struggle with both the book and its ideas, at least until the traditional date set for the feast of St. Bradbury, August 22 ("the great man's birthday," as Disch reminds us), or until someone or something pushes me to read past my roadblocks. I am hoping with an idealistic postmodern gusto that our hero and heroine will finally realize that Mike/Michelle's identity changes depending on his/her audience and that that in itself is an indication of the social constructs of gender reflected in the novel and its characters. Then, at last, I will be able to pitch my tent in Heinlein's camp. 
 I am not holding out strong hopes for this eventuality. Still, if there are any readers out there who have read The Moon Is a Harsh Mistress and are up for debate, I am honestly open for discussion and ready to hear about the novel's finer points, which I will then respectfully blog about to set the record straight. Push me to read a little faster. I am ready. 
 All quotes from Disch are from On SF (University of Michigan Press, 2005). Quote from The Moon Is a Harsh Mistress is from the Orb Edition (Tom Doherty Associates, 1997, copyright 1966), and appears on p. 71, among other pages.
