Audiobook with a good reader. He used a faux-Russian accent through most of it, but given the nature of the book, that's pretty much inevitable. 
 Heinlein's 'If only the world would listen to ME' Libertarianism never ceases to be tiresome, but it's basically the point of the book, so there's little point in complaining about it. The story itself is entertaining. For once there were too many digressions about various topics, even for me. Events move along well despite that, though, and it stays interesting to the end, even if the presence of a master computer makes things far, far too easy for the heroic Lunarians.

I felt like something science fiction. I always liked the title of this book. I thought I would give it ago. 
 Despite getting my interest from the get-go with an intelligent computer, the book is slow and wasn't terribly exciting, even in the midst of a riot. But okay, I'm patient. However, the sexism in this book is painful. It wasn't actually enough to stop me from reading it until about 60 pages in when the only real woman character in the book says that the protagonist insulted her by not raping her--or at the very least, making aggressive sexual advances on her when she had already made clear several times that she did not want to have sex with him. When the guy demurs, Heinlein has her say, "Michelle would understand," referring to the computer with AI. Sooo... 
 Sigh. :\ I hopped online to check out other reviews of the book. It has an amazing 4.17 star rating on Goodreads, but many of my friends on the site gave it 2 stars or below. I'm not saying that all books with high ratings on Goodreads are necessarily bad, but I am saying that often I am suspicious of books with ratings over 4--especially if they're 4.1+ and "classics" in any genre--because it seems like people who might have read a book and enjoyed it as a child just think, "oh yeah, warm fuzzies for that one--5 stars." 
 Luckily there are some great reviews of this book out there. I'll leave you with my two favorites, after the reading of which I was assured that the book would not get any better, would in fact get worse, and decided to DNF it: 
 "Joint Review: The Moon is a Harsh Mistress by Robert A. Heinlein" at The Book Smugglers 
 "The Moon Is a Harsh Mansplainer (1966) by Robert A. Heinlein" at From Couch to Moon

reference_book.title: Virals (Virals, #1)
reference_book.review_text:
Not really sure if this book falls under paranormal or sci-fi. 
 Tory Brennan, niece to the famous Temperance, lives with her father on an island off South Carolina, where he works as a marine biologist. Together with the only other 3 guys her age on the island, and thus, her only friends, they make visits to the other island that is the research facility. This causes them to stumble onto a secret experiment being conducted on a wolf-puppy. They rescue him, which leads to the strange sci-fi/paranormal direction of giving them extra powers. Add in their investigation of some dog tags they find that tie in to the mysterious disappearance of a teen girl a generation earlier. 
 These characters don't really read like teens. They're more like college students really. The book reads like it's meant for reluctant readers, but at 450+ pages, it'll be a hard sell.

book_a.title: Mister Monday (The Keys to the Kingdom, #1)
book_a.user_review: New series by the creator of Sabriel. Arthur, an orphan from a large family, comes into ownership of a key to a house in another dimension. He must then battle against the personified days of the week in order to stay alive and keep possession of the house.

sample_reviews.review_text: I didn't like it as much as Abhorsen, but it definitely holds it's own. Good series for Jr. High.
10-14 year old boys. Great for connections and inference.

I confess that I only read this book because I saw it on a list of "steampunk" books and I was ridiculously curious as to what "steampunk" meant and how it translated into book form. But now that I've read the whole book I am anxiously waiting for the second book to come into the library so I can read it and finish the series! (In case you were wondering, steampunk books are those that are set in an alternate future (past too) where we have developed steam power to run things. Most books set in a steampunk era also have Victorian elements. Not an official definition either, just something I came out with.)

This book was alright. The only things that bugged me were 1) there was no character developement AT ALL. i do not feel like i know arthur. 2)the author was not bound by any kind of rules, because he is making up his own realm, a completely different thing than has ever been done before. Therefore, he can do whatever he wants. if he finds himself in a situation he can't get out of, he will just invent something to save his characters. that bothers me, because you have to be a lot more creative when you are bound by rules than when you can do whatever you want. 
 The seven sins thing is really interesting, though. i am almost staying with the series just to see how he portrays the seven sins with the seven days.
Ok- wasn't enamoured of the characters or the world, but the writing itself was very good.

Much like Arthur Penhaligon, the reluctant protagonist, I could barely catch my breath throughout this first book in the Keys to the Kingdom series. The plot moves along at a breakneck pace sometimes at the expense of character development and oftentimes logic. Nix has set up a complicated world in which reside trustees, fetchers, denizens, dinosaurs(!)and countless other characters, both living and automated, sinister and helpful. A first book in a fantasy series is always a delicate balance between world building and an engaging, enticing plot that will encourage readers to stick around for more, and Nix mostly manages to maintain that balance. The strength of supporting characters, specifically Suzy Turquoise Blue and The Will in the guise of a frog, help compensate for a lack of development of the character we're meant to care about the most. Here's hoping that in the subsequent six books Nix deepened Arthur's character as well as stuck to the complicated world rules he established in this volume. I'm not sure I'm compelled enough to find out.
Great start to what seems to be a fascinating series.

A new favorite series for me. A real page turner! It took me a few chapters to understand what was happening, but it was exciting all the while! A great choice for boys who like fantasy and sci-fi. Definitely a bit dark at times, but a very good book!
Wasn't all that I expected. Still I will finish the series. Maybe it will pickup.

Okay, so I was all set to love this book. Like REALLY LOVE IT. I picked it up a few weeks ago but had to return it to the library, but because I was so SET TO LOVE IT etc., I went out and bought my own copy to take to New Zealand. 
 :| 
 I just didn't believe a bit of it. I thought the dialogue was rubbish. Arthur came across really nothingy to me. I loved the actual concepts, but it felt badly executed. I'm bothered, because it could've been so fantastic, and I heard an interview with Garth Nix the other day and he sounded so wonderfully lovely and just my sort of bloke, but ARGH. Maybe I just don't get it! I feel like I have to justify myself with this, because it seems so universally loved. But then, I'm not a Sabriel et al fan either, so. 
 Anyway, none of that really matters because I managed to lose the book somewhere between Te Anau and Dunedin. Perhaps it was my subconscious at work, SAVING ME FROM FINISHING IT. I hope so.

book_b.title: Alanna: The First Adventure (Song of the Lioness, #1)
book_b.user_review:
I originally read this book when I was a teen myself, but didn't really remember it. After finding a love for Tamora Pierce a few years back, I finally listened to this one on audio. 
 Alanna comes up with a plan to switch places with her twin brother; she will maskerade as a boy to become a knight and he will go to the priests to learn sorcery. It was very interesting to read this book after having already read the Protector of the Small books. Though Alanna is bullied, bullying doesn't appear to be as rampant, and Alanna has a fairly easy time hiding her sex from nearly everyone, until the very end. Which did seem a little rushed and easy for Alanna and Jonathan.

sample_reviews.review_text:
This book was better back when I was 10, but it will always be my very first favorite book. Keep in mind that this was written back in 1983 when there was a dearth of strong heroines in fiction before you start complaining you've seen this character a hundred times. 
 Loved this book when I was 10, so much that I still go back and reread the series every few years. :) I wish I could still love it with the bang and pizazz that I used to when I was a tweenie, but I look forward to introducing my children to these books and watching them fall in love with them. I really looked up to Alanna as a child, and am glad to have had her as a strong female role model. I'll make sure my daughters (and sons!) get to know her as well. :)

I'm sorry I'm such a hater! But I cannot tell a lie. I started reading it, and it just wasn't doing it for me. The world, the characters, the situation--none of it was grabbing me, so I put it down. Maybe it gets better, but, you know, maybe I'll read a little further in the future.

This was a very good book. I'm sure I'll read it again, once my To Read List stops being 7000 books long. I'm eager to read the next book in the series. 
 Although I didn't warm to her right away, Alanna as a character is someone I like quite a bit. She's very brave, and although her confidence issues occasionally make me eye-roll, she has a lot of traits I value. I don't always understand her -- her aversion to using magic, for one thing. I get that she thinks it wouldn't be a fair fight to use magic in her battles, but she has the same aversion to utilizing healing magic, and I don't understand that. Her friends are also people I like. Coram wasn't my style at first -- he seemed really grumpy -- but he grew on me. And most of the people Alanna surrounds herself with are fantastic characters. Gary, Myles, George, and Jonathan are my favourites. I think I'd quite like to be friends with all of them. I'm also sort of in love with George and Jonathan. 
 There wasn't much lead up to the climax, in terms of discussion of the Black City. It was foreshadowed a couple of times via Alanna's visions, but as soon as they were in Persopolis, it was like they discussed the city and then Jonathan and Alanna were riding off to see it. The writing style was also very matter-of-fact, almost childish, which I would understand more if this book were for children, but it's clearly a YA novel. The writing style is the reason I initially thought I wouldn't like the book very much. But I was only 15 or 20 minutes in the 6 hour audiobook before I started to get interested in what was going on. 
 So at the end of Alanna, two new people know Alanna's secret -- George and Jonathan. I'm glad it's them; they're my favourite. Other things I'm glad about: Alanna kicking ass at everything. I don't even care of it's sort of Mary Sue-ish (Pierce avoids this, by having Alanna struggle to learn things she isn't good at). It made me ridiculously happy when she kicked the crap out of Ralon. That guy was such a dick. And I smiled widely when she performed her second test in swordplay and whooped ass. 
 There were a few times as I listened to the audiobook that I reacted audibly. More than once, I laughed out loud -- usually at the reaction a character had to something Alanna said or did. Other times, I was just exclaiming -- like when the Ysandir magicked away Alanna's clothing, I said aloud, "OH COME ON!" because rude. 
 I liked this a lot more than I was expecting to. Not that I was expecting to dislike it, but I don't read much high fantasy. I'm glad I read it though. It was a quick read, and I'm sure I'll fly through the other three books in this series too.

I borrowed this book from a friend, and really have nothing good to say about it. I thought that the plot line was overused, and the writing style left a lot to be desired. The story of a girl dressing up as a a boy to prove herself is something we're all familiar with, and sometimes it's done very well and it's a pleasure to read. However, there was nothing fresh or new about this book, or this series. The characters weren't fleshed out and their difficulties-- hiding identity, physical exhaustion, etc-- weren't very surprising. I felt that this book borrowed heavily from the genre of literature surrounding it, and that it didn't even come up with its own thoughts or takes on what it took. 
 So, if you're taking a long plane trip, this book will keep you from clobbering the person next to you out of boredom. It may also entertain some people, but if you're looking for good fantasy I would beg to point you in the direction of Robin McKinley's The Blue Sword or Patricia Briggs' Steal the Dragon. Both of them feature strong female heroines in semi-magical realms, have horses, knights, and combat. However, Patricia Briggs and Robin McKinley are both, in my opinion, better writers, and the characters and plots are much more fleshed out.
Has been one of my absolute favorite series for years

I know a lot of people liked Alanna and this entire series, however I had a difficult time reading this. I remember disliking Alanna, and also the way the story was told. I also found it odd (because I won't like I wasn't used to stories with more mature relationships in them at the time I read this) that she could so easily sleep with one guy (I actually think it's in another sequel). So I gave up. I couldn't relate to this series. It just wasn't my thing but it might be someone else's obviously!
I know this is YA and all, but come on! The book sounds like it is written by a middle schooler and Alanna is a total Mary Sue. Yuk.

I really, really wish I had read this book when I was 10 rather than 35. At ten it would have gotten five stars, for sure. As it was, I loved it, will be reading all the sequels, and will probably be reading the rest of Ms. Pierce's extensive oeuvre. Why the missing star? Certain things didn't sit quite right to me, and I think I have read too many other books like this (Fire/Graceling, the Song of Ice & Fire saga, to name a few) to see any of them as truly original. Still, a terrific, feminist, well-plotted and paced book which I will certainly be giving to any children of the appropriate age.
much enjoyed, sending on to calandra

It's a testament to Tamora Pierce's writing skills and evocation of charactars that I could like a book that is more fitting for a 10 year old. I won't be reading the others, but great imagery and an interesting world. I am still interested inhow Alanna's journey turns out, but, it's written ona child's level, and that is just too boring for me.

reference_book.title: Defending Jacob
reference_book.review_text: I enjoyed this story and there was always a hint of how it would end, but of course you don't see it until the very last page. I do however feel the author could've done a better job in grabbing his readers emotionally. The story was well told. Very detailed, but I felt somehow unattached or emotionally uninvolved. Even in the surprising ending (I really didn't see it coming) I feel like I should've felt more.

book_a.title: Six Years
book_a.user_review: I love Harlan Coben, but I found this book slightly predictable. I can see some similiarities between Tell No One and Gone For Good. Still a good read.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Wow , what can I say but first off let you know that this would have to be one of Harlan Coben's greatest books. It was so amazing and is one of the few novels and a mystery one at that , which has left me breathless and feeling exhilirated. The novel itself was so intense that the reader is left blown away and with millions of little thoughts running through their heads. 
 Six Years started off with the premise of a guy meets a girl , falls head over heels and then the girl breaks up with the guy and remarries somebody else and makes a promise to the guy she has broken up with for him to never make contact with her. 
 The guy is Jake Fisher and the girl is Natalie Avery , "Six Years" pass and Jake reads an obituary in the newspaper of the guy that Natalie married and travels down to his funeral only to discover that he has a whole different family and Natalie is nowhere to be seen. 
 This starts Jake on a journey to discover where Natalie is and what has happened to her as it seems that she fell off the grid "Six Years" ago. 
 Without giving too much away, hence why this has to be a short review as I could really go on and on all day about this book is that Six Years is (not that I'm trying to be cliched) a novel that is truly and utterly unputdownable. It is a novel that will take you on a journey of emotions and feelings , a journey where you are stuck between - Are you deluding yourself Jake or did it really happen ? 
 The best thing is that I have just discovered that Six Years is being made into a film starring the Hunky Aussie Actor Hugh Jackman
Worst book ever! I usually really enjoy Coben's books but this was awful. It seemed rushed and the writing suffered. So, so disappointed!

A new Coben novel that keeps you intriqued all the way through. After seeing the love of his life marry someone else, Jake promises not to interfer in her life until . . . Six years later he sees what he thinks is an obituary on Natalie's husband. But nothing is what it seems, there is no Natalie or husband, and Jake gets involved with something like the Mafia while trying to find Natalie. The reader continues to try to piece together the whos and whats, but not until the end of the book do we know the whole story. A good story that will make this mystery one of your favorites.
Not his best.

The narrator's faux-contemporary voice made me want to scream. As did many of the developments in plot and harebrained actions of the characters. 
 This was a tedious read and sticking with this stinker to its conclusion has reminded me why I read very little popular fiction.
First half was strong. However, it ended up being boring and unbelievable.

Suspense: 
 I read about 30% of the book at which point I figured out the ending. Then I read till 40% mark and lost all interest because all indications pointed to that ending. 
 Writing style: 
 I dragged myself for yet a couple more pages but the story was progressing at snail's pace. I felt the author digresses from the point way too much. For ex. when the protagonist is taking a drive then he describes the farm that's passing by, who owns that farm, what are the owners hobbies, who are his guests, what artists do and finally comes back to Natalie - what she did as an artist. You get the idea. There's way too much of unneeded detail. I was literally skipping a couple of paragraphs and reading a few lines, again skipping a few paras then reading again without losing any info. 
 Story: 
 The story sounded really interesting when I started reading it. However the plot progresses a bit slow. There's a lot of action happening but that's not really what I want. I want the character to ask important questions, do the first things first but he doesn't do them. For ex. When two people try to kidnap him in college one of them hits Barry. Clearly Barry must have seen that guy. So later on when they're discussing about how there's no trace of those two people the most sensible thing would be to meet up with Barry, ask him whether he saw those two people, is he okay, what's his verion of the story. But instead the main character ignores him completely. 
 Then there are weird character personas. For ex the FBI turned teacher friend he has. What happens is she agrees to trace Natalie for him. Then later meets him and her update is that she found nothing. But instead of telling it to him like a normal person she starts asking him lots of personal questions. I found that really weird. It doesn't fit in with a character. If you had no info for someone what would you do? You would just tell them that you have no info. But instead if you were asking them detailed qs it meant that you had some kind of hypothesis in your head that you were trying to work out. It's just a weird character. And then both of them don't communicate with each other which was again a weird thing. Are they normal people or do they have some kind of trust disorder? 
 Overall: 
 It sucked. Bad characters. Lot of action but no noticeable progress in plot. Lots of - yeah, yeah, uh-huh, but little concrete conversation. People around acting weird for no reason. Sucked! I'm glad I'm able to drop books without any guilt. There are millions of books coming out every year and I would much rather spend time reading something that I connect with.

Meh - a little far-fetched. Not the greatest mystery, and a few distracting tangents and a couple big "whaaaa?" elements to the plot. (So, they killed the husband in front of the wife and essentially say "shhhh..." and we're supposed to believe that?)

Really disappointed in this book. If it was possible to give no stars, I wouldn't give it one. It came with such great recommendations, which for my part I can't understand at all. It is a lazy book, badly researched, badly written with so many platitudes that there is hardly any "real writing", the plot is ridiculous and every single character is unbelievable and totally uninteresting. Absolute rubbish, won't give Harlan Coben time to spoil my precious reading time again.

SIX YEARS (Pub 2013) by Harlan Coben is an interesting read. This story bucks the trend, slowly picking up speed, and really gets cooking at the mid point. Once you hit page 120, you'll be hooked. But I have to admit, things felt a little boggy on the front end due to a lot of necessary background info. 
 The story opens with Jake Fisher watching the woman he loves marry another man. The first chapter is a short prologue and is only five pages. 
 Chapter two opens with the words Six Years Later posted at the top. We see Jake reading about the death of his lost love's husband in the college newsletter. The rest of the story is about Jake trying to find the woman, and that's when things start to get complicated. People are blatantly lying to Jake, but in a way he can initially refute. As the author builds the story's legs, Jake's insatiable need to find Natalie combines with wanting to know what's behind the cover-up and lies. Danger grows with the clues--some come from layman's clumsiness on Jake's part, the rest from solid sleuthing and a little help from his friends. 
 My favorite part of the story is two-thirds of the way in, when Jake discovers information about his best friend and co-worker, Benedict. I like the way the author subtly brings out strong characterization of both men through that encounter, which organically relates back to the story in an unexpected way. 
 Harlan Coben is famous for his highly tangled plots, and SIX YEARS holds up to that as multiple murders, past and present, start coming into play. The reader doesn't learn just how deeply tangled things are until the very end. The climax is definitely worth reading through the story-building on the front end. 
 The novel concludes with a big bang, and an unexpected surprise. We get answers to both small and big questions right up to the last page, along with a satisfying ending.

book_b.title: Inferno (Robert Langdon, #4)
book_b.user_review: Don't waste your time. :/

sample_reviews.review_text: I have mixed feelings about this one. It's not as intriguing as Brown's previous works but I still managed to find myself mesmerized by the beauty of the Italian skyline as described by Brown's extensive historical vocabulary. Another plus is the philosophical standpoint (a sentiment which I deeply share) with regards to overpopulation and management of ecological resources. Humans have become so egoistic that nature suffers in our wake of population explosion. The ending is a little divergent from the usual resolution in other thrillers, but illustrates something thought-provoking that needs to be addressed in the real world.

A fun read! I now know more about Dante's Inferno than I thought I ever would...and there were great descriptions of classical Italian art and cities, etc. This book was a typical exciting Dan Brown, with many adventures, fun pursuits and escapes, and a some surprising twists along the way. A very entertaining read!

I give 2stars for its pertinent subject-population explosion and a diabolically scary solution. Book is more a travel brochure for Venice etc than a thriller. Pace is sluggish/action mediocre. There are no hair pin bends that wake you from reverie or keep your nerves crackling. I finished the book, well, coz I always do (barring 'The Satanic Verses' that I couldn't go beyond 8-9pgs). I could pre guess the turns that the storyline was going to take-hence found the book to be 'mediocre'. Boring.
So not impressed with this book. I thought he was a better writer than what I found here.

At chapter 5: 
 Not off to a great start... I can usually get past Dan Brown's writing because he's so good at high-intensity, page-turner storytelling and peppering in history and facts. But starting with a dream sequence? Packing THIS many cliches into each paragraph? An incredibly unrealistic exchange with a hot nurse? Where was his editor on these? Maybe my standards have changed, but I don't know if I can make it through this one. Hubby and I have read other Dan Brown novels together, but I think he's dropping out and leaving me to fend for myself. I'll give it a few more chapters, but I might be switching over to the original "Inferno." 
 *Update* 
 At Chapter 49: 
 Not gonna finish this one. I tried, I really did. I encouraged hubby to keep reading, and he's enjoying it now, but I've gotten bored and can't stay focused on it. Unfortunately, I think the Dan Brown formula is just too stale for me at this point. I've been able to predict every scene so far, and that's no fun. And DB's social commentary started to get old (really, most 20-somethings are not obsessed with Googling themselves). 
 Also, DB, why not add some depth to Langdon? By book 4, I was hoping he'd be more than just a claustrophobic know-it-all with a Mickey Mouse watch. Haven't all these life-threatening adventures affected him at all? At this point, it seems more likely that he'd be a paranoid PTSD patient, unable to hold a job and dragging his therapist through a bunch of imaginary adventures, than a stable professor off to save the world from anther conspiracy. Poor guy. 
 That being said, if you like Dan Brown and just can't get enough of high-intensity chase scenes through art museums, this book is for you.
Torrent of description & Misleading character developments and incidences, with no real necessity, just to divert the reader!

Good quick read but it is pretty formulaic, especially for Brown. He continues to put the existence of humanity at stake in every novel and in every novel there is a nicely wrapped ending with a bow. It was a good read, but NOT my favorite.

Our Review, by LITERAL ADDICTION's Pack Alpha - Michelle L. Olson: 
 I'm a Dan Brown fan... I've read all of his works, not just the Robert Langdon series - Digital Fortress is probably my favorite work of his. Anyway, being a fan, I was excited to hear that he was coming out with a new book, had Inferno pre-ordered, and actually waited up until after midnight on release day so I could start it immediately keeping the next day free of commitments so I could dedicate it to reading. Sadly, the only thought that kept running through my head while reading was "Oh Dan, where is the heart!!?" :-/ 
 I like Brown's writing style despite the harsh critique it's received. I enjoy how his books are layered with codes and mysteries, how they're incredibly fast-paced & often surprising, & how he takes facts and then pulls and twists them like taffy as far as they'll go without breaking to turn them into riveting fiction. 
 I don't even mind the repeated format within the Robert Langdon series - professor and expert on symbology and iconography finds himself embroiled in the middle of a high-stakes mystery, teams up with an attractive, smart and capable foreign woman who helps fill in the gaps and challenges him, and the two cement alliances, skirt villains, and undergo a hair raising adventure to save the world's (or the world itself). 
 With all that said, Inferno just fell flat for me. It had the expected format as mentioned above. It had the twisted facts as also mentioned above. What it didn't have was any of the action packed thrills and gasp inducing surprises I've come to know and love in Dan Brown's books. In addition, those style critiques I mentioned were very evident in this book to me, where I hadn't even noticed them before: foreign languages used during dialogue - a lot of times without clarification leaving holes for those of us who don't speak fluent Italian or Latin, references that make no sense - a train of thought referral to Dutch city where MC Escher lived (who cares if that's where the artist lived, it has no bearing in the story & took 3 sentences to tell!), simile & hyperbole used in the weirdest of places without much order, etc. 
 I wanted to love this book. I really, really did, especially given my fascination with and deep appreciation for Dante and all of the other art and literature his Divine Comedy spawned, but alas I just couldn't, and am giving my very first ever 2 Skull review. *sigh*

Oh dear why was I surprised? 
 The action picks up in Florence where Robert Langdon has just woken up with amnesia, what happens next can only be ripped from scenes of a Hollywood action blockbuster as he and the latest femme rush across the city in a murder mystery plot, all revolving around the text of Dante's Inferno. 
 Things take a drastic turn for the ridiculous as the novel continues and finishes in a way so unbelievable that I was actually speechless for a moment. Just think of a magician waving their hand over your eyes and murmer, 'Science!'.

Look, everybody knows Dan Brown's writing is formulaic. If you picked up a Dan Brown book and then complain that the characters/plot feel recycled, either you've been living under a rock for a decade or you're jealous that his mediocrity made him rich. 
 I got this from my local library while waiting for a book I requested to come in. I've read some of Brown's other stuff, didn't have high hopes for this one, and wasn't disappointed at least. Much of the book takes place in Florence, a favorite city of mine. I enjoyed reading Brown's descriptions and little tour guide anecdotes about the city and it conjured vivid memories for me. And, for Brown, I thought the ending was a little brave. 
 I hope I don't have to tell you that if you're looking for a book to challenge you/your worldview/your ideas, keep looking. If you're looking for a Renaissance beach read, this one wasn't half bad.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Reading The Little Prince was such a strange experience. It's delightful. It's funny. It's adorable. The almost condescending attitude towards adults and the jokes at their expense makes this book appealing to kids since they can relate to being baffled by grown-ups. But as I'm laughing at the crazy adults and the crazy things they do, I had to stop for a second as it sank in that I do those crazy things, too. I found myself reflecting at the deeper story behind this prince and his cute travels to different planets. The little prince's complete bewilderment at the behavior of adults challenged the way I think in so many ways. And boy do I love a story that challenges my thinking. 
 Here's one that blew my mind - if sheep eat flowers with the thorns, then what good are thorns? I HAVE NO IDEA. My instinct is to explain evolution or genetics. But that's not the question. The thorns don't do any good and I hadn't realized that. Maybe as adults we simply stop questioning things because now we know science and math and stuff and we assume there's nothing left to learn. I do have a lot left to learn. I need to figure out why plants have thorns. 
 The little prince describes grown-ups as loving numbers and asking questions to get to know someone where the answers are numbers instead of questions about things that matter (like getting to know their personality). To prove the little prince is right, here's a numbered list of the types of adults he meets on each planet: 
 1. The King - talks about his control and power, but the little prince clearly sees that it's just an illusion since he commands things under the "science of government, until conditions are favorable. (pg 31)" Or, when they were going to do it anyway. 
 2. The Vain Man - wants nothing more than to be admired constantly. The little prince wonders "...what is there about my admiration that interests you so much? (pg 34)." 
 3. The Drunkard - the vicious cycle of shame. He's ashamed that he drinks so he drinks to forget his shame. The prince has literally nothing to say about that. 
 4. The Business Man - endlessly counts all the stars and says he owns them and they make him rich. The little prince sees that work should be a two-way street. "But you're not useful to the stars. (pg 40)" 
 5. The Lamp Lighter - stuck in the endless cycle of chores. He is a hard worker and the little prince likes him since his job is useful to others, but the little prince doesn't understand why he can't rest and enjoy the many joys (like sunsets) that his planet has. 
 6. The Geographer - never actually goes anywhere. He writes about places and discoveries that other people have made. He's the kind of adult that never fully lives their life. 
 7. Earth - the last planet he visits that has a combination of all these grown-ups (which he numbers to please the adults). 
 I think I relate the most to the lamp lighter. I get stuck in the daily grind of things. Who do you relate to the most? 
 My favorite thing about the little prince is his view of love. The time you spend caring for something is what makes it important to you. A huge rose garden is not as meaningful as the one rose you took care of. Like the fox said, don't forget this truth: 
 "One sees clearly only with the heart. Anything essential is invisible to the eyes." 
 -Antoine de Saint-Exupery, The Little Prince pg 63

this book was a kind of joke! It tells an unreal story about the Islamic republic of Persia that No one who know just a little about Persian culture can`t believe it. I can`t understand how people can like it.
I've seen the movie, but it's been a few years but from what I remember of it, both movie and book are incredibly moving and powerful. So much heartache to process but so well written. What a story.
Engrossing and informative; a remarkable graphic novel but not a remarkable book.

Truth-loving persians love to dwell upon that oh-so-trivial skirmish fought near Marathon. Not really, but we really are dealing with Persians, particularly one: Ms. Marjane Satrapi, the author of the graphic novel Persepolis. 
 I first heard about Persepolis as an independent film some years back, and then it slipped completely from my mind. Fast forward to a week or so ago as I wandered aimlessly through a Barnes and Noble. I was looking for a book, the kind that you don't know that you're looking for until you see it, when I saw it. I suddenly remembered that spark of interest from years ago, bought the graphic novel and finished it in a day. 
 It was good you see. 
 Persepolis is a memoir of Satrapi's childhood in Iran before and during the Islamic Revolution. Historically, the title refers to the ancient capital of the Persian nation, which is modern day Iran. In skipping about the Internet, I was surprised to see that Iran had openly decried the film based on the graphic novel, although I can't say why I should have been. 
 I liked this story because it really makes the people and culture of Iran tangible to readers. Marjane is a vivacious, headstrong and intelligent girl who is just trying to make sense of life. She is passionate about her religion (as a child she wants to be a prophet), tender toward her country (like a good patriot) and rational in her quest to figure out why her secular lifestyle suddenly takes a turn toward a more zealous one. 
 What struck me also was how I had to be careful with my prejudices as a reader. For instance, in the beginning, Satrapi writes that the West, i.e. Great Britain and the U.S.A., were greedy meddlers in her country's history. She also writes that Iranians have suffered under a long list of dictators. My knee-jerk reaction as a Westerner was to say, "Nooo! You're wrong!" But my rational self quickly surpressed that thought. As Americans, I don't think its often that we learn non-Western perspectives of history, and who is to say they aren't "true"? Satrapi writes her memories of Tehran as a diverse center of thought. Her parents are liberal intellectuals. Her father is a loving husband and family man who respects the independent natures of his wife and child. Her mother is a strongminded individual who is not afraid to stand up and speak. Satrapi does hint that her family did have a very close connection to influential politicians, which could explain this nonstereotypical Middle-Eastern family lifestyle, similar to Malika Oufkir in Le Prisonniere. However, the simple illustrations and clear story really sweep you up in the emotion and chaos that takes over the family and country.

As an Iranian growing up in a family with political background, a communist sister (Parvaneh Emam) executed at the age of 22 and, having read many books on the history of Iran's struggle for freedom and justice, I see that the book talks about the true Tudeh Party members, real communists as they were, who fought hard and sacrificed their lives for equity, freedom and justice. 
 What I like about Persepolis is that it leaves out the back-stabbing counter-revolutionaries of today's Tudeh Party who are very active in Iran and abroad and have been able to infiltrate literary organizations and political movements to destroy them from within. 
 This group of Tudeh members are also very busy writing the history of Iran and among them I can refer to "Rosewater", which is full of lies and simply a propaganda tool for today's Tudeh Party. Of course by giving the example of Rosewater, I do not wish to promote that book, although those books are also useful to show the real identity of that Party. 
 I highly recommend Persepolis to my Goodreads friends and I will be happy to participate in any discussions.

I found this book in my classroom and was instantly taken with it. Satrapi tells an internationally relevant story with all the wonderful hallmarks of memoir and graphic novels. I read it while my students read and then I ran to the library for the sequel.

3.5 stars. I can see why this graphic novel has gained so much popularity -- for example, I would not have read a prose memoir with this same storyline. The cartoons bring levity to the dense content (there are a lot of cultural facts to pick up along the way), while the seriousness of the text brings meaning to the cartoons. It's a good balance, though be aware that there's a lot of heartbreaking content in the narrative. 
 I would recommend this book to anyone interested in Iran or the Middle East. If that's not your interest then don't be afraid to skip this one.

reference_book.review_text: This small book is a treasure - evocative of To Kill A Mockingbird and written in the voice of a young adolescent boy. It doesn't take long to read, but it will stay with me for quite a long time. The prose is spare, precise and haunting. I felt as if I knew the Hayden family at its conclusion.

book_a.title: The Wife
book_a.user_review: The Wife is a sad chronicle of a woman's life from her early college years to the end of her marriage. Her insecurities and doubts allowed her to feed the enormous appetite of a narcissistic, self-absorbed man. She chose to subjugate her talents, her self respect and her instincts as a mother to a man whose selfish egotism knew no boundaries. He was despicable and she enabled him. The ending is a fitting tribute to their fifty-year marriage.

sample_reviews.review_text: I didn't particularly *feel* anything while reading the first 2/3 of this book. However, as it picked up towards the end, I began to to enjoy and appreciate it for what it was. It seemed like the first parts were overly and unnecessarily sexual. The flashbacks into the past were not always helpful, and often confused rather than shed light on Joan and Joe's relationship. Wolitzer's writing skill did, however, shine through towards the end.
I did not enjoy this book. I dislike women who give everything they have to their husband but then blame their husband for taking it. Probably the story of lots of women but shame on them.

I could not get interested in this book. The author was trying to be too clever with her prose instead of just telling the damn story already. I couldn't connect to the wife. She seemed emotionally distant and all the crude language felt like the author was trying to prove her hipness when it was like adding cud to a soup. Unpalatable and off-putting. This isn't The Catcher in the Rye.

Wow! Bitingly sharp, funny and tragic at the same time. The twist at the end is breath-taking and strangely sad. An homage to feminism and the inexorable ties of marriage (not for the faint-of-heart!).

Love this author, and in the beginning, I laughed so hard. She paints such fun images---LOL stuff. About marriage--about marriage of my era--early 60's. He's a writer, she was his college student.... 
 However, at the end, I was very let down. The humor went away, the honesty seemed to go away---well, it's hard when a story doesn't end as a reader thinks it should. Perhaps it was good...but not to me.

Joan and Joe Castleman are visiting Finland for Joe to receive a literature price. Many people would no doubt envy Joan to be married to Joe, the famous author, but it turns out that their marriage is flawed, to say the least, and that Joan has sacrificed much to be with a man who is narcissistic and self-centered. 
 Meg Wolitzer alters between present day and earlier years. The reader learns about how the two of them met and that the power balance was askew right from the start. It is a portrayal of a couple that many people probably recognize, and the book has a certain feminist vibe to it. Sometimes the writing is wonderful, like when Joe is hilariously stupid at a party, or when the children see through their parents facade. However, I would have liked more of these events. Sometimes, I think the book is repetitive and tedious. It is as if Meg Wolitzer relies on the theme of the book, which is indeed very interesting and a little feminist, but it is not enough to build a book upon it without more strong moments.
I didn't care for this book, I found it to be boring. It didn't hold my interest and I wouldn't recommend it to anyone.
Couldn't get into it.

What a fabulous read this insightful, ironic, entirely believable novel was, and what a sharp portrait it is of a marriage. It beautifully written, perfectly paced, and devoid of cliches, despite the fact that it deals with a story that could be hard to make fresh. It reminded me a bit of Richard Yate's Revolutionary Road, but with a frank, specifically female point-of-view, that of the memorable and eloquent voice of the wife. I couldn't put it down.

Not as interesting as The Interestings. This book offered insight on the role of a traditional wife (I have wished for a wife when I was busy with work and parenting), but the story was unfortunately pretty dull. The most interesting character was their troubled son, whom we hear little of.

book_b.title: The Girl on the Train
book_b.user_review: Paula Hawkins' debut novel, The Girl On The Train, is taut with suspense. It is told from different characters' perspectives with a shifting time line that enhances the revelations at the end of the book. The main character, Rachel, rides a commuter train into London every day. The train passes the residential area where her ex-husband lives with his current wife and child. This is also the home where Rachel lived with him when they were married. A few houses away she catches intriguing glimpses of another couple, and she becomes embroiled in a mystery surrounding them. This is a novel that will keep its readers guessing until the end. I am grateful to Random House for the opportunity to read this book, and I recommend it without reservation to those who enjoy suspense-filled novels.

sample_reviews.review_text: Here's the thing about this book. Everyone in it is terrible. I pretty much hated all of them. It dragged a bit in the middle, and I thought I had figured out the killer from the beginning. (I was wrong). However, I couldn't stop listening to it. (Yay for audiobooks!) Wow! This book takes so many twists. It kept surprising me all the way through the last chapter. So unexpected!

1 star for the predictable story. Ugh and the terrible characterisation. Every female was pathetic, needy and pitiful. The male stereotypes were no better. 
 1 star for the fact that despite the story being crap, it kept me up most of the night wanting to know what happened next. The same part of me that likes d-listed and other gossip websites enjoyed the book and I am not proud of that fact.
Figured it out on page 47.
Though the main character's actions made me cringe throughout the story, I couldn't put the book down. There were some nice twists that I didn't see coming.

I couldn't put this book down for all the right reasons. There is mystery, suspense and good character development. I was surprised by how the story developed and couldn't wait to find out what happened.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I had to drop this book. 
 A couple of the things that really killed this book for me. To begin with, I made it about a quarter of the way through, and as yet we have only begun to hear rumors of a threat. Some wall far to the north is crumbling, and horrible beasts are coming through to this side of it. We've of course not seen any beasts, unless you count the ones that Administrators have set on our protagonists. (By the way, does a more limp pair of faction names exist?) It is a misstatement on the dust-jacket to say that Davian learns to wield the power of the Augurs. He accidentally does something once, then otherwise has things done for him by his friends and keepers. The one power he's able to reliably use doesn't work on anyone who knows about it, which is apparently everyone who matters. 
 So far, the book consists of two separate groups of characters, each essentially "on rails". They make no choices, and are only shuffled from one place to another by more powerful individuals. At each waypoint, we the readers are stuffed with a bunch of facts that we need to know to get why anything in the book matters. These are universally delivered in expository "Question?" "Explanation." "Questions2..." type conversations. 
 Then, we move on to the next waypoint. To the extent that there is any action, the main characters do not participate (with the notable exception of when Davien takes up the sword and kills the hunter -- which is also the only cool thing that happened in the book up to the point I stopped reading). 
 It would be better to have the characters start out knowing everything than to have to wade through more of this interminable conversation. 
 Worse than just not having any decisions to make for themselves, the chapters follow a predictable mirroring of events. First, we learn something in the Davian and Wirr chapter. Then Asha learns the same thing from a different group of people in the next chapter. This pattern has already repeated itself at least a half dozen times just to the point where I stopped, and it gets old fast. 
 I can understand why this book would be recommended to Robert Jordan fans. It has the same sort of architecture -- at least as far as I read, the first book was essentially going to consist of an enormous wind-up, the end of which would at least make clear the stakes. Personally, I don't have that kind of patience when there are other books that start exciting and get even more exciting.

2.5 Stars. 
 The story tries hard to be interesting and fast-paced, however, the characters just fell flat for me. I couldn't care less for any of them and thus didn't care if anything happened to them. 
 I had high expectations going in; will not continue the series.

I enjoyed The Shadow of What Was Lost. The story itself, and its concepts, are good, but they're also a little unexceptional, which was disappointing for a fantasy story. 
 Let me begin with the plot. The overarching plot is somewhat tired (there's evil things locked behind a barrier that's on the brink of collapsing) but the actual driving points of the story are both entertaining and compelling (apart from a segment between the 1/4 and 1/2 marks in the book which read a little tedious and boring. 
 We are introduced to characters than evolve and change throughout the story and who are thrust in a variety of differing political and social situations. Some of them gain power, and others lose theirs. I do wish some of them had more distinctive personalities, but they're suitably complex and appealing. I think, the greatest part of the characters is their diverse stories. Of the four-ish main characters, three have distinctive stories: one is accused of mass murder but has no memory, another is stripped of their magical power and forced to live as a "Shadow," and the third shall remain a mystery because it's a little too spoilerish. And even the fourth character has a compelling character-arch, his just toes the line of "child of prophecy" a little more than the others. 
 Something I deeply enjoyed were the Blind as villains. These are some of the lesser spooks imprisoned behind the failing barrier and there's a couple thousand of them. I liked them because they're not the standard grunt, they are vastly superior to the humans and this gives the presence a deliciously perilous feel. This sense of danger is deepened by the knowledge that they are only a small evil, and that there are many greater things behind the barrier. This gives the story's events a wonderful sense of growing desperation. 
 Beyond that, the prose was fine ( a little long-winded at times but fine) and the story caps off with a strong conclusion and an intriguing, if not entirely unexpected, revelation.
Made it like 30 pages.

This is a good story, an interesting world and likable characters. The writing is sound and I found that I wanted to just keep on reading... Worth a go - of course we now have to wait for the next - maybe early next year?

Solid 4 star book. Magic system is reminiscent of wheel of time series and perhaps Brent weeks way of shadows? 
 Will warn fans of NOTW or WOK (you know what books I mean) that this story isn't exactly like those. Instead of world building brick by brick from the bottom up, you're kind of thrown in the deep end in regards to trying to figure out what's happening at first. Complex names also don't help. Will say there are a few twists and turns. Overall a lot like early wheel of time. 
 Did the book drag at points? Yes 
 Would I still recommend it? Yes, but for fantasy fans who are okay with a bit of waffle and confusing stuff along the way. 
 Look forward to the next instalment!

Picked it up because I liked the cover art. Also want to support indie authors (even though this author got a publishing deal, the book started as an indie, so whatever). Gave it a fair shake but I couldn't get into it.

This book took elements of Jordan and Sanderson but moved at a much quicker pace. I've never read a 700 page book like this that never felt like it was dragging. 
 The world building and mysteries set up here are fantastic. 
 My only small complaint would be that thus far, the 3 main boys (Dav, Caeden, Wirr) have somewhat interchangeable personalities. Overall, a fantastic read and highly recommended.

Well, it is a bit too clever for itself, a bit too formulaic on a few points, and too complex to allow sheer enjoyment. 
 But the story is good, the writing is good, the pacing is generally good, if not a bit harried, and I'm looking forward to the next one. 
 I relistened to multiple hours of this book just to get a grasp. If I listened to the entire book again I would understand better, but the overall story isn't compelling enough to have me too it now. Maybe in 4-8 months.
What an epic read this has been! Intricate world building and some wonderful characters! I loved this, a full review will be on my blog soon!

book_b.title: Battle Hymn of the Tiger Mother
book_b.user_review:
I read that excerpt in the Wall Street Journal. I have an asian mother, and she tried to be pushy at times but was too caught up in her own life to really push. 
 I think it's a little presumptuous to think that children owe their parents everything, to force children along certain paths before they've even developed their own aspirations. 
 So what if they performed at Carnegie Hall. So what if they went to good schools. What if Amy's kids could have been brilliant engineers? What if they could've been exemplary actresses? What if while out playing, they could have found someone who loves them? What if they could have been happy? There's more to happiness and life than academic achievement.

sample_reviews.review_text: Although I did not necessarily agree with everything in this book, it was stimulating to me. It made me think, and I love it when books do that. It really made me stop and think about the way I parent my children and maybe some changes I could make to be better.

I don't know what to say. It took me forever to complete this book. It was so repetitive and boring. The sequence that is repeated over and over again is : 
 The author wants her daughter to play violin. 
 The daughter plays violin. 
 The author forces her to practice more. 
 Daughter rebels. 
 They have a fight. 
 Daughter finally plays it. (and she is oh-so-perfect) 
 This happens several times in the book till the daughter finally stops listening to her mother. Who could see that coming? Why would your child resent you and hate you? You are just being overbearing, pushy and forcing her to do something that she does not want to do.. or at least does not want to do it your way. Is it not the job of a parent? 
 No. It is not! Having been raised in an Indian family I understand how parents can be pushy about being hardworking and being the best. You have to compete with a lot of people. But that does not mean that parents will blackmail, threaten, bribe or scream at their kids. We are scolded/beaten for not getting good grades and constantly reminded that opportunities are scanty and the competition is cut throat but what this woman does to her children just sounds too cruel. Maybe she is not. But she has written the book herself, hasn't she? Also she never fails to mention about her accomplishments every now and then. Self praise is no recommendation. The number of "I"s that you use in a book determine if it is a nice read or a bragathon. This one is latter. Ok you are accomplished and stuff, we get it. But nobody wants to read a book on that. At least I don't.

I had to read this for a parent-teacher book club I am in. It's a quick read, and apparently the term "tiger mother" is now the hip term for overbearing mothers. Move over, helicopter parents. Amy Chau has an impressive resume, but I don't think she's the greatest writer. My five-year-old niece who is learning to read was reading a lot of the words over my shoulder. Maybe Chau felt the need to dumb down her vocabulary for us Westerners. She certainly didn't tone down the amount of bragging. Really, Ms. Chau, your husband studied drama with THE VAL KILMER?!? Your daughter discovered the cure for cancer before she was potty-trained, but refuses to share it because she resents you!?! Blah. Quit showing off and go back to micromanaging your daughters' every move.

The author wanted to be provocative and she was, but reading the book made me feel cranky, like I was constantly being lumped in with all those overly-indulgent western mothers that she was so critical of. Still, it was a very fast read, and I think some of that has to do with her writing ability. It will certainly have me thinking about my parenting style for some time to come.

Appalling, no mention of school. Where was the husband in all of this? These children were being abused-and abuse is what it was. The husband needed to "man up" and calm this woman down. I hated this woman, having two wonderful children and treating them the way she did. I hope she regrets it. And I hope she realizes that her children are half "western" as she puts it, and that she is living in the US taking in the advantage of all of the "inferior" (in her eyes) the western world has to offer.
This woman is insane! I really hated it while I was reading, especially her, but it was interesting enough that I persevered. The silver lining: I am so grateful for the mother I had.

I'll have to come back to write a full review on this later, but this book ended up kind of a mixed bag for me. There were things she said that I was surprised to find reminded me of my (Chinese and tiger but not nearly as conventional as Chua) mother. And I think there's merits to her methods and also some serious flaws. So yes. Consider this a bit of a placeholder until I get to a real computer.

I'm glad I read this. And I'm glad I'm not her daughter. All the screaming and yelling! The author seems very self-aware, which makes this an interesting book. As she admits, she is not creative and doesn't know how to have fun. On the other hand, you can't argue with her results (although I don't know if her daughters will speak to her when they're grown).

I have to rate it low. It made me gasp it horrified me, and made me grateful for my Western parentage and my own life and way of thinking. It made me tense and angry; it will surely be a great discussion for the parent book club at my school which I read it for. It is extremely well written, and clear, easy to read. I could not rate it higher because I cannot say that I loved it at all, and that is a personal opinion based on nothing but my horror at the way this woman thinks and acts; of her obvious lack of regard for American values; for American society, really. I am not even sure I am glad I read it. I am sure Amy Chua does not even care that I read it, based on her attitude and opinion of Western civilization. The one thing I am glad for? I am glad that I did not spend money on it and was able to borrow a copy.

I have had this review of "Tiger Mother" simmering on the back burner for a while, and I realized what better day to post than--Mother's Day. Ultimately this is a story of one mother's journey, but rather than a journey to acceptance or realization, it is a journey of denial and control. I was curious after all the hype about this book, to find out if the flaming of this book was unfounded, as the author claimed. She maintained in many of her interviews that this book was written tongue in cheek. It was a *joke* she said, can't cha take a joke? Since I am fluent in sarcasm, I was able to read this book in its intended language. And there is a lot of sarcasm here. What mom hasn't threatened to throw out all the kids' toys, make them study all night or yelled "No More Wire Hangers!!"? But there is something else here, something desperate and sad. Amy Chua is a woman consumed by fear. Fear of losing control, fear of failing, fear of not being viewed as successful. This is a bad place to parent from, since parenting is mostly a journey of errors. Ms. Chua can say that she was joking when she got upset with her husband because he didn't set high enough goals for their dog, but there is no joke when she bullies her daughters into writing a eulogy for their beloved grandmother. That is something no child should be forced to do, and Ms. Chua's motivation can only be the prestige of the praise she will receive afterwards. Her youngest daughter pegs her perfectly, accusing her of being vain and self-centered. That is what this book is about, one mother's attempt to keep the focus on herself, rather than let her daughters shine in their own spot light.

book_a.title: Swan Song
book_a.user_review: I had very high expectations going into this book. It has been compared to The Stand numerous times, and the ratings and reviews speak for themselves. That being said, Swan Song exceeded those expectations. It's a wonderful story with with a little touch of everything. sample_reviews.review_text: More like a 4.5, it's awesome. I don't read horror fantasy much but this was truly well done. Will evoke comparisons to The Stand. The writer is as good if not better than the honorable Mr. King. Same goes for the story. I don't know how this even got in my queue but I'm grateful to who's ever goodreads update made me aware of it.
One of my favorite end-of-the world titles. I so wish this was a made for TV series. I could not put it down.

I can see how it could be viewed as derivative of The Stand (also a much loved book of mine). It's a post apocalyptic book and I would imagine there are similarities in many of them. For me, there were enough differences to make it good in it's own right. 
 I noticed that the author revisited the president towards the end after only introducing him at the start of the book. Something he has done before. 
 Either way, I would happily read this book again and for me that's the litmus test.

There's something wrong with judging books entirely by some presupposed standard of literary merit. Because it seems to me that a lot of the time the most cliche-ridden and intellectually barren books are the best. Not that cliches are all good, but they're cliches because they've managed to resonate with enough people to be deemed worthy of imitation. There's probably some Campbellian monomyth type of explanation for this, but what I'm getting at it is that they're the currency of our stories, and in good check they can be used very effectively. 
 In so many words, Swan Song is a cliche-ridden mess, and that it happens to be a very good book. Pretty much every action movie trope imaginable is utilized here, the characters are all archetypes with almost no personality, and the moral spectrum in post-apocalyptic America is pretty much relegated to black and white. We've all seen these characters and situations before. And normally, I would throw the book down in disgust and write strongly-worded letters to the author, but McCammon does something right. It's never too over-the-top and he doesn't rely of any his tropes to carry the story. It's really well-balanced. 
 And the story. It's basically The Stand with nuclear bombs instead of superviruses. The characters and plot structure are a bit too similar for this to be a coincidence. No, McCammon unabashedly borrows from The Stand, and does something that makes this totally acceptable: he improves it. Where King overwrites and overdevelops characters, McCammon writes with a remarkable subtlety. Where King makes the apocalypse out to be a minor annoyance, McCammon paints a picture of a hellish nightmare. Where King tells, McCammon shows. 
 That's another thing. McCammon is an excellent writer. The novel is ~1000 pages and there's no lag time. There was no point where I felt that I was growing tired of the book. Also, just check out the opening line: 
 "Once upon a time we had a love affair with fire, the president of the United States thought as the match that he'd just struck to light his pipe flared beneath his fingers." 
 Daaaayum. King ain't got nothin' on this guy. 
 But I think the most important this about this is just that is was a joy to read. It's dark visions regularly sent shivers down my spine. It has a really deep sense of beauty and a lot of really touching scenes. I have to admit my eyes were watering up quite a bit while reading and I even cried a bit at the ending, tropey action scenes and all. 
 Read it if apocalypses are your thing.

Swan song was a great story, why this has not been made into a movie baffles me. I can imagine the actors that would play the characters. It was long with a few plot minor plot holes. Mr McCammon is a brilliant author, his craftsmanship is fantastic. He made you care about the characters easily enough, the bleak landscape he painted with words. Left me with a mixture of fear, loathing and facination. I would say that Swan Song is akin to Stephan Kings the stand. But only in the basic premise of a Doomsday story. I like that there were fewer characters to have to remember. Which gave them a more refined personalities.

A worthy bookend to Stephen King's The Stand. No Captain Trips this time, but a nuclear holocaust engineered by evil shape-shifter Doyle Halland. 
 And there are two separate survivors' communities - good and evil - each linked to Swan, a little girl who can knead life from scorched earth. 
 This is a terrific post-apocalyptic chiller, and one worth reading.
A lot of violence and not enough hope...though it ended well. I am just glad I'm a fast reader. I would not have wanted to spend more than three days with this book.

This book has been compared to The Stand by Stephen King and has received glowing reviews from the masses for almost 20 years. At over 900 pages, I found it to be dreary in parts and if whiddled down to 500 pages perhaps I would have rated it w/ 4 stars. A Bram Stoker Award winner that never gave me any chills or frights. Stick to The Stand if you want to read about the apocolypse.

I gave up after about 200 pages. It's a generic post-apocalypse novel that's very 1980s. Child who is the chosen one -- check. Magical negro woman -- check. Evil mystery man who may be the devil -- check. The writing was filled with forced awe and mini-tragedies that unfold as if by checklist. It seemed to be basically The Stand without Stephen King's flair for characters.

Read this months ago, but I recall it being the best post-apocalyptic novel I have ever read, even better than 'The Road' by Cormac McCarthy. Made me a fan of McCammon, so I bought another of his but havent read it yet. 
 Enjoy this. Its long, but it gets into you so you can get into it.

book_b.title: Firestarter
book_b.user_review: I don't believe he has wrote a bad story. Sure some are better than others, but I have yet to come across one yet that made me feel like I had wasted my time and I've read almost every one of King's books. Firestarter is no different. A really good story that gets ahold of you from basically page one. It is scary, but for different reasons than the usual King tale. The frightening thing about this one is the way that the government could and would act in situations of "national security." King made it feel like it was a true story, not surprisingly though, there is a reason he is the best. Firestarter fits in well with his better novels and whether you are a King fan or not I believe this novel is worth your time.

sample_reviews.review_text: Dated, but fun. I like the breezy pace of King's early work, and this one contains thematic elements that I especially appreciate after reading King's memoir, On Writing.

** spoiler alert ** 
 i kinda love the ending, i mean the very last page, where she gets up the nerve to finally take her story to the one life-saving, incorruptible news outlet in the country, powerful enough to take on the government... and it's Rolling Stone. that was such a great window into a certain time and headspace in this country. it almost brought tears to my eyes. 
 the rest of the book is interesting (CIA/LSD/mind-control) and often fun, and of course very readable. but a) it's a SF/suspense/thriller type thing, not horror, so who cares, and b) the structure is very strange, it basically happens in 3 large chunks, and each chunk is less exciting than than the one before it. the bad guy is the best part (king does psychotic evil better than anyone) but we know he's never a match for drew barrymore, i mean charlie, who can set the planet on fire with her brains, so there's not really much tension. 
 basically, it's Carrie, but re-envisioned as a thriller. and a not-super-exciting thriller at that. 
 i am running low on stephen king novels i haven't read and am starting to get a little antsy.
I remember liking this book, but I don't remember much about it. What can I say? It was the 70s...

Admittedly not one of King's best books, but fascinating for its connection to the [real] military's experiments on the unknowing public with LSD and other illicit drugs. Andy and his college girlfriend sign up for a drug study, and Andy ends up with some wacky powers. Next thing you know, they marry and she's pregnant, the kid's a whiz with flame, and the government is verrry interested. Not that big a stretch, really. But I think one critic I've read nailed it - the real protaganist of the book is Andy.
I'm not much of a King fan, but find I like his earlier books better than his later ones. This is less wordy than some & the premise is interesting. Plenty of action without too much wandering.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Honestly, I was a little surprised to find out that Stephen Kind does science fiction and does it fairly well. I've seen a lot of the story elements done before -- the government conspiracies and corruption, the innocents on the run, the unlocked powers of the mind -- but SK brings his own particular touches to the story, spending a great deal of time turning Charlie, Andy, Cap and Redbird into real, rounded characters. 
 It doesn't surprise me that Firestarter and The Dead Zone were published within a few years of each other; SK seems to have been experiencing a reflective, somewhat sad period in his writing. 
 I've spent a lot of time thinking about what happens after the last page in the book. With her father dead, Charlie's lost her moral compass. The Shop is still after her and if she succeeds in telling her story, a lot of other people are going to be after her too. She's going to get harder, almost as a necessity. She's going to get more powerful. And I suspect that she will turn into the monster that everyone already fears. My own ruminations makes this book especially bittersweet; it's the last shining time of goodness and innocence in a little girl that never had control over her own fate.
This book was really boring and I had a hard time even finishing this book. In my opinion one of kings worst books

Probably one of the worst books of King, I found it dull and there was really nothing to it. Maybe because I read it during exams period, during bus rides/taking the underground I lost all the joy there is to it. But I doubt it. Overall a mediocre book.

The concept behind this book was unique and interesting, as with all of Stephen King's work. However, the story seemed to drag at several points with the author delving into minute details at nauseum. This was definitely not King's best work. However, I preceded this read with King's 'Joyland', maybe not the best comparison to make!

Listened to this audiobook from the library, using Hoopla. 
 Classic King. Kinda horror, kinda scifi, kinda family in peril chase story. Book jumps right in, showing, main character Charlie and her father Andy, on the run from mysterious organization. We find that the organization is a secretive government organization (called the Shop) who want Andy and Charlie because they happen to have psychic powers. Charlie is the firestarter and Andy can "push" people with his mind to influence them (kinda like a cross between Scanners and the Force). In true King fashion, we jump back and forth to find out their backstory, where we learn that Andy and his future wife were part of a drug experiment when they were in college that gave them these psychic powers. When they later get married and have a child, we find that their abilities are passed along in full (and more) to their daughter. 
 Andy and Charlie are eventually captured and taking to a facility where they separate the two and try to find the secret to Charlie's ability and how they might control her. Needless to say, again in true King fashion, things come to a head and do not go well at all for the Shop. Its a good, fun, pulpy read. Just what you'd expect from 80's era Stephen King 
 6/10 
 S: 3/26/15 F: 4/9/15 (15 Days)
