reference_book.review_text: What a novel! This one is for men and women alike with adventure, romance, and revenge. After you read this one watch the Frecnh movie with Gerard Depardieu. It is an great way to reward yourself after reading it. Though reading it is a reward in itself.

book_a.title: Under the Banner of Heaven: A Story of Violent Faith
book_a.user_review:
Nov 30: It started off good - but one thing Krakauer is lacking is in an unbiased perception of fact. First, and foremost, most of his facts are inaccurate and lacking. Most of it makes me laugh because he really doesn't know the truth but tries to sound as an authoritarian on it. Yes, there are many zealots out there and from all religions. Yes, they can do horrendous things and stuff we don't even want to know about. However, that should not take the place of accurately getting the facts straight to make judgments. Second, in the telling of the Lafferty and Smart cases he comes off very unbiased and as a fact giver, but when he starts in on the theology you can see how extremely biased and judgmental he is. Either come out and say "This is how I see it and believe" but don't pretend to be unbiased and accurate on theology and religion - especially when your facts are not true or accurate. 
 Still gotta finish the book though and see how he pulls this off. 
 Dec 13 update. 
 I am thoroughly disgusted with this book. It bums me out - I like Krakauer. Yet, here we see a man who says he spent a lot of time researching and familiarizing himself with his subject, yet, he spends most of his time in the book spouting off inaccurate information and sticks closely to one or two people's opinions without really exploring the opposite camp. He takes facts out of context and relies heavily on his bias (even though he claims not to have one). He twists what information there is and then produces a book that is inaccurate, false in so many ways, and yet highly influential (according to the comments). Before you make a judgment read and know for yourself before you rely on one man's faulty research to determine your beliefs. He did a GREAT job with into the Wild but that doesn't mean he did a good job here.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I definitely trust this author, I think he is very well researched and tries to keep to the facts. I still have some issues with the flow of his books, however. This is the second of his I've read and I think it would make more sense if he stuck to a linear time flow. This book is mostly Mormon history, although it does focus on the violent and infuriating history (not as bias, as journalism), but there are so many names and dates that it's hard to follow after a while. I was really wishing for some sort of "name" glossary or something, or a drawing of the timeline. 
 I think it would have been better as two story threads: 1. the history of Mormanism and 2. The Lafferty story. They relate to each other quite a bit, but by the last few chapters I couldn't wait for the history lessons to end because it was too overwhelming. (I recently read Unbroken, for example, which tells the entire story in time order, and it worked exceptionally well.) Switching back and forth between these two would be easy to follow. The current format of this book jumped around too much for me, which was the same complaint I had with the first book of his I read. I still think it's a worthwhile read, and absolutely fascinating. 
 However, I also am left asking myself, "What was the point of this book?" Not in a derogatory way, just because I'm not sure how to answer that. Was he trying to just give information? Point out where religion can go wrong? Make a philosophical point? Warn us about taking things too far? I think there's an argument that this book is about all of those things, but I wasn't sure what the author wanted to portray.

I find the subject matter fascinating, and I did like Krakauer's writing style in Into the Wild, but Under the Banner of Heaven was just too long-winded for me and I stopped about half-way through with absolutely no interest in continuing further. It would have benefited from some heavy editing.

Under the Banner of Heaven is Jon Krakauer's "expose" on the Mormon Fundamentalist movement. Krakauer is really a master of non-fiction writing. With his writing mixed with an interesting subject of this sect of religion/cult, makes it a highly engrossing read.

In the Author's Remark section towards the back of the book, Jon Krakauer states that the book didn't turn out to be the one he started off with, and that the focus switched in the writing. While that may be forgivable in fiction, I'm not sure if I can give him a pass in a non-fiction work. You can clearly see the great divide between the book that he wanted to write and the book that he ended up with. Even though it's a 4/5 on the rating system, a more accurate rating would be about 3.5/5. Insightful and thorough look at the history of Mormonism and religious fundamentalism, but loses a bit of focus towards the end. But more on that later. 
 The book begins with the murder of a woman and a baby in the hands of two Fundamentalist members of the Church of the Latter-Day Saints, aka Mormons. They are the Mormon version of what the mainstream media would refer to as the Islamic Fundamentalists, basically. Opening the book with a seemingly mindless murder did draw me into the story, and I wanted to know more about these men's motivations. On that front, Krakauer definitely delivered. He spoke with one of the murders in a high security prison, and you get to learn about how a normal, everyday husband was influenced by his brothers and transformed into a religious extremist. Like any true crime novel out there, this section of the book is incredibly interesting, and it reminded me of Truman Capote's work on In Cold Blood, which is similar in many ways save for the religious twist. 
 On top of that, Krakauer also gives readers a rundown of Mormon beliefs and history, with how the religion came to be and how it works. We get to see how Joseph Smith came to be and how he attracted believers from all over the US. Again, very intriguing, because the church has always been somewhat closed off, especially to people (like myself) on this side of the Pacific. Krakauer's look at the fundamentalist church's practice of polygamy was also insightful, if not unsettling and deeply disturbing. Again, as above, very arresting materials here and thoroughly, thoroughly researched. 
 My problem with the book comes towards the halfway mark, when Krakauer decides to talk about the blood-soaked history of the LDS Church. The section after Joseph Smith's death involves a large cast of characters, and it quickly descended into a convoluted history lesson. Four or five chapters were devoted wholly to how the LDS Church was persecuted by the government, the wars (and almost-wars) waged during that time, how the Indians got involves, and an exploration team that was murdered by LDS members. All very detailed and all very intriguing, but Krakauer decided to delve into this part of Mormonism history AFTER describing, in detail, how our murderers killed the woman and the baby. Yes, the titular scene happens halfway through the book, so you are left with little to "look forward to", as macabre as that may sound. I wanted deeply to go back to the murderers and see how they lived out the rest of their days as free men, how they were arrested and how they were charged. Yet, Krakauer devoted at least a hundred pages to this OTHER part of Mormon history, which added little to the central plot (even though this is, essentially, non-fiction). Yes, you do need to know the church's history to understand these men's motives, but I felt like he has already driven the point home by this point, and he really did't need to bang more holes into the board. 
 Also, I am a fan of Krakauer's work, especially his real-life experience on Mount Everest, which he chronicles in Into Thin Air. Having lived through the ordeal himself, he was able to provide a fairly well balanced view of what exactly happened during one of the worst disasters in mountaineering history. When approaching this book, I was expecting the same level of level-headedness, but got something else instead. Krakauer's depiction of Mormonism is more than a little skewed here. It is funny, because as an atheist, you would think that I would enjoy a book that bashes Mormonism. Instead, I wanted something a little more fair and balanced. Perhaps some conversations with your average everyday Mormons would be nice. I mean, he even states in the Author's Remarks that he used to hang out with a bunch of normal everyday Mormons. Couldn't he have talked to any one of them to get a different perspective? 
 I bring the point up because there are a lot of misunderstanding in the world going on right now with regard to religion and religious beliefs. While I believe that humanity does not need religion to survive--in fact it has cause much suffering over the years--I also believe that there are two sides to every coin. While there are people who'd manipulate religion to their own benefits--like fundamentalists of any religion--there are people out there who just want to get by. We already have enough demonising when it comes to religious fundamentalism, so it is more than a little tiresome to read yet another biased view on a religion. I believe that religion will eventually die out, whether that will take decades or centuries, but I'm not sure if biases will get us there any quicker. I mean, I suppose a book that attacks FUNDAMENTALISTS is fine, but Krakauer doesn't seem to make that distinction towards the end. Yes, he starts off by saying that polygamy is practice ONLY by the fundamentalists, but he doesn't shy away from the opinion that BOTH sects of LDS shared a bloody history of violence and bloodshed. As mentioned, the book turned into something else, and I suppose it does show.

Dead In The Family is the tenth book in the Sookie Stackhouse series by Charlaine Harris. I was extremely excited about this release but I have to say now that emotion has been changed to utter disappointment. Dead 
 In The Family revolves around very subdued Sookie coming to terms with the brutal torture and near death that she faced at the end of Dead and Gone. She's struggling to recover her physical strength but the biggest changes seem to be in her personality. She's understandably quieter, more nervous and ill at ease. Eventually she regains some of her normal perkiness but when faced with a threat to her and Eric's happiness her first thoughts are that it would be better if person threatening them just died. 
 Eric has many parts in this book but many of his fans will be disappointed in his role. He seems to have evolved from all powerful to gloomy and depressing, almost needy. 
 The highlights to the book include a mystery when an unknown person leaves a murdered body on Sookies land and try to set her up to take the fall by reporting her to the police. The whole rush to figure out who did it, who it was, and why she was set up happens in about 3 chapters and are the only in the book that caught my attention. 
 The lowlights unfortunately include the constant rambling which is at times had me just turning the page to get past it. Really, I didn't like how her mornings were laid out and details were explained on exactly what she did (i.e. walk to the kitchen and makes a cup of coffee, using a new coffee she picked up at the store on Saturday). 
 I feel as though this book did not add to the series, in fact it hurt it. And unfortunately I would not recommend it for readers out there. This is just my opinion but unfortunately I did not enjoy this book.

book_b.title: American Psycho
book_b.user_review:
So it is the second time I've read through this diary of madness and I still found the first one hundred pages intensely infuriating. The first time I read this book, when I was about sixteen, I assumed I hated the beginning of the book so much just because I didn't really understand it. Turns out . . . that was not it at all; understanding it made it even more infuriating. Bateman rolls off list after list of materialistic possessions, random and mundane facts that only he finds significant, constant comments on his appearance, and so on. And it all just seemed . . . a little, well . . . over the top. It seems to me - by looking at previous reviews, anyway - that I'm not the only person that feels this way. Well, I think I know why the author has created this soul withering intro, and it's not to paint a picture of Bateman's madness for us; it's an attempt to stir up own inner insanity instead. Think about the title; American Psycho. . . it screams blood, gore and violence from the get go. Doesn't it? Yet when you start reading the book, it is nothing but menu lists, champagne, suits and steroid talk. Deliberate? Yes, I think so. But not for the reasons you might think. I recon Ellis has constructed this in a way that it is so infuriating and pain staking to read, that by the time your only half way through the beginning, you're already begging Bateman to go out and stab and mutilate someone, screaming at him to get a f***ing move on; thus, only really becoming a little blood thirsty yourself. Who's the psycho now? You blood hungry vermin! Anyway . . . once coming to the conclusion that it turned me into a villainous madman, and although the beginning will always terrorise me, at least I know now it what only doing what the author intended; driving me crazy. And I must say that it did a mighty fine job of doing so. 
 The part in the book that gets to me the most is the chapter, killing a Dog. So deep . . . my book is twisted, yet this horrified me. Poor dog. I'm in Viet Nam at the moment and I've eaten pretty much everything that would be considered weird - snakes heart and bile, pig brain, live squid, fresh quid, some egg that has a baby chicken inside but you eat it like a boild egg - that was just strange, and so on. Yet, I'd never eat dog . . . too intelligent for my liking - thinking about cutting out the pork for that reason as well. Probably never happen, I love bacon too much. 
 The ending of this book is whatever you make of it. I know what I think but I'll leave it for you to decide. 
 All in all, I really enjoyed this book - Again! The murder scenes are amazingly written . . . actually, the whole book is written well, yet the blood and guts stand out on the page the most. Pure hack fest! This book will literally drive you to insanity.

See Pat date. 
 See Pat screw. 
 See Pat mace. 
 See Pat use a nail gun. 
 See Pat eat flesh. 
 See Pat do obscene things with a severed head. 
 See Pat store body parts in random places. 
 Go, Pat, go! 
 1.5 stars Don't worry. That's the tame version. I didn't spoil the extreme parts of the story. Trust me. 
 It might be a long, long time before I read something which knocks American Psycho out of the top spot for "sickest thing I've ever witnessed," and I've read books which have had rape, murder, and gore aplenty in them. 
 How often can a person say that the movie was better than the book? I actually liked the movie because it carried the point from the story without being quite as tedious or gruesome. 
 Part of me wanted to spoiler-tag a couple of the more gruesome scenes, just to give readers who were curious something to look at. But I'm not giving anyone any ideas. O.o 
 The first half of the book was overworked satire. Pages and pages of excessive description gave no great sense of entertainment or enjoyment in terms of reading experience. I do understand why the author did what he needed to do in order to set up the character's state of mind to the reader. Many of the conversations and interactions were needed, and a few were actually informative or interesting, but the same point really could have been made in a few chapters. 
 It all comes down to reading preference for me. Half a book of recycled conversation about fashion, society, tanning, etc. is torture for people like me who could not give a shit about that stuff. I hate wasting my time by reading about stuff I don't want to read about, satire or not. Overkill is still overkill, especially when you see the same catch-phrases (hardbody, gazelleskin, etc.) used dozens of times in the book, and you're sort of sad that you're not playing a drinking game to combat some of the repetitiveness. By the time I got to the chapter on detailing Whitney Houston's career, I was downright tired of reading scene after scene of tedious information. 
 Although...the chapter on name brand water amused me, probably because of how I learned that I'm sparkling water poser. 
 Speaking of excessive...let's get to the second half of the book, otherwise known as a precursor (no, not really) to the show 1,000 Ways to Die. 
 Try thinking of the sickest way you could kill someone. Chances are, you aren't even close to thinking about what Pat put his victims through. 
 Did Pat become the way that he was because he was so rich and bored, and had nothing left to achieve or desire, or was his mind so completely ordered and methodical about everything from the start, that he viewed murder without emotion as just another thing he could organize and categorize? 
 I get why American Psycho has a good portion of its ratings on either one end or the other of the spectrum. Since the subject itself doesn't lend itself well to words such as "love" or "admire," a reader is either going to respect the method of writing, or hate the product of the writing. 
 I wanted to fall on the respect end because I understood why others rated the book high. But I can't overcome the fact that I hated reading the repetitive formula of : character talks about meaningless shit, character talks about or participates in unappealing (and super-extreme) sex, then character makes a gruesome kill. 
 The end of the story gave the reader nothing to wrap up the madness of it all. 
 The guy was a psycho. That's about it. At least the book was aptly named.

For a book about a serial killer, American Psycho is surprisingly boring. It's about Patrick Bateman, a 20-something year old bigoted narcissist who's deeply afraid of turning 30. He works on Wall Street, does a lot of cocaine, and also likes torturing people to death, especially women during sex. 
 Patrick Bateman's narcissism may have been satirical in 1991, but his intense superficiality has become tediously mainstream in 2016. There isn't anything particularly outrageous about a man who is obsessed with going to the gym, drinking mineral water, rejecting food because of its nutrient content, getting tans, having manicures and wearing designer clothes. Contrasted with Bateman's materialism are many scenes of horrific murder. These murderous acts have no purpose, and they are described in a graphic but also incredibly curt, matter-of-fact way that actually makes them extremely unconvincing. The violence is cartoonishly over-the-top and yet depicted in such an understated way that it has no real impact. The many scenes of sexual violence against women are especially notable examples because they are so gruesome but also so ludicrous (eg, murder by acid + broken glass + cheese + rat + chainsaw, with sex before, during and after). The more elaborate the murder, the less I could maintain attention. I found myself rolling my eyes constantly and sincerely questioning why I was wasting my time with this book. 
 The story doesn't have much of a narrative and repeats itself to the point of pure tedium. It doesn't work as horror, it doesn't work as satire, it doesn't work as a black comedy. I wasn't even offended by it because it's so patently ridiculous. I thought American Psycho was wearisome.
Lets just say it: Bret Easton Ellis is pure genius

 "L'universo nei tuoi occhi" e l'ultimo libro di Jennifer Niven, edito in Italia per DeAgostini. La Niven venuta alla ribalta con lo young adult "Raccontami di un giorno perfetto" e una scrittrice capace di scavare nelle storie, di entrare nella testa dei suoi protagonisti tirando fuori delle storie che apparentemente sembrano banali e invece tirano fuori spunti di riflessione che inducono a guardare dentro di se, anche quando non si vorrebbe. 
 Ho letto questo libro diverso tempo fa, ma ci ho messo un sacco di tempo per recensirlo. Un po' perche mi spaventava, un po' perche e difficile ridurre una lettura del genere in uno spaccato degno di nota, capace di catturare la luce che emerge dalle pagine. Un po' perche il mio tempo libero si e ridotto considerevolmente e trovare il tempo per fermarmi e scrivere delle recensioni e sempre piu difficile. Ma d'altronde ogni libro ha qualcosa da raccontare, anche quelli piu impensabili e nonostante la pochezza di certe trame, e importante non perdere di vista che una lettura ha sempre il compito di accrescere la nostra persona, in termini di emozioni o di conoscenza, ma non e mai un vuoto a perdere, non e mai la cristallizzazione di un'incognita fine a se stessa. E la Niven non lascia certo indifferenti, pur sfruttando due casi che potrebbero sembrare uno sfoggio eccessivo di problematiche unite in una sola vicenda. Eppure, forse, e proprio questo troppo che spinge ad interrogarsi sul serio, e proprio questo intenso concatenarsi di tragicita che da un certo punto di vista induce a non fermarsi. E da un lato c'e Libby, una ragazza che ha attraversato una delle prove piu difficili della sua vita e ancora non se ne e liberata, perche la lotta con il proprio corpo e quanto di piu complicato esista. Perche perdersi nel cibo, scomparire nei chili che si accumulano, annullare il dolore di un lutto in un flusso continuo di cibo e fin troppo facile. Perdersi, senza lottare, abbandonandosi al peso specifico del proprio dolore e estremamente facile, salvarsi estremamente difficile. Ma Libby in fondo e una lottatrice, una ragazza che nonostante tutto cerca di salire la china e salvarsi. D'altronde se non iniziamo noi a salvarci da soli, nessuno potra farlo per noi. Ma Libby non e una damsell in distress che aspetta l'arrivo di Jack per essere salvata. Libby e una tipa tosta che sa cosa vuole, ballare, sopra ogni cosa e dopo essere stata educata in casa per anni torna a scuola come una normale adolescente, ma con il peso del suo passato a pungolarla continuamente. E dall'altro lato trova Jack, un ragazzo che finge continuamente di essere sempre sul punto, ma che il punto non riesce neanche a riconoscerlo. Jack mente continuamente, naviga nella sua quotidianita con una manciata di punti fermi che si sbriciolano continuamente, che si frantumano dietro cambiamenti repentini delle persone che lo circondano. Jack, che si destreggia con la forza dell'abitudine e mille espedienti, e completamente solo, senza nessun aiuto, neanche quello dei genitori che ignorano completamente la condizione in cui versa. E allora e una continua lotta a fine l'ennesima giornata senza fare troppi danni. Jack e Libby hanno lo stesso approccio all'esistenza, il dramma che non li abbandona, esasperato dalla loro incapacita di accettare che hanno bisogno di aiuto. Il messaggio, fortissimo, della Niven resta quello che se non chiediamo aiuto, se non parliamo, non potremmo mai renderci conto che non siamo soli, che accanto a noi ci sono persone che ci amano disposte a fare qualsiasi cosa pur di metterci nella condizione di raggiungere la serenita. Non e facile, ma la vita non e mai facile. 
 Il particolare da non dimenticare? Delle fotografie... 
 Una storia potente, che supera i confini della vicenda che si dispiega nelle pagine per parlare al lettore, e indurlo a credere che non e mai una sconfitta parlare delle proprie difficolta. Una storia non comune, forse molto sopra le righe, ma che di certo non lascia indifferenti, con la delicatezza della Niven, che e come una carezza. 
 Buona lettura guys!

sample_reviews.review_text:
This was actually a ridiculously fun read! I just recently finished What the Dead Want, a book I had ridiculously high expectations for that let me down hard. So going into this I lowered my expectations considerably. I figured it would be another cheesy YA drama with far too much emphasis on romance and too much girl-on-girl hate. 
 Which is has.... in spades. The author just presents it in a way that while it's using the same old ideas in all YA contemporary fantasy books, it comes off as being refreshing even if not wholly original. Sam Mathers is a descendant of Cotton Mathers, one of the Puritan baddies who basically started the Salem Witch Trials. So when she arrives in Salem, the descendants of the witches have a bone to pick (because Salem is apparently a ridiculous town with far too much emphasis on this stuff). Then suddenly there's deaths everywhere. And because of this, Sam is all alone trying to deal with this stuff. It gave the girl-on-girl hate legitimate backing so it was entirely plausible for Sam to not have any girl friends. Even the love triangle is weirdly explained well, and for once in my life I wasn't rolling my eyes at the way it developed. If anything, it felt more organic that 99% of all other love triangles in YA fiction. 
 I loved the plot. It starts out fast and just gets worse and worse as time goes on. The mass hysteria hits hard and there's very little time at all for Sam to get acclimated before the shit hits the fan. It's a surprisingly fun romp through some crazy, and that ending.... it's just a damn good ending. All the major players make an appearance and it is the perfect way to end the book. I actually think this is great as a standalone novel so I'm mildly curious to see what the second one will be; I'll probably still check it out either way. 
 The only thing I was sad about was Vivian, Sam's stepmother. In the beginning I thought that for once we would have a stepmother who wasn't a crazy controlling psycho, but alas, it was not to be.

No one wants to be the new girl--especially when your last name is "Mather" and you're the new girl in Salem, Massachusetts. Samantha hopes she can just blend in, but the elite group known as "The Descendents,"--because they are directly descended from the original witches from the infamous trials--makes it very clear that she is not welcome at Salem High. Even her family home is unwelcoming, or is it possible an angry ghost haunts her grandmother's house? In drawing comparisons between "mean girl" style high school bullies and the Salem Witch Trials, Mather brings a modern relevance to this very popular subject. Unfortunately, stiff dialogue and shallow characters prevent the interesting premise from reaching its full potential. The obligatory love triangle feels forced, lacking the steamy tension that should tug on readers' emotions. Samantha, who prior to the move had virtually no knowledge of her family's involvement in the famous trials, slides into practicing witchcraft much too easily to be believable--blithely mixing spells as if she'd been doing it all her life. Suspense, however, is nicely developed throughout the story and the fast-paced climax with a bit of a twist rewards patient readers. Give to teens obsessed with this popular historic event.

Solid 3.5. At first I thought I was reading another version of Conversion by Katherine Howe, but then the plot really kicked in. I had trouble liking the main character at first (oops I'm so clumsy, everyone hates me but this hot boy) but she grew on me by the end. And I loved Elijah. I've also spent a lot of time in Salem so it was fun to read about places I've been.

This story was more interesting to think about once the author's interest in events was established. 
 The Salem Witch Trials is a fascinating event in history, and the consequences of actions and group dynamics is intriguing. It's a story that could be replicated at key moments in history, so it was interesting to see how this was adapted to a more modern setting. 
 When Sam moves to Salem her presence is immediately unwelcome. Her name has a lot to answer for...for one of her ancestors was responsible for the hanging of those accused of witchcraft. Their descendants are unhappy that Sam has returned, and when strange events begin to happen they have their perfect scapegoat. 
 This could have been a simple retelling, but Mather introduces a new twist. This serves well enough to bring a different take to events.

Have you ever read a really highly rated book and just know you're going to be in the minority? Because I do, and it's this one. It pained me to read this book, like I was literally regretting sitting down and reading up. But, there was no way I couldn't finish it, because I needed to know exactly what made this such a painful experience. And, honestly, I'm still having a hard time with that question. there are so many elements in How to Hang a Witch that just didn't work. Maybe it's me, but this book was just...bad. 
 But, I have to give credit where credit is due. This book is incredibly well researched. From the Salem Witch Trials to the descriptions of witchcraft in the book, it all felt very authentic. It was clear Mather did a lot of research into the culture and history, which is also her history since Mather is a descendant of Cotton Mather from the actual Witch Trials and writing a YA, maybe-fictionalized-maybe-not-I'm-just-saying, account of her family history is pretty cool. So, I can't say that there's nothing positive about this book. 
 My problems with this book stems from two main points. 1) The Characters. 2) The writing style. This is pitched as a sort of Salem Witch Trials meets Mean Girls kinda thing. A lot of books capitalize on the whole "hysteria" thing and the way gossip and fear can take a hold of a community, but this book takes it to a whole new level, linking the Salem Witch Trials to modern day high school, which would be really cool if it were utilized properly. 
 This is very much a character driven story, but there's no character in this story. Sam, Jaxon, Elijah, the Descendants. They're all lifeless shells full of spite, self-hatred, and occasionally funny one-liners when the plot calls for it. Does Sam need to be vulnerable because plot? Yes. Does Lizzie need to do something bitchy, because reasons? Yep, done. Does Susannah/Alice/Mary need to spout some half-assed/half-explained exposition Sam will ignore until the time is right? You betcha. 
 All these characters were puppets, moving because the plot, which is pretty flimsy at best, calls for it. None of them were developed past the point of a vague description and a name. Hell, some of them didn't even have that luxury. Two of the five Descendants were interchangeable, one made an impression because he's a guy and another because she was the only person who actually interacted with Sam outside a few mean comments. And the final Descendant? Guys, I can't believe I'm saying this, but how do you mess up a mean girl? Like seriously? Lizzie, the only "mean girl" in the book, is the weakest mean girl I've ever read about. I'd call her a stereotype, but that's stretching it because stereotypes are at least interesting/fun to laugh at. Lizzie was just a shell of a ghost of a stereotype that honestly wasn't in the book for that long. 
 Oh, and there's a love triangle between a hot junior named Jaxson, yes that is how his name is spelled, and a dead ghost who falls in love with Sam named Elijah. And, seriously people? Has our need for a love triangle superseded the fact the love interest has to be alive and not three-hundred years older than the protagonist? Because, if it has, were in some deep shit. And neither of them are interesting. Seriously. Jaxson was a wet blanket and Elijah was a literal ghost whose dialogue was like something out of a bad porno parody of the Salem Witch Trials. It got on my nerves super fast and not only did I not find it authentic, I found it absolutely irritating. 
 And Sam? She's...she's...god, I don't know. I can't cal her a blank slate because she does do stuff, but I can't call her a character because there's almost no personality behind her. She's funny when she has to be, vulnerable when the plot calls for it, and angry when there needs to be a reason for one of her two guys to make her feel better. This entire book is Sam reacting too what happens to her in a way that gives her no agency. She's just a pair of eyes that pretends to have a personality to trick you into thinking it's a real character. 
 Moving on to the writing style, it's too fast. And not necessarily fast paced, but fast writing. The scene changes with a sentence, stuff is discovered and talked about and moved on to new stuff in a paragraph, things just go by too fast. The story is written so tightly there's no room to breathe, no room that would allow the story to grow and build on its own. Something is always happening, Sam is always feeling something or do something it overshadows what she was doing previously. It's disjointed and manic and gave me a huge headache. During the climax, like twelve things were going on and I couldn't focus on anything. I had to re-read like the last twenty-ish pages just to get some handle on the setting and what the hell was going on. There was just too much happening all at once to feel any tension or suspense or fear or whatever I was supposed to be feeling in those moments. 
 And, what's just really really sad, is that this could have been such a good book. It was so well researched it could have been an absolutely phenomenal story about bullying and hysteria and dark family secrets if it just had a better writing style and characters who were interesting/engaging/good. But, instead it turned into a well-researched dreck that made reading it literally painful for me. However, I will probably be reading Mather's next book, because I really think if she tweaks a few things I could see what other people see in her writing and get on board with what she has to offer.

sample_reviews.review_text: I just couldn't get into this one. Raylene was sort of interesting, but she drove me nuts too. She was so full of herself that it turned me off the rest of the story. This one just wasn't for me.
Drawn out, cliche riddled, plot, flat lead and ridiculous romance that had no spark. This was a dud for me.

Bloodshot by Cherie Priest is not the first book of Priest's that I've read. If it had been, I don't know that I'd be convinced to pick up another of her books in the future. (I read Boneshaker when it was on the AussieCon Hugo ballot and enjoyed it.) It's the kind of book that makes me glad I didn't pay full price for it and assuages some of my "buying all the discount books when Borders was dying" guilt. 
 Raylene is a vampire for hire. Usually she's hired to steal things -- art, archaeological artifacts, home made porn... -- and this time is no different. A mysterious vampire client (where her usual clients are human) hires her to steal some paperwork from a classified military operation. It's a fairly simple story in which she sneaks around, trying to avoid the people suddenly out to kill her and completes the mission in a more roundabout way than they all initially suspected. Fine. It wasn't a plot made of deep but it was the part I didn't have a problem with. If it sounds like the kind of urban fantasy you might enjoy, then by all means, don't let me ruin it for you by reading what I disliked in the rest of the review. 
 First, Raylene is fairly unlikeable. She's somewhere between kickarse and paranoid and she talks too much. Some of the talking too much can be attributed to her personality/character development, but some of it was just poor writing. Many statements are rehashed or irrelevant details are harped upon in painstaking detail. There was so much justifying of her comments it felt as though the author was working too hard to point out the blindingly obvious to the reader. It very much could have done with more subtlety. Here is a random example from near the start: 
 I'm white as a compact fluorescent bulb, which you might expect from a woman who avoids the sun to the best of her ability, and my teeth... well, I try not to show them when I smile. 
 They're not all incriminatingly pointy, don't get me wrong. When I yawn I'm not flashing a row of shark's choppers, but my canines are decidedly pokey. Thank God they don't hang down as long as they once did. (I know a guy. He filed them or me.) These days they may be short, but they're still sharp enough to puncture an oilcan, and that's how I like it. 
 My hair is more or less the same as it always was, a shade of black that doesn't require any further descriptors. 
 And so on. Bolding mine. It's all overwritten in a similar vein. That particular sentence at the end made me angry when I read it because if it doesn't require descriptors why put the descriptor in? 
 At times the characters talk in a stilted way, which would have bothered me more if I hadn't given up and started skimming at that point. To be fair, not all the conversations were stilted, but enough to bother me. Too often the action scenes (which were numerous, it's that kind of book and that isn't a bad thing) were broken up by gratuitous description which made the situations less tense and caused me to skim down the page. 
 The final thing that bothered me relates back to Raylene being unlikeable. She's a bit everything-ist, which is OK except once you stop and think just how much worse it would sound if she was male. Yeah. And then there was a drag queen character who I didn't think was handled very well. There were some cringe-worthy aspects. (I'd be more specific, but they do actually involve spoilers.) 
 So yeah. I wouldn't recommend this book. I won't be reading the sequel. I might read Cherie Priest's steampunk books -- on the assumption that they're more like Boneshaker than Bloodshot -- and I have Four and Twenty Blackbirds (which is apparently southern gothic, though I'm not sure what that means) which I'll still get to eventually. I've read worse books and I've read worse writing, but I couldn't enjoy Bloodshot. 
 2.5 / 5 stars 
 You can read more of my reviews on my blog.

I actually finished this book last night, but haven't gotten around to writing a review before now. 
 I'm a fan of Cherie Priest, have been for a few years now, but I'm not the biggest fan of vampires, so I let this book kinda slide into the shadows. But now I have a goal of trying to read all her books, and so I had to get around to it sooner or later. 
 I did it sooner. 
 To be honest, I thought about DNFing this book multiple times in the beginning. 
 I found the start to be really slow, I didn't like the writing style, and I didn't connect with the characters. But I pushed through, 'cause I didn't really want to pick up another book either, and I'm glad I did. 
 After getting through the first 100 pages - which I found slow - things picked up. We actually got a working story line, not just jumbling around being weird. 
 I liked parts of the story, while I didn't like others. Some parts seemed a bit coincidental, even if the MC proclaims it was planned. 
 Some parts, were fun and action packed. 
 I am also glad that there isn't a big romance story line in this book! 
 There are some hints to one, I will admit, but the way the characters were written, it didn't seem like a main point in their personalities, which I really enjoyed. 
 Speaking of characters, I loved that there were some really diverse characters in this book, but unfortunately, I didn't believe many of the characters. 
 There were two, maybe three, characters that seemed fleshed out. Raylene, Adrian and Pepper, maybe also Domino, if I'm generous, but other than that, the other characters we met seemed like paper. Sure, we didn't get a lot of time to know them, but it didn't even seem like Priest tried to know them herself. 
 And then there was the writing style. 
 It took me a bit to get into, but when I did, I managed to not get annoyed with it anymore. 
 For while it is still good, grammarly and technically, the way the story was told... *shudder* 
 The book is written in 1th person POV, and this would have worked, if not for the constant break in action and other things for the character to tell us she is neurotic, have OCD and is paranoid. I love that it is part of the character, but when you stop action and story line to tell us again and again? Then it doesn't work. 
 Other than that, I also had a problem with some of the chapters being really long. Now, I know I'm a special case, with my health issues, but when one chapter almost took me 1 hour to read, I got tired and couldn't concentrate, and lost track of the story. 
 So I will read the second book in this series, but I am kinda glad that there are only those two books in this series.

Mercedes (Mercy) Thompson lives in a world where the fae have come out of the preternatural closet, the werewolves have recently shown their true faces, and the many other mysteries of the world are still kept hidden from the humans to avoid mass hysteria. Being a walker (a girl who can shift into the form of a coyote) who was raised by werewolves, she more deeply tied to the preternatural scene than most. So when the vampires call on her as nothing more than to be a witness to fulfill a debt she incurred while helping the werewolves, she's more than happy that she wasn't called on to do something much worse. How was she to know that this one simple act would pull her into the hunt for a vampire sorcerer, host to a demon? That she would come to learn why vampires had feared her race for so long? 
 Briggs is quickly becoming one of my favorite authors. I read Moon Called a while ago, and enjoyed it, but I had so many other things to read that I forgot about the series altogether. Until the Blood Bound made it's way to the top of the to-read pile, and I got to fall in love all over again. 
 I love how Briggs pulls Mercy into trouble. She never goes looking for it. (Well, at least she doesn't in the beginning of the book. It always finds her at first, she just doesn't let it disappear once it's found her). This time it was to fulfill a debt to the vampire Stefan, though even he didn't realize that he was bringing her into the lair of a vampire possessed by a demon. 
 This book also expands on the relationship between Mercy, Adam and Samuel. (Not all three of them together, but rather Mercy's relationship with both of them.) Though it definitely doesn't answer any questions about them. (I have my opinions, of course. I want her with Adam. In my head, they belong together, and she doesn't see that. At least not completely. Come on Mercy! You need to figure it out!) 
 Anyway, I loved this book, and am even currently halfway through the next one. I'm thinking that Briggs is one of those authors that I may need to read her entire body of work, which means I have some catching up to do.

sample_reviews.review_text:
The philosophy of this book is strange. There is a definite good and evil force, but the church that claims to be a source of good has been possessed by the dark side, and the regular folk, "superstitious" witches, are the ones who get the way the world works. How one knows which side is good, and which is evil seems ambiguous (at least from the point of view of the characters). 
 I can see how this could be a parallel reality to Mormon Christian history/theology, like C.S. Lewis' Narnia is parallel to Protestant Christian theology. The preacher (representing Christianity, should be a guide) seems irredeemably lost, and everything points to Alvin as this savior of a sort. 
 There are some rules which are similar to Christian theology, or Zoroastrianism~ 
 There is a Maker, there is an Unmaker (is it an entity or a force?) 
 There is a Devil, an enemy of the Maker (most definitely an entity) 
 There are angels ("shining man") 
 There is magic/miracles (science and reason seem to be the enemy, or is it pride?) 
 I enjoyed the Ender series so much I wanted to start another of OSC's series. So far, I'm interested. Religion makes good sci fi! I like the idea of an alternate reality in our history with characters (founding fathers etc) that we are familiar with. I am a little disappointed in the good/evil dichotomy, and some shallowness in the few "bad guys". I wonder: Is there redemption? Do his characters change and grow or do they stay the same?
It was a solid read. A great spin on historical fiction and Card is a great writer. Well worth a try.

I discovered Orson Scott Card by reading Ender's Game first and loved it. Once I had finished that series, I looked for more by the same author. 
 Although totally different than the Ender series, The Tales of Alvin maker series are a great read, and I love it.

book_b.user_review:
This is certainly being added to my list of recommendations for children! This is a realistic and moving look at a teenage boy who's life didn't go as planned. Steven is a drummer, Steven is a thirteen-year old with a crush on the hottest girl in school, and Steven has a brother. 
 Steven's school paper about the most annoying thing in his life was all about his five-year-old brother, Jeffrey, but when Jeffrey comes down with Leukemia, Steven's world is turned upside down. The worst part is everyone is so concerned for Jeffrey, that during this terrifying time, no one is paying attention to Steven who's stopped turning in school projects and is growing ever more depressed. 
 It's hard, but step by step Steven becomes the brother Jeffrey needs. 
 It's a pretty touching story. A few times I felt like the way Steven thinks about girls was very stereotypical. And Dangerous Pie was only barely mentioned at the beginning of the book! Why is it in the title, except for the reason that it sounds interesting? 
 I listened to the audiobook. The narration was great.

sample_reviews.review_text: I know the storyline means well and in some moments can appear cute with the Jeffrey scenes but the dialogue. Oh man. I can't take any book seriously if the speech of the characters isn't up to par. It makes it less believable and it ruins the story.

I want to rate this higher because if I was a teen or pre-teen this would easily have been a 4 star book for me. But I'm not that young, I'm in my early 30's and I have to rate this for me when I read it - now. 
 This is a really good story. On one hand it's quite simple and you feel like you're just skating through the reading of it. On the other hand it's pretty complex with the matter at hand and more. 
 And this isn't just about a boy who has a little brother whose life is on the line. It's about a lot more. Family ties, sibling issues, school and friend issues, the way people act around a sick person, and much more. 
 What I liked most about it was Sonnenblick's humor. I'm willing to bet a large amount of money that he has a killer sarcastic streak. Coming from someone who absolutely loves sarcasm that did me in right there. It's strange to recall laughing at a book about a kid with cancer. 
 The second biggest factor for me was how realistic it was. I don't and have never had a child with cancer thank God. I don't now and haven't ever known a child with cancer. I can't comment on that aspect but with the medical terminology and what went hand in hand with that it seemed very realistic. 
 I do want to mention that it's not over the top in any way. The medical parts aren't so complex you won't understand. It's all kept very simple and very age appropriate. 
 When I say I liked the realisticness what I mean is with Steven, his brother, his friends, the girls he's coming in contact with each day, his parents, etc. I'm not a writer but I've read enough books to know this isn't always done well. Sonnenblick wrote Steven so well I felt I'd love to know him. And I don't really aspire to spend any time at all with 8th grade boys. For the record I don't really even like being around 8th grade girls. For even more of a record I'd say I like to stay away from all young people from the age of, oh, let's say about 5 all the way up to the mid-twenties. (Later if the common sense and courtesy kicks in late.) This is excepting my own wonderful, smart, beautiful, sweet, caring daughter of course. :) 
 Read the book - it's a good fast read and even someone who is (gasp!) middle-age can benefit from it and enjoy the story.

reference_book.title: Guy in Real Life
reference_book.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 This book is such a mess. I'm still trying to sort out my feelings about it (I may add more after today's book club discussion), but so far this is what I've got: 
 Characters: The characters are flat, static, and just plain terrible. The parental figures are interchangeable, and at one point even Lesh notes that his parents and Svetlana's are basically the same. The protagonists themselves are unlikable. Svetlana is a spoiled brat portrayed as an ethereal fairy princess. She's described as a hippie, but she just seemed like a quirky artist. She also faints constantly, which I found bizarre and grating. Lesh is an ungrateful metal dude who gets horny. That's pretty much it. There was some gender identity confusion that had the potential to be really interesting, but instead it's given superficial lip service and glossed over without too much discussion or thought by either of the main characters. That was disappointing, but probably for the best. The portrayal of females in general is pretty insulting; they're either quirky and interesting or mean sluts. Or clueless, overbearing moms I suppose. 
 Plot: When my students have difficulty determining the conflict of the story, I have them figure out the climax first, and then work backwards from there. I had to do that myself with this book. I can't decide if there's too much going on or not enough, but none of the various threads are resolved satisfactorily. I also couldn't figure out the main conflict. There's literally nothing keeping Lesh and Lana from being together: their parents are okay with it, the other potential romantic partners fade to the background or exit from the story of their own volition. The only obstacle to the romance is the protagonists themselves. The main conflict appears to be Lesh wanting to role play as a female elf priestess in his MMORPG. He ends getting sexually harassed constantly in-game (which seems like a major programming flaw) and actually leads on one of his guild party members without revealing this real-life identity. The problem with this is that Lesh has basically created a Svetlana clone for the game, his besotted guild friend learns enough information to find Lana in real life (!) and starts sending her gifts (!!) and even shows up at her new job (!!!) where he freaks her out and punches Lesh when he shows up to finally tell the truth. And then he goes away again and that's all we hear of that. This happens in the last 30 or so pages of the book, and it's completely ridiculous. The fact that Lesh created a Lana avatar is creepy, but I can actually understand that he was fascinated by her and she does seem to fit the race/class he wanted to play. The fact that he revealed so much about himself that a complete stranger on the Internet was able to track her down is wrong, though. And that's not even the focus! 
 Theme: Who knows? I guess it could be something like, "It's important to be yourself, even when you're a terrible person." But I really didn't feel like I got much out of this book. I wanted to rage quit at several different points, but I kept going for the sake of being able to participate in the book club discussion. It reminded me a lot of Backwards Compatible, which I also didn't like, so if you were into this book you'd probably like that one too.

book_a.title: Alienated (Alienated, #1)
book_a.user_review:
This is a slightly better-written Twilight clone with an alien instead of a vampire. There are some interesting twists, but we know these two crazy teens are going to fall in love despite their differences. I'm also pretty sure I caught the first whiffs of a love triangle that will probably be explored more in the sequel(s). 
 First, the things I didn't like: 
 For an alien who supposedly had no concept of human emotion, Aelyx smirks. A LOT. I felt like I needed to start keeping a tally, because it happened constantly. 
 The idea of falling in love with an alien (I don't care HOW hot he is) is pretty icky to me. It's one of my peeves about the Doctor Who fandom, too, actually. If these aliens want to be neighborly, that's awesome! But (SPOILER) mating with aliens, even if it strengthens their genes (I didn't really get the logic behind this part) seems too far-fetched. I understand that there's a parallel to civil rights, but I guess I'm just not that open-minded. 
 It's very obviously the first part of a series. That drives me crazy; I wish authors would finish their stories in one book, rather than stretching them out. Especially when said book ends on a bit of a cliffhanger. 
 The stuff I did like: 
 There's some pretty cool world-building, but we don't get to see too much of it in this book because we only really interact with Aelyx. 
 Cara blogs about her experience, which is a pretty fun conceit. I would've liked to read more of her posts about the L'eihr. 
 Cara's best friend is Latina. Hooray, diversity! 
 Alienated is also pretty action-packed, especially toward the end. I don't know if I'll read the sequel, but I will definitely recommend it to my Twilight-loving students.

sample_reviews.review_text:
This is yet another entry in the recent spate of books featuring earth girls having relationships with aliens. In this case, 17-year-old Cara Sweeney doesn't have much trouble falling for one of three L'eihran exchange students, Aelyx, who comes to stay with her family. Not only is he from a race with the same DNA as humans, but he is 18, and hot, hot, hot. 
 However, there are many on Earth who are terrified of these "others," such as the growing membership of HALO, or Humans Against L'Eihr Occupation, also known as The Patriots of Earth. At first, they just bully and harass Cara and her family and friends. But as ecological devastation of the Earth accelerates, the Patriots blame the aliens, and the opposition turns deadly. 
 Things I liked: 
 In a fun side plot, Cara runs a blog, and her posts are interspersed throughout the text. 
 Cara is a good character, and defends Aelyx out of integrity rather than lust, although we don't have a chance to question whether or not she would behave in the same way if he weren't "hot." 
 Cara has supportive, loving parents - a rarity in YA books! 
 Things I didn't like: 
 The story would have been more subtle and persuasive had Aelyx had his same personality but with more alien features, and not necessarily so great looking. 
 Cara is the school valedictorian, but doesn't seem all that bright. Aelyx has to explain a lot to her that shouldn't need explaining, like about how big the universe is. Really? 
 The author's use, in the beginning of the story, of bad metaphors was almost a deal-breaker of me. (The school principal was "happier than a pigeon with a French fry." When Cara felt nervous it was "like she'd eaten a dozen Taco Bell double-decker burritos in one sitting." To raise her grade point average, she was "sneaky as a senator.") Fortunately, as the plot evolved, the prose settled down. 
 The author has Cara successfully defend the worth of humans by sharing tales of human kindness. They seem way too anecdotal to be persuasive, however, given the treatment of the L'Eihran ambassadors and the history of violence on Earth. 
 Last but not least, this is just Book One of what will presumably be a trilogy.... 
 Discussion: One wonders (rhetorically) why so many YA authors have races of vampires, aliens, werewolves, and even angels decide that the best place for them to infiltrate and influence society is in high school. This is a major eye-rolling element you have to get over if you are to read these books! 
 Evaluation: This is a quick read with not much gravitas, but if you accept the underlying premises, it's quite fun, with some laugh-out loud lines delivered by the snarky but lovable female protagonist.

Instead, he remains stagnant and uninteresting. Until he suddenly decides to declare a who-can-turn-who-on-better contest. ....huh? 
 The plot also bothered me. It meandered seemingly without direction or purpose. There were very few scenes that the book couldn't afford lose. The rest felt like filler fluff and drama, inessential to either plot progression or character development. 
 Overall, I found this book more frustrating than anything else. It felt like a great concept and opportunity that had been squandered and dumbed down for a lesser audience. This could have been so much better with a little common sense, research, and editing of the cliches.

 The Ups: The entire concept of aliens not being some weird "I come in peace" green things and intellectually advanced, selectively bred, "better" versions of humans was really cool. book_b.title: S.
book_b.user_review:
Such a strange, awesome book. It definitely needs a reread (or three), but I love the idea of sharing the experience of reading with someone. That's why we post updates and reviews on GoodReads, right? There are so many different timelines in this book - the original story, Neal's initial pencil annotations, the first back-and-forth he has with Jen, their continued exploration of the mystery surrounding the author(s), the relationship that grows out of their mutual trust and admiration - that it's hard to get the entire story in one read-through. Especially when you're rushing to finish because you're a procrastinator who waits to pick up the book club book until the last possible second. 
 At any rate, I enjoyed my first pass and will eventually be back for another.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Very disappointing. S. initially seemed like it was going to be bit of fun escapism wrapped in a striking package. Instead, the more I read, the more I was forced to admit that all of the beautiful production and design concealed an awful, awful book. 
 Two main texts comprise S.: the novel Ship of Theseus, by a fictional writer named V.M. Straka, and the annotations, written in the margins and across various inserts, being shared by two students as they are drawn further and further into the mystery of Straka's "true" identity. Theoretically, this should be interesting and fun and exciting to read, but it isn't. Why? Well, firstly because the actual novel Ship of Theseus is bad. It's so bad that it is painful to read. Secondly, as a result, it is literally impossible to believe that Straka is a giant of Western literature (no matter how many breathless student annotations profess it to be so). So why would anyone care about the "true" identity of the author of such a bad book? Why should I, as the reader of S. care? I mean, I can hardly believe that we are supposed to believe that Ship of Theseus was "published," let alone that it's supposed to be an important piece of literature! Thirdly, no one in academia reads literature to get "clues" as to the identity of the author. That's not how academic scholarship works! Even with an author like Shakespeare, no serious scholar actually cares about his "true" identity. That question is the sole preserve of old-fashioned cranks and weirdos at the margins of academia, who seem to have missed Barthes' memo about the death of the author. And that's Shakespeare, ffs! And finally, those marginalia... embarrassing. I can't believe two grown adults (Dorst and Abrams) wrote such sophomoric rubbish, most of which boil down to trite cliches like "be true to yourself!" and "love is all you need!" At one point I was cringing so much that I developed a cramp. 
 The layers of interwoven text mean that S. demands a serious investment of time and effort. Unfortunately the reward is incommensurate with that effort. As a physical object, S. is gorgeous. It's a pity that the actual text(s) contained therein are so bad. 
 [edit] Maybe my review sounds a bit harsh. It's clear that S. is a labour of love for Dorst and Abrams, a book about books and reading. It's just not a good book. Oh, and to all the people saying that this is a "smart" book: no, it isn't. It's dumb as a bag of rocks.

Spoilers in this review. 
 This book read like a less coherent Da Vinci Code for art majors, and I am unimpressed with both the fake-novel (if the foreword prepares the reader to experience one of the most fascinating books ever written by an incredibly genius author, the book to follow should probably actually be at least close to fascinating and genius), and the fake-meta-commentary of the fake-novel. Though at first I enjoyed the novelty of the story's main conceit - that the two main characters have to communicate with each other almost solely by writing in the book's margins over the course of a year - there was a point at which I ceased to be convinced by it; it felt contrived and unnecessary. Around the same point or maybe slightly after that I completely stopped caring about the panicky, trivial girl with standard daddy issues and the surly, damaged boy who just needed to find the right girl to plumb his secret sensitive depths. I may have groaned out loud when they both reach their epiphanies about how important love is and what their really real identities are and how they should let go of the past etc etc etc. I felt like the beginning of the novel unintentionally(?) prepares the reader for a much more epic and convoluted mystery than the college-age romance that eventually unfolds. 
 In short: this was a solid concept with really great, but squandered, potential. "House of Leaves" used the ergodic lit approach far more effectively, creating layers within layers within layers of narrative all referring to each other in a way that drew the reader deep into its eerie, monstrous world. It was, like S., essentially a mystery story, but it allowed the reader to discover and interpret the mystery independently. In contrast, "S." felt like it was using all of its two layers as nothing more than a cheap marketing gag, and while its narrative is intended to be a puzzle, the reader merely watches other people solve it instead of participating in the solution. 
 Also, not that this affects my overall enjoyment of the content, but this book is annoying as SH*T to read in the bath with all those freaking inserts.

With at least four different plot lines running simultaneously, trying to decipher codes and jumping around in time , it was a nightmare to keep track of everything. ** spoiler alert ** 
 I'd like to point out that this book is a book of deception. 
 The moment you break the seal and look at the book inside with a totally different title, you have started reading the fiction that is S.. 
 It doesn't matter whether it is the fine print of the library stamp card at the back. Or the copyright page at the start of it all. Or the first margin note that tells you to return the found book. 
 These are all composites of the elaboration of S. A book within a book, a tale within a tale, a mystery wrapped within a mystery. 
 I fell for that deception. I was pleasantly surprised by breaking open the seal after much deliberation, after conceding that there was no way to get to the book without breaking the seal or demolishing the book sleeve it came with. 
 All those inserts, postcards, letters, newspaper clippings, maps (!!! omg there was a map!)... they delighted me so that I forgot the hidden danger. 
 I read the margin notes on the title page. I mean, it's only the title page! But then I was drawn to the two people that existed on the margins, the 'off to a wrong foot' start that is so typically rom-com. 
 And after ten pages or so simultaneously reading the Ship of Theseus novel text and the intricate handwriting superimposed between the margins, I realised I was conned. 
 I was conned into starting the novel that is S. before I even realised, and I was drawn into it deeper and deeper with each line that I continued, each word I tried to decipher. 
 The story that is The Ship of Thesues is not a particularly brilliant one. It is bewildering, interesting, and quite avant-garde, I suppose. A bit far-out, maybe. 
 But it propelled the margin story of Eric and Jen, and that story on top of that of S., made it into something a lot more enthralling and entrancing than its original. 
 And the margin story between Eric and Jen told yet another different story about the fictional writer... and that mystery is like a jigsaw puzzle that is scattered all over the place. 
 In that regard, the book S. is a brilliant masterpiece. I still haven't wrapped my head completely around the mystery within a mystery on top of the mystery, and I think the only easily understandable story is that of Eric and Jen. 
 This will bear re-reading. Re-visiting. Re-investigating. Re-puzzling.

Now, the story is real the author is not. It is a fabulous story of the high-seas and derring-do, filled w intrigue, exotic locations + femme fatales - like a BOYS OWN adventure. As well, there are apparently, 2 people corresponding in the margins who love this book + its author. There is also various artifacts contained in the book itself - postcards, letters, pictures, maps, etc. This is all 2 heighten the reading experience + it really does. This book is a truly a SINGULAR experience for all + highly-recommended for ages 14-140.

Well, I don't know what kind of sorcery this is, or how one even begins to write a book like this. Just reading it requires a decision: in what order will you read this book? I read it from beginning to end, but I think at some point in the future, I will reread it in chronological order: SoT, then the notes in chronological order. I think this book will reward multiple readings, and I am impressed by a book that can live up to such an ambitious concept. SoT itself is a great read, even without the mystery. 
 Finally, I am certain that Eric and Jen did not figure out al of the ciphers in SoT, and on a future pass, I intend to.

Like House of Leaves this incredibly meh story is saved by the execution. Written by the writer/producer/director/allaroundlegend JJ Abrams it adds a lil summinsummin to the standard book formula. The majority of this story is told by the notes written in the margin between two students. 
 Gotta respect a man who puts effort into making coffee stains look real. 
 It comes like this!

I'm giving it 5 stars because the idea behind this is amazing, as is the execution, even if the story between the readers / margin-note-writers annoyed me at times. Then again, I tend to blame myself and assume that maybe I just "didn't get" some things. While I really liked reading their remarks on the mystery surrounding the book author, the way some things are interpreted seems a little far-fetched (well, they are literature students, so... symbolism and connections everywhere). Also, the personal story that develops between them is cute and all but I did cringe at some of the messages they write each other (but well, in theory they're writing as if no one else will read it, I guess!?) 
 It took me about a week and a half to finish, but I'm on holidays! I read the novel, the margin notes and the added things and documents all at once. There are many guides online on how to read it, all I can recommend is that you try several ways before deciding what works best for you. Do try to finish it in the same month, though, lest your memory betrays you. I now plan to read the "recently found" original ending of the book (tweeted by Doug Dorst!) and look into all the internet stuff there is (the readers have twitter and tumblr acounts, I believe). I recommend this blog once you've finished reading: https://whoisstraka.wordpress.com 
 Last of all, I must say something about the "taboo" of writing on books. I usually feel like I shouldn't write on ANY book, but lately I've allowed myself to make pencil notes on some that I own and that I might read again. Will I ever dare to use a pen like the readers of Ship of Theseus? Maybe even different color pens? I'm thinking... hmm... no.

After it was found out that the video teasers J.J. Abrams had released were actually about a book, and that the premise of the book had to deal with two people finding each other in the margins of a novel, I was beyond excited about getting it. I love novels that have unconventional structure or design, and I bought this one on the day it came out. This is a complex novel, but I'll try and keep this review brief. We'll discuss the three main categories at play: 1) the design and inserts, 2) Jen & Eric's margin notes, and 3) the main story entitled "Ship of Theseus." 
 Let's talk about design and inserts first because that is the first thing that one notices. The authors and the design company that the authors partnered with truly deserve all of the book design awards there are for this year. The design makes everything feel very genuine: everything from the handwriting in the margins, to the drawings, to the various fades and stains on the paper, to the library sticker and stamps in the back making it feel like a real library book that's been handled by many over time, all of the inserts the book has throughout it like letters, postcards, pictures and the like, and finally to the packaging the book comes in. Again, all of it is top notch and you can tell a ton of time and hard work was spent on getting the designs right. Some of the inserts fall out of the book from time to time, and some reviewers have suggested taking them all out and putting a post it note on them so you know where they are supposed to be, but I didn't really have that much trouble with them. The design aspect of this book deserves 5 out of 5 stars. 
 Let's talk about the margin notes. Essentially, you have a boy named Eric who read Ship of Theseus, loved it, and became obsessed with trying to figure out who the author was/is, writing out some of this thoughts in pencil in the margins. A girl named Jen later found the book and his notes and wrote her own thoughts in response, and the two began to communicate through the book in the margins. Reading the margin notes can sometimes be confusing as Jen and Eric use different color inks for different times that they are reading and rereading through the book. All of these different color inks are mixed in together, making a chronological read of the book confusing and a little tedious. When I began reading this story, I read everything on each page before moving on to the next page. This turned out to be very cumbersome, and I found the best way for me personally to read the novel was to read the story for the whole chapter, and then read the margin notes for the whole chapter. The exchanges between Jen and Eric feel very realistic, and it can really make you feel as if these are real people. (It is kind of crazy to think about how many times Jen and Eric would have to take the book back and get it out again to write each and every line at the library though.) My favorite parts about their writing in the margins to each other was actually not the mystery of them trying to figure out who the author was, in fact I felt that part could get very repetitive and confusing. Also, I thought the paranoia they developed that people were following them etc. felt very over dramatic (why would anyone care that they were discussing who the author was that much/how would they even know?) My favorite parts were when they talked about things that had affected them emotionally growing up, such as when Jen ran away. I also enjoyed the love story that grows slowly between them, although when they first meet felt very anticlimactic for me. The notes can be complicated but I enjoyed them, and the unique characters and dialogue between Jen and Eric. I would rate this section a 3 out of 5 stars. 
 But let's talk about Ship of Theseus, the main story, because to match the great design, there needs to be a fantastic story supporting it. While I felt the overall story of Ship of Theseus was entertaining, I felt that there were a number of things that turned me off from the story. So many things go unexplained, including, and maybe most importantly, who our main character "S" really is. In the beginning, we (and he) know absolutely nothing of his past, or who he is, and that really never changes all the way through the book. This becomes a flaw in the story as it becomes hard to care about S and what he's going through when we know almost nothing about him. I really wanted to be enraptured by this book and not be able to put it down, but for a long time, I couldn't get through more than a couple pages at a time. Here is a list of just a couple of the many things that go unexplained: why have all the sailors on the ship had their mouth sewn shut? Why does he seem to age faster on the ship than he does on land? Why is he on the ship repeatedly at all? Why is S constantly writing random words on the walls and on paper if it never factors into the actual story at all? Why does S seem to always be losing his memory, and just appear at random places with new skills and supplies, having no idea how he got there and who told him what to do? Why is the mission never truly explained? Why is Sola never truly explained? Again, I thought the story had entertainment value, but I felt there were a number of things that could've made it better. I would give the story a 2 out of 5 Stars. 
 Who knows, maybe if I had gotten more into the codes that are apparently throughout the book, maybe I would've gotten some more answers (I never used the code wheel that's in the back for example.) The cool parts about this book are enough that I would recommend it to others.

 I'm finding it difficult to sum up my feelings for this book. At first I was bored, then mid-way it was okay, but then it just got silly and I sat there contemplating what my rating would actually be. I settled on a good 2 stars. 
 I got this book with RavenPost with the theme 'Isolation', and it's a book I've definitely seen around but never really considered picking it up. Still, it was an interesting read. I've not read a story of someone who has to stay inside and never leave their house due to terrible allergies, so it was quite new to me. I just the story lacking in some areas. 
 Firstly, it was a bit slow. Maddy was inside and basically just reading and spending time with her mum or nurse, all the while pining for the normality of a regular teenage girl. Of course that's to be expected, she's isolated. But then her neighbours move in. And one of them a handsome young man called Olly who takes her fancy. From there, this book is mostly just Maddy wanting to be with Olly and cursing her illness for trapping her in her home. Which leads to my other issue with the book overall - romance. 
 Maddy and Olly speak a few times online, meet face to face twice and then THEY'RE IN LOVE. It's instalove, and it's too unrealistic for my liking. Not only that, but Maddy makes some terrible decisions and does pretty questionable things just to be with him, right up to risking her life. It's pretty careless of her. Literally risking everything just for a boy she's just met. Instalove isn't a seller, I don't know many people who like it, so I wish authors would stop writing that in. I, for sure, am not a fan of it 
 Also, there is a plot twist in this book. Sadly, I kind of suspected that there would be one. The book was a little too slow for there to not be. When it happened, I wasn't that surprised. I did have a reaction along the lines of 'WHAT' because I wasn't sure that would even be an option. If you know what it is, you'd think 'surely this can't be after everything that's happened.' Yet it did. It's not easy trying to explain without spoiling, so go read the book and let us know what you thought about the twist! 
 There was also a part of the story which I really didn't like (can't say due to it being a spoiler), but I felt that Maddy was really stupid and acted on impulse without thinking. It ended up being extremely bad for her and others around her. I was reading it thinking 'Why do this, and what made you think this was a good idea?' 
 She learnt the hard way. 
 With the characters, I wasn't a fan of Maddy. Her bad decisions, dramatic nature (mostly near the end of the book, crying over such a small issue), and her slight lack of consideration for others. As soon as she saw Olly outside from her window, she was obsessed. I got bored of that very quickly. 
 Near the end though, she was just so emotional and crying so much (for about an hour - maybe longer!) over something and I was like 'what is she even crying about?'. I know she's a teenager, but I was genuinely not sure what was wrong. If it's about Olly, it's honestly her own fault for making silly decisions, getting people in trouble and nearly dying for her reckless attitude. 
 Speaking of Olly... he was alright actually. He was quite patient with her, and he wasn't pressuring in any way. His penchant for climbing on everything and stuff was a little strange, but it's not really a bad trait. He was quite a nice guy. I do think he should have knocked some sense into Maddy, though. Sometimes it felt like he should say 'Alright, stop now. You need to be careful', if he really cares about her. He was just as reckless as Maddy in the end, and should have been a bit more decisive in some cases. 
 The other characters were interesting, but didn't really stick out much. I quite liked Carla - she was a warm and caring character, a bit more lenient and sometimes funny. There aren't many characters in this book, but considering the type of story it is, you don't need too many. The number itself was enough. I just wished that some were fleshed out a bit more. There was time, for sure. 
 Olly's family was quite interesting to read about. His overall story and what was going on in his life was sad and I wish we learnt more about that. Of course, the male lead as well as the female lead needs a sob story. We had quite a bit of pagetime with Olly, so again, more fleshing out of his life would have been good. Ultimately, it was all about Maddy. 
 I did like that the main character was half-Japanese and half-African American. It certainly makes a change. I'm all for diversity, especially in YA. I just wish I enjoyed the story more, considering it was a kind I'd never read before. I haven't read many books revolving around isolation and it's one of those rare ones that I read that's about sickness. As a hypochondriac, I tend to avoid them. 
 I'm not entirely sure how I feel about this book. I forced myself to read it, I did get into it but then I was left feeling like it was lacking something. Hence my 2 star rating.
