sample_reviews.review_text: Historical fiction....1665-1666 near London....plague isolates a mining town north of London. Found it slow and not engaging.

I can see by the reviews and ratings on Goodreads that this is a much-loved book, but not for me. Although it is well researched and well written, it did not engage me as much as the author's Caleb's Crossing. Life was harsh in the 1600s in a small village in England, and made even worse with the Plague and people's ignorance and religious superstition. The author took the story in some directions I did not want to go, but I think she is quite accurate in her portrayal of human nature.

Nope, I didn't like this at all. OK, just about everybody agrees the ending is bad, me included, but that is not at all why I so dislike the book. For me endings are not that terribly important. It is the time spent with the book that is important to me. Do they get me thinking? Am I drawn into the lives of the characters? Do I occasionally smile or laugh outright or cry? I never laughed with this book. Not once. Neither did I cry. I was made miserable by the depravity so frequently seen in the village. I was annoyed by the rector's religious thinking that made him judgemental and all-knowing. He was as far from humble as you can get. 
 The following sort of has some spoilers so beware! 
 I have difficulty accepting the rector's sexual behavior towards his wife and her closest friend Anna. The rector's religious explanation for his sexual abstinence toward his wife, whom I believe he did deeply love, an explanation revolving around repentance and atonement, is beyond my understanding! I think it was pure sophistry even in the 1600s. The explanation simply didn't ring true. Furthermore if this is what he truly thought, well then the rector sure had a high opinion of himself and what he thought he had the right to teach others. 
 I do respect and admire the rector's noble efforts to save numerous lives by guiding the village to close itself off from its neighbors, albeit sacrificing many villagers to save others living outside the village. However this tremendous noble act of courage, in the hands of this author, completely squashed out the normal, small every-day occurrences of kindness and humor that usually lighten and ease the burden of life in difficult times. There was just too much misery without any joy or humor, which must have occasionally occurred. 
 I agree that the author seamlessly tied in her historical studies - but that doesn't make it a good book. 
 I guess I am the odd ball out in not liking this book!

 I also loved the way she created the rectory character, so saintly in the beginning, but so human in the end, again another twist that I cherished. I was just a bit annoyed when he came to Anna proclaiming she knew everything that happened in the Bradford's, how?

I thought the writing was beautiful and the characters memorable, but overall the story was pretty depressing. Have an hour? This book is a summary of Pollen's "In Defense of Food" and follows a simple philosophy--"Eat food. Not too much. Mostly plants." Comprised of 83 simple rules--many of which are common sense or things that we heard our grandmothers tell us repeatedly. However, I must confess that I wish that I hadn't been snacking on potato chips while I was reading it. Hold the dip.

This is a quick little handbook of 64 rules designed to help you eat healthier. For me, the author was mostly preaching to the choir -- I am one of the healthiest eaters I know.* But this book still gave me some things to think about: 
 From the introduction: "Nutrition science is today approximately where surgery was 1650 -- very promising, and very interesting to watch, but are you ready to let them operate on you?" Do you really want scientists creating your food in laboratories and processing plants? 
 Rule #23: "Treat meat as a flavoring or special occasion." Vegetarians are really healthy, yes, but people who eat meat 2-3 times/week are just as healthy. The author suggests in the least swapping portion sizes: eat a smaller meat portion and a bigger vegetable portion for your meals. 
 Rule #26: "Drink the spinach water." Okay, maybe not drink it. But he does suggest saving the water you boil veggies in to make soup or sauces with later, because it contains lots of vitamins and minerals. 
 Rule #43: "Drink a glass of wine with dinner." Imagine! Health benefits to alcohol (not just wine, apparently)! 1 drink for women, 2 for men (so unfair) every day is healthy for you -- especially if you drink while you eat. (This made Ted feel a lot better about his drinking habits, LOL.) 
 I think many every-day busy Americans would find these rules in their entirety very daunting. Hopefully they read the introduction where the author encourages us to at least adopt one rule from each section of the book. 
 *BTW, I wasn't always a healthy eater. I was your typical vegetable-hating, junk-food loving, fast-food eating, soda-drinking American until I slowly, over time, phased out the crap. You can do it if you set your mind to it -- your tastes will adjust, and pretty soon you'll be loving those veggies and wondering how you used to tolerate all that sugar and salt. Realizing I was naive to think that "If they sell it, it can't be that bad for you," was key. Also, that I was poisoning my body instead of nourishing it.
A strong dose of common sense.

As much as I appreciate Pollan's mantra of 'Eat Food. Not too much. Mostly plants', this book seems a little unnecessary. Food Rules has about 65 rules that help explain his popular catch phrase and each one takes up about a page or so. Quick and small, I couldn't help thinking that this book could have been so much more. I kept thinking, really? A book? Why wasn't this a blog post, or a 30 minute video? Or several short videos that could be embedded and shown around the world. Multi-media could have added dimension to this book, which seems a little over-hyped for what it is - a tiny little book filled with common sense about eating and a few good tips.

I had a really hard time with this book. It was my first by Margaret Atwood and will probably be my last.
Will be great for book club discussion.

I'm sure this book had a greater effect in the late '60s/early '70s, when it was written. However, reading this now, in 2013, the surrounding details are too dated to let the overall theme of the story have its intended impact. 
 Marian McAlpin is a recent college graduate in Toronto, working for a survey company, and essentially killing time until the next thing comes along. For Marian, as it is for many women during this period, the next thing turns out to be an engagement to her boyfriend - steady, socially acceptable and upwardly mobile Peter. Yet after her engagement, Marian finds that she can't eat foods that were previously acceptable to her, and she also dallies with an otherwise totally unacceptable graduate student as her impending nuptials grow closer. 
 It's a great concept - subsuming one's identity in preparation for marriage - but although the surrounding details are just that - details - there are too many of them for the theme to stand alone, and frankly, details make the story. As it is, this story reads more like a quaint tract showing how things were "back then" than it is an entertaining, thoughtful story.

First, starting with this review, I'll try from now on to insert information about the book and author from wikipedia. 
 If you follow this blog, you probably already ran into my comments about my love-hate relationship with Mark Twain. I admit I have the same kind of problem with Margaret Atwood: I enjoy very much the style and quality of her writing, but the content has the tendency to totally creep me out - yes, I know, it's supposed to. The problem then for me is that I'm both attracted and repelled. As this book was published in 1969 and fit well into my own Reading Challenge [books published in the first 5 years of my life], AND because this is Atwood's first novel, the attraction prevailed. 
 I enjoyed the beginning of the book, her writing always flows so well, I felt drawn into the lives of the characters, but at the same time, I was wondering when the creepy things would begin! Well, they do little by little, and this is part of the grandeur of the book. And when Marian hits rock bottom, things get better again. So as a whole, it is actually a much more positive books than others by the same author, as the outcome seems to be for the best - as far as I could judge. 
 The relations between love and possessiveness and freedom would be a very valuable theme to study and follow as you read along. 
 All the characters feel very true, each with his/her own bizarreness. 
 So I really enjoyed this book, and it may help me overcome my hesitation to read at last the Year of the Flood.

During this time she told me "Maybe you're becoming the edible woman." And I said "What?" and thus this book was thrust into my face and I fell in love. 
 The writing is simple and deep and cute and complex. But not that obnoxiously cute like Bjork thing. Cute and sophisticated without being pretentious like, well I don't know, like Gidget or something. When I read this book I got this feeling, and it wasn't the description of the setting so much, as a feeling the writing gave me, of bright black white and gray tones with brightly colored pictures of ideas of cartoonish exaggerated ice cream cones floating above heads and blue and white checkered davenports in the background scenery. Solid and dreamy. Although when Duncan entered the scene everything turned sepia. I love the Duncan character. He's such a freak. And she's a freak for digging him. This seems like the cutest little freakish lyrical story, but it's actually a bit deep and black as well. But I never felt the solid color of black. Just the comedy black. Maybe deep red towards the end. And yellow at the beginning. And purple in the middle. It's funny how my brain remembers this book in colors. You should read it and tell me if you feel colors when you do.

I kind of loved this book. I enjoyed it for its portrait of Toronto in the 60s, and young women entering the working world, and for the weirdness that Atwood weaves in. There's humour in the absurdity of the characters' action, but also very sincere grappling with the transition to adult life, and deciding what type of person you want to be, and life you want to live.

According to Virago, this is the author's first novel. According to Atwood it's her second, the first having been rejected for being too gloomy. Although the publication date is 1969, it was written in 1965. 
 Atwood thanks Virago 'for bringing it to life again in England', then signs off 'Edinburgh, 1979.' Edinburgh is not in England. Canadians, including my relatives, keep doing this so now I call them Americans. 
 Reading this book you wouldn't guess how good she would later become. The heroine, Marian, has two choices - a dead end job or a dead end marriage. Opting for the second, marriage to Peter, her subconscious fights her all the way, and gradually forces her to give up one variety of food after another. Other apparently irrational behaviour follows, like running away with Duncan from her first (and last) party with Peter as the engaged couple. Duncan is not an attractive character. Neither are his flat mates. 
 Her picture of the three of them in their flat gives Atwood an opportunity to satirise faculties of English and what they like to term 'research'. She makes good points, I agree with them, but if you choose a target you can hardly miss there is little virtue in hitting it. 
 An example of feminism at work might be the behaviour of Ainsley, who uses a male by the name of Len as a sex object. Her only interest in him is getting pregnant, after which she drops him. But the conclusion, in which Marian makes an edible woman sponge-cake, doesn't work for me.
Just couldn't do it. Can't put my finger on why but these characters depressed the hell out of me.

book_b.title: Olive Kitteridge
book_b.user_review: Not a fan

sample_reviews.review_text:
DNF after 50 pages 
 *Phew!* I'm a little bit impressed with myself that I managed to make it this far! Wow is this boring. I couldn't find any semblance of a plot anywhere, and I found myself losing focus and thinking about other things while attempting to read it, because it was so boring that I couldn't even make myself pay attention. I also had trouble understanding why it was even called "Olive Kitteridge" when most of the first 50 pages focuses on her husband...not her. Maybe it got more interesting or found its footing later on in the book, but I'm just glad that I don't feel the need to read on and find out! 
 I was attempting to read this so that I could watch the HBO series based on it, but now that I've tried, I'll be joyfully skipping right on to the episodes without a second thought! Let's just hope they're not as dull as the book.
I guess if you want to win a Pulitzer Prize you should write a novel about sad people living depressing lives with no hope of anything getting better.

One of the fastest books I've read! I really enjoyed this, actually found it hard to put down sometimes. The way the story is told, from a lot of characters perspective, really rounded out Olive as a character and gave many dimensions to this town and this story. Olive grows so much and I found myself crying with her and smiling at her witty remarks. All of the characters in the book you find yourself attached to by the end of their chapters. I found myself rethinking a lot about the way I treat people and how to appreciate the tiny moments. Excellent read!

Even after finishing this book, I could not see what all the fuss was about. It is a series of minimally related stories -- related because they all take place in a small Maine town and the epynomous retired schoolteacher has a role (sometimes major, sometimes cameo) in all of them -- that are pretty bleak. Is the author trying to tell us that into each life a little rain must fall, or that we can't judge someone unless we walk a mile in their moccasins? I persisted through the depressing stories because people I admire -- including smart friends and the Pulitzer committee -- thought this was a great book. If any of my Goodreads friends can explain why, please tell me. Behind the picket fences and comfortable wooden cottages, there is someone who is lethally anorexic,or committing adultery,or in denial that their son stabbed someone 29 times, or about to be jilted at the altar. How anyone kept their spirits up in this town is beyond me -- and maybe Henry, who tried so hard to do so in the face of all odds, was punished for his efforts by suffering a stroke that left him debilitated, blind and speechless. As we say in Yiddish, genug! Enough already.

This sequence of short stories that are connected by the stony New Englanders of a small town in Maine and the central character, Olive Kitteridge, is an empathetic book that forces the reader to understand the motivation of each character whether redeeming or not. I am guessing that I am one of the few who liked the main character right from the start, flub-dubness and all. The dog-loving energy and directness of Olive combined with deep flaws, humanize her struggles of becoming a better person even if it took her seventy years to give up her controling nature in order to live at peace with what life presents to her. Elizabeth Strout is a natural story teller that honors the hidden lives of everyday people.

I couldn't finish this book, simply on the notion that the main character is so nasty and mean to everyone she comes in contact with. I think there is enough of it in the world already. The other characters are interesting, but not enough for me to be in this negative space. Oh well.

Content: profanity, sexual references, adultery, suicide. 
 Did not enjoy this book. Could not get past the first couple chapters. Boring and depressing book.
Hmmmm! Had to finish it so I could get back to something better!

For me, it is just blah. 
 I rarely read short stories, and when I purchased this book I didn't realize that it is essentially short stories. A reviewer on Amazon describes it as though a chapter was ripped out of 20 different books about Olive and compiled into one book. The characters all disappear from the canvas when the chapter ends. I just began to like the people when the story changes and revolves around another character. Yes, Olive is in each story, but I fond her to be an unlikable character and so this doesn't rescue the story. I will not read this again.

In an attempt to read the more recent Pulitzer fiction winners, I decided to listen to Olive Kitterage. I definitely enjoyed these bleak linked stories. Honestly, linked stories are one of my favorite literary devices and Stout did a great job dropping Olive into each story. I like this one much better than Goon Squad. 
 I loved Olive - her acerbic nature was hilarious to me. She used the phrase "hells bells" which is also one of my routine utterances. Unfortunately, I figure I will be/act very similar to Olive as I continue to age. 
 I am looking forward to reading more of Stouts fiction in the future. (less)

book_a.title: Smart, Sexy and Secretive (The Reed Brothers, #2)
book_a.user_review: Audist as hell, full of ignorance and misinformation, and the plot doesn't even work. A huge disappointment I would definitely not recommend.

sample_reviews.review_text:
The first book came off as audist, but I forgave it because it was a cute, enjoyable story that did get a lot right. This sequel, however, is horrible, though. It becomes glaringly obvious that the author has not interacted with deaf (let alone Deaf) people in real life, and Logan is apparently capable of superhero-level lipreading (including lipreading from the side or if someone has their mouth partially covered.) 
 Example (from page 90): "He's looking at the TV and not me, but I can still see his lips." Or, later in the book, when Logan miraculously can perfectly read Emily's father's lips even though Logan tells us "[h]e doesn't look up from his paperwork" (p 140). What? 
 No. It doesn't work that way. 
 But I could let that go, too, because there are times when the author does make an effort to get that aspect right (having light, facing each other, etc.). 
 But what really got me was the audism. It's really, really bad in this book despite the occasional line thrown in ala "Not to sound racist, but..." 
 For example, the book tells us repeatedly that it is "rude to sign in front of hearing people" and yet what about hearing people talking without signing in front of Logan? We also get far too much simcoming (signing while talking, which is really awkward) or straight up talking, which doesn't make sense. (Yes, I DO know some deaf who prefer to read lips/talk over signing, but Logan was never really presented that way, especially since he didn't even talk before he met Emily.) In fact, there's even a part where Logan complains that Emily is signing and talking and he wishes she would stop--not simcoming (and sign only) but that she would stop signing and just talk (p 44)! I don't know a lot of deaf people who sign who would prefer to have no signing in a conversation with several hearing people. It's very difficult, if not impossible, for someone with no hearing in the vocal range (even with hearing aids) to really follow a conversation with several non-signing hearing people. That just struck me. 
 Worse, throughout the first book it's there, but it's even more so in the second book that speaking (spoken English) is obviously better than signing. That is extremely audist. For example, on page 113 Emily says in her narration: 
 I'd trade my right arm for his voice, if someone told me I had to choose between the two. Hearing his words, his laughter and hi thoughts means the world to me. 
 That struck me like a slap to the face. 
 It gets worse. At one point, Logan admits to his brothers, "You guys all made it really easy for me to retreat and not speak since you all learned to sign." (p 137) 
 GASP! A hearing family that actually decides to learn to sign! Oh no! We better go out and stop that, because heaven forbid the deaf/Deaf family member not speak! Because (spoken) English is the only "correct" form of communication. Logan hadn't withdrawn. He wasn't depressed. He was communicative and active and interested in the world and his future. Not speaking was his choice, and he was perfectly in his right to elect to sign or communicate it other ways. 
 So that was really bad. But then there's proof of my suspicion from the first book that the author has no idea what the difference is between deaf, mute, and someone who chooses not to speak. 
 In my online fiction In/Exhale, the main character, Kai, was mute growing up. That meant he did not have the ability to speak. His vocal chords did not work correctly. That meant that he could not produce ANY sound that required his vocal chords, so he had to rely on clicking his teeth or clapping his hands or some other extra-vocal sources of sound. 
 On that note, laughter, though in some situations can be controlled, is NOT a voluntary experience. Many times, it just happens, and if you have working vocal chords, you WILL produce sound. Sometimes loudly (which can get deaf people in trouble since they have no idea how loud they're being). 
 Even Deaf people who chose not to use their voice voluntarily often are very vocal, making noises while they sign, and of course laughing. The fact that the book tells us that not only did Logan not speak before, he apparently did not use his voice AT ALL, even for laughter (his laughter was silent) is just completely ridiculous. Even if he did genuinely choose not to speak, he would still laugh like anyone else. (See for example, "He laughs with no sound (p 144).) 
 Now, even if I was able to swallow down the egregious audism and ignorance this book perpetuates, and just look at the story, I still couldn't give it higher than the current rating. Why? While I do appreciate the setup, as melodramatic as it is (the one-dimensional evil father and the one-dimensional evil ex boyfriend), there is no real story/character development. In one fell swoop the father goes from bastard to understanding, and I didn't believe it. Then, to make matters worse, there's a ridiculous turn of events that I actually had to re-read a few times in order to believe it really happened, thinking I had to have misread it. 
 Emily's father is nearly hit by a car because he's standing in the MIDDLE OF THE ROAD waiting for her to tie he shoe. Seriously. The guy is supposedly a native New Yorker (as we learn later), and yet he WAITS IN THE MIDDLE OF THE FREAKING ROAD. Who does that? Maybe if you live in a subdivision with no traffic, but really?? This felt like yet more proof that the author has zero familiarity with New York City. 
 Then, if that all wasn't bad enough, including a moment where Logan momentarily forgets he's deaf. (He's been deaf 10 years. How can he just "forget that?), the book ends rather abruptly and suddenly switches to 2 years in the future and one of the other Reed brother's POVs. I get the author was trying to set us up for the next book in the series, but I was just like, wait. What? Did I suddenly skip to the preview of the next book? Where did this come from?? 
 Frankly, it felt a little manipulative, and I was already pissed off, so it just irritated me further. 
 It's really a shame, but I can't recommend this book chiefly because of the blatant ignorance of signing, deafness, and the audism even without the other problems.

This is the next story or continuing story of the Reed brothers by Tammy Fulkner and I must say it is as good or better than the first, sometimes a 2nd in a series sort of shifts and vears you away from where you were before in the first book. Not so with this series. I flowed right through this book in record time..and only became deeper in love with all these brothers and their personalities. This book is just as full and amazing as the first..wow...how very enjoyable! It can be a stand alone as Tammy weaves you back and forward, without it being repetitive and boring.. 
 Stars..***** all stars in my eyes!

Let me just say that I'm obsessed with this series but I absolutely hated so much of this one! 
 I hated Emily's dad, I hated Trip, I hated the way that Emily's dad talked to Emily and even more the way he talked to Logan. I hate the way he held his money over both of their heads for different reasons... I hate that nothing got done about it, Trip especially and I hate that her dad had a chance to redeem himself. There is so excuse at all for the way he talked to Logan and the way that he treated him. And calling Emily stupid? Saying flat out that all she'd amount to was arm candy because she couldn't read.... saying that he hopes that anykids she had didn't end up like her? What the heck man? I seriously hated him with the force of a thousand suns. And her mother did nothing? Gahh, I was frustrated beyond belief in this one. 
 What I loved though, was the love between Logan and Emily. I loved how they all came together when they needed each other. I loved how they accepted Emily back and welcomed her home, because she was at home with them and they all wanted her. And I loved the ending, even though the thing with Logan came out of nowhere and I was seriously shittin myself when I read it! 
 Alls well that ends well though..... I love this family and I can't wait to read more!

Pretty much what I was expecting... 
 Well.. There really aren't any surprises in this book. You can pretty much guess what this story is all about from book 1, the cover or even the plot. 
 The book is really short, you can read in one siting. 
 The only thing different from book 1, is that in the sexy version of book 1 there really isn't a lot of sex scenes, so I didn't particularly see the point in the sex-lite version. This book has a lot more sex scenes, so if you're uncomfortable with that, I would recommend the sex-lite version.

Another really great book! I loved the sweet relationship! This book was different from others I have read because the turmoil comes from outside the relationship rather than inside. I loved the characters sweet way of caring for each other. A bit too much "recapping" at times, but overall a quick and heartwarming read!

I liked this okay, but I think maybe the characters were a bit young and immature for me. The drama melted into melodrama too many times, even more so than the first book making me cringe in places. AND the extraneous exposition of book one was seriously bugging me. AND the emotional wrenching in the last 20% or so almost stopped me from finishing, It was too short and too much at the same time.

This was definitely good, I expected a hell of a lot more conflict between Trip, and Emily's father being in town and preventing Logan and Emily from being together. But that didn't really happen, it changed fairly quickly and maybe it's because this was a short book, or maybe it's just because of who they are as people, but I expected a lot more drama, a lot more drama that I almost wasn't read to read this book yet and see how the author prevented them from being a couple, clearly I was wrong and made assumptions and I'm really glad I read this.

2.5 stars. 
 I forgot how dramatic this series was. 
 I can't give this a higher rating because too many things annoyed me during reading. I liked the book, I just didn't like everything. The dad thing was the worst and magically fixed in 2.5 seconds, the Trip thing annoyed the shit outta me too, the car thing felt a little extra, but all in all it's still 'enjoyable' and I was on the way to saying I liked the book rather than it just being an alright read, hence my rating.

Man, I just love Logan and Emily. Emily is strong enough to fight her family for what she wants and Logan is not going to back down from her father or ex. I have read a couple of 2nd books about couples lately, and this is, for sure, one of the best. They angst isn't crazy like most NA books, thank god. AND we get to see all the Reed Bros again. That right there is awesome.

Loved this one as much as the first one. Practically screamed at one point and had to put it down so I didn't cry. Logan is such a great man. The fact that people belittle him and don't think he'll ever make anything of himself just pushes Logan to work harder. He sees what no one can see in Emily, that she's smart. 
 Emily may have dyslexia but she's smart and she's going back to school even when her own father doesn't believe in her. She has Logan cheering her own and his brothers. 
 A beautiful story with heart about love and forgiveness. It's also about striving to become better and showing others that they're wrong. Being deaf and having dyslexia aren't things that don't stop anyone when they want something bad enough. 
 The best part of this story is that it has two versions, the sexy version and the clean version. Anyone who doesn't want anything descriptive can read the clean version. Those who want a smexy version can read the other one. Read the first book Tall, Tatted and Tempted. Highly recommend these books.

book_b.title: The Book of Lost Things
book_b.user_review:
I read this book about a couple of years ago when my husband was having surgery. I basically read it in one day, and have since recommended it to friends and family. It's creative and well written. 
 A really unique take on the traditional coming of age tale, this book is kind of like Narnia, but darker, and definitely a story for adults. 
 I would love to be able to write something like this some day.

sample_reviews.review_text: It was interesting but not interesting enough to keep my attention. I may come back to it in the future but for the moment, moving on.

"For in every adult there dwells the child that was, and in every child there lies the adult that will be." 
 John Connolly's 
 The Book of Lost Things 
 is a tale that reflects everyone's story of growing up. Some would say that it's a story of losing one's innocence, but are we ever really innocent? Through time we have come to develop feelings of grief, rage, hatred, and jealousy. These are some of the things that eat the pure off of us. At some point, we have all become the things we feared the most. We have turned into our very own monsters, destroying the good that is ahead of us. This is the story of how David overcame his monsters. 
 As a young boy, David lost his mother, and his only means of coping up with his grief was reading, an interest he got from her. The books started whispering to him and only he could hear them. Months after his beloved mother's death, his father remarried. Rose, his father's new love got pregnant with Georgie, David's new half-brother. As a part of starting a new life with his step-mother and half-brother, David and his father moved out of their London home and into Rose's which was located out of the city. There, in the old house, he was given a room that was used to be of a boy named Jonathan Tulvey. It was filled with old books that David tried to read for himself although some he could not understand thoroughly. 
 In his dreams and around the house, David began seeing a figure of a man with distinct, odd features. Drawing closer and closer to him, waiting in the shadows, was the Crooked Man. 
 I borrowed a copy of this from my cousin and it had been sitting on my shelf for months. At first, I was not too thrilled to start reading it due to the synopsis at the back of the book. It was not very attractive to me. I decided to read it just so I could return it to her sooner. I was so wrong to judge this book by the few words written on its back cover. I was not expecting it to fascinate me, to touch my heart, and to show me what it means to live and to be alive, but it did. It was an extraordinary experience that was beyond my anticipation for it. The synopsis didn't do it justice. It was a dark, strange, tragic, and bloody adventure that every child in us would fear, but the adult in us would come to understand the truth beneath its surface. In it are very familiar tales that were distorted to suit the book's eeriness, constructing a twisted realm parallel to David's reality. 
 David was a child at the beginning of the story, and you could really visualize how his character developed. He became more mature as he learned to decide what's right and what's wrong. In time, he also became more selfless, learning that love could cause a terrible ache, and living, sometimes, could hurt. His journey in the world beyond the sunken garden emblematized a lot of things that he was battling in his heart. They were struggles he had to face to help him cope with the pain of losing his mother and adjust to his new life. 
 The world that the author wrote into being was quite disturbing. It was stripped off of peace, innocence, and hope. In every corner of it lurked danger that a child like David, realistically, might not be able to endure. I don't even think adults could come out alive of the situations David found himself in. There were beasts, creatures that could kill or mangle you. There was also a bit of sexual content implied in it that I was not expecting. It was not graphic, but it would be perturbing if a very young child would mistaken this as a children's book and read it. He could either be very curious to try those things out or be afraid of them. 
 A hundred pages on the origin stories and source materials were included in the latter part of the book, explaining further how each distorted tale woven into The Book of Lost Things represented something significant in David's life. It gave me a clearer insight of what David was going through, reminding me more that, somehow, I have been there too. It was quite amusing to reread those fairytales and to read some of them for the first time. They felt familiar but at the same time strange because after all these years of not reading them and then revisiting them now, it seemed to me that they were telling a different story that exhibited deeper reason than how I perceived them when I was just a child. There were also explanations on how each of the characters represented an archetype or a persona that contributed greatly not only to the development of this story, but also to those that inspired it. 
 This is a really cleverly-written adventure and I highly recommend it. I hope you guys would give it a try. Surely, I will be reading more books written by this author in the future.

A book about an envious twelve year old boy who travels to a fantastic world based on modern stories. Very realistic in the beginning then turns to fantasy in the middle, where most of the book is spent.

I struggled to finish this one. I may even have only done so because I got this from paperbackswap and it seemed a shame to waste a spent credit. It seems to be quite a love it or hate it book for most people, so at least I'm not alone. 
 I didn't care much for the protagnoist (spiteful little boys can be grating, even when the book keeps telling you they are actually quite clever and probably good at heart), and the book didn't really give me stakes I cared about till near the end. That said, I did enjoy the last quarter or so, but I'm still suprised I got there.

The book is about a lil boy named David living in WWII England. David loves to read. His escape from the real world where his mother is sick and there's a war brewing are the stories his mom introduced him to. When his mother dies his whole world is thrown into upheaval. After time his father moves on some and begins dating another woman. David starts having "episodes" where he can hear the books all around him talking. When the war becomes a reality in the city his father moves them to his new wife's home in the suburbs where David discovers another world. This world is made up of fractured versions of fairy tales and fantasy stories. It's made up of dreams and nightmares. David is trapped there and has to seek out the king to find his way home. On his journey through this new world he encounters werewolves, a communist version of the 7 dwarves, a twisted version of Hansel and Gretel and he is being haunted by the Crooked Man who is a powerful Rumpelstiltskin kind of character. 
 Connolly makes an interesting world for David to journey from childhood to manhood in. It makes for a great allegory for the passage through puberty into maturity. The beginning of the book is necessary but moves a little slow. But once David lands in the other world the story takes off. I would definitely say to check it out it was a fun read. Now it's time to read "I Hope They Serve Beer in Hell". We'll see just how good Gina's tastes are.
I didn't like it. That's all.

This story was really lovely. David is a young boy who loses his mother and shortly after begins to start hearing the whispering of books. When he suddenly finds himself in the midst of a fairy-tale world, he has to fight to return to his family. 
 There was so much emotion behind David's mourning that it really struck home for me. The fairy tales and stories of the land are dark and twisted with a tone that hearkens back to the story tales of the Grimm brothers. The murder, rape, deception, and torture isn't glossed over or sugar-coated. It was really interesting to read. 
 *spoilers: 
 I think my favorite fairy tale visitation was the dwarves with snow white. The fractured fairy tale showed the dwarves as abused workers fighting capitalism while trying to poison and murder the unbearable Snow White. The sarcastic humor was gorgeous and actually reminded me of Chris Colfer's children's book The Land of Stories. 
 ----------------- 
 I read this with the Nothing But Reading Challenges group!

The characters weren't that interesting and I found myself rewriting passages in my head. The tone of the story wavered a bit and that was kind of distracting. One part at the end of the book was a complete cop-out and I'm too lazy to write it all out and hit the spoiler button. After the climax of the book, I was reading a chapter that looked like it was wrapping things up, but the book still had over 100 pages left in it. Turns out those extra 100 pages were notes on the book: origins of different fairy tales, explanations of characters and creatures we met in the book, etc. That part was pretty interesting and I liked that it was thrown in there. 
 If you want an easy fantasy-ish read, grab a copy from your local library. This isn't something I would recommend running out to buy, unless you want to keep on hand the reference material in the back of the book.

Really enjoyed this one, especially as I'm grieving the loss of my Mother, I found myself understanding the grief a young boy might have if he lost his mother at such a young age. I also enjoyed the twists and turns of the story and marvel at how Connolly has made his own new fairytale out of a mixture of old fairytales. I highly recommend this book to most anyone, but especially those who are fans of magical realism, fairytales, and coming of age stories.

This book was an enjoyable read. Starting out as a wartime coming of youth tale. A young boy dealing with grief, which transforms into a tale of adventure. The adventure itself uses metaphor to help david come to terms with the turmoil of his life. I found the book humourous, and thought provoking. And thuroughly enjoyable. As I was reading I wanted to compare to the original fairytales and to my delight at the back of the edition I had there was a section that actually had excerpts and explanations relating to the fairytales that are parody'd and/or alluded to in the story.

reference_book.title: The Girl with All the Gifts
reference_book.review_text: I'm torn with this book. It had me hooked immediately, the middle was a bit stodgy and slow, and the ending felt a bit rushed. I have so many unanswered questions, especially about Beacon! All in all, pretty good writing, well rounded characters, an interesting story but there was just something missing, and I feel the author has really missed an opportunity with the ending!

book_a.title: The Road
book_a.user_review: The Road is a difficult book to review. I enjoyed the concept of the story, a man and a boy trying to survive in a hostile world in the middle of what sounds like a Nuclear Winter (though it is never actually revealed what happened to the world). The 3 stars I have given this book are for story and characters, because I just did not like the writing style. The stream of consciousness technique is difficult to pull off at the best of times, but if you couple it with bad grammar/punctuation then it is, in my opinion, going to fail. Even the descriptions, limited of course by McCarthy's choice of setting, got monotonous and at the end I was just wanting to finish the book. I didn't feel the great emotional train that others went on, and the boy's ending just seemed a bit too neat for me to take it seriously.

sample_reviews.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 I'm sorry, but I didn't love it. Yes. It's a quick read. Yes. It's an intriguing look at the world after the end of the world. But it's just so brutal...in the *spoiler* cannibals trying to eat your child kind of way. And I agree with the reviewer who tried to count the number of times "ash" was used...whatever the final count, it was way too high.
I appreciate this book in the way it was written, but it was very depressing, and I hated the end.
A beautiful ode to the heroic nature of parenting (and canned food).

I am not quite finished with the book, but so far, I've found it an absolute masterpiece of modern literature. I got the audio book from the library, because I'd read so many comments about how readers were distracted by McCarthy's minimalist prose. If you are planning on reading this book and think that his style will bother you, I recommend the audio version. Tom Stechschulte reads it and does a wonderful job. 
 The book is dark. It is dark in a soul-wrenching way. I found myself tearing up at some of the simplest passages, because McCarthy taps into very real human emotion and thought. How many of us haven't wondered about a post-apocalyptic world? McCarthy makes it real and understandable, even if we don't know exactly how it happened, how many years it is post disaster, or even the characters names. It's easy to envision the gray world that McCarthy paints with his words. The contrasts of the two main characters makes for some interesting comparisons. The boy knows nothing but a post-apocalyptic world - the man remembers what once was and what's been lost. They have two opposite perspectives, and that sets the book up for real introspection. The rambling journey they take is as aimless and purposeless of a post-apocalyptic life. 
 There are some real moments of terror that might not be suitable for younger readers.

Crap. Total Crap. Totally trying to get you to feel apocalyptic-sad-and-play-on-those-existing-feelings-and-fears crap. what is SO amazing about a guy who is trying to be a good father? Oh, a guy trying to be a good father. I get it now. Please. 
 You can have all of the extra credit that exists on the planet if it's the end of the world and you are still trying to be a good dad if you buy the ideology of this book. It's just crap. Crap wrapped in nice words crap. Crap from a literary god? Crap happens.
Cormac McCarthy, the greatest living American writer, as far as I'm concerned.

As a big reader, I often get asked which book is my least favorite. I used to say that every book I read had some kind of significance to me, but after reading this book, I now tell everyone my least favorite book is The Road. 
 Now, I don't want to say I HATE this book. It's fast paced and dark, and I read it all in one sitting. It had entertainment value, to say the least, and provides a worthwhile warning about nuclear weapons. Unfortunately, I have many problems with the style and writing itself. 
 First of all, this book tries too hard to be unique, while crudely copying the style of Hemingway. Furthermore, the use of the boy and the man makes this book preachy. As a reader, I don't like having symbolism shoved down my throat. Symbolism can be done right in the likes of Fitzgerald, but when it becomes repetitive and all the book is depending on thematically, it quickly grows old and makes the reader feel like they are being talked down to. 
 Overall, I think McCarthy has potential with writing an entertaining story, but he should try to just let the themes naturally grow from his story-telling instead of attempting to create a theme himself.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I know that a lot of people love this book and find it worthy of high minded literary praise. If that is you, that's ok we can just agree to disagree on this one. I am just going to list the things that I think are wrong with this book. I am guessing that some of these things might be why certain readers like it, but to my mind these things are lacking. 
 Things wrong with this book. 
 1.) There are no apostrophe marks in the words couldn't, didn't, wouldn't, shouldn't. Yet there ARE apostrophe marks in It's, They're and We're. I am sorry but if you have the guts to wipe out apostrophe marks in the first place, be bold enought to wipe them all out. 
 2.) I have never read a book with more flowery descriptions in as many ways as possible about what someone is eating. I couldn't count the number of times I had to read that the boy wiped bean juice off his chin and licked the can. It was the same basic description over and over and over. The food did change occasionally and then he licked the can of peaches instead. 
 3.) There are no names given besides papa and the boy. I get that it's not supposed to matter what their names are, we are supposed to care about the characters anyway. But I found it very hard to grow attached to someone whose name I don't know. How many friends do you have who you don't know their names? Would you care more that one whose name you didn't know got eaten by a cannibal or would you care more about the one that was eaten whose name you did know? Me too. 
 4.) We keep being told that things happened "before the world burned" but not enought to know what made it burn or how or why. I wanted an explanation and I don't think that is too much to ask for in a story. 
 5.) This is about the extent of the boy's dialougue. "Are we still the good guys papa? Okay." Oh, and I ADDED the quotation marks because apparently after the world burns another thing you lose besides random apostrophes is quotation marks. 
 6.) There are pages and pages and pages and pages and pages of nothing happening. I suppose you could argue this is what it might really be like after an apocalyptic event and that the day to day events might be dull. But that sure as hell doesn't mean I want to read about that part. Then there are short sections of something kind of exciting happening and then straight back to pitching a tent, maiking a fire, eating some food. 
 7.) If these two people could find enough food for themselves all this time, why does everyone else have to be a cannibal? That just plain didn't make sense. And is again where an EXPLANATION could have come in handy. 
 8.) The dad, far from being a heroic protector most of the time seemed to me to mostly be an idiot. He is constantly getting out the map but at the same time realizing he has no idea where he is. He perpetually leaves the kid alone, even when that is just stupid. He always runs from trouble which I understand but then doesn't seem to think very much before going into say an abandoned house and opening up a cellar. Idiot. 
 9.) After going through the whole plot, slogginly, slowly, wondering if anything of note will ever happen, the dad finally dies. I didn't really care that he died. But more irritating than that was that a page and a half later the "good guys" show up and rescue the boy. They also seem to indicate they had been following them for a while so why didn't they help the dad. 
 10.) Okay last one, the whole time I kept feeling like something had to happen to make this more interesting. It never did, it was just dull, dull, dull, dull, dull, dull.

Like Hemingway...but not! Spare language that peaks at times, but rarely jolts. Considering the topic (post-apocalyptic survival), you would think the characters would pop off the page a little more. But like most Cormac, it woudl still make a good film. Screenwriters have little to work with and with film, sometimes that is good.

This book makes you think and I just wanted something to take my mind off of my troubles. If you want to cry/be depressed/worry about the future, this book is for you. If you want a good, entertaining read, then look elsewhere.

book_b.title: Look Who's Back
book_b.user_review: I'm going to call time on this one. While the premise is interesting, and Hitler's initial interactions are amusing enough, there's only so many forced misunderstandings I can bear. It's not a good enough plot to hold up an entire book.

sample_reviews.review_text:
While I found this book enjoyable to read, there were a few aspects of it that irritates me throughout. 
 1) I couldn't understand why Hitler was unable to change himself ever so slightly to mix in with modern society. It was clear he understood the world has changed so why couldn't he make the effort to change with it? 
 2) Would Germany really be so accepting of a Hitler 'impersonator'? I have the feeling that no, they would not! 
 Other than these two points I enjoyed the book, and by this I don't mean I found Hitler and his atrocious crimes funny, this book is clearly a piss take...

Germans have no sense of humour, they say. 
 Well, in the first place that's wrong, and in the second this is a best-seller there. 
 Sarcasm and irony abound, and you can't help liking old Adolf. 
 Which is the point of the book, I think. It's easy to be charmed by evil.

** spoiler alert ** 
 It was one joke stretched over a whole novel. I thought it was a tedious read and was quite relieved when I got to the end. I found it difficult to concentrate on the novel, which I thought was an interesting idea. I did enjoy the beating Hitler got, especially because the perpetrators did it because they thought he was Jewish. A clever novel but way too long. There must be better ways of ridiculing the modern media.

The premise is preposterous, but handled in such a believable and mundane manner that you find yourself involved and observing an entirely plausible progression. The novel ends in a way that surprised my expectation, but didn't disappoint, which for me is always a sign of a well-written piece.

I started reading this book, because I heard is a good comedy book. Ohh boy I was so wrong. 
 Hitler somehow time travel to the future and everybody thinks he is a comedian posing as Adolf Hitler. He acts a stand up act on tv... If we can say that, because was not funny at all... 
 Whole book seemed to me just a justification how Hitler was a cool guy, who did nothing wrong, just loved his country. 
 Was expecting much more from this book, because this was crap

A very clever satire on contemporary German, and more broadly Western, culture and politics. Though (not knowing beyond basic German) I have not read the original, the translation seems very competent, however, not being a student of current German culture and politics, I am sure I missed some of the references that would have made it even funnier. But it did not lack for humor especially of the barbed kind. 
 Surprisingly, Vermes manages to make Hitler almost sympathetic at times as a person lost in the modern era (but still, you know, Hitler). Not for everyone but an interesting and often amusing read. 
 I received this book (an ARC) as part of the First Reads program.
The only good thing about the book is the cover.

This book was a slog. It has been in my 'currently reading' list for nearly a year and each time I tried to complete it, I grew bored. 
 It had its moments -some parts were funny and it is an interesting satire on modern society and I did learn a lot about Germany however it worn thin and felt like it wasn't going anywhere. 
 I did manage to complete this book though but I can't say I enjoyed it or that it is a book I would particularly recommend.

With all the fuss about this book, I felt I had to read it in order to form my own opinion. 
 It's very much what I'd call a marmite book - some will love it and some will hate it. Those that will hate it will in the main be those that have either studied the 3rd Reich in detail or have been personally affected it. 
 I must admit I did feel a real unease reading this book. Whilst I'll find Mel Brook's "The Producers" funny this book is a very different proposition as it's told from an imagined Hitler point of view. The imagined Hitler is essentially portrayed as a grumpy old man struggling with the modern world with all the hatred and prejudices of the real person. 
 The book does ask some interesting questions about the keys to his power in the 1930s, how many of those elements still exist and for example how a modern day Hitler would exploit social media. 
 I was hoping that Hitler would experience an epiphany at some point, and did think that was going to happen when one of the characters talks of the sadness and anger of their Jewish relative at the fact that they are working with what is believed to be a very accurate Hitler impersonator. 
 However, any epiphany never happens and all we have is a character that you could feel sympathy for viewing the modern world seen through an imagined Hitler's eyes. 
 Whilst some may argue that it shows how a new Hitler figure could appear again and that it's very profound, I can't help being very uncomfortable with Hitler being portrayed as simplistically as a grumpy old man struggling with the modern world despite the message. 
 I can't recommend this book. It's too close to a horrific period of world history, but it does makes you think. All I can hope is that by reaching a wider audience than a dry history book it may make that audience read further to fully understand the horror that was the 3rd Reich.
Not for the easily offended, loads of loose ends and lacking in humour. Not really sure the purpose behind this 'story' at all. Nothing actually happens.

Prior to The Stranger Camus received a BA in philosophy, an MA in Christian Thought and wrote a number of non-fiction pieces. This was his first work of fiction and...I think it reads like that, as a philosophical idea with characters and plot built around it. I enjoyed it because I like literature that makes me think but if the idea was "life has no meaning so how should we proceed" I think he might have done better with a protagonist that tried even a teeny bit to find some meaning. In the same way, I don't believe the protagonist's "epiphany" at the end of the story that he had 'been happy' and that he would have realized that earlier if only he had opened his heart to "the indifference of the universe". Huh? 
 First of all, this was not a happy man. In fact, the dullness of his interactions throughout the first half of the book made me think maybe he was mildly depressed. He takes buses, he smokes cigarettes, he views the landscape and carries on short conversations but never does he engage in a way that an even mildly happy person might engage with the people around him. He sees his mother's "fiancee" have a fainting fit but offers no help. When a good friend of his mother's cries at the funeral, he says "I wanted her to stop crying, but dared not speak to her". Yet what a surprise when later accused of callousness! Is it really the universe that is indifferent or is it indifferent people that make it seem that way? 
 Throughout the first half, also, the protagonist claims that things "have no importance". He could marry Marie or not, he could accept his employer's offer to move to Paris or not. "I didn't care much one way or the other" he says because "one life was as good as another". Does this sound like a happy person? Does this sound like the universe being indifferent? Or does it sound like the kind of B.S. a moody teenager might spout. 
 This phrase (near the end) got me too: "...supposing she were dead, her memory would mean nothing; I couldn't feel interest in a dead girl". This just confirms that all the protagonist feels are physical sensations: the desire to touch Marie, the heat of the sun or the coolness of the evenings. If death only means the cessation of physical sensation then - sure - the protagonist is right that who cares if death occurs at 40 or 80, by guillotine or by old age? It's all the same. Yet most people's lives have motive, a reason for doing something that creates value to our lives that the protagonist neither has nor understands. (The word motive sprang to mind when mulling over Mersualt's crime since he, predictably, has none). 
 Sorry - if you shoot someone 4 times at close range and then feel "less regret than a kind of vexation", I will have to argue that you've either got a psychological problem or you are a creation of a philosopher's active imagination.
Had to read this book for school... It was sooo boring! Could not wait for it to be done! Would not recommend to anyone... One star...

BOOKTUBEATHON 2017: BOOK #1 
 Well, this was disappointing. I read this in an hour and all I can say is that this is NOT nearly as good as I remembered it being. In fact, it wasn't really anything good at all. It was extremely average at best. Sure the characters are rather engaging giving the length of this book, but this book, for me, boils down to a story about a murder where the main character questions everything without ATTEMPTING to answer them during these events. If you want to ask such deep questions, at least attempt to make some sort of answer with it. Camus' writing style annoyed me with its vocabulary, short sentences, and very choppy flow. If you are going to make your story slow as a snail, make sure EVERYTHING is slow. The murder itself was rushed in 2 pages and the whole process of him sitting and thinking about what he has done takes up the remaining 60 pages of this book. In short, I didn't like "The Stranger." I didn't dislike it, but I didn't like it like I initially did. I have now read this twice in my life and I don't think I need to read this ever again. In fact, I don't think I need to read any more Camus ever again. I just don't think he is for me. Unless if you are fascinated in the themes he explores here, I say skip this one. 
 I am giving this one a 2.5 out of 5 stars.

Estraneo, straniero. Racconta la propia vita col distacco di una telecamera. 
 Caldo, mal di testa. Spari. 
 Oggi mia mamma e morta. 
 Inizia con distacco, finisce con lui ancora distaccato da tutto quanto.

The protagonist of this story is a 'stranger' indeed, in the way he reacts to events in his life. He seems impassionate with regard to everything and without deep moral feelings. In the view of his and each man's destiny, death, nothing matters for him anymore. This presentation of the character of this man tastes a bit artificial too me, too theoretically philosophical. Also, the trial seems rather absurd in the argumentations used (or is it only outdated?). The description of the thoughts of Meursault when he approaches the Arab he is about to shoot are very effectful as are the last pages of the novel.
This was a quick and powerful read, revelatory of social issues, existence and death. Albert Camus is a master writer to pack so much philosophy so casually in this short, simple book.

***Spoiler alert 
 Mersault was a sociopath. He was friends with shady characters. He had no problem with women being beaten. He was strangely okay when his mother died. And he shot and killed a man with the only explanation being "It was because of the sun." It struck me when, during his trial, the prosecutor placed much emphasis on premeditation and intention and Mersault thought to himself, "He was right though." The tone that Camus used throughout to tell the story left me, the reader, just as detached as the character himself. And the result of that was losing sight of terrible crime he committed. Mersault didn't show much feeling. And by much, I mean that he didn't show any at all. In fact, his negative reaction to his execution was almost too much emotion for him and a detraction from his apathetic character. 
 I know this book was supposed to make me "question my existence" or something of that nature. But reading it didn't make me feel any more or less human. I felt exactly how I should feel about the particular story - disgusted. I did not feel this disgust because society told me it is appropriate to feel it when a man is killed by another man. I felt disgusted because killing a man is a disgusting crime. The only thing Camus accomplished with this novel in my opinion was giving us readers insight into the mind of a puzzling character. A character who has no control over what he does and doesn't care how he feels about it. In other words, a sociopath.

Listening to the radio today I heard "Killing an Arab" by the Cure. I remembered that it had to do with a book I read in high school. So I looked it up, where else but goodreads. I must be one of the few, but I remember thinking "this is dumb" when I read it in school. Maybe I just wasn't very high brow, I'm still not.:-)

I give this book two stars not because I think it was a bad book, but because I was completely and totally indifferent to it. So, I can't really say that I liked it. But it's still a good book, and from a literary standpoint, it's not bad. It's just not particularly engaging. However, from what I can tell, it is intentionally structured that way, because indifference is part of what it's trying to convey. It's definitely worth reading if you're into existentialism or absurdism (Albert Camus vehemently declared that The Stranger is an absurdist work, not an existentialist one, but there are definitely existentialist concepts in there, whether he liked it or not). I, personally, am just not into that stuff enough to have legitimately enjoyed this book. I will say that it was a quick read though. It's short, and even when I wasn't too interested, I at least was not bored.

Sookie's ongoing romance with Eric the vampire, the reapperance of her faerie relatives and of course the warewolves and shifters and the occasional murder. All this plus the introduction of another historical character in vampire form. Delightful read, especially if you like to suspend reality.

What a disappointment. I love the Sookie Stackhouse series. I wanted to give this book a higher rating just because I love the series. But I can't. Nothing happens in this book. It is so boring that I was 3/4 of the way through the book wondering when something, anything would happen. I'm still going to continue to read the series, in hopes that the books get better but I was really frustrated. 
 The only way I can describe this book is as an episode of True Blood kind of in the middle of the season. That is all the book is. It is a filler for later books.

It's hard to keep coming back to the same well, and this is the tenth time. But, Harris did the right thing by not putting Sookie in so much physical danger this time that it starts to get ludicrous. 
 The book has a slow start. No one wants to read how depressed Sookie is. But it picks up quickly and then we're off and running with all the various subplots intertwined into the series. What I like about this series is that each book doesn't feel very stand alone. Things start up in one book and don't get resolved. And then the story just picks up where it left off the next time. That's how life really is, and I like that she doesn't try to wrap everything up in a neat little bow.

I actually had to push myself to finish this one. As an avid reader of Charlaine Harris that shocked me. Though, same as the book before this, nothing really happened. It just seemed like a bunch of minor plot points summed up in a rushed ending that made me think, "Did she really just do that?" Even the writing seemed different. It seemed that every time Sookie talked to Sam we were reminded that only the first born in an all shifter family would carry the shifter gene, and when she talked about Claudine we were reminded everything about her and what happened. I feel that the constant reminding of information is a little insulting. Being reminded once was awesome because it has been months since i read a book in the series but when you are halfway through the book and read the same sentences four times it got a bit much. Still I will continue reading and would recommend this series to any vampire lover.
Definately not Harris' best. Not much action in his book, but still i couldn't put it down. Still enjoyed it very much.

Saying good bye to this series was literally hard on me. Even when I bought the book on release day, I let it sit on my shelf for months till I was ready to say good bye. I was nervous as to what would happen to my favorite characters. Being that I have followed this series from the very beginning, even before I was a blogger, it was hard. I still remember the day I bought the first book. A store employee was putting books on the shelf's and I said," Excuse me, do you have any YA paranormal that isn't vampires?" The girl chuckled and looked at her hand which just so happen to have My Soul To Take. She said," Here. Try this one. I read the back and it sounds pretty good." I smiled, gave my thanks and bought the book. Hook. Line. Sinker. 
 Plot: I knew without a doubt that this plot would be filled with lots of tying up loose ends and a big showdown at the end. Once I started the book it was as if I never left. Taking place in Kaylee shoes once again, the reader gets a first hand experience in action and major decisions. 
 Love: Of course I love this LOVE! It's a love that I have been rooting for. It's consuming and breath-taking. To see what these two people have gone through and still come out on top, leaves me speechless. I adore how they shared moments of great love and sadness. But most of all, I adored how well it ended for them. 
 Ending. I anticipated the ending more than anything. When I was half-way through, questions began popping in my head. I wondered how in the end will they get peace. Through clever tactics and smart wording, Kaylee managed to save those she loves with a great sacrifice. 
 With All My Soul is gripping and successful. A creative story that promises deeper emotions and a superb ending, With All My Soul excels all prior installments. Completing the series, With All My Soul rocks!

I can't believe that this series is finally over. This is probably one of the best YA paranormal series I've read. Kaylee, Nash, Tod, Emma, Sabine, Sophie and Luca has been through a lot. I'm just soooo glad that each ad everyone of them got the ending that they deserved. I love this series beyond reason and I can't wait to get my hands on the fourth and final omnibus. Yes, that's how much I loved this series. It's such a bittersweet feeling. I'm glad that their suffering has come to an end and yet I'm sad because of the fact that this is it. I won't have Kaylee and the gang to look forward to anymore. But other than that it was an awesome read. I love love love this series beyond reason. 
 Thank you Rachel Vincent for creating Kaylee ad everyone else from the Soul Screamers series.

This is going to be a difficult review to write. Let me start by saying that since the first book I really enjoyed the Soul Screamers series. I think If I Die is the best book of the series and the two books afterwards just weren't that good. With All My Soul was a great ending to this series, but overall this only an okay book. 
 The story is just more of the same and I have to admit it was a bit boring for most of the book. There were some interested scenes that I liked and some surprises, but it didn't have that keep-reading-feel. I could put this book down too easily. Although I have to say I still love Rachel Vincent's writing style and will probably still read everything she writes. The writing style is great and what kept me reading even when I wasn't that interested in the story. Also I just had to know how it all ends. I did like seeing how the characters went on with their lives after what happened in the end of book 6, because some stuff happened and I had no idea how they would continue onwards. 
 The best part of this book are the last 16 pages, the ending is emotional and brilliant and also still full of questions and some plot holes. I think this series is wrapped up really well and the ending was done really good, but I also didn't like some of the events that happened at the end, because some things are just contradicting each other and as mentioned earlier there are still some plot holes and explanations that don't make that much sense. And the explanation stuff was a bit confusing at times. The ending did leave me feeling good and I liked how it ended. 
 The characters do change in this book. I actualy started to like Kaylee a little less in this book, there are just a few things she says and does that I didn't like or agree with and sometimes she just couldn't see the perspectives of everyone else and it felt like she didn't take those in consideration at some moments. Emma on the other hand grew stronger in this book, certainly after what happened in the last book I was amazed at how she dealt with everything in this book and I think she became an even more awesome character in this book. I also liked how Sophie developed in this whole series and actually ended up as a decent character. And how in the end I really like Sabine and I think she is a great character, even though she did some bad things and was pretty unlikeable when she was first introduced. There are also some great developments between some of the characters and I liked where they all ended up at the end of the book. 
 There isn't much world building added in this book, but now most of the world building already has been established and I even thought that the descriptions of the Netherworld were less vivid than in the earlier books. 
 To conclude: I just have some mixed feelings about this book. I was a bit bored for most of the book and I actually had enough of Avari and all his evil plans. I did like the writing style. I also liked the ending and what happened to the characters at the end. I think this book concludes the series well, but I didn't like some of the events that happened and I think there are still some plot holes in the story. I also liked Kaylee a little less in this book because of some of the things she did. I did liked Emma more because she showed so much strenght in this book.

book_a.user_review:
I first read this book when the 1979 BBC-NBC mini-series came out. I remember exactly where I was won over: in the second chapter, "Ylla", I read the following: 
 "Here's your scarf." He handed her a phial. "We haven't gone anywhere in months." [...] 
 From the phial a liquid poured, turned to blue mist, settled about her neck, quivering. 
 I absolutely loved the image of that ephemeral scarf wrapping itself around the Martian Ylla's shoulders. 
 However, I had a really hard time re-reading it as an adult, and dealing with the casual contempt for all things female. I felt as I did when I tried to watch "Mad Men." The use of language is powerful, but I could see the "No girls allowed" sign above the club house door.

When does a classic go from being a classic to merely a book like any other, its quality determined in the eyes/mind/heart of the reader? Writing out that question, the answer is painfully obvious; why, when it's read, of course! The reason for this feeble rhetorical game is me trying to find some novel way of reconciling my ambivalent reaction to The Martian Chronicles with its status as a classic. Where my reading of the first subject of SFX Magazine's Book Club, The War of the Worlds (review), revealed a vital and timeless work, I was all the more disappointed to find Ray Bradbury's younger (by over 50 years) effort uneven and stodgy. Which, in one way, would seem to make it more, and not less, entitled to be labelled "classic" - taken as pejorative, the term evokes something dusty, irrelevant, unassailable (but also inaccessible). My star rating should dispel any notion that I found TMC to be crap, though; it's nothing of the sort. At least half of the longer episodes constituting the bulk of this loosely linked tapestry novel are deliriously good. Bradbury's prose sings and burns, fluidly moving from florid to terse; even the clunkier episodes never lack for spellbinding sentences, crackling dialogue or dazzling descriptions. 
 What does let the side down, and where Bradbury pales in direct comparison with H.G. Wells, are the ideas, science fiction's supposed revelatory effects caused by holding a warped future mirror up to humanity's more shameful facets. Bradbury's sketches of Martian culture in the opening episodes are mesmerising, but as soon as the human colonists take center stage, it's clear that he hasn't bothered with any other imaginative leaps, beyond making the USA circa 1950 capable of interplanetary travel. If charitable, one might take this society unchanged in half a century to be a pessimistic prophecy of Bradbury's, but it seems to me more of a misstep than anything else. Brilliant as his prose might be throughout, as soon as the dated social commentary pops up halfway through, the anachronisms start to grate instead of merely being charming and quaint. There's nothing wrong about railing against censorship and racial segregation, but the episodes in question lack the transformative qualities needed to take them beyond simple polemics with tacked-on rockets. My regard for the author's social consciousness might also have been a wee bit compromised by the last-man-on-Mars episode featuring a gluttonous and despicable woman as the protagonist's bete noire. 
 Perhaps this exasperation was necessary for me to grok the message of my opening gambit, though. Not only is it foolish of me to expect to like every classic, it's downright stupid to expect something as fantastic as The War of the Worlds every time. More importantly, in another mood, with a less churlish heart, I would have been so overwhelmed by the beauty and virtuosity of "Rocket Summer", "Ylla", "The Third Expedition", "-and the Moon Be Still as Bright", "The Martian" or "There Will Come Soft Rains" that I would've forgiven the aforementioned grievances as merely the patina of age.

First, there is a lot to be said about Bradbury's sometimes masterful art of the short story. I think the strongest contenders were the expedition narratives--especially the third. Also, the stories where the narration remains objective are all excellent in their own right. I am thinking here of "There will come Soft Rains." 
 However, this collection of stories also showcases just how badly Bradbury can write. First, these stories seem hardly imaginative and what might be a tiny detail (the years these stories apparently take place) makes it hard to see this work positively. For instance the story "Way in the Middle of the Air" seems especially troublesome as the events described (blacks slowly gaining rights and the enacting of anti-lynching laws) were both relevant at the time of publication. Therefore, why not set the story in the historical context? To me, it seems that Bradbury was faced with the conundrum of how to make The Martian Chronicles more "futuristic" or more "sci-fi" and decided, "Hmmm, 2000, now that's flashy number!" Also aggravating is the fact that this story subtly creates an idyllic south; a south where blacks are happy with their situation, evidenced in: "Here and there...there had been voices singing, the honey laughter under the mimosa branches, the pickaninnies rushing in clear water laughter at the creek...jokes and shouts of amusement from the shingle shacks covered with fresh vines" (96). Now, Bradbury isn't entirely unsympathetic in his treatment of race, but there are still odd moments in the text in which the narration subtly reinforces stereotypes, i.e. the repeated references to the watermelon patches being empty now that the Black Americans have left earth. To me, this type of narration is just about as stupid and facile as the phrase, "I'm not racist, but..." 
 Last, I am tired of the assertion that Bradbury is "original," or "peerless." Really, all of these stories are about white men fucking shit up and going "whoops, won't do that again." If Bradbury was really as "original," or "peerless," maybe he should have tried challenging the status quo, rather than reinforcing it.

This is one of those books I should have read a long long time ago. I think it was on my TBR for over five years. I finally got around to it now and I loved it! Of course, I am overly fond of science fiction short stories, like The Illustrated Man, and this is just classic Bradbury. My favorite stories had a touch of The Twilight Zone in them. All of the stories deal with man's exploration of and subsequent conquering of Mars. You see, Martians live on Mars, and so the first three groups to arrive from Earth, over the course of a couple of years at the turn of the 21st century, are not greeted with the warmest of welcomes. However, eventually, Earth gains a foothold on Mars and humans start to build their own towns and cities. Trouble back home in the form of impending nuclear war impedes the colonization process, and the books end in the 2030s with life on Mars not being exactly what you would think. I loved the bite size stories, the chronology as it played out, and the wonderful descriptions of the Martian landscape. The books were written long before we knew of the harsh conditions on Mars, so one must remember that only 70 short years ago, we had no idea what Mars might hold. I highly recommend for anyone who likes classic science fiction like Bradbury, Asimov, or Clarke.

Historias impresionantes desde una perspectiva distinta en ciencia ficcion. Cronicas Marcianas es el libro perfecto para quien este cansado de la ciencia ficcion en la que se endiosa la labor del hombre y se alaba la inventiva del mismo. Bradbury tiene genio para escribir historias graciosas, algunas veces tragicomicas, pero siempre con esa moraleja incrustada muy en el fondo que deja a la mente masticando el verdadero mensaje que queria dejar. 
 El libro tiene historias largas y cortas, mis favoritas fueron: El verano del cohete, Encuentro nocturno, Usher II y El Marciano. Todas tienen en comun la intransigencia del hombre y el desprecio por las personas, cosas e ideas diferentes. Estas cronicas son historias atemporales que se veran como caricaturas y pequenas columnas de opinion bastanate reales cuando el hombre llegue a otros planetas. Una perfecta guia de lo que no hay que hacer. 
 Es para: fanaticos de la ciencia ficcion y personas que busquen historias desde perspectivas distintas 
 No es para: gente que guste de la ficcion cientifica pura, no hay nada de eso aca.
