I really wanted to like this book from the start. I had heard nothing but great things about Ann Rice's work, and came highly recommended by one of her biggest fans, my mother. Now, to be fair, I love lore and mystery, especially with witchcraft and the supernatural, but this story wasn't really about any of that. Instead, it is a long and highly detailed recording of a family history with a sprinkling of creepy demon stalking, and an abrupt and unsatisfying ending. Some of the bits about the Mayfair history were very engaging and interesting, but as the main plot wore on I found myself loathing the protagonists and completely disinterested in the supernatural being tormenting them - get on with it already! So when the climax begins, along with the vivid eroticism (...yet again...), I'm questioning the purpose of the story other than to excite the sexual fantasies of bored individuals. Fair enough then, but not my cup of tea.

This book is a detailed look into the lives of a family of witches. There is no stone unturned when it comes to the telling of their tale. I was very intrigued by this story and the author did well in the developement of the entire set of characters. Unfortunately I felt at times there was a little too much detail. The same thing was described many many times through the book and it became challenging to keep reading during some of this. I am a fan of Anne's and look forward to continuing the story of the Mayfair witches in the next chapter, Lasher. I do hope the descriptions are better placed in this book but this is more a personal preference I am sure.

** spoiler alert ** 
 What a queer little book (although at 1207 pages, little isn't the right word)! This was my first attempt at Anne Rice and I fear it might well be my last. 
 Halfway through "The Witching Hour", I was absolutely enthralled. I loved the idea of The Talamasca. At that stage of the story, I would have loved knowing it was a real organisation and applied for a job. I revelled in learning the entire Mayfair history. Anne Rice has a gift for choosing the words that bring it all to life. I could imagine the house on First Street and see everything as the characters walk through the Garden District. 
 So why only one star? Firstly, I thought it was too long. I love books & reading and don't shy away from a challenge but I felt it just took too long to get to a disappointing ending. And that really is the crux of my complaint. How it all ends. In a word, pitifully. 
 Rowan, the all-powerful 13th witch in the Mayfair Dynasty & destiny, so completely consumed in her eternal love for Michael - gives up, betrays Michael and helps Lasher? Please. For me, it not only belittled her character (and relationship with Michael) but made a mockery of it. None of it rang true. After wading through this, all I am left with is a feeling of being cheated.

Great read as always. Whilst I'm pretty far into 'Lasher' the second in this series now, I dread re-reading the third 'Taltos' because it lacks everything this and the second novel contain - a great story. 
 I digress... The Witching Hour is such a saga, you must read it to understand just how deep it is. Despite my many years of reading, I always hope for happy endings and sadly this book just doesn't contain those happy endings. There are hints of what could have been if not for the curse that has shadowed the Mayfair family for centuries. 
 The main characters of the story enter the story in different stages. Michael, is the first to enter the story. At first, you won't have any idea why we're following this Irish kid from New Orleans. He grows into a wealthy and well-capable man after the death of his father. 
 Michael suffers a tragedy himself, an accidental drowning. He is literally dead when he is rescued by a passerby in a boat. When he comes to in the hospital, he finds that he has come back with a purpose, and a gift - or is it a curse. 
 As we ride through Michael's tumultuous thoughts surrounding this 'purpose' he was sent back to the living for. He's conflicted about his gift and the images that he sees when he touches things, people - everything. He doesn't want to touch anything, he wants this 'gift' to go away, but all he can think of is returning home - to fulfil this destiny he believes those from the other side have sent him to complete. 
 ***Spoilers ahead*** 
 When the second main character, Rowan enters the story, we find out that Rowan was actually the person who rescued Michael when he drowned. She finally gets in touch with him, not because he wants her to, but because she wants him to use his 'gift' on her. See, Rowan isn't what you think she is....a normal neurosurgeon. She's so much more. 
 The third main character in this story is of course, Lasher. Lasher, the devil, the daemon, the 'man'. He's been appearing the women of the family, affecting those around them and lets just say he's inherently evil. Not all those women who he 'haunts' believe he's evil. Like the devil is purported to be, he's silver tongued, tells the women he loves them and even goes so far as to rape them - whether willingly or unwillingly. 
 Rowan's family took her from her mother the moment she was born and kept her mother in a medical-induced state of near vegetation until she subsequently dies. Whilst this is harsh, her aunts felt that was their only to keep Lasher from getting her. Rowan's adoptive mother is also a Mayfair and prior to her death made Rowan sign paperwork saying she would never, ever look for her mother, try to find her roots and would most definitely never return to New Orleans. 
 With all her good intentions, Rowan tries to stay away - even when she wants to follow Michael there to help him with his quest to sort out what those 'other' people told him he must do, the reason he returned from the dead. The night he flies in to New Orleans, Lasher appears to Rowan in her home in California and everything changes. See, Michael had been seeing Lasher since he was a boy - Rowan despite her familial connection to the Mayfairs, had never seen Lasher. That is...until her mother dies. 
 The story follows Michael and Rowan through their pursuit of the truth, what to do about Lasher, the relationship and the Talamasca. 
 For a story that is steeped in deep, dark history and a harrowing tale of what people would do for those they love, The Witching Hour is an incredible tale.

I originally read this when I was around 14. I remember carrying the book around with me everywhere so any free moment I got, I could dive in. 
 Well, it's probably me, but I didn't think it was GREAT this time around. It could have been at least 200 pages shorter. I really had a tough time finishing it.

To me, this book reflects some of Ms. Rice's best work. This book might not be for everyone because of the extensive background and detail that makes up much of the story - especially the file/history of the Mayfairs, which is VERY intensive and takes almost half of the novel altogether - but I enjoyed it immensely, and those who like detailed stories would too. 
 Infact, the history of the Mayfairs is critical to the book, and it added to the book, what with the saga of the thirteen witches. Just be prepared for a surprise ending!

My mother and I both read this one and agreed. Any value the book had, any interest it evoked along the way, was negated and then some by the most horribly stupid ending of any book we've ever read, period.

Amazing...the depth to which Anne Rice went to with this novel! The history of the Mayfair family is fascinating and incredibly detailed, and the story flows so well that it is hard to put this book down. Shocking at times, I couldn't wait to pick up "Lasher".

<< Va au Sud. De l'autre cote de la riviere. Suis les oiseaux. >> 
 Je n'avais jamais entendu parler de ce livre avant d'y tomber dessus par hasard a la bibliotheque. J'ai vu la couverture : << Oh, qu'elle est belle ! >> J'ai lu le resume : << Oh, il a l'air vraiment interessant ! >> J'ai ete fouiller Goodreads et j'ai vu plein de super chroniques : << Oh, je dois le lire tout de suite ! >> 
 Donc je l'ai lu tout de suite. Et je suis tombee de haut. Vraiment. Pour tout vous dire, j'ai bien failli abandonner au moins cinq fois (mais j'ai tenu bon *fiere*) 
 Nous suivons Syrli (qui normalement s'appelle Lark en VO, allez savoir pourquoi ils ont change son nom...), qui vit dans une ville protegee du reste du monde par un dome, et qui fonctionne grace a l'energie magique que l'on recupere chez les enfants lors de la << collecte >>. Cette collecte a generalement lieu avant l'adolescence, mais a 16 ans, Syrli n'a toujours pas ete collectee. Lorsque son tour arrive enfin, elle decouvre qu'elle n'est pas exactement une adolescente normale : c'est une Renouvelable, c'est-a-dire qu'elle possede plus de magie que les autres, et qu'on va donc se servir d'elle comme source d'energie principale de la ville. Se refusant au sort qui lui est destine, Syrli s'enfuit en direction du Bois de Fer, ou vivent, caches, d'autre gens comme elle. 
 Avant de comprendre ce que je viens de vous resumer, il m'a fallu plusieurs chapitres. Meagan Spooner a fait le choix de commencer son roman en plein dans le vif de l'action. C'aurait pu etre un choix judicieux, pour accrocher le lecteur des les premieres pages, si elle n'avait pas oublie qu'elle etait en train d'ecrire le premier tome de sa trilogie, et que dans un premier tome, on a quand meme besoin de poser un minimum le contexte avant d'entamer une sequence a 4000 a l'heure. Elle commence tout de suite a nous parler de ressource, de collecte, de renouvelables, comme si on avait connu ca toute notre vie. Chere Meagan, je vais peut-etre t'apprendre quelque chose, mais les lecteurs ne sont pas dans ta tete. Si tu ne leur explique pas ton univers, ils ne le comprennent pas. (On est peut-etre intelligents, mais pas au point de lire dans les pensees des auteurs. Pas encore du moins) 
 Outre le fait qu'il m'a fallu un bon nombre de chapitres pour comprendre de quoi il en retournait, j'ai trouve globalement que l'univers manquait cruellement de developpement. Il y a eu << des guerres >> qui ont eu pour consequence que de monde est ce qu'il est actuellement dans le livre, mais on n'en sait pas plus (pourquoi, quand, comment...) J'ai comme l'impression que l'auteure elle-meme ne le sait pas et qu'elle se repose sur cette explication pour tout, sans creuser plus loin. Il y a eu des guerres, point. C'est un peu leger, je trouve, surtout que la construction de l'univers est quand meme l'un des points les plus importants dans une dystopie (enfin, a mon avis). 
 L'heroine, Syrli, ne m'a fait absolument aucun effet. Je trouve qu'elle aussi manque de consistance, tout comme l'univers. Je ne sais pas du tout comment la decrire. Je ne saurais meme pas dire si elle a vraiment evolue entre le debut et la fin. Elle n'a pas vraiment de personnalite ni d'histoire derriere elle. Vous allez me dire, elle n'a que 16 ans, elle est encore tres jeune, mais quand meme. Prenez d'autres heroines de dystopie (Katniss ou Tris, pour ne citer que les plus connues), elles ont une vraie personnalite et une vraie histoire. On se souvient d'elles, elles ne laissent pas indifferent. Syrli en revanche... elle est completement lisse. Je suis sure que dans quelques mois, je l'aurais deja oubliee. 
 Une grande partie du roman raconte la fuite en solitaire de notre heroine, tres peu d'autres personnages interviennent. Et elle n'a absolument pas assez d'envergure pour soutenir un tel recit. Du coup, on s'ennuie un peu. 
 Tant qu'on est dans les personnages : est-ce qu'il est cense y avoir un triangle amoureux Kris-Syrli-Oren ? C'est une vraie question, j'aimerais vraiment savoir. Parce que j'ai eu l'impression que oui, mais que c'est tellement rate qu'en fait... y'en a pas. Vous voyez ce que je veux dire ? 
 Quant a la fin... elle ne m'a pas convaincue. Je ne sais pas trop comment expliquer ca, mais j'ai eu comme l'impression qu'on revenait au point de depart. En fait, tout le livre est un peu comme ca : Syrli est quelque part a rebondissement a elle fuit a elle se retrouve quelque part a rebondissement a elle fuit etc. etc. Ca tourne en rond, en fait. Et durant les 400 pages de ce premier tome, je n'ai pas l'impression que l'intrigue ait beaucoup avance. 
 En bref, ce fut une lecture tres laborieuse, mais j'en suis venue a bout ! Mais comptez pas sur moi pour le second tome, par contre... 
 Mais je ne vais pas vous dire de prendre vos jambes a votre cou pour autant. Si le livre vous tente (et que je ne vous ai pas decourages !), alors allez-y. Les chroniques negatives comme la mienne sont plutot rares, donc qui sait, peut-etre que vous adorerez...

When I first read the summary for "Skylark" I thought, "Wow, what an original concept." However, no matter how unique the storyline, the writing just did not deliver. 
 Lark Ainsley has been passed over for harvesting her resource year after year. You see, in this dystopian society, the magical powers of children are tapped to power the city. Finally, when her time comes, Lark finds out that what will happen to her is not what she was taught. It is all a big lie and her life is very much on the line. Sounds good, right? Well, unfortunately, it was just okay. 
 First and foremost, sometimes authors attempt to write a book with a creative flourish that is poetic. Often it works and often it does not. In this case, it just did not work for me. I read and reread various parts of the book for a clearer meaning and in the end, I was left frustrated more times than not. Also, while the concept was great, too much of the story was without dialogue. Much of it chronicled what Lark was thinking as well as her mental state. It all felt very antiseptic and clinical. I need more interaction among characters that includes dialogue, action and suspense. This book had a little in the beginning and more towards the end. 
 At times, I liked the book; but, not enough to give it higher than two or 2.5 stars. It is a shame because it could have been really great if the author just made the changes I listed earlier. There are too many great YA novels out there right now to read mediocrity. Therefore, I will not be continuing on with the trilogy. Sorry Ms. Spooner, I really wanted to love it.

When this book came out, I skipped all the hoopla and consequently forgot all about it. A few weeks ago I replenished my holds requests for the library (yes, it is as nerdy as it sounds) and came across Skylark again. I couldn't remember why I didn't want to read it, so I put it on the list and decided to give it a go. 
 Lark Ainsley's world exists in isolation. Wars have wrecked havoc on the world, making it impossible to survive anywhere except within the Wall. In order to protect those inside each child is Harvested, giving up the small amount of Resource within him or her in order to power the Wall. But when it's Lark's turn to do her civic duty, she discovers how different she is and that those in charge may have a more inimical plan for her. Lark must escape into the unforgiving world outside where everything she thought she knew begins to unravel. 
 "...I could hear the sounds of their slaughter as far away as I was. I stared, unable to look away, as the six people-but they could not be people, they could not be people-fell upon the wounded one. The clearing echoed with the sounds of tearing flesh and cracking bones interspersed with whoops and gurgles of delight." 
 What had me from the beginning was the sheer terror of Lark's experience inside the Institute when she was taken to be Harvested. The mere word sends shivers down my spine. It was brutal and cruel and inhumane. And from that point forward I felt the need for Lark to escape and went on the journey with her. 
 One of my favorite things about Lark was that she was too curious for her own good. The moment she steps into the Institute and has an opportunity to go snooping for clues in her brother's disappearance, she takes it. She's dogged and audacious and I love her for it. Lark's naivety in the outside world was especially endearing. Sometimes you read a book where the character is supposed to be out of sorts, but there's no surprise, no true moments of awe. But with Lark there was a true wide-eyed innocence. 
 The shining beacon of Skylark is Oren, the wild boy Lark meets in the wilderness who eventually takes her to the Iron Wood, a place inhabited by special people like Lark. Oren was savage and sweet and at times a little unpredictable. He was also extremely sad and I've got a soft spot for the dejected. 
 There were, however, a few characters that fell flat for me, including Kris, a potential love-interest. He was far more interesting at the beginning of the book than at the end, where his sudden appearance was nothing but a red flag. Subsequently his feelings for Lark felt disingenuous. He was never really around her except possibly when she was unconscious. I'd have bought into his concern for her if that was the extent of his feelings, but I felt the author pushed too hard with him. 
 Overall, Skylark was a really enjoyable and the best part of reading a book more than a year after it's release is that I don't have to wait long for the sequel...seriously, I just went to the library and picked it up (another nerdy thing about me).

Skylark presents a unique and flavorful sort of dystopia/post-apocalyptic setting and fictional universe. Starting in a grim city reminiscent of 1984 but with magic, it's protagonist escapes after realizing her own capacity for magic and goes in search for others like her. The "magical" apocalypse the transformed the world outside the bubble of her city is recognizable and, at times, surreal. All of it makes for an interesting adventure with some fun twists. While the protagonist can be frustrating at times, being both naive and short-sighted, it does make for an interesting arc as her journey transforms her. This may be a "YA" book, but I hardly noticed that other than the age of the protagonist as it contains plenty of surreal horror elements and some fairly graphic violence at points.

I don't know how to say this gently, so I'll just say it: this book was awful. I absolutely hated it. I really, really don't want to be mean but I just couldn't bring myself to like this book one bit. It was exasperating! I literally wanted to scratch at my eyes and rip my hairs out every time I read a chapter. 
 First of all, the good things about Silence. I have to be honest and solemnly thank the author for making this a fast read, otherwise I don't think I could've been able to finish this book. I'm not kidding. Thank the heavens that the writing style was easy to follow and that the overall action was extremely easy to read. 
 Also, let me just point this out: thank God that there wasn't a love triangle! That's about the only good thing about this series, overall. Love triangles are usually cheap, corny and frustrating and this book didn't have it, which I can only praise it for. 
 Now, moving on, I must say that I was frustrated during 3/4 of this book. Really, memory wipe? Okay, that's actually pretty cool if you think about it. But, really, Patch would rather let Nora mumble alone in complete darkness - or, silence, if you wish - than fight for their future and fight for her? Granted, Nora is a terrible person but still. Patch swore up and down that he loved Nora and that nothing would keep them apart, and yet, here he was ready to just let go of it all. 
 I'm honestly getting mad just writing this review. Seriously, we're book 3 into this series and I don't know if there were 100 pages combined of Nora and Patch actually being together, without fighting or "letting go" of each other. This is not okay, not at all! I've said it before and I'll say it again - drama is alright. Everybody likes it, everybody wants to read a little of it and maybe even shed a few tears. But this book just went over the top. And don't even get me started on Vee - worst bestfriend of all times. 
 On the other hand, I have mixed feelings about the action. The truth is, this book didn't keep me interested too much, which is why my mind kept slipping when reading it. Therefore, I don't really remember much of what happened, except the basics. I know that at times I felt like nothing was really happening. However, things changed a bit towards the ending and it all felt a little more fast-paced. 
 To sum this all up, I'm not going to pretend that this isn't a fit of rage where words start pouring out of me. Yes, I am very mad with this book. Yes, I am also very unimpressed and still wondering how on earth I was able to finish it but mostly, I'm wondering what would make someone want to read the final book after reading this one?

Ok, I must say this one is waaaay better than the others and this story is less whining-Nora and more I-think-I-grow-up-Nora. But I'll be honest *whispers*: I skipped some parts. I know, I know, bad Bia...but I think this was the best way to read this book. 
 Nora has lost her memory from the last 5 months thus she doesn't know Patch/Jev and has no idea Hank Miller is who he is. Armed only with the need to discover what happened to her memory, Nora went and grown up (at least she tried to and her behavior was an improvement from the previous ones).  On a completely side note, I really liked Scott in this one. He's her friend and tried to help her remember what she learn throughout the first two books. He also changed completely and yet was just the same. 
 All in all, the best book of this serie.

This book was... absolutely terrible. I've heard such good things about this series, about how addictive and fun it is, and how great the characters and the world are. I feel like I must have read a different book than everyone else, because this book was so fucking boring. It took me forever to read, I hated the characters, and the world was so uninteresting and weird that I barely managed to finish this book. 
 To start, Mac was one of the most annoying and boring main characters I've read about in a long time. At the beginning of the book, she finds out her sister has been murdered while studying abroad in Ireland. The police investigation into her sister's murder goes nowhere, so Mac decides that she will go to Ireland herself to force the police to reopen her sister's case. The police refuse, so she decides to investigate on her own, hoping to discover evidence that will force the police to reconsider. From that point on Mac makes a series of weird and questionable decisions that lead her to discover the world of the fae and her role in it. The book is narrated by Mac of the future, recounting the events of her life, so there were a lot of instances where she would add comments that made her sound very juvenile and made the writing seem very choppy. Mac is characterized as being a girly-girl who likes fashion and the color pink, and she is also able to hold her own in a fight. I really appreciate the message that girls can be badass and also like traditionally girly things, but I thought the author tried way too hard to get that message across. Mac went off on long tangents in nearly every chapter to describe her nail polish color or her outfit, which got boring after the second time it happened, and every time after that I wanted to rip my hair out. I could not possibly give less of a fuck what shade of pink her nails were that day. 
 Another thing that drove me absolutely insane about Mac was how against cursing she was. On multiple occasions, she uses "petunia" instead of "ass," and to be completely fucking honest, it hurt my eyes. This book is basically erotica in some places, and the fact that Mac was so against cursing was just laughable. And annoying. Just use the real fucking word, holy shit! 
 Then we have Barrons. The entire point of his character was to be Mac's brooding and sexy, while also extremely douche-y, mentor to the world of the fae. He was such a one dimensional character that I forgot he existed a lot of the time he wasn't around, which is saying something because he and Mac were basically the only relevant characters in the entire book. He is characterized as being very mysterious, but literally the only reason we didn't know anything about him was that Mac NEVER ASKED HIM A SINGLE QUESTION ABOUT WHO OR WHAT HE WAS. Like, what the fuck. The only questions Mac ever asks him about his background are where he is from and whether or not the has any siblings. 
 And, of course, because we also need a pointless fae character to keep things interesting, we have V'lane, or whatever the fuck his stupid name is. I spent most of this book referring to him as Vlad in my head because me brain literally refused to remember a name that stupid. V'lane is a death-by-sex fae. Yes, you read that right. His fae power is making women want to have sex with him so badly that they die. They literally die. I can't with this book. 
 Every time Mac meets V'lane, she takes all of her clothes off in the middle of the street. Without realizing what she's doing. Seriously. 
 Not only were the characters all flaming piles of human garbage, the plot and world building were horrendous as well. Barrons and Mac's journal were used as plot devices to dump definition after useless definition on the reader in the most boring possible terms, with future Mac jumping in to add even more information that I didn't care about. The writing was choppy and the narration style did not work for me at all. I spent half this book wishing it was over and the other half rolling my eyes at how ridiculous everything was. Needless to say, I will not be continuing this series.

 Mac is a young Georgia girl who reminded me of the song Georgia Peaches by Lauren Alaina (I'd post a link but the video is horrible). She was bubbly, in love with her hair, and is pretty much a little Barbie Doll, except this doll is able to stand up for herself without being invulnerable, naive without being idiotic, and generally great. Her voice is very unique and she reminded me a bit of Percy Jackson, except she's not 12... 
 Mac has joined the group of my favorite characters along with Percy Jackson (hey, it's my inner 9-year-old), Seraphina from the book with the same name, and Rose from Vampire Academy. 
 Barrons is a little petunia (you'll get it if you read the book). Many readers find him appealing, maybe he softens up a bit but right now, I find him annoying and a huge jerk. What I love is the Mac feels the same way. She's not swooning over his big muscles and hard abs. Neither of them like each other and that's that. 
 I'm hoping we get to know V'lane a bit more in the latter books. He's so funny! V'lane is a (as Mac calls him) death-by-sex fae, which as you probably guessed there are some pretty funny scenes between Mac and V'lane. 
 Plot & Writing: 
 Plot: 
 I can honestly say that I did not see all the twists coming. By the end, I had no idea what would happen. It was foreshadowed a bit and I bet a lot of readers guessed it but it might have been because I was reading at 11 PM and wasn't fully awake. I better read the end again. 
 The story was wonderful. I loved the, well everything. I guess I getting the I-hate-every-book-I-read rep, which is NOT true. I like some of them :P 
 Writing: 
 Between the stellar descriptions and the awesome narration, I can truthfully say, I love Karen Marie Moning. The descriptions were vivid without being overly descriptive which can seriously mess with the flow of a book. Mac's voice was snarky and entertaining and I have my kindle book highlighted everywhere. I can't wait to see her writing grow into something even more amazing. 
 What I liked and didn't: 
 Liked: 
 * Mac 
 * The descriptions 
 * Barrons and Mac's chemistry 
 * The Writing and Plot 
 Disliked: 
 * Barrons lack of respect for Mac 
 In conclusion: 
 I loved this book! I'm so glad that I have the rest of the books sitting on my shelf ready to be read. 
 ------------------------------------------------

 Favorite Quote: 
 Movies tell you what to think. A good book lets you choose a few thoughts for yourself. A movie shows you the pink house. A good book tells you there's a pink house and lets you paint some of the finishing touches, maybe choose the room style, park your own car out front. My imagination has always topped anything a movie could come up with. 
 Case and point, those darned Harry Potter movies. That was so not what the part-Veela-chick, Fleur Delacour, looked like.

sample_reviews.review_text: I freakin love Amy Poehler. She's not an author; she's just someone who loves to tell stories. Her take on being in film, television and the Hollywood spotlight is refreshing, honest and straight forward.

I love Amy, but I didn't like this book. It took me ages to read it (I started way before the 10th, I just didn't update it until the 10th). 
 First of all, I thought it dragged. The stories seemed pointless and for most of it, I didn't understand why she included them in the first place. 
 Second, half of this book is just about name dropping. The amount of times she mentioned someone famous was ridiculous. I understand she's famous herself, therefore she works with famous people, but if you go back to my first point, it just seems like pointless name dropping. 
 I liked maybe two chapters out of this book and couldn't wait to finish it, to read something better. So, yeah... 2 stars.

I like Amy Poehler and this book is really just Poehler riffing on stories from her life, or random thoughts she has. I listened to it, which likely helped; I can't really imagine reading it. I realized that her rapid fire comedy, which works so well on screen, doesn't work so well in narrative. There were several sections I skipped because I just didn't care, but overall I found it an entertaining car listen.
I thought since I liked Parks and Rec and SNL that I would like this book a bit more, but it was "just okay."

A light, fun read. I wasn't particularly familiar with Ms.Poehler's work beyond her Hilary Clinton impressions on SNL, but after reading his book, I'll say that I like her. The essays varied between personal memoirs and more straight humor, and it was a good balance.

I listened to the audio book version (yes, Amy, through my phone). I am simultaneously happy and not that Amy recorded it herself. It's always nice when a autobiographical work is told by the subject, but for an actress, I found it surprising that it was still difficult at times to know when she was joking. In particular, the chapter where she talks about how she hates being approached by strangers. I'm not the type to approach strangers on the street, celebrity or not, but the chapter rubbed me the wrong way and for the first, but not the last time, I thought that I liked Amy more before I started listening to her book. There are some genuinely funny passages, but not a lot of insight into the events of her life. It's on par with recent books by Tina Fey and Mindy Kaling.

This book, disappointingly, did not live up to my expectations. For me, it lacked flow and any real content. There was a lot of "I worked in this theater and then moved to a different one and then I worked at SNL with so-and-so," but the events aren't described at all, and those stories aren't really told. Then amidst all of this cursory information, there will be one random event presented in a lot of detail, and all those parts seemed to be unimportant, peripheral stories, like the time Amy handcuffed herself to her best friend in elementary school. There was a lot of going backwards and then jumping forwards in time, which made some of the stories hard to follow, and the themes seemed all mixed together. Parts almost seemed like they were written stream of consciousness style- the organization was genuinely confusing. In the end, I felt like there was no real take-away. I didn't learn anything new about Amy Poehler, and any of the "advice" was really obvious and unoriginal. It might be a bit more amusing to listen to the audio version.

The only reason I picked up this book in the first place was because my book club was reading it. I got about 1/3 of the way through, but really didn't care about what she had to say, just not interested in Amy Poehler and didn't want to waste any more of my time.
I liked the takeaways, and her insights about mothering and kids.

I hated this book. I'd say that if Amy Poehler wasn't a celebrity, this wouldn't have been published, but that isn't true. The truth is that if Tina Fey's book wasn't so successful, and she wasn't friends with Amy Poehler, than this wouldn't have been published. Bossypants was a funny, cute, and sometimes offered some decent life advice. This book is Amy Poehler talking about how wonderful she is. We get it. You think you're lower middle class, you did some drugs, you were poor in the "cool" way that liberal arts kids love to be after college to prove that they don't care about money. Whatever. I'm actually sad I read this because I love her comedy, but now I'll know what an annoying person she is in real life every time I see her :/

reference_book.title: Marked (House of Night, #1)
reference_book.review_text:
Early on in my reading of Marked, I wasn't at all sure I would like this young adult novel. The story of Zoey Redbird, a sixteen year old girl who is unhappy at home, becoming "marked" as a fledgling vampyre, just seemed a bit forced. I wanted to feel a part of her story but her angst was overwhelming and I couldn't really see where the plot was headed. However, about midway through, the book picked up steam and by the last few chapters, I was eagerly turning the pages in order to find out how Zoey's unusual powers would manifest and where it all would lead. 
 Marked is an imaginative take on vampyres, weaving "old" pagan religious themes throughout and incorporating ancient history into its background. I liked the idea of a society where vampyrism is openly known and accepted, and I liked the School of Night where fledgling vampyres are taken for further training. I loved Zoey's learning to accept herself and step up as a leader at the school, and even the cursing seems realistic. What I didn't like was the obvious prejudice against traditional religion, and the "mini-sermons" we receive early on against drugs, drinking, and oral sex from Zoey's point of view. I liked Zoey's friends but felt that her acceptance into such a tight group so immediately didn't ring true, and I had to wonder at just why Erik, the hot young vampyre, was so attracted so quickly to Zoey. There are also some very lucky coincidences, such as Zoey's Native American grandmother having taught her purification rites which come in very handy. Thankfully these annoyances were overcome by the general storytelling and the excitement of the last half of the book. 
 Marked is the first in the series and I'll definitely be looking for the next two. I am captured by Zoey's world and want to see how her special spiritualism develops over time. This book also left enough unanswered questions that I'm drawn to find out more. With a caution that this book would probably be better for more mature readers with its incidents of sexual tension and cursing, I can say I'm intrigued enough to recommend this one.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Awful. I tried reading this on vacation, but it wasn't even good enough to be a beach read. I loved the first 8 novels in the series, as well as the other add on Ali's Pretty Little Lies, but this was terrible. 
 Firstly, it's not a cohesive story like the other books - it's just four short stories, one for each girl. To be perfectly honest, I only got about two paragraphs into the second story (Emily's) before giving up entirely. Mrs. Fields signed Emily up to be an elf at Christmas? I'm sorry, no. Pretty sure that's a plot from Saved by the Bell or Full House. Hanna's story (the first) was pretty bad as well and didn't really seem to fit in with the timeline of the regular series. As I said, I haven't read the other ones but they sound pretty bad based on what I've read here. 
 I mean no disrespect to Sara Shepard, it's just that I know she can do better than this. In fact, if you told me this was ghostwritten, I'd believe you. The plots had no thought put into them and the writing seemed off - characters saying things they typically wouldn't say, for instance. If you're a die-hard of the series you'll probably want to read it, but I recommend skipping it.
Better than I thought it would be. It was quite intriguing and there were a few twists and turns here and there, but it wasn't really as good as the other books.

I really thought this was going to be a fun in-between novella. So wrong. 
 It's broken down into 4 novellas, one for each girl (Hanna, Emily, Aria & Spencer), and turns out to be longer than any of the first 4 books. 
 Each novella looks into how the girls are spending their Winter breaks. None of them intertwine, and each seems to be completely boring, or so far fetched & ridiculous. (Aria?! Seriously?!) 
 I read this pretty fast, but only because I was hoping it would get better at some point. I definitely could have skipped this one since it re-capped everything that'd happened so far into a few short sentences, and I'm sure we'll be finding out in book 5 that there's another A lurking around the corner.

** spoiler alert ** 
 OMG , I have to admit that this series is one of my all-time favourites and I am loving every bit of it , when I read that their was to be a new book - I couldn't wait , though at first I was a tad disappointed as the title was originally called Ali's Little Secrets and I thought it might have been more a prequel to the whole Pretty Little Liars saga but I soon got over that. 
 Pretty Little Secrets is in fact, in a way a collection of four short stories and has been slotted as an in-betweener novel which authors like Janet Evanovich has done and proved to be popular. Pretty Little Secrets takes place after Book #4 Unbelievable , the girls school days are over and it's time for the Christmas/Winter Break and of course, these 4 pretty little liars are still up to mischief and can't seem to find themselves out of trouble especially when school is out. The Pretty Little Secrets is split into four stories , each one telling the Winter secrets of the characters. 
 First up is Hanna, Lucas is away on holiday with the gorgeous family friend Brooke and Hanna is bored so she hits the gym and meets the hunky and good-looking instructor Vince. Vince talks Hanna into joining the Winter Boot-camp and Hanna wanting to dig her claws into him , goes along but it seems Hanna has competition in the form of a girl named Dinah. Can Hanna win over the affections of Vince even if it means getting her Pretty little liar hands dirty once again ? We also see some blackmailing going on between Hanna and her step-sister Kate and we discover that Hanna and Ashley Marin are in fact Jewish. 
 Next up on the Pretty Little Liars list is Emily. Somebody is messing with the Christmas decorations at her mum's church, community groups and the neighbourhood and they have their eyes on the elves at the local mall as the suspects. The old Santa has been fired for lewd behaviour - for more take reference to the creepy Santa in Hanna's story. Emily with much reluctance from her mum has been hired as the replacement elf and been sent in to spy. Can Emily find herself a part of the group and get them to spill their secrets? When a prank goes wrong and her friends are arrested , can Emily spring them with a little blackmail heading the officer's way as Emily has photos of him in a compromising position and he could lose his job, credibility if they were ever to get out . 
 Third , which was the most surprising and interesting story and I can admit I was shocked and would never have guessed it. Aria's family is celebrating the Winter Solstice, when a retreat visit goes bad , Aria finds herself back home alone in Rosewood . However, not for long as she recieves a visit from her ex-boyfriend in Iceland Halljborn. He is on the run from the police and staying on a temporary visa , he needs a way to stay in the country - so get ready for this "ARIA AND HALLJBORN HIGHTAIL TO VEGAS AND GET MARRIED". Will her parents find out about this little adventure and what will Aria's reaction be when she discovers the real reason Halljborn fled Iceland ? 
 Last but not least , Spencer's tale. It seems that a common thread has developed between Spencer and Melissa , they both like the same type of guys and they have a habit of sharing them between the two of them. On a family holiday, Spencer meets Colin at the local Tennis Club and falls head over heels with him but it seems that Colin has another admirer that Spencer doesn't know about - Melissa and when he chooses Melissa over Spencer - it's a War of the Sisters once again but what will happen when the sisters realise they have been duped and that Colin is in fact married , will the two be able to stay friendly to exact revenge on Colin ? 
 Find out what these Pretty Little Liars did over Winter Break in "Pretty Little Secrets" by Sara Shepard.

book_b.title: Never Too Far (Rosemary Beach, #2; Too Far, #2)
book_b.user_review:
Well, she does it again! Talented author Abbi Glines has produced an excellent sequel with her outstanding book Never Too Far. 
 It was the lies, harboured secrets and nastiness that broke Blaire's heart. It was the purity, innocence and beauty of Blaire, that broke Rush's. 
 Because of the lies and deceit, Blaire was rudderless, her world lacking the foundation she needed to continue. It was heartbreaking to see her resolution to only trust in herself - but understandable. I cried for the abandoned, desolate girl, whose only source of comfort, came from the tombstone of her mother. 
 It was equally devastating to see the anguish Rush both experienced and caused in his attempt at a relationship with his sweet Blaire. Not so surprising for this beautiful, deeply loyal man with so little example in his life of love without manipulation. I would so love to see a third novel in this series, if only to read of Rush learning to forgive himself for his erred sense of justice and to read of his growth as a man under the tender, genuine loving of Blaire without guilt baring so heavily on his heart. 
 Such is the talent of Abbi Glines. She can evoke such powerful, emotional responses with her words. At just the right times, she would also wonderfully provide lightness, often in the form of Bethy. How I would love to know her story as well. By changing the writing style, with each chapter shifting between Blaire and Rush's POV, this cleverly allowed the reader to enjoy the insight and depth of both characters. This was a good decision. 
 As silly as this might sound, I would also love for a third book to see the spoilt, immature and manipulative Georgianna to be held accountable for her responsibility in the ruination of the many lives her lies resulted in. I would want Nan to have the opportunity to heal, with truth and trust as a foundation as opposed to spite and hate. To see her capable of both being loved and loving. 
 Never Too Far was not, in any way, all doom and gloom as the above suggests. There were many sad moments, but it was also a story of hope. Hope for redemption, hope for change and of course, hope for love. Please write some more Ms Glines!!!

sample_reviews.review_text:
I did not know what the book was about before I read it and it was everything I wanted. 
 Reading about Hemingway and his experiences in Paris with some of the best writers and artists like Scott Fitzgerald, Ezra Pound, James Joyce, T.S.Eliot and a whole lot of others, it felt like I was in my own fairy tale!

This is the newly restored edition of my all time favorite book. The Preface by Patrick Hemingway and the Introduction by Sean Hemingway provide new perspective on the writing of this book by their father/grandfather and the changes to the original manuscript made by Hemingway's fourth wife Mary. 
 After reading it I can't say that there was much different although I loved the way they included several versions of the same lines to show how his thought process worked when he was writing. It is true that his actual descriptions of Scott Fitzgerald were far more compassionate and positive than what was published based on earlier drafts of his work. 
 To me the most interesting thing is his writing about Hadley. When you remember that this book was written over 30 years after their marriage ended and while he was with his fourth wife, his loving, lovely words about her are almost difficult to bear. Much of this book is really a love letter to her. 
 Such a fascinating writer.
I like Hemingway's fiction but could not get into this.

So why does one read A Moveable Feast? I like Hemingway and I love Paris, so it's a must read, right? A friend said she finished it and still didn't feel like she knew Hemingway; yet, it's a memoir. She's right. He wrote like a journalist even in these short takes on his life in Paris in the early 1920s. But I find it interesting to see what he includes and what he omits. Surely this tells us something about Hemingway. He includes lots of references to how poor they were, but they are always drinking beer and wine in one cafe after another. He talks in several stories about the beautiful women he encounters yet he resists them like a man committed to his wife Hadley, whom we never describes or mentions in a very positive way. He talks about writing at cafe tables, but not much about the craft of writing. Whether you like Hemingway or Paris or neighter, you should read the chapter on Scott Fitzgerald if nothing else. Gatsby may make much more sense.
At least it was short
One of the best books ever. I wasn't lucky enough to live in Paris as a young man but when I did visit this book came with me
The only Hemingway work I could tolerate!

This was an okay read, 
 I enjoyed the first few parts where he talks about writing. For example, he mentions he writes in the morning or in a place where is by himself like a cafe or something; and that once his work is done for the day, he closes his book, and doesn't/didn't think of writing until the next day so he had ideas ready to go. 
 But towards the middle it got boring. He talked too much of Scott as well nearing the end. I just didn't care for some dialogues. 
 I also disliked how he kept looking at women or making certain comments despite having a wife. 
 I lost interest towards the end and skimmed instead and was shocked to read about his affair. 
 I am not a fan of such thing but I don't even hate on the guy because he is no more or because it's just ehh Idk. Nothing comes out of hate from this book because you take your lessons and shut the book. 
 For me what I took away was the writing tip that was mentioned a few times. 
 Other than that, not much.

Hemingway's spare writing style is very evocative and draws you into 1920s Paris and the so-called "Lost Generation." This version includes unedited pieces of sketches Hemingway prepared for the book before he died, some of which he had intended to discard. I found I missed an editor's touch but overall, it's well worth reading.

A very enjoyable surface-level dive into Hemingway and Paris, for true fans of either. This 'memoir' is little snippets, written long after the fact, of Hemingway's time spent poor, hungry, and writing in Paris during the roaring twenties there. 
 It features a cast of characters familiar to any Hemingway/Midnight in Paris fan, most prominently Gertrude Stein, The Fitzgeralds, and more painters. It contains scenes of writing in cafes and walking through the Luxembourg Gardens, as well as a road trip debacle with FScott. 
 Hemingway writes well, as you'd want him to, and brings you into his world - albeit at arm's length in diary-like entries. There are many classic Hemingway aphorisms here. It prepared me nicely for our Paris trip (since much of the locations and feelings remain frozen in time there), but it's not a change-your-life book or fully baked novel. One can tell it was composed of scraps to be published posthumously.

book_b.title: Purple Hibiscus
book_b.user_review: A very strong debut.

sample_reviews.review_text: Although I finished this book - it took too long for anything to really happen and then at the end it was almost as if the author ran out of things to say as, I felt, it was very abrupt and just ended. This is quite far removed from my normal reading material so maybe this is why I never enjoyed it.

I literally have been wanting to read this book for years and finally was able to get to it; how sad that it was so disappointing. I feel that the story had a lot of potential that wasn't capitalized on (Kambili's conflicting emotions about her father and her upbringing, for example) and it left the overall novel feeling underdeveloped. The interweaving of political unrest and cultural norms was interesting and provided a good backdrop to an overall depressing story centered on Kambili's dismal home life, but I don't feel that anything was sufficiently fleshed out in order to tie it into the central storyline. While the events that occur in the last 20 pages of the book might seem to some to have been an inevitable progression/reaction, it still felt like it came out of left field to me and was not thoroughly analyzed by the characters - almost like it was just included for shock value. In spite of my disappointment, I'm willing to give Adichie another try and I'm hoping that I can better connect with Half of a Yellow Sun.

Purple Hibiscus, Nigerian-born writer Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie's debut, begins like many novels set in regions considered exotic by the western reader: the politics, climate, social customs, and, above all, food of Nigeria (balls of fufu rolled between the fingers, okpa bought from roadside vendors) unfold like the purple hibiscus of the title, rare and fascinating. But within a few pages, these details, however vividly rendered, melt into the background of a larger, more compelling story of a joyless family. Fifteen-year-old Kambili is the dutiful and self-effacing daughter of a rich man, a religious fanatic and domestic tyrant whose public image is of a politically courageous newspaper publisher and philanthropist. No one in Papa's ancestral village, where he is titled "Omelora" (One Who Does For the Community), knows why Kambili's brother cannot move one of his fingers, nor why her mother keeps losing her pregnancies. When a widowed aunt takes an interest in Kambili, her family begins to unravel and re-form itself in unpredictable ways

This book was moving and definitely sad but very well written, as all of Adichie's books have been. The characters really felt dynamic and real and it was great to see into Nigerian culture- British influence vs. original tribal influence. The family dynamic was terrible and I hated their father so much! The end of the book happened so quickly and really surprised me. This book was good, for sure, especially for anyone interested in religious extremism or shaming and abuse that happens in hyper-religious homes. I wanted more for Kabili, but I also love that the ending felt sweet in a way that was believable and real.

I really enjoyed this book - the plot and characters were great, real, honest, and totally believable. The description and metaphors were a bit obvious at times, which held the book back from being truly great. 
 The father figure as loved by the community but a monster in his family is an important one to look at. We often see many men as heroes and pillars of their communities, when in reality they're horribly abusive people. This duality exists, to varying extents, in all of us and the author's intense writing about it is something that can teach us about ourselves and the complexity of people. As a first book it's pretty impressive and I look forward to reading the rest of her work.
this is simply a wonderful book
i honestly just love how chimamanda ngozi adichie writes. it's very believable and genuine.
a manual on dysfunctional families but also Nigerian life in modern times - the ending was a surprise but the journey to that point was interesting.

I started reading this book yesterday evening and read only 50 pages or so. I liked reading it, but it was late in the day and I had other things to do. This morning, I read about 50 more pages. Then I had to go out to meet someone for coffee. Already, I felt the story take hold of my thoughts. I had to shrug it off to concentrate on other tasks. When I came home, I picked up the book and began to read. I read almost without stop to the end. My stomach was in knots over what Kambili was going through. I was reading slowly to savour the fantastic details of the world Kambili lived in - her home in Enugu and her aunt's home in Nsukka, as well as their vacation home in Abba. I felt the heat of the sun and that freshness of the world after the heavy rains. I choked on the kerosene fumes in Auntie Ifeoma's kitchen, and I twitched at the flight of the 'aku' after the rains, recalling the swarms of flying termites I saw and wanted to avoid in Kenya. I longed for an invitation to a Nigeria feast so I could taste garri, fufu, and all the many dishes that Kambili ate just to see all these details come to life. On the other hand, I wanted all the repression and sadness and fear in Kambili's life to go away. I ached for her and wept for her. I couldn't put the book down while she was going through such difficult times. The room I was in darkened as the sun set and only when the words became hard to read did I get up to turn the light on. I was that engrossed in ready Kambili's story. Only after a major event happened did I get up and make myself some soup for dinner. It almost got cold because I let it cool a bit too long while I returned to the story and forgot about eating. 
 I must read more Adichie. This is my second book by her. The characters in this story are so rich in detail. I read the paperback published by Fourth Estate, which looks like a branch of Harper Collins. I mention this because the paperback included an essay by Adichie called 'Tiny Wonders' and little biography in which she tells how Chinua Achebe was a great influence on her writing. "Reading Achebe gave me permission to write about my world," she writes. Thank goodness for that, I say! I was also quite chuffed that I recognised her opening line that begins "Things started to fall apart..." I didn't realise that Achebe was her hero until I read the biography after finishing the book. I just ordered his "Things Fall Apart" from my library - I thought I had a copy - because Adichie makes me hunger for more books from Africa. I have a soft spot for Kenya from my years there, and I don't know Nigeria. Adichie is helping correct that oversight. She is helping to flesh out bits of history that I have forgotten, and she is doing so with a storytelling skill that can leave me breathless at times. I was breathless during the tenser moments of this story because I felt fear, anguish, and sorro. I was breathless from the description of Nsukka in her little essay 'Tiny Wonders'. Her stories are like fine silk tapestries with such depth and colour that they come to life before your very eyes.

Ok, so the story goes something like this: "Today I woke up early in the morning, had pancakes and orange juice for breakfast, and then my dad beat me and my brother half to death. Then I mopped the blood from the floor and got ready for church. The sermon was lovely. Oh how I love my dad, he's such a great man blah blah blah". Something wrong with this picture? Yes indeed. The girl is so emotionless and matter-of-fact about the beatings, that it made me not care about her at all. I mean, come ON, if my dad beat my pregnant mum until she miscarried, I'd want to kill the bastard, not worship him like he was god.

Amy's mother moved from their home in California to Connecticut a month ago. Now that school is out she needs Amy to bring her car to her in their new home. The only problem is that since the death of her father three months ago, Amy does not drive. Enter Roger. Roger's father lives in Philadelphia and it's time for him to go visit. They agree that Roger will drive them across country in four days, leaving Amy safe with her mom. Amy's mom plots a direct, if boring, route for them. Predictably, they choose to take another path. 
 This is such a well done depiction of a road trip. Matson clearly does her research, as they eat in regional restaurants and see all the right cultural landmarks. Each chapter has it's own play list of songs that when read carefully offered hints to the coming pages. The book includes a few pages of a travel scrapbook that a 
 Amy fills in as they go, as well as pictures they could have taken and copies of their receipts from various restaurants and stops. It is exactly what I would have done at her age. 
 Amy is still in high school but she is dealing with a lot of life changes. Her father, to whom she was very close, has recently died. Her twin brother is in rehab in North Carolina. Her mother has moved away and Amy feels very lonely and isolated. She is still struggling with both her father's death and his absence. This trip gives her the opportunity to mourn her father and to figure out who she is. 
 Roger has his own reasons for wanting to take the trip. His girlfriend broke up with him without explanation and he wants to take a little detour to find out why. Roger is both good looking and charmingly geeky and it's hard to imagine why anyone would break up with him, but so be it. He's also very understanding and not at all pushy about her reasons for not driving and always knows exactly when to push and when to hold back. If Amy hadn't fallen in love with him I would have. 
 The secondary characters are mostly fun as well, but the book is mainly just about Roger and Amy, since they are the only two in the car. 
 Verdict? Excellent YA fiction. Some serious notes, but overall a sweet little love story backed up with the fun of a road trip.

 Ten Things We did was the perfect summer novel. It is full of fun content but also has a seriousness to it. I found the balance between the two just right. Like I said earlier, Sarah's writing style made me breeze through the novel. She didn't overwhelm me with unnecessary details but was able to pen her settings so visually, I felt as if I was one of Vi's and April's roommates.  What I loved about Ten Things We Did was that the author got into the minds of teenagers almost flawlessly, including the male characters. The book touches on a lot of subjects that seem to come in contact with most teenagers; Alcohol, partying and Sex, but I thought the author wrote it well.  I loved Ten Things We Did(And probably shouldn't have). It had everything I look for in a summer read but with a little extra punch to it. A great read for soaking in the sun!

Not only did April encounter sex in this book, but she learned the responsibilities of sex and the consequences of it. I like how April took care of herself by going to Planned Parenthood, getting check, tested, and prepared.  April as well as her friends go through a lot but learn so much. They had planned thinking that it was going to easy to be alone, with no parents. Then reality hit. Ready Player One is the most referential book I have ever read. Its pages drip with 80s pop culture references, some of them obvious, many of them not. It's entertaining at first, especially when you understand the reference, but then it becomes a bit obnoxious and excessive. This, in fact, is a good analogue to the book itself. Its beginning is much stronger than its conclusion, and the aspects of the book which were its most entertaining element at the start become tired and worn-out by the end. 
 The book is on the whole enjoyable. I described it to a co-worker as "aggressively okay." The narrative pulls you along at a steady pace, interesting things happen, the mystery of the "Easter Egg" is sufficiently compelling, but it's the finer details that start to nag. As mentioned, the references, the worship of 80s culture, although explained through the narrative, becomes irritating. The details of the story are impressive, and the author's passion for the subject matter screams on every page. The writing and dialogue serves the story fine and provides only a few moments of profundity. 
 Sadly, the author, Ernest Cline, commits one of the most grievous mistakes of any science fiction or fantasy story, which I call "The Magic Wand." Essentially "The Magic Wand" is a narrative tool to magically fix the story's most perplexing problems. (Did you know reversing the Earth's orbit reverses time itself!? Thank you, Superman). Often times authors use this Wand when they've painted themselves into a corner. "Oh, look, now the main character can fly!" or "travel through time!" or some such thing. Ready Player One's Magic Wand is the main character's outlandish sudden ability to perfectly plan and execute a plan of such devious and conniving genius it leaves both the characters in the book and the reader of the book completely stunned. Furthermore, throughout the book, there are far too many instances of the character needing to know some obscure or obtuse fact about 80s pop culture and the main character conveniently notifies the reader: "Good thing I've watched this film exactly 175 times." Good thing, indeed. 
 Having said all of this, I enjoyed Ready Player One for what it was. I was especially interested in the possible and entirely plausible future of virtual reality that the book showcases. It's both exciting and dismaying. Although the messaging of the book is muddled, which is too bad, the fiction aspect of it was very interesting. (It's worth mentioning that according to an article in Businessweek, each new Oculus Rift employee--a company which has created a virtual reality headset--is issued a copy of Ready Player One). A few years ago I was extremely skeptical of virtual reality's ability to be adopted by the mainstream. Although that hasn't happened in a significant way yet, I do believe it will; in addition, I believe it very well could herald a massive shift in how we consume and participate in entertainment, education, business, commerce, and even how we interact with and make sense of reality itself. Ready Player One shows a world that is either terrifying or exhilarating depending on your worldview. I'm not convinced the author knows exactly which one it is. 
 Ready Player One is being adapted into a film by Steven Spielberg, and I think it might have a better chance being a great story as a film than a book. I think the story needs to be trimmed, sliced and diced a bit, and leave behind many of the arcane details meant to be enjoyed by only a few. There is definitely a fun adventure to be found here, but it might take some other storytellers to tell it a bit better.

book_b.title: The Rose & the Dagger (The Wrath & the Dawn, #2)
book_b.user_review:
This review is spoiler free! 
 A satisfying end to an enchanting story. 4/5 stars. 
 I enjoyed this very much and more than the first installment of the story: 
 The Wrath and the Dawn 
 . This was partly because The Rose and the Dagger delivers entertaining magical shenanigans, and also because my enjoyment of book 1 was hampered by some irritating stylistic quirks which were mercifully absent from book 2. 
 Character-wise, things also improved. Tariq is far less annoying in The Rose and the Dagger. And while I still didn't warm to Shazi or Khalid, their personalities were consistent and their actions made sense at all times. Some new characters were also introduced and I got so involved in one of their stories it managed to make me cry. 
 I read most of this book in one long sitting and I think that's best. In fact, I think these two books would benefit from being read back-to-back. Firstly, because I found I'd forgotten many things which happened in book 1 (although don't worry - the author drops in lots of little reminders). But mostly because I think the triumph of these books in their tone. The story is based on 1001 Nights, and the entire tale is cloaked in a convincing ancient, mystic, exotic atmosphere. Within this fairy tale cloud, the way the characters speak and act makes perfect sense. I suspect if you keep dipping in and out of the story this spell could be broken and certain elements of the narrative may appear strange and even ridiculous. 
 Finally, major points to Ahdieh for writing a two-book story. It seems like all YA series these days are trilogies or longer. Bucking this trend, The Rose and the Dagger wraps up the story started in book 1 nicely with no loose ends. 
 Overall: fans of The Wrath and the Dawn won't be disappointed. A satisfying end to a magical, mystical tale which successfully balances romance and adventure.

There were too many circumstances, too many subtlies of relationships and friendships that were skated over because the details were all in the previous book and knowing them would have made this a better book for me. So do yourself a favor and be sure you read it in the correct order! 
 So why was is 'meh' for me you ask? Well, I didn't find it particularly well written - there were times that the descriptive adjectives were - hmm - just not right. I also found the constant unsheathing of swords a little disconcerting - man, these guys had too much testosterone and seemed really quick to flare up and take blood. "It was because they were two parts of a whole. He did not belong to her. And she did not belong to him. It was never about belonging to someone. It was about belonging together."

 Overall Thoughts: This is currently my favorite series/books of 2017, and in my top 5 series of all times list for sure. I didn't not expect to feel this strongly for these characters so quickly, and to be absolutely entwined in both the world and the plot so quickly each time I picked up the book. I could honestly never put it down, and even a few days after finishing, I'm still amazed by how thoroughly this installment made me feel. It managed to wreck my heart, and fix it moments later, which is not something many books can claim. 
 The Good: Badass characters (from a broken king to a powerful queen, and almost all characters had their shining moments!), a good wrap up for all characters with few, if any, loose ends, and a fantastic plot all the way through. 
 The Bad: I honestly cannot think of anything to put in this category at the moment. 
 SPOILERS BEGIN HERE 
 The Characters: I didn't think I could like this group anymore than I already did. We saw Tariq somewhat redeem himself, and Shazi to prove herself as strong as capable, but still human (losing a fight with Spider, etc.). In addition, all characters got an ending that they deserve, with the punishments they deserved. This made the ending so freaking satisfying, as we saw this villains that took advantage of teenagers meet their ends at the hands of them. 
 The Plot: While I have to admit some parts of the magic plot seemed a bit thrown together, the rest of plot more than made up for it. It showcased the strength of the characters while keeping them human, and added twists and betrayals into the mix as well. I also enjoyed the small war that did took place, started by the enemy but finished by them. Oh, and while I don't often enjoy having my heart wrenched from my chest when thinking everything will be okay, I mind a bit less when they put it back and cover it with some duct tape. That final scene made me audibly gasp, and if Renee Ahdieh hadn't fixed it all with a bit of magic shortly after, I doubt I could have ever forgiven her for so thoroughly breaking my heart. 
 The World Building: While the world building wasn't too elaborated upon from the first book, we did learn more about the magical side of things. However, many questions still remain in that area, since magic seemed both important, yet not. 
 The Favorite Character: Khalid & Shazi 
 Buy it, Borrow it, or Bin it: Buy it (seriously, you'll thank me later.)

reference_book.review_text:
I haven't been through many books about the Vietnam War. It's tough sledding to relive it because it tore our nation apart. Upon finishing the book this morning I'm feeling so sad and moved by it it's difficult for me to write a review worthy of its greatness and it was a great book. It took almost 2 weeks to get through it and I'm left feeling sort of numb and drained by the experience. 
 I liked Karl Marlantes's "What it's like to go to War" so much I had to put this one on the book shelf whether it was difficult to or not. It's a fictional account of the War but Marlantes brings his experiences as a veteran of the Vietnam War to life in this book. 
 There are the terrible battle stories, the horrors of seeing fellow Marines get put through a meat grinder but it's much more than that. Marlantes gives a lot of time to the mundane, the sublime, the politics, the racism and the emotional bonding that takes place between groups of men that experience the ultimate in horrors. 
 The story of the men who administered the war makes you think they were all a bunch of insane idiots trying to advance their military careers no matter what price the grunts had to pay for it. And the grunts do pay for it in a big way, in this story you learn they do more than once for the same piece of ground no less. 
 In hindsight after finishing the book it's hard to judge any of the leadership of the military involved in the war because they didn't get the kind of support from the government or the citizens at home. So it lead to confused sporadic bloody battles in impossible fighting conditions in the jungle were they killed many NVA troops and won some individual battles but in the end lost the war because of the media and meddling politicians in DC that didn't support nor understand what was going on in Vietnam. 
 Still the story of the men in this book will move you, infuriate you, disgust you, amaze you, shock you and leave you with that awful feeling of how so many young men lost their lives in one of the worst Wars and causes in American history. Still the bravery, the nobility, the humility, the pride and the humanity of the men of this war must never be forgotten because they like all veterans of foreign wars deserve respect. Some would argue they deserve more respect. Take the journey it's worth it but be warned it's not for the faint of heart. 
 Bronson Pinchot narrated this audiobook and he did an outstanding job of it just like he did with Marlantes' other book. He's one of the best in the business, he held me with a death grip throughout.

book_a.user_review:
Most everyone has seen the movie I'm sure but maybe not read the book. It goes into more detail about his crimes and the ending wasn't what I expected. I always like to do some research on the non-fiction and biographical books I listen to afterwards. I read that some of the book's crimes couldn't be authenticated in some instances and that the man who help him write it may have embellished parts of his story. Abagnale claims that many of the people he conned were just embarrassed that they had been swindled and that's why they denied it. Regardless he did get away with some amazing crimes and did it between the ages of 16 and 21. 
 In one YouTube video interview he had with the BBC that I watched he explains he never received a dime from the movie and after he went to work for the FBI to help train agents about fraud he wasn't paid either. He said he couldn't take the money because he owed a debt to society and since he had 3 children he had to be accountable and honest. In fact every cent he wrote in bad checks he repaid which is incredible considering over a 5 year period it added up to $2.5 million dollars. 
 He was an extremely intelligent con man, boy really, who seemed to always be one step ahead of law enforcement. One of the parts of the book that was unbelievable was when he passed the bar exam to become an attorney in Georgia. He made some bogus college transcripts studied for about 6 weeks took the exam failed, took it again and failed then on the 3rd try passed. He was a 16 year high school drop out that hadn't taken a single college class and was able to pass the bar exam. 
 I really admire him for that because after going through an 880 hour Police Academy course I really struggled to do all the studying necessary to pass all the difficult law tests. It was like a 5 month crash course on all the laws and given that I didn't have the best memorization skills it didn't come easy for me. For Abagnale it was just another day at the office. Good reading, I recommend the book.

book_b.title: Invisible Man
book_b.user_review:
Invisible Man was a book written about racism by Ralph Ellison in 1952. Here's a brief plot summary in case some of you haven't heard about the book. 
 "Invisible Man is the story of a young black man from the South who does not fully understand racism in the world. Filled with hope about his future, he goes to college, but gets expelled for showing one of the white benefactors the real and seamy side of black existence. He moves to Harlem and becomes an orator for the Communist party, known as the Brotherhood. In his position, he is both threatened and praised, swept up in a world he does not fully understand. As he works for the organization, he encounters many people and situations that slowly force him to face the truth about racism and his own lack of identity." 
 It was an interesting book about the injustice of racism but the book's ending was horrible. I don't really see how a book like this advances the Black American's cause in the fight for equal rights. I get the underlying angst and the futility that many Blacks may have had in the early 50's but in my opinion Martin Luther King had a better idea about 10 years later. The main character in the book turned out to be a self loathing cad and instead of taking the moral high road he resorted to the stereotypical angry Black Man placing all the blame on everyone else for his own problems and in the end didn't have the courage or will to rise above it. 
 Honesty this is the first book I just can't recommend because the ending was so horrible.

It's taken me a long time to get through this book. Not because of any lost of interest, but because it was a lot to take in. Navigating the emotions and struggles of the the unnamed protganist was a challenging and rewarding experience. The sections addressing the prejudice and manipulation he faces, while at the same time being forced into performing like a perfect gentlemen, is about the angriest I've ever felt on behalf of a character. It's an important book, and I can see why so many recommend it as "the one book every person should read." 
 Had I been strictly reading this book, I probably would have given it four stars instead of five, due to the twisted nature of the prose that skips back and forth between the protganist's reality and his fantastic interority. It's well-done; it's just a technique that I find hard to follow. But as I listen to this book, narrated by Joe Morton, I'm bumping it up to five due to his amazing performance.

Well, I can say that I've read it. But I did have to force myself to finish it because it is one of those books that I felt like I "should." For the first half of the book, I just did not like the protagonist. If Ellison's motivation was to show the crushing effects of racism, then his character should have been less of a self-centered fool and less complacent in the events that happened to and around him. By the second half of the novel, the character has become much stronger, more community-oriented and more likeable. Unfortunately, it's at this point that the author's political agenda clouds the story. In the end, if readers do take a serious look at themselves and ask how they contribute to the invisibility of others- because I assure you, no matter who you are, there is someone in this world who you do not "see"- then it is an important contribution and should continue to be one of those classics that must be read. I simply wish that I had enjoyed the process.

Often I feel like I pick up a book at a perfect time. This one hit home. A lot of good things can be said about this novel. I'm sure other people have other feels, but if you're wondering what's the point to it all and searching for meaning in this vast wasteland of miscommunication and failure that we call life, you'll find patient and profound rhetoric in Ralph's Invisible Man.

This book was assigned to me as an AP English summer assignment. Reading a book over the summer for homework is daunting however I'm glad my new english teacher picked this one. 
 Invisible Man by Ralph Ellison takes place during in the early twentieth century and told by an unnamed narrator. The reader follows the narrator through his telling of what eventually led to his 'invisibility'. This novel examines numerous themes such as racism and identity (and more). This novel made me think on a different level.

Let me risk the scorn of the ages by saying that I think this may be the most overrated classic in American literature. The first couple chapters would have made compelling short stories, but the book as a whole is an incoherent mess. It's no surprise Ellison could never finish his followup, since this is barely finished. I'm baffled as to how this became part of the modernist gospel.

However, I found myself most interested in the nuances of day to day life in Shanghai before the revolution and in Los Angeles. I did not care for their toxic sisterly relationship or bond. I don't know how two sisters who claim to love each other like these two do could end up with one being so manipulative and the other such a doormat (and realizing this!) and continue to coexist in somewhat harmony for so many years.

Better than Peony or The Secret Fan, IMHO. The pace is slow at the beginning, and then it's rushed at the end. Despite that, I feel that the characters are much more fleshed out and See does a good job of pulling at the complicated strings of family, duty, and love. 
 I can definitely relate to the sisters; I am the eldest and raised in America, and my younger sister is American born and raised. The tension between sisters and tradition-bound family is realistic, something I most resonated with.
I really enjoyed this book. Can't wait to read the next one.

book_b.title: Lost Souls (Dean Koontz's Frankenstein, #4)
book_b.user_review: I listened to this as an audiobook. I didn't listen to the previous books in the series but was easily able to follow the plot.
