sample_reviews.review_text: Relief... that's what I felt after finishing this book, complete and utter relief, at last being free of a plodding story that was so engineered and formulaic that it resembled a ten tonne truck heading straight at you. The characters garnered no warmth or empathy from the reader and certainly didn't evolve in any way what's so ever, in fact some of them suddenly found they had hidden talents just because the story needed to go in a certain direction. I really feel this was a case of Mr Koontz flogging the life and death out of what was initially a reasonable rewrite of a good story just for profit. Now just because I'm a masochist I'm going to finish the series because I started, not because I 'm intrigued or hooked.
Ended on a cliffhanger! Sooooooo glad I already had Book 5 to immediately pick up and start reading!

I saw this in the store and thought Koontz would do a good job with Frankenstein. I didn't realize until a couple chapters into the story that it was the fourth in the series. I still liked it, though, and ordered all the other books in the series to read. It was horrid and violent, but the plot so captivated me that I had to find out what happened next!

Lost Souls picks up two years after Victor Helios was destroyed at the end of Dead and Alive. The two cops are now married, have a baby daughter and run a Private Detective Agency. Deucalion has returned to the monastery he lived in when the events in the first novel Prodigal Son kicked off. Erika Five and Jocko are living in a small mountain town in Montana called Rainbow Falls and are quite happy. 
 Victor Helios lived on at the end of Dead and Alive because his death activated a clone at the climax of the novel. We know the shit is going to hit the fan soon and it does. Deucalion senses his maker lives on and goes after him with the help of the two cops. Erika Five sees her maker / abusive bastard former husband walking about town in Rainbow Fall and pisses her diddies or something to that effect. 
 The huge failing of Lost Souls is how predictable it is and the fact it adds nothing new to Koontz's series. 
 Helios now goes by the name of Victor Leben (Leben is German for life) and often refers to himself as Victor Immaculate (chortle!). He's as mad as his predecessor, even more so. He still thinks human are flawed because they think and feel and are untidy, dirty and messy (whatever). 
 The New Race has become The Community but it's the same old shit. 
 He's perfected his ability to destroy the humans using a weird creature called a Builder that's made up of nano-organisms (WTF) and basically eats people and gestates (pass me a sick bucket) them in a cocoon for them to emerge as new Builders within a few hours and start the whole cycle again. The replicants only physically resemble the gestated people but are cold, detached and unemotional like - well cyborgs (!!). 
 The new, improved and totally insane Victor Immaculate Leben wants to replace all humans on earth with his Builder creature then commit suite and wipe his creations off the face of the earth thus ending the blight known as humanity. For a master plan it's pretty lame. It seems pointless to go to the effort of replacing all humans with his creation just to kill them all. Why doesn't he just nuke us or something? 
 Lost Souls just isn't worth the paper it's printed on. There's no point in continuing the story. It could have ended when Helios and his New Race got wiped out at the end of Dead and Alive and it would have been an average series of novels. Koontz however insists on flogging this dead donkey and churning out another two pointless novels where he regurgitates the same old crap. Shame on him.

The fourth book in Mr. Koontz's Frankenstein trilogy. And yes I know what I just wrote. It was my understanding (and it wouldn't be the first time I was wrong) these books were introduced as a trilogy, but it seems it is a series of two trilogies ... before Victor and after Victor. 
 Victor Helios ... aka the clone of Victor Frankenstein is busy carrying out the work of his predecessor, repopulating the world with perfect half flesh/half machine superhumans. Our usual cast of characters are out to stop him. Another good installment for fans of the series. 
 Question to anyone out there reading this series and particularly this book ... is it just my imagination or does Jocko bear a striking resemblence to a certain house elf in the infamous HP series??

It ticked me off that it ended where the climax should have been, now I have to find the next book to see what the buildup was about. I haven't read the previous either, started in the middle I guess.

 sequel coming
I find the switching of stories and POV slightly irritating now. If they were longer than maybe I would have given the book 3 stars. But I wasn't engaged enough.

I didn't enjoy this as much as Koontz' earlier Frankenstein installments. I also did not appreciate the ending; rather like a commercial break rather than the end of one installment. IMHO Koontz would have done his readers a better turn by bringing Lost Souls to a conclusion. Koontz is capable of completing a book while leaving openings for the next installment; wish he had done so with this one.
It's a pretty solid reimagining of the Frankenstein mythos. I'll continue to follow the series but more out of comfort than excitement.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I hate twist endings. 
 Okay, that's not true. I like twist endings, but only when the surprise works, and the hints have been there all along and it doesn't mean the some three hundred pages you've just read are all a lie. The book could have just ended. The hints could have been placed more clearly at the beginning. All could have been left all alone. But it had to be pushed just that little bit further and everybody had to be cannibalised and for what? A bit more of a 'ho ho! look what I can do!'? 
 And goddammit, I enjoyed the book. 
 Yes, there are hints that it was all made up. There's only so much time you can spend utterly alone before you start to crack. He starts hallucinating that Richard Parker is talking to him, the other sailor, the floating algae island, the very fact he was in the middle of the Pacific Ocean for 227 days. 
 Pi asks the investigators, and us by extension, whether we prefer the story with the animals or without. You know what? I'd prefer it without the animals. I'd like to read about a young man stuck on a boat and every one of the people onboard slowly start to die and get eaten, and when everyone is dead and gone, he slowly starts to become mad. That's what I'd like to read. 
 Sure, it was interesting, reading about how trained the tiger and all the wonders of the ocean, but it felt like a light version of Twenty Thousand Leagues Under The Sea. The island part was just nuts. 
 I did enjoy it, but the ending ruined it for me.
I'm sorry, but I officially deem it impossible for me to get into these kinds of books for, say, at least another fifteen years.

reference_book.review_text: This book lets you in on two worlds: the world of a struggling actress and the world of Brooklyn/New York, both of which I found very interesting. I would say it is a coming of age story more than a romance though there is a triangle going on between the main character, Franny, and two guys. I wish there was more description of New York, though there is a trip to Times Square to see Phantom of the Opera and drinks at Sardi's. I like the dad character who is very supportive and teaches English literature and leaves funny messages on Franny's answering machine. I like how parts of scripts Franny auditions for and dayplanner notes she writes are scattered throughout the novel. Of course, I wondered how much was autobiographical, as Lauren Graham is herself an actress and at the end she does have to straighten her hair for a part on a tv show in L.A. Graham is skilled at ending chapters with double meanings and making scenes farcical, especially when Franny has to cater and wear orange (orange?) nylons and a hair net and run into someone posh from her past. I hope Lauren Graham makes her next book about an actress living in L.A. and working on a beloved tv show....

This book was actually pretty cute! The set-up with living life like the 60s seemed a bit forced and farfetched, but once the story got rolling, it didn't even bother me anymore. As a protagonist, I absolutely loved Mallory. There have been so many contemporary YA books I've read where the main girl starts off as likeable. Then, as you get further into the plot, you end up wondering why you even liked them in the first place. With 'Going Vintage', I liked Mallory the entire book. I'm a sucker for a funny protagonist and her thoughts in general had me cracking up. She just felt real, like any normal high school girl. At first, I thought the whole cyber-wife thing was ridiculous. I mean, on paper, it sounds stupid, but the more I read, it became kind of sad. People always think of cheating as physically getting with someone else, but there's never really much focus on emotionally cheating on your boyfriend/girlfriend. In a way, it's worse because it's not like they stepped out because the other person was hot. It's because this person made them feel things that you no longer do. Emotional bonds are a lot harder to break than a brief fling or one-night stand. I couldn't help but feel horrible for Mallory when she had this revelation. 
 Maybe it's just me, but I thought Mallory's mom was ridiculous! Oh my god, this woman was a piece of work. I know that she loved her children. However, she had a terrible way of showing it. There's this one part of the book where the family goes to Disneyland to cheer Mallory up after she breaks up with her boyfriend. When her mother basically said that she was surprised that Mallory had dumped Jeremy and not the other way around . Her mom just came off as so insensitive. Later on, I was ready to laugh off the randomness of the blog her mother was writing , but I wanted to slap someone after reading the blog post about Mallory and her ex. It wasn't so much the content because the woman can blog about her life if she wants. It was more about the way things were worded. It was rude and I couldn't believe someone would write about their own kid that way . I thought that that whole situation totally crossed the line and I didn't blame Mallory for being hurt by it. 
 As for romance, can I just say that I loved Oliver? From their very first interaction, I was like shipping it so bad. That's all it took and I wanted them to be together so badly. It was refreshing to read about a relationship that was based on more than how attractive someone was. I liked how they got to know each other as friends before they ever went that direction. There was none of that 'ohmigod you're so sexy' instalove. I don't know. I just thought that there was something really sweet about their relationship. Not gonna lie, I was a bit thrown off by how things ended up for them, but it was realistic. Like, it's probably not the healthiest decision to jump right into another relationship so quickly after having your heart broken . The epilogue felt odd and kind of stuck in, but it left me happy with where Oliver and Mallory were.

She then decides to "go vintage" by swearing off technology of all kinds from the microwave to her computer.,,,Mallory's grandma begins to move into a new home while all of this goes on and she finds a notebook with a list in it. A list that will decide her future. Well, maybe. 
 Enter Oliver, Jeremy's ex-boyfriend's cousin, who signs up to help her with one of the things on her list... Pep Club. He's the president. And he is cute. 
 Sure, this book is filled with drama and family issues which kind of help me with giving it the .5 of the stars, but I really don't think I will pick up another Lindsey Levitt book..

sample_reviews.review_text: Oh my god soooooo good!!!

Okay, I've heard so many good things about Colleen Hoover's books so I wanted to pick up something of hers and see how I like it. This definitely really disappointed me. 
 From what I've heard about her writing, I expected a dramatic new-adult romance that I would be able to fly through but I didn't get that at all. There was just so much unnecessary drama and so many eye-roll worthy moments I was beginning to grow so frustrated while I was reading this. I really didn't like this book. It took me forever to read and I had no motivation to pick it up at all. It's not even like it's a long book. It's literally only 300 pages and it took me like 2 weeks to read which I rarely do because I can usually read a 600 pages book in less time than that. Reading this just left a bad taste in my mouth every time I put it down and I didn't look forward to getting back into it. 
 I didn't like the characters. They were just so super uneccisarily cheesy and I felt like it was trying to hard to be 'every book-lovers dream story.' Every time I read about Ben and Fallon getting together it was like there was a neon sign flashing over their heads. I just couldn't take it. 
 Also, I've heard a few negative reviews about this book because of Ben's actions and sexual harassment and whatnot and I have to say that I 100% agree with those reviews. I didn't like Ben at all. He just wasn't appealing at all as a character and the dumb things he'd say that were supposed to be oh so romantic just made my blood boil. I couldn't stand him and Fallon and the way he'd treat Fallon and just their whole relationship in general was toxic and I don't like it at all. So I caution you about that if you're thinking of picking this up. 
 Honestly, I thought the premise was interesting and unique but there was nothing outstanding about this book. I was hoping to really enjoy it because of how many people rave about Colleen Hoover's writing and I know I have an unpopular opinion here when I say I just really didn't notice anything special or dare I say (gasp!) enjoyable about it. It was bland and I didn't like the style of writing much either. The writing and dialogue just felt stilted and I wasn't particularly enjoying any of it. 
 I appreciate that Fallon had scars because it isn't seen much in books (at least the ones I read) so I thought that'd be an interesting factor in the book but it was literally only used as a plot device and gave Ben another reason to tell Fallon how "f****** beautiful" she is every 5 fricking minutes. Gag me with a spoon. It's nice and all, but she shouldn't need a boy to tell her she's beautiful in order to realize that she IS beautiful. Whatever. Ugh. I'm done with this issue. 
 Honestly, I don't think there was really anything I enjoyed about this book. Some parts made me angry and some were just meh. I hope Hoover's other books aren't like this because I was really looking forward to devouring a cute, cheesy new adult romance. I don't even know if I want to give any of her other ones a shot now if this is what her writing style is like. 
 Overall, I didn't like this book and I personally don't recommend it. There were just too many things that happened in this that I don't support or couldn't stomach, but that's just my opinion. If you liked this book I am in no way trying to belittle you or your opinion, this was just my experience while I read the book. And I am aware that Hoover released a video after the allegations about the issues in this book but that doesn't make me enjoy it anymore than I did. It was nice she made the effort to speak about it and I can appreciate that as a reader. Welp. Those are my thoughts. A bit disappointing.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I purchased the ebook (which begs the question-who gets the money?) and actually couldn't put it down. Obviously, the material isn't something to be impressed by, nor, for that matter, is his writing style. The one thing I will give Hitler is he was a damn good orator-not so much an author. But reading this book has never been about criticizing metaphor usage and writing technique- it's about the controversy that goes along with it. I tend to stay on the neutral side of history. Yes, bad things happen. Yes, (insert impressive number here) people were killed because of him. But, if I am completely honest, I am a sucker for a good psychopath, and tend to detach myself from personal histories and emotions. Does that make me a horrible person? Not sure I care to know. I am intrigued by certain people and certain stories, I can't help it. Does giving this book 4 stars make me a horrible person? No, of course not. Those stars aren't a pledge of allegiance to Hitler and his way of thinking, obviously. I give it 4 stars because it was a good book. A bit difficult to read sometimes, but a very interesting and intriguing book. They call it the 'Nazi Bible' and I sort of read it with that frame of mind. Just like I would read any other holy script. I don't have to agree with it to appreciate it. 
 I have read in so many reviews of this book that there are things to be learned from history, and also that there are not. I tend to think that it doesn't matter if you can learn something from it- it has already happened and there is nothing that can change it. Was it terribly horrible? Of course. Do I appreciate Hitler? Of course not. This book, for me, was more a matter of intrigue and curiosity than anything else. History has called him a monster, a tyrant, and psychopath- and rightfully so. But every story has it's intrigue.

Rather than give a knee jerk reaction to the book based on the author, or just a joke review. I felt it was write to attempt to read the book to be able to talk about the book in an informed manner. Yes, I decided to give Mein Kampf a try. I got about 12 percent of the way through the book, and eventually gave up on it. 
 I was reading it with the John Murphy translation, complete with notes. What was interesting about it is the translation was done in 1939, so much of Hitler's history was unavailable to Mr. Murphy. Rather than judge the book based on his future actions, as that is unfairly prejudicial, I'll judge the book based on John Murphy/Adolf Hitler's writing as composed in the book. However I will admit my preconceived notions on Adolf Hitler is impossible to forget, I believe it would be impossible for most people to put them in a box. To attempt it however such I'll be referring to the writer as "Adolf" as his last name has a very negative connotation. 
 With that being said, I only read two full chapters, and I fully admit that's not the "whole book" or even a large part of the book, but I felt I could not continue further, I had no interest in it. The main problem of the book is Adolf uses a lot of flowery language, and it's annoying. Perhaps the true Germanic words worked better, or perhaps the Germanic language didn't allow him to write in a more accessible version, but either way. I found it hard to really understand what Adolf really wanted to say at a few points. To the point where I just muddled through just so I could see the next thought or idea. 
 At the same time, when he was clear. It was a mixed bag. He discusses his homelife and shows who his parents were. Part of me wonders if his parent's deaths are the way he lays out, but as I said I couldn't keep my preconceived notions out of the book. 
 His second chapter though appear to be where I changed on it. While his foreword makes a veiled reference to the Jewish Press, the second chapter he discusses his disdain for Marxist and the Jewish population. He basically skewers communist, calling unions run by them awful (and making a case for it) and says the Marxist (or Social democrats in his words) want to destroy the economic prosperity of the countries they are in. 
 The Marxist are the lucky ones. He then goes on to discuss anti semitics feelings and his exploration of them, he talks about how he learned about the Jewish people. To put it mildly, he's abusive. But it goes in more than that. If you imagine a man walking into a bar, and looking around. And then saying "You know what's wrong with this country?" pausing to build a little tension and then says "The JEWS" you'd have a fairly good representation of this chapter. Adolf starts out by acting like he has no preconceived notions, and then starts to discuss the jewish population. Talking about how almost all journalists had Jewish ties. Most prominent "Social democrats" are Jewish and from that feels that they are the entire problem with the book. 
 From there we get into someone of the worst of the worst. He claims that he can't stand the Jewish smell, he talks about for every crime and degradation a Jewish person had done them. After he makes a case against him he talks about the "Jewish" religion as if it's a race, and essentially says no true German can be Jewish in far more words. 
 That's where my interest in the book changed. I'd heard Adolf can be a charismatic leader, but this book isn't it. I read for another half a chapter, and just wasn't enjoying it at all. He had interesting ideas, but he has a bit of a revisionist history thing going on, and his out and out hatred of the Jewish people make it hard to really take anything he says reasonably. I keep coming back to a line he says. 
 "The odour of those people in caftans often used to make me feel ill." 
 Caftans in this case being traditional Jewish garb that Adolf makes clear is a Jewish symbol. 
 After that though... I really can't say much more. That line is what I think broke me. For at least an hour more where he discusses representative democracy in ways that might be correct, but at the same time, the source had been tainted, not by history but by his blatant hatred. 
 I came to the book in the search of a new insight. I hoped something different would turn up but sadly I found exactly what I expected to find. Though I did find one piece of insight. If this was Hitler's great tomb and the majority of the German people had read it. How did they not laugh his ass right out of town from the beginning. His blatant hatred of the Jewish people and Marxists is extreme and while it doesn't say he would murder them, his logic isn't exactly solid enough in my mind to make me believe it. Perhaps people hear what they want to hear, or perhaps a majority of the German people already were already anti-semitic, but to me, this was terrible. I put aside the knowledge of what he was to become and still found an angry little man who I couldn't stand.

At the beginning let clarify one thing ... if we have prejudices, then it is the best not to start with reading this book. If we start from the side that we want to see what's in the head of one such figure, then it's okay. We have to admit that history has a lot of such characters, and if we go with the point of view, that we need to evaluate the character, then perhaps, this book does not deserve a single star, but, if we go with the point of view, that we should evaluate the book, then that's a completely a different matter. I readied a book in Serbian language and I can say that writing style is very clear. The attitudes in the book are just the views of a leader and you can like it or you can hate it, but still is good to read it. So please, do not kill me because of my point of view. ;)

book_a.title: January First: A Child's Descent into Madness and Her Father's Struggle to Save Her
book_a.user_review: This book was a compelling read, especially for someone with no knowledge or experience of mental illness. That it tells the story of a little girl's affliction certainly adds poignancy, but I found it extremely difficult to understand the author's (her father) decisions and reactions to the challenges posed by his daughter, particularly in relation to his baby son and wife - his total preoccupation with Janni to the exclusion of the safety and well-being of the rest of his family was, frankly, shocking. sample_reviews.review_text:
January First is the memoir of Michael Schofield, a father struggling to raise a daughter diagnosed with child-onset schizophrenia. January is only five when the most worrying of her symptoms start to appear. She is violent towards her family, hallucinates a huge cast of imaginary friends and flies into uncontrollable rages over things as simple as hearing her own name or receiving a compliment. It's very rare for schizophrenia to be diagnosed in a child so young, so when Schofield turns to medical professionals for help the answers don't come easily. He has to battle an array of less-than-hepful doctors and fight with his insurance company to get January the treatment she needs. This book is a brutally honest window into the life of a family trying to deal with a horrific mental illness and work within an inefficient and uncaring medical system. 
 I won an ARC of January First through Good Reads, and I am so glad that I did. The fascinating subject matter made this a quick read for me. I finished in just a day. As other reviewers have pointed out, the writing style isn't as polished as a seasoned author's would be. However, I feel that this strengthens the story because it makes it feel more authentic. In fact, I would say that the honesty portrayed through Scofield's simple language is one of the memoir's biggest assets. He doesn't portray himself as a perfect parent. He documents all of the stress, the fighting he and his wife go through and his frustrations with January's behavior in detail. Most people will never have to deal with a mental illness as extreme as schizophrenia, so to get an inside look at a family struggling with it is both interesting and disturbing. I certainly learned a lot of things I didn't know about schizophrenia, as well as a lot of things about how people affected by mental illness struggle to get help. 
 I was most deeply affected by the passages where Schofield would talk about how schizophrenia will limit January. It's an incurable disease and his daughter has a very severe case of it. He laments the fact that she won't ever be able to live independently. Someone will always need to be taking care of her for the rest of her life. He also touches on how since people with schizophrenia have shorter lifespans, it's a very real possibility that she will die before him. It's just gut wrenching to read these thoughts because they're undeniably true. No parent should have to think like this about their child. 
 In the forward of the book, Schofield says that, "Schizophrenia is a little like cancer. You can't trust that it will ever go away completely." Even though the novel ends on a hopeful note, the reader can still feel the shadow of January's illness looming on the horizon, ready to swoop back in and turn everything the family has built on its head again. This was a great read and I definitely recommend it. It has made me feel more empathy for and be more aware of people dealing with children who are sick. It's worth the time it takes to read it to gain a wider perspective on the world of mental illness.

I am not too familiar with schizophrenia so I was thankful that I was able to learn a little bit about it from this book. HOWEVER, I couldn't help feeling like Jani's parents were complete enablers. I know it is wrong of me to judge because I am not a parent struggling with a child who has schizophrenia, but I think they could have handled the situation a little better. I also found myself feeling sorry for the mother, who was dealing with a schizophrenic daughter and a husband who always thought he was right. Tough situation all around.

I have to admit, I didn't walk away from this with a very high opinion of the father who wrote it. He seemed to just write off his second child and revolved his whole world around Janni. That bugged me. I do however admire his determination to get help for her and to build as much of a normal life for her as he could. This was an emotional and touching story.

It's hard to put into words my thoughts on January First by Michael Schofield. I can't help but feel sorry for January "Jani" Schofield, her brother, Bodhi, and her parents Michael and Susan. At just age six, Jani was diagnosed with schizophrenia. It took months and months of violent outbursts, hallucinations, and suicide attempts before Jani was given a definitive diagnosis. The path to get there was long and fraught with hopelessness. 
 I've seen a lot about this family on various television shows, but I think those programs only scratched the surface. I think the book goes much deeper than a television show can. The book is solely from Michael Schofield's perspective. I definitely felt like I was in his head. I could totally understand why he and his wife felt like giving up. Jani's violence was just so unpredictable. A cry or a whimper from her little brother was enough to set her off. If she didn't get to hit or throw something at Bodhi, Jani just couldn't rest. She has to hit him or her mind can't rest. When her parents tried to protect their infant son, Jani is quick to hit them -- violently. 
 Read the rest of my review at: http://www.asiturnthepages.blogspot.c...

Definitely one of the most frustrating books I've ever read. The author was narcissistic and arrogant, continually calling every doctor he met a "stupid idiot" because all the doctors refused to diagnose his out-of-control daughter with schizophrenia. The author diagnosed her himself by looking up her symptoms on line, and then once he convinced himself, he convinced his wife and daughter. I found the stories in the book to be completely unbelievable. I think the parents need to be diagnosed with Munchausen By Proxy. I feel sorry for their children.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I laughed, I cried, and I wanted to throw my book across the room at certain parts! January First is a memoir written from the perspective of a Father with a schizophrenic daughter. I felt so close to her, and her family as I read their story. It was hard for me to finish the book, knowing there was no resolution, and January will continue to live her life this way, haunted by her mental illness. 
 Some things annoyed me greatly. For starters, Michael Schofield has a tendency to act as a martyr. He treats his wife as if she were never involved with January's care, even though she is present all along. He gets aggravated with his wife for not being able to "handle" January, as she is beating the crap out of her infant brother, meanwhile he takes her out with their dog and she turns her anger on the dog and HE can't handle it himself! So why is it hard for him to understand why his wife can't control her ALL DAY LONG, when he can't himself for a brief walk around the school? 
 I greatly feel for this family, and especially for January. I cannot fathom having a mental illness that caused me to hallucinate 95% of the time, or to have a child afflicted with something so horrible. I try not to judge this family as I have no clue what it would really be like to be in their shoes. With that being said, it was nice to have a brief look into their window, and I think it was courageous for Michael Schofield to let us into their world.

This is the true account of a child tormented by mental illness. It is written with the intensity and emotion that only a parent can feel. 
 From infancy, Janni had conflicts that other children did not seem to have. She was more connected to her imaginary friends than other children. She was absorbed in a world she called Calalini. As time went on, it became apparent that these were, in fact hallucinations. 
 Janni's parents, unable to help her, sought counsel and medical advice. Ultimately, they were forced to obtain psychiatric intervention. They needed help, but also answers and a direction to resolving Janni's problems. 
 January became a hazard to herself and her parents; she also became a serious hazard to her baby brother. They could not allow Janni near him for fear that his crying would send her into a rage. Her many problems were tearing the family apart. However, her parents would not give up on the family, or on January. 
 At the tender age of six, January was finally diagnosed with Schizophrenia. With this diagnosis, her parents were finally able to begin to understand Janni, and to help her. 
 This is a very emotionally charged account of mental illness and its effects on a very young child, as well as her family. Both heartbreaking and brave, it is a compelling read.
Mixed feeling I would say.

January First by Michael Schofield was a page turner, but not in the way that you would expect. Michael Schofield has to be the most unlikable person/parent ever. Surprisingly the book is written by him about him. Well actually it is about his daughter, January, or Jani for short. Jani is the youngest person ever diagnosed with schizophrenia. I have never been as annoyed or as angry about a person as I have been about Michael Schofield. He is irritated by and disparages everyone he comes into contact with. He is judgmental and condescending. This could have been a fascinating and rewarding story about a troubled girl with some exceptional gifts but instead we have this self serving navel gazing. Michael and his wife Susan make some astounding choices; having another child while dealing with their obviously deeply disturbed daughter, ignoring medical advice and assistance because they feel like their daughter is a genius and is just not being challenged. I hope that Jani thrives and has a successful future and her potential is realized. I hope their other child, Bodhi also thrives. I really hope Michael Schofield gains some sort of self awareness. He really is one of the most unlikable people I have ever read about.

Are you getting the impression that this book is just a bunch of garbage thrown together in the cauldron and stirred, 'cuz that about nails it! I really didn't enjoy this book at all. I couldn't finish this. The multiple-page info dump that chronicled the main character's life story within the first 1% of the books should've been a big enough red flag to save me from wasting several more hours of my life, but I pressed on, hoping for an improvement. There wasn't. After trudging through to the half-way point, at which I'd endured more conversations about wine, tea and yoga than I thought possible, I gave up. It's clear the author did her research -- that's great, but it doesn't mean we have to wade through her notes. Part of effective story-telling is to weave the research into the story without dragging it down. Harkness missed the mark there. 
 I also saw no good reason for the alternate POV's, other than to give the author a chance to over-explain and suck all the tension out of the book. It was like a glaring neon sign -- "Hey, just letting you know...there's no danger from Matthew...'cause he loves her. Already. After two days. Two days of drinking wine and tea and hanging out in the library." His entire first POV chapter is pointless -- multiple scenes where he and his friend blather on about nothing, in the form of 'as you know, Bob' dialogue, and we get more information on how to play various games of pool than necessary in anything other than a book about how to play pool. 
 I'm incredibly grateful for this site, because I considered trying to go back and finish, but after coming here and seeing this is only the beginning of a series I know stopping is the right decision. Had I forced myself to read through the rest only to find a million hanging threads I would've thrown the book at the wall. Which would've been a problem, because I have it on my kindle.

There's a scene in Sideways where Thomas Haden Church's Armenian prospective father-in-law asks Paul Giamatti's character about his writing and, when told that Miles writes fiction, declares it pointless. This book lends weight to that argument. There's a lot here that should resonate with me; these people are a lot like me, went to a similar university at a similar time. If I don't know them personally I know their kind. The writing is good in an academic exercise, postgraduate creative writing bashful-showiness sort of way. But here's my problem: there really isn't enough of a story. A series of polished vignettes does not a page-turner make. I'm taking my advice from the Armenians here and will actively avoid anything that smacks of 'true to life'. My life is true to life; when I open a book I want to be taken somewhere else. I want contrast, not a mirror. I would have given it a ho-hum three star review if it hadn't been for the (in a phrase beloved of the Witterati) 'unfortunate event' that occurs towards the end. I don't want to create a spoiler here, suffice to say that if you use such an event to get the narrative ball rolling, fair enough, to use it at the end is one of the laziest, most manipulative literary devices I can think of. Whilst, fair enough, it rendered a raw emotional punch with the feeling of being manipulated by a plot contrivance only coming in as an after shock, it did leave the remainder of the text feeling like an after-thought. Still, not as much of a waste of time as say, soap operas...

When I first heard about the concept for this book (it covers about 20 years in the lives of two people, but only the same day every year), I thought it sounded kind of interesting. The book got great reviews. It was picked up by Hollywood. And so I started reading it. 
 "Hey, this book isn't that great," was my initial impression. "If it weren't for the concept, this book would be nothing." 
 A few chapters in: 
 "Wow, I'm kind of getting into this. This is interesting, and kind of neat to see how people change and mature over the years. Are they ever going to get together?" 
 Three-quarters through: 
 "Yay! They finally got together! I knew they would! Jennifer Aniston's agent must be desperate to get this part for her!" 
 At the "twist": 
 "WTF was that?!!!?!" 
 After finishing the book: 
 "Jennifer Aniston, forget about this role. I wish I could forget this book. How freaking depressing and pointless this was."
I just saw the trailer for this film and it reminded me how well-written this is as a modern romance novel. Don't expect too much, and you'll be surprised how quickly you fall into the pages.

This is one of those books that should really be a five star, but I gave it four stars because the author just wore me out. Alison Bechdel is a genius, no question of that. I loved discovering her family, her father's secrets, and the feeling of growing up in small town Pennsylvania as part of the family that owned the "fun home." (Funeral Home.) 
 It's just that Alison Bechdel, who really is a genius, can never just tell the story. There always have to be classic literary allusions. And great Seventies pop culture. And learned references to local lore, geography, entomology, herpetology, and every branch of human knowledge and endeavor. In a way it's like Moby Dick, (the only literary classic she doesn't riff on) except that after a certain point Melville just told the damn story. When she learns how to get out of her own way she could be as great as Melville. There's one picture in the book of young Alison and her father watching a sunset together that is really beautiful and tells you everything. But then there's page after page of stuff on Proust, Oscar Wilde, the AIDS epidemic, the Watergate Scandal, and that just knocks it down from a five to a four. But I would still recommend this amazing graphic novel to anyone who likes stories about small town life, family tragedies, Seventies pop culture, creative writing, insects, or basically the sum total of human endeavor. 
 *** 
 Okay, this is just me being silly, but : anyone who watches the classic movie version of WEST SIDE STORY will probably pick up on the fact that Anybodys, the only girl in the Jets gang, is probably a lesbian. Alison Bechdel never mentions this, but I kept thinking about Anybodys all through Fun Home. And I'm so glad Alison's Dad didn't take her to see WEST SIDE STORY, because then we would have got ten pages of stuff like, "What did Anybodys mean when she said she was real good with shadows? Was I truly my father's shadow? Had I followed him into inverted sex the way Anybodys follows the Sharks into P.R. territory? When Chino pulled out the gun he wanted to use on Tony Anybodys describes it euphemistically as "the bad news." Was homosexuality the bad news that killed my father the same way the gun killed Tony?" 
 Sometimes it's time to cut the frabba-jabba!
A little too close to home sometimes.

I really wanted to like this more than I did. I just couldn't get over my opinion that the author was horribly horribly self-centered.
I bought this book at the Vancouver Art Gallery because I'd read an excerpt and loved the drawings. I still love the drawings and think this is a fabulously told story.

Overwritten and overwrought with Bechdel's need to make her life mirror and in some cases eclipse great literature, which this book assuredly is not. I felt like she just took transcripts from her therapy sessions, switching out the words to be the longest and most obfuscating words possible, where she probably used a leather-bound thesaurus. Fun Home is trying, and failing, to help Bechdel reconcile the father she knew with the man he really was, a closeted homosexual who preyed on his students, who I might add were teenagers. Yes, Bechdel does capture the dichotomy of who her father was and what he went through, but in the end, his seduction of teenagers, which is unforgiveable, is swept under the carpet to make way for Bechdel's own Homeric odyssey of finding herself, aka masturbating to Collette. On a personal note, I seriously don't think I've ever taken such a strong dislike to an author's voice before. Bechdel comes across as the most arrogant of snobs who uses language to elevate herself and make her readers feel stupid. This turned me off so much that I was barely able to finish this book, and I quite literally finish EVERYTHING I read.

 Most of the graphic novels I have read in the past have been sequels or prequels or blahquels to various media franchises that I like (Buffy, Angel, Firefly, Star Wars, etc.), and I have always struggled to pace myself through them. I blame on the lack of a soundtrack. Anyways, I'd been wanting to read this ever since I saw its musical adaptation at the Public, but I was hesitant about its format. However, knowing that Fun Home is working its way to Broadway and that I'll be seeing Bechdel speak later in May, I decided it was time to read it. And I'm so glad I did. 
 It's an autobiography of sorts, but rather than being told chronologically, it unfolds in these thematic arcs. Each chapter deals with a moment or particular issue in her life and the resonances of that moment later on. There are moments when the prose is just plain beautiful or insightful. It makes sense why some of those translated so well into song. Both the book and the musical are beautiful and enrich other, so I recommend both. If you've read the book, see the musical. If you've seen the musical, read the book.

Well, not my favorite read. I liked the illustrations, and how she wove so much of her family's letters and books into the storyline. What really turned me off was the overuse of the jargon of feminist/queer theory - which I myself studied on a graduate level, and find thoroughly pretentious and out of touch with most people's reality. I would have much preferred to have the story told, and the human elements come out, without so much reliance on shaky theory. 
 Just my opinion - don't flame me for it.

I know everyone loves this book, and don't get me wrong, I think it was good and I can see why everyone likes it. It just didn't speak to me for some reason.

* Disclaimer: I received a free eARC from NetGalley in exchange for an honest review. * 
 I love Josh Sundquist. He is one of my favorite YouTubers and one of the first that helped me discover the platform. I find him to be very smart, kind, funny, articulate & understanding. I've read one of his non-fiction works and found it to be very interesting. He is a great writer, orator and content creator. In fact, this was one of my most anticipated reads of the year. 
 You've probably guessed by my need to have a disclaimer, but this wasn't my favorite book. Inherently there was nothing wrong with it. Though I do wonder how those who are visual impaired will react to this book, and honestly that was a contestant though running through my head throughout this book. I think this book, for me, is the epitome of why own voices books are important. I don't know if this (especially the beginning) is a fair or accurate representation of someone in Will's position. I don't know that it's not. All I know is that Josh understands the importance of representation as an amputee, but as someone who hasn't been blind he does not know what it's like. Neither do I. Josh did his research, but you and I both know it's not the same. 
 I appreciated that Will had his own aspirations (journalism) in an attempt to define him as more than being blind, however those seemed to slip away as the story progressed. Again, something that's sad. These aspirations that had begun to fill him out as a person who is more than his disability was essentially dropped after more "pressing" story plots came about. 
 Speaking of more "pressing" story plots, let's talk about the surgery. There was nothing wrong with the surgery, in my opinion. It was actually interesting to see the aftermath of that and Josh did indeed his research on this front. It's also something that rarely happens, so it's nearly impossible to have seen this from a perspective that's not fictionalized. I found Will's process of understanding depth, perspective and colors fascinating. However I can see how this would put someone off, as most do not have the opportunity to have a surgery like this and that reality MIGHT (again I don't know, as I'm not in this position) be frustrating and how that changes Will, which might take away any relatability he has to someone who is visually impaired. 
 The side characters were woefully underdeveloped. Even our love interest was not as fleshed out as I would have hoped. 
 Lastly the writing was very cheesy. The circumstances, at least to me, did not seem to be over the top. But the words josh wrote, especially a lot of phrases at the end of paragraphs or chapters felt forced, awkward and cheesy. 
 I did like lots of things about this, though. Even though our side characters and parents weren't fully developed, I loved the roles they played in Will's life. They were contestant and funny. I liked how Will described scents and has this silly fascination with scratch-off scent cards. I liked the scenes where Cicely described things to Will and the way she described them. 
 One thing that was lovely about this is the writing style and the story was compelling enough that I SPED through this book. 
 I appreciate the attempt to write diversely. I don't know if it is an accurate representation, and I don't know that it's not. I do know that the thought of that was distracting to me and I overall wanted more development from the story.

Not as bad as I'd feared - but not as good as I'd hoped. 
 (Full disclosure: I received a free electronic ARC for review through Netgalley. This review contains clearly marked spoilers.) 
 "A door swings open, dinging a bell. I recognize the next sound: the deliberate but controlled steps, treading gently, as if she's trying not to leave footprints. I've never seen a footprint, of course, but my understanding is that the harder you press, the more of an impression you leave behind." 
 Sixteen-year-old Will Porter has attended boarding schools and summer camps for blind and visually impaired kids his whole life - but now it's time to go mainstream. Will wants to finish out his high school career in his hometown of Toano, Kansas - even if it's over the vociferous objections of his over-stressed helicopter mom. Unfortunately, Will's first day in public school is a bit of a disaster: he gropes a random girl in the stairwell, makes a fellow classmate cry, and plops down on yet another student's lap in the caf. 
 But Will quickly finds his niche in Toano High School. He takes a shining to journalism, where the teacher - Mrs. Everbrook - treats him like every other student. He partners up with and eventually befriends Cecily, whose knack for photography complements Will's way with words. He falls in with Nick, Ion, and Whitford who, along with Cecily, represent the entirety of Toano High's academic quiz team. Will even convinces Cecily to try out for the morning announcer cohosting gig, despite her obvious - and inexplicable - reluctance. 
 And then, just a few months into the semester, Will's mom drops a bombshell in his lap. At the hospital where his father works, there's an experimental surgery to "cure" blindness that's accepting applicants. The operation is a two-stage process: a retinal stem cell transplant, followed by a corneal transplant within two weeks. Even if it's successful, the surgery comes with a whole bunch of risks: Will's body could reject the new corneas, while the immunosuppressant drugs will leave him susceptible to common illnesses such as the flu. If the new eyes "take," Will will have to rewire his brain to properly perceive and process all the unfamiliar, overwhelming visual input. It's not as simple as waking up and being able to see; rather, Will will have to learn how to perform this new task that his eyes and brain have never done before. 
 The primary conflict in the story is how this surgery impacts Will's budding romance with Cecily. Love and First Sight is one of those books that sounds like it could be really awful and offensive ... but might (just might!) prove unexpectedly subversive and progressive. (See, e.g., The Continent. I added it to my TBR early on, only to drop it when the Twitter commentary started rolling in.) As it turns out, Love and First Sight falls somewhere in between. 
 ** Caution: Possible spoilers ahead! ** 
 The synopsis kind of skirts around Cecily's appearance, making it sound like maybe she's merely "ugly" (with a big nose, a la Roxanne, perhaps?), while her friends, in a bid to hook these two crazy kids up, talk Cecily up to be some kind of international, smoking hot supermodel. When Will finally gets his first sight of her, his shallow side wins out. Or at least this is the impression I got from the description. Thankfully, what I feared might happen does not actually come to pass. 
 Rather, Cecily has a large, purplish birthmark that covers the upper half of her face, earning her the nickname "Batgirl." (In my fantasies, I dreamed of an alternate universe where Cecily owned this slur, reappropriated it even, and strutted around the halls of Toano High wearing gold Doc Martens and a purple cape, wielding her digital camera like a weapon.) Her friends - and Cecily herself - simply fail to mention this one very obvious and defining feature when describing her to Will. 
 When Will is finally able to see her - or rather, understand that the lines and angles he's seeing do indeed make up the face that is Cecily's - he notes the existence of the birthmark. He understands that Cecily's face doesn't look quite like all the other faces he's seeing, but doesn't automatically classify this as a bad thing. Having never been bombarded with images of ideal or traditional beauty, Will has no opinion on the birthmark either way. He already loves Cecily, and he finds her beautiful. The whole of her, inside and out. 
 Yet the story needs conflict, so rather than be upset that she's "ugly" (Will openly bristles when his mom refers to the birthmark as a "disfigurement"), Will is angry that Cecily lied to him. That she kept this one Very Significant thing to herself. That she didn't want to go out of her way talk about being bullied, to delve into the source of this shame and embarrassment when she could just as easily not. Will interprets it as Cecily taking advantage of his blindness to feel better about herself, but that's a really selfish and self-centered way of looking at things. Especially coming from a guy who, for example, left his sunglasses at home on the first day of school because he didn't want to draw unnecessary attention to himself. Like Cecily, Will wants desperately to fit in, to not be defined by a congenital condition that he didn't choose and that does not define the whole of him. You'd think he'd cut Cecily a little slack, you know? 
 Instead, he goes on a pretty childish rampage, deleting his comments on her Facebook page and then defriending her altogether. He even tosses the box of photographs she gave him in the garbage, and then dumps a jar of mayo on the pile for good measure. I guess, as a 38-year-old, I should cut teenagers some slack, but it all feels pretty overly dramatic and out of proportion to the (perceived) offense. 
 On the positive side, the rift only lasts about twenty pages, so there's that. 
 Look. I get that the story needs some sort of tension, but I much rather would've seen it play out between Will and a society that says he couldn't/shouldn't/wouldn't love a girl like Cecily. That's where the cultural critique is at. 
 ** End of spoilers. ** 
 As for the rest of the story, it's pretty evenly split between things I love, and things I hated. The scenes between Will and Cecily are mostly lovely. I really enjoyed watching them interact, particularly those times when Cecily struggled to find the right words to describe a sensory experience to Will (and vice versa). Based on actual research, Will's quest to gain sight is fascinating. And though I'm not blind - nor do I have close friends or family members who are - Sundquist seems to do a good job of detailing how visually impaired folks experience the world, and navigate one shaped by "the tyranny of the visual." 
 On the downside, the male characters all feel pretty juvenile. For example, upon leaning that Will's dad is a surgeon, Nick insists that all male urologists must be gay, because why else would a straight guy want to look at penises professionally? (Also apparently there are only two settings, straight or gay.) Will comments on the principal's fat rolls several times, and Whitford is weirdly, regressively possessive of his girlfriend. Given how sensitively Sundquist handles Will's visual impairment, all these other microaggressions are especially annoying. (Ion rightfully calls Nick homophobic, thankfully, but all the other aforementioned incidents go unchallenged.) 
 And then there's the joke about sexual assault, right there in the very first chapter. When navigating the stairwell, Will accidentally grabs a girl's breast. An honest mistake, and it would've been excusable if not for this bit: 
 That's what a white cane will do for you: Not only can you get away with copping a feel, the girl assumes it was her fault and apologizes for it. Let me assure you, random girl, you have nothing to be sorry about. Completely my fault. And my pleasure. 
 Nope nope nope. Intentionally grabbing someone else's body parts without their permission is sexual assault, full stop. (And yes, this is what we're talking about here; otherwise there wouldn't be anything to "get away" with. Plus, if it's truly an accident, wouldn't you feel chagrined, as opposed to smugly self-satisfied?) In fact this seems to be the go-to M.O. of our President-Elect, which Sundquist probably didn't know when writing this story, but makes it all the more offensive to see now. 
 Honestly, I almost threw in the towel then and there. Proceed as you will.

I'll have to admit that I did not think I would end up enjoying LOVE AND FIRST SIGHT so much. 
 It's not like it's ''mind-blowingly'' written and I'm normally a little wary of books written by YouTube sensations, however famous the latter are. 
 But it was evident to me that Josh Sundquist wrote this book with much care, did a tremendous amount of research on visual impairment and carefully outlined the story. 
 You know how sometimes you read a book and you have trouble figuring out what is happening - you feel as if the action and even the writing are all over the place? Well, it's the contrary in this case. I felt like every sentence had a reason to be part of the story. 
 I got extremely attached to Will, the very relatable main character with a visual impairment. This is probably because the majority of authors are women, but I never once read a book about a boy being blind, just girls. So it was great to have a guy's opinion and thoughts on the matter of living without seeing. 
 And then being able to see for the first time. Let me tell you that his reaction to the world as we know it - with colors and shapes - is worth remembering. In fact, this book helped me learn a lot about visual impairment and how blind people perceive the world. It really was interesting. 
 It's a moving story with dramatic scenes, but don't worry, there is also humour to lighten the atmosphere and inspiring scenes that make this book unforgettable. It's a fantastic character-driven story to which I sure hope you'll give a chance.

This was a really enjoyable, quick and mostly light read. I wasn't really sure what to expect when I started reading, but I found myself completely engrossed right from the very beginning and pretty much read this straight through. Will was a really great character: engaging, charismatic, a little bratty as he should be considering he's a teen aged boy, but thoroughly likable. The premise of this was what drew me to want to read it and I wasn't disappointed. This is a book about much more than just a boy regaining his sight after being blind his whole life. It's about acceptance, trust, friendship, and family. There's humor and light-hearted moments, but there's also some very moving, emotional ones, too. 
 Full review to come on: www.swoonyboyspodcast.com

In this book that explores the idea of beauty being in the eye of the beholder with a twist, sixteen-year-old Will Porter gets a chance at love and sight. Blind from birth, Will transfers to a public school so that he can figure out how to navigate the sighted world. He loves journalism and writing, but he worries that his blindness will be all his classmates see. As it turns out, blindness can come in lots of different forms, and Will fails to recognize the possibilities for love right in front of him. As he is befriended by members of the quiz bowl, Nick, Ion, and Winthrop, he also gets to know Cecily, a talented photographer who is gentle and considerate but shy. Clearly, she's been teased and bullied for most of her life, but Will is unable to figure out why. He resists the attraction he feels to her, at first because he fears that love will make him too dependent on another, and later, for other, more complicated reasons. When two different operations offer Will the chance to see, he decides to have the operations despite their risks and the struggles that will occur as he tries to recognize objects in the world around him. But his sight shows him a very different Cecily than he has imagined and he hurts her feelings. Both of the teens feel betrayed. Will and his friends use spring break to track her to LA where her father lives, seeing some of the beauty of the Rockies and the Grand Canyon along the way. Although the road trip seemed a bit too much for me, I enjoyed the rest of the story and how Will was portrayed. I'm not so sure that a mother would be so quick to sell a car to finance a road trip, but I suppose it could happen. Perhaps we'd all be better off is love was, indeed, blind, and we remembered to see past the surface. This glimpse of what it might be like to tackle this particular life challenge--being blind from birth--will leave readers thinking even while they also reflect on Cecily's situation, judged because of her facial birthmark that leaves some onlookers unable to see anything else.

What a wonderful story and characters. And it makes you really think about something we sighted people take for granted. I can't imagine not having a point of reference for things we see such as the colors, shapes, depth perception, and having everything your eyes see crowding into your brain and causing a massive information overload. Yes, it definitely makes one ponder. Recommend this read!

***I received a copy of this from Netgalley**** 
 The best part of the book was the afterwards where Josh explained his research on blindness, because it was interesting. My rating may be slightly unfair as I just finished several 5 star reads, which is rare for me, and this one didn't measure up emotionally or have the characters depth I wanted. I just wasn't sold on the love relationship aspect of the book and I had to force myself to finish. Basically, this didn't have the cuteness of Simon vs the Homosapien Agenda or the emotional impact of A List of Cages. It was just ok.

Love and First Sight surprised me, simple as that. I didn't think I was going to like it as much as I did. I didn't think I was going to find it as cute, lighthearted, and adorable as I did. If you go into the book and put aside all of the science-y aspects, it completely transforms into something unique, imaginative, and heartwarming. Love and First Sight is a story of discovery and of how love knows no bounds. Love isn't something we create because we can see, love is fundamentally feeling - and this book is a brilliant celebration of the differences that make us human. 
 Will was entertaining, to make a long story short. I enjoyed his commentary, most of the time. There were moments in his narrative that felt inauthentic and almost like a childish caricature of what an actual teen would think or do - but in the grand scope of things, it was forgivable. Will was stubborn, but he was also gentle and kind. He wanted to do everything himself, and he wasn't afraid to let you know when you overstepped the boundaries. Oh, and he's also blind - which was awesome. Small note, I'm not saying that being blind is awesome, I mean having a protagonist with a disability I can relate to is awesome. There is something magical about writing without one of the senses, and I think that magic really worked in favor of the novel as a whole. Every word, sentence, and paragraph had a reason - there was always meaning. Not only did the selectiveness of the sensory detail illuminate Will's character, it also enabled a different type of growth we don't often see in literature. 
 Now, on to the parts that sort of messed me up. I loved this book, I really did - but some things just need to be addressed first. To begin: Cecily. I adored her, and I wish she had even more time in the story. My problem is not with her character or anything she did, no, my issue is with how she was handled as a narrative tool. Cecily should have been so much more than something to mess up his friend group because she wasn't as pretty as Will had hoped she would be. Do you see the problem here? Will basically throws a bitch fit because, after the surgery and he can sort of see, he discovers Cecily isn't model beautiful. He feels betrayed. WHAT THE HELL. To put so much reliance on beauty really bothered me because Cecily was a genius, she was kind, and she put herself out there to help Will with things throughout the course of the novel. The "issue" of her non-traditional beauty shouldn't have been an issue at all. 
 My second issue is much smaller than the first: the surgery. While I loved the narrative following the surgery, Will's relearning shapes and whatnot, the surgery itself was a bit over the top. There was no believable element to cling to here, and it really bothered me. I don't know if it was Will's lack of interest or thought process in deciding to go forward, or if it was something else, but the surgery took away from the magic the book had created. I think Sundquist realized this, too - which you will realize when you read it. The surgery took a metaphor that had beautiful qualities and destroyed it by being literal. 
 Even considering the two things above, I completely adored Love and First Sight. The romance was a perfect slow burn, the friendship was refreshing, and I loved the growth of every individual involved. Stories aren't all inclusive, our lives touch and change the people around us, too - and I feel Love and First Sight did a beautiful and subtle job of it.

book_b.user_review: Listened to the audio version. Excellent recording.

sample_reviews.review_text: My daughter got this out of the library and decided on this as the latest read-aloud bedtime story book. It's a fantasy about a girl in a kingdom that prizes singing ability. And it's sortuva preteen romance-y type thing and really geared towards younger girls. So... it was okay for my daughter but OMG this did nothing for me. I thought it pretty clunky and slow and just, well, dull. Maybe it's okay for you, though.

Nice. Very reminiscent of Shannon Hale's Bayern series but Hale's writing is much superior. I liked some of the singing magic and I really love the family and sisterly moments at the very beginning of the book. Very imaginative retelling of Snow White but only a decent book on its own.

Fairest attempts to bring song to print and lost me in the translation. 
 This is one of those books that I wanted to like but was unable to involve myself in the story because of the entanglement of songs written into the plot. Trying to imagine the songs being sung and creating a melody from nothing brought me out of the story and into my head. This bothered me especially because song is such a major element of the world that Levine is trying to build that this disturbance is ever present throughout the book. 
 In the moments I was truly involved in the story I found the plot, the characters and the message being told to be intriguing and well written. It was these sections that made me read on to finish the entire book, but my problems with the incorporated music is what stayed with me in the end. 
 Overall I do want to return to Fairest at some point and give it a second chance, only this time it will have to be an audio book instead.
As this is a fantasy genre for Young Adults, I had a higher expectation. Sadly, I was disappointed. It's more of a novel directed at young teenagers. I honestly found the piece childish and a cliche.
Liked Ella Enchanted much better.
A delightful, non-obvious retelling of Snow White. Very much in the style of Ella Enchanted. A quick, light read. Loved it.

** spoiler alert ** 
 The only elements I liked about this book were the magic mirror she could go inside, the scene in the library where she is trying to find out about the mirror, and the gnomes that represented the dwarfs in this tale. I was really excited that FINALLY much less emphasis was placed on the concept of the seven dwarfs, because that aspect of Snow White always seemed much less important to me. The gnomes were absolutely adorable and lived in an underground cave; their world was really interesting. They spoke their own language and the protagonist finds out she is actually part gnome. 
 It was really disappointing how the "Snow White" aspects didn't show up until a 100 pages and then really not until the last 100. I kept wondering "when is this story going to turn into Snow White?" The entire singing concept was silly; a musical does not transfer well to a book, but I did enjoy the lighter passages that were just song and not text (lazy reader). It just seemed like the author wanted to expand the world of Ella Enchanted (which I haven't read in well over a decade, but I probably should read again because it has fantastic reviews and I remember really enjoying it) and have the singing aspect, AND cram in Snow White. Like in Mirror, Mirror, it was too ambitious and came off as cluttered rather than seamless. 
 This story was pretty irritating until the very end when it finally got interesting. All of the names of both the places and the characters were strange and almost all alike, starting with the letter "A" and ending with "A" as well. I'm all for authors inventing their own character names but it gets really confusing when they sound all alike. I couldn't even tell you the name of the country they were from, it was just that memorable. 
 I wish the story had been more of a straight up Snow White retelling rather than all the other stupid things it included because that would have been much more enjoyable for me. The evil queen is actually the main character's age and doesn't hate her because she is prettier than her, but because she has a better singing voice than she does, but she does try to kill her via the huntsman and then later poison her. I thought the message of "accept yourself as you are" was poorly done and it didn't resonate with me as it did with some of the other readers, which is a shame because it is a good concept for young adult literature. I wouldn't suggest anyone go out of their way to read this one.

I was excited to read a novel by Gail Carson Levine; but this book turned out to be less than I was hoping for. It make work out better for young girls, but I seriously doubt young adults or adults will find it all that engaging. On a side note I listened to this as an audio book and that was definitely...well...an experience. They used a full casting for the audio book and all of the songs were sung in all of their full operatic glory. I was riding my bike when I started listening to this book and I almost fell off of it when all the sudden music started pelting out in the middle of my audio book.... 
 Aza thinks that she is ugly; she is too big and has different coloring from other people in the kingdom. Her parents run an inn and love her dearly, but they are not her birth parents (they found her on the steps of their inn as a baby). When Aza accompanies a Duchess to the wedding of their new king she feels drawn to the new Queen. The Queen ends up asking Aza to be her lady-in-waiting and from there Aza gets embroiled in a dangerous plot to help Queen Ivy save face. 
 This book is supposed to be a retelling of Snow White and the Seven Dwarves. It has some similarities to that story but more differences. If you think Disney took the grim out of Grimms Fairy Tales well then this book is Disney sugar coated with a cherry on top. There is so much happy ever after it is almost sickeningly sweet. The dire circumstances of the heroine are never really dire at all; the book is completely predictable. 
 Aza makes an unlikely role model for young girls. Aza (who is wed at 16 years old, I might add) is fifteen going on sixteen but has the mentality of a ten year old. Her obsessiveness with her ugliness is really...well...obsessive. She easily tosses morals aside to be beautiful. At the end she says she can't believe how much she has changed throughout the book; when not a few seconds earlier she was *again* whining about her ugliness. At times the author tries to excuse Aza being ugly because she sings so beautifully. Is it a requirement that everyone do one thing outstandingly wonderful to make them a good person? 
 All of the characters pretty much have this shallow level of depth. All the characters are type-cast. Not one single character does anything surprising. 
 Is there good in this book? If you read it knowing what to expect it is an okay book. It was actually what I expected, but not what I was hoping for. It is super cute, and super sugary. I as said it is a Disney film with heaps of sweetness added. That is not all a bad thing. The book ends how you expect and all the characters are just so good that you can't help but smile at times. Of course at other times you want to slap them for being so stupid, but I feel that way about Disney films too. 
 If you love Disney and you love cutsey and you want to be a princess then this book is for you. I think it will probably find appeal with younger girls who still dream of being a fairy princess. I think anyone over ten years of age will have trouble finding much to love here. This book did not make me eager to read more of Levine's books. Maybe if I am in the mood for more brainless sweetness I will check other out. Instead of reading this I would recommend "Princess Ben" by Catherine Murdock; this is also a sweet fairy tale but with more guts and more interesting characters.

Kind of disappointing after Ella Enchanted. Ok, I guess, but it was a little too heavy on the PC "empowerment" message and too light on the character development and quirky magic confusing life. The plot was a little too similar to Shrek at times.
Loved the twist on the tale, but struggled with the excessive meanness.

reference_book.review_text:
Ugh I couldn't stand Julie and I find that especially sad since it is a memoir of sorts. 
 The movie was vastly superior but having read the book I feel like the movie is a farce. Never been so disappointed in a Book to Movie adaptation and it was really only because they portrayed the characters Julie and Julia as two completely different characters from their memoir counterparts. Also the timelines within the adaptations are like Ying and Yang, different and definitely chopped up and served where ever best fitted In regards to the book. 
 The only pleasant thing about Julie (since let's face it, Julia is a vague mystery) is that she remained determined to finish her goal regardless of barriers and actively took part in constantly trying to make her relationship work, even if it was not in the kindest of ways. I just wish Julie had taken as much determination and tried to apply it to her attitude? 
 I read this in a day well waiting to buy a new book and at times I really had to force myself to get through it. I found myself silently cheering as I grew closer to the end and not in a happy way.
