sample_reviews.review_text: full review here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bV65p...

I was at first hesitant about reading this book, because I haven't been a huge fan of King's earlier works so far. I'm glad I picked it up, but to be honest, the most scary thing about this is still committing to 1000+ pages of his writing. 
 First off, I liked it. For the most part at least. It took me a while to get into, but the farther I got, the more invested I was in the story and the characters. The character development is amazing in this one, by the end I was attached to pretty much all the characters. King also has his way of making you absolutely despise characters and there were more than one in this, that made it onto my list of most hated characters ever. And just to make it clear: I was IMMENSELY disappointed when one of them died of a mere heart attack, when I wished him so much worse! I really liked how the two storylines, taking place 25 years apart, were woven together and how great their childhoods were portrayed. 
 To be honest, there weren't that many scenes in here that actually scared me. Some, yes, but much more which just made me go wtf? I'm not really a fan of King's writing - I hate how he oversexualizes and overdoes everything for no fucking reason. I'm just sitting through all of his books like "Did I really need to know that right now?", "Why would you write that? That's just sick.", "Does this scene have any purpose except weirding out the reader?", etc. It's a horror novel, so I'm not really mad about most (MOST! You know what I'm talking about.) of these scenes, that were just there for shock value, but I still find this part of his writing style pretty tasteless. 
 My main problem was still that this was MUCH too long. The story could have been effectively told in about half the amount of pages. Much could have been cut, described less detailed, etc. without losing anything. It's quite exhausting to read, especially the first half and you feel like it will never end. And while in some parts it was overdetailed, I would have wished to know more in others. Especially in the end, some things felt rushed, some storylines were dropped before they were really finished and I would have liked to know more about what happened after everything (also I found the ending really sad :( ). 
 But in the end, I enjoyed most parts of "It" and can appreciate it for what it is, though I have several issues with it.

I hate this book and it's convinced me I don't really want to watch the movie either. 
 First problem is the unnecessary length. He could have cut this down to 400 pages and had a decent story. It just kept going and going, the descriptions, the time flopping, it was all too much. 
 Second thing, now I know it was written forever ago but I wish I'd have known about the bullying and abuse before I even picked it up. I mean the bullying is something I understood to push the story but the abuse I could have lived without completely. Beverly is probably the worst female character I've ever read, ever! No woman likes to be abused and perpetuating she did to be reminded of her father and her friends was messed up and I hated it. There's more on her later. 
 Third, the time jumping was done so horribly. There was never any real distinction when you were suppose to be reading. I know it's all in memories but the italicized writing to say your in current (1985) to past or past to current, it didn't work and gave me a headache trying to read that nonsense. Had he separated it out more clearly I probably would have enjoyed it more. 
 Fourth if 11 year olds are having sex then police need to be involved. I don't care if they are all 11 year olds something is really freaking wrong. This was wrong in 1958 and in 1985 and unbelievably wrong still. I don't know what possessed him to put a scene in a book about 11 year olds having sex with each other, that's effed up. I was sick at my stomach reading it, I'm still sick at my stomach thinking about it honestly. The whole it was her way of getting them out?!? No. It was clear abuse of a female character for sexual uses and it was disgusting and I'm probably never going to be reading another of his books because I'm so disgusted with this one. 
 Lastly it's just not good. I got the concept and tried to like the characters but the situations they were put in and decisions they made caused me to hate this book. I just finished it to say I did. If you don't agree with my review that's fine, don't at me. I hate it.

I read this book in five days. I've been reading this book non-stop for the last five days, and holy crap what an experience this was. This is my second Stephen King novel (my first was The Shining) and this is easily the longest book I've ever read in my life. This book centers on seven kids in a haunted town called Derry. Pennywise the clown lives in the sewers and he comes back to haunt the town every twenty seven years. 
 The first 200-300 pages of this book were really slow in my opinion. It started with the adults and with all of them receiving phone calls saying "It" has returned to Derry. It felt repetitive, and it was a lot of info-dumping about the characters and their lives now as adults and about the town of Derry. But then, part 2 finally goes back to the kids, and we get to experience the true horror of Pennywise the clown. I was reading this book really late at night sometimes, and it was creeping me out in certain parts. Especially with the sink in Beverly's house, that scene really got to me. 
 The interlude's were boring as shit and I mainly skimmed them. Some of them were so long and I didn't really care that much about all of the town's history and I wanted to get back to the main characters. I also enjoyed the kids parts a lot more than the adult parts, at least in the beginning. By the end, I love the way the writing flashes back and forth between the kids and the adults so effortlessly and so quickly at the end. He would be able to start a flashback in mid-sentence and I thought it was really cool, like watching a movie. I will say that I really disliked the very very end, I thought it was so anti-climatic. I'm talking about how IT takes form as a spider at the end, I thought it wasn't as scary as if it were a clown, and the action scenes of them killing the spider were so hard to follow. Also what was up with Beverly having to have sex with all of them at the end? They are only like twelve years old and she had sex with all six of the boys like wtf?And then the book actually ended on a happy note and I was kind of disappointed by that. I wanted a creepy ending. Also, I was shipping Beverly and Bill so hard right up until the very end. 
 Overall this was a really fun experience reading this book, one I'll never forget for sure. I can't wait to see the new movie adaptation! It looks promising and horrifying.

Buddy read with my BFF for our book club - Book for Mar. + Apr. 
 I know I'll get some mean comments and definitely some shit for this review but I honestly don't care. If you can't understand that people have different opinions that yours than I'm more than happy to piss you off, because you deserve it. I hope your day is ruined after reading a freaking review on Goodreads by someone you don't even know ;) 
 You have to understand that, when you start such a hyped and loved book, you obviously have at least some expectations. I kept justifying this book for no reason: I found it slow and assumed it was because it's more than 1000 pages, I was forever waiting to be scared and terrified but it happened maybe twice. 
 I understand that so many people are scared of clowns so this book plays on that fear (irrational or not, clowns are fucking creepy and they should stop with whatever they're doing because of reasons) but more than scared I felt disgusted. 
 The writing was, as expected, amazing. I always say that King sure can write books and there's probably a reason why he's such an acclaimed and loved author - loved is probably a big word in his case. It's more of a case of love to hate and hate to love relationship. 
 Like, when I read Misery I nearly vomited at some point. I felt sick. Did I loved that? No, I fucking hate feeling nauseated. But did I love the fact that A BOOK made me want to vomit? Yes. It's a pretty amazing thing if you think about it. 
 So, I went into this book knowing it was about a scary clown and kids getting killed in brutal ways. I started buddy-reading this with my best friend so I could have some kind of emotional support. 
 The format of the book was really interesting, going back and forth past and present, with some interludes (I found them boring as hell but they still made the format original and helped the reader understand how fucked up the city of Derry really was). 
 We followed seven main characters and it was fairly easy to distinguish them all, probably because King REALLY focused on 4/5 of them. 
 Like, because Stan killed himself pretty ealy in the book the only thing we learn about him when he's a kid is that he's always fraking out about the whole It story and Bill has to calm him down more than once. And that he likes bird watching. 
 I grew a little bit attached to the Losers and this feeling is probably what I will remember the most about It, not the scary parts. 
 The first 1000 pages where pretty okay. I mean, it was written in 1986 by a white male, it's obvious I wasn't expecting what we call now diversity - this word was probably ignored during that time. I wasn't expecting a fair treatment of the only female main character, that would be too much to ask. 
 The ending was SHIT. There's no other way to put it. It was disappointing, it was lazy writing, it was confusing, it was underdeveloped. 
 [I will discuss the main reason I gave this book two stars in the spoiler section and because it's such a big plot point please don't read it if you're interested in reading this book, thanks.] 
 First of all there was the fact that It took all these different shapes during the book, some of them scary as hell, but during the final battle, because Its real form is so difficult to grasps for the human brain, It became a spider. WHAT. Lazy as heck.I was expecting to shit my pants to say the least. 
 The battle scenes were ridiculous. That thing with mind reading and... honestly, what the fuck was that? The Turtle? I can't believe he wrote 1000+ pages just to end the book like that. 
 The thing I'm mostly pissed off though about is the sex scene. So, you know when they're escaping and they can't find their way out? And Beverly says the ONLY WAY for them to solve the problem is to make love with all of them so she can show them how much she loves them? Yeah, I'm talking about that scene. 
 First of all, let's not forget they're 12 years old. I know there are some twelve years old discovering sex all over the world probably right this minute, but I find it pretty unrealistic that the first thing that comes to her mind as a solution is to have sex with all of them. 
 Not only that but Beverly was clearly used as an object, because they when they were all done (insert gagging sounds here) they magically find their way out. 
 Oh so NOW it's clear. Now you know where to go. WHAT THE FUCK. 
 I also found the epilogue cringe-worthy to say the least. 
 Although I found the writing exceptional as all of his other books, I can't get over the ending and all of the episodes of lazy-writing that happened during the whole book. There was no reason for this book to be this long. 
 Personally I would not recommend this, maybe watch the movie instead if you really want to see why so many people are terrified of this.

Actual rating: 2.5 
 It took me 20 days to finish this book. And in those 20 days, much excitement, frustration, wonder, and annoyance was had. I'm struggling with the final rating for this, because truthfully, as much as I found it to be every bit the modern horror classic I so eagerly craved, the final 250 pages or so practically ruined the entire reading experience. 
 It started out fantastic. King had me totally hooked for the first 600-700 pages. Around the 800-page mark, however, I think I started to realize how long and drawn out this tale was to be. You see, I've come to discover that when Stephen King has a good thing going, he usually winds up screwing around with it too much, to the point where it (and, literally here)-- It -- becomes a convoluted mess. All these weird, fantastical elements came into play, which I feel has no basis in this story: the fucking space turtle?? and the ritual of Chud, which threw me out of the story entirely. 
 The idea behind whatever It is should've remained more ambiguous; this unknown entity haunting an entire town, but as soon as we found out It's true origins, I gave up on enjoying the book. You see, it wasn't scary. I found the plot to be more of a super dark coming-of-age adventure. Was it gruesome? Sure. Bloody and violent? Heck yes! But not once did I feel fear. I guess I expected more from a horror novel of this stature. 
 Other major issues I had were, again, towards the latter third of the book, the infidelity of Bill, which was completely unnecessary, and actually made me start to loathe his character and of course the whole God-awful nevershouldhavebeenwritten gangbang scenario in the sewers between the six boys and Beverly . I understand King's motives for its inclusion, and how it explained part of that plot, but it was just too damn odd and wholly off-putting. 
 All that aside, I really did like the first half of the book- the longer It remained a horrific abstraction, the better. The writing is still top notch King, and the characters developed to a T. But I cannot overlook the failings of the last 300-odd pages. I was bored, annoyed, and so thoroughly let down.

This novel is quite an undertaking, both for King to have written it and others to read it. Overall, here's my take: this tale, as inventive and original as it is, could have been told in half the amount of pages it took (toward the end I had little sympathy for "The Losers Club" and I just wasn't afraid of Pennywise anymore). My other gripe is that King uses cliches too often for someone who talks a big game about originality in writing. Lastly, for anyone who loved The Stand and thinks, if you will pardon the pun, that this monster of a novel is worth tackling after all these years then do yourself a favor and read something else by King. This bloated novel should have had its fat trimmed before it was first published; if not, it should have been published in two parts (maybe Pennywise's reign in the past and then in the present?).

It is a novel steeped with emotion, and drenched in love. Moyes takes us on the unforgettable journey of Louisa Clark, and Will Traynor. Two people thrown together and changed forever by meeting each other. Me Before You encompasses everything a brilliant novel should. There are many moments of hilarity as well as moments of discovery, and truth. I found myself being able to totally relate to all the characters in this story. This story is so gripping I found it very difficult to put this novel down. This novel literally brought me to tears at several points. There are many lessons to be learned from this story. This novel opens with a glimpse of Will Traynor's life before the accident. He's a handsome and charismatic businessman who enjoys "crushing people" in business deals. One busy day he accidentally steps into the path of an oncoming motorcycle. Will's rage has defeated his parents and any friends who tried to hang on after the accident. The only power he believes he retains is the power to end his life; and, as a man of action, he wants to exercise that power. 
 Louisa (Lou) Clark is the 26-year-old daughter of a struggling family who live in a town dominated by a National Trust castle. She has just lost her job at a tourist cafe and has little prospect of getting another. To take a job caring for a man like Will is terrifying, but her family's financial difficulties allow her no choice. 
 Lou, who is actually quick and funny, is intimidated as she cares for Will. Eventually there are moments when Will's great personality comes alive and the two seem very companionable. When Lou learns his plan is to commit suicide in less than six months' time, she is determined to change his mind by engaging him in life. It frustrates him that she refuses to do much with her own, to experience anything beyond their small town. So she presents herself as willing to broaden and learn, if only he'll teach her. 
 The author makes their coming together sweet and real. But there's a deadline, one that haunts their love story, as well as the novel. I found I was unexpectedly moved by this story, and the issues it made me think about.

The feels. Although I hate romances this was one book that I actually enjoyed the romance. It was no instant love it was developed and I enjoyed that. I knew how it was going to end by the movie trailer and the title of the sequel but I still wasn't prepared for the end. Loved it.

I thought it was interesting that Moyes chose to write about such a sensitive topic yet only told the story through the perspective of those who wouldn't understand (the able bodied). Despite the story seeming to champion Will's right to choose, it was always about Louisa, which totally skewed the potentially profound narrative. Plus, the random bits of activism (mostly complaints about accessibility) seemed like they were last minute additions to appease people who might take issue with the story instead of real concern for the quality of life for disabled people. Regardless of the few good parts, it was all overshadowed by the overall implication that Will was right when he said his life wasn't worth living anymore. Can definitely see why there's a controversy.

"I just needed a bit of time to be away from it all. I just wanted time to be a different person." 
 She looked a bit like a different person. It was weird. Just a few weeks away from home could rub the familiarity right off someone. I felt like she was on the path to being someone I wasn't quite sure of. I felt, weirdly, as if I were being left behind. 
 It's just that the thing you never understand about being a mother, until you are one, is that it is not the grown man-- The galumphing, unshaven, stinking, opinionated offspring-- you see before you, with his parking tickets and unpolished shoes and complicated love life. You see all the people he has ever been all rolled up into one.

I guess I have a right to say that I'm offended by the existence of this book among "romantic" stories. 
 Both as a disabled person, and as a Catholic who aims for everyone to live their life to the fullest potential, realizing what God wants them to be, after 
 this, it sounds like I won't be reading it any time soon. 
 Well, being offended won't be the same as being right, but I'm also right. I'm offended that this is getting all the attention for everything it's not. Literature like this should be absolutely destroyed by critics: the quality doesn't seem too good, the topic is terrible, and the actual lesson of the story is "get rid of those you love, especially if they're billonaire, so they can leave a good amount of cash for you". 
 Of course, people who have read it will argue that Louisa Clark didn't want him to die. But finally, she, like everyone else, gives in. And is that something to do for someone you love? This isn't an heroic act, but selfish death.

 I went into Me Before You with one very specific expectation: that it was going to to be one of Those Books. You know, one of those books, the kinds of books I very specifically do not read because there's a very good chance they might break me. (See: Exhibit A and Exhibit B.) This is probably a spoiler alert--and honestly, it kind of is, if you think about it--but this book is known for something: that it's good, yes, but also that it's S A D. I do not like sad books. I do not read sad books. I do not like feeling so uncontrollably emotional and spending my day(s) trying so damn hard not to cry my eyes out. (See again: Exhibit A and Exhibit B, those filthy bastards.) But I finally took the plunge and read Me Before You after seeing the first movie trailer and because this book was everywhere and I decided to suck it up, further wreckage of my soul be damned, because this mood reader was in the mood for this book. And I read it. And I--and my book-damaged soul--am okay. 
 Here's a fun fact: I bought this book from Goodwill a couple or so years ago because I recognized it since a few friends had raved about it, but I don't think I knew much about it--except that it was sad, I think. And here's the kicker: I thought a large part of the story had to do with an old man who was, of course, dying. Well. Let me tell you that I was wrong. Because Me Before You is about Louisa and how her life changes when she becomes a caretaker for Will Traynor, a man stuck in a wheelchair after an accident left almost every single part of his body paralyzed and ultimately took away any control Will had over himself. Except it's not about that, not exactly, not really. It's about love and life and choice, and it's something I did not except this novel to be: a gosh damn thinker. 
 I'm going to talk about why this book is a gosh damn thinker and it's going to get a bit spoilery (I, at least, didn't know this when I started the book), so if you want to avoid spoilers please skip to the next paragraph. Now. You heard what I said about Will. The guy can move his head, maybe a bit of his neck, and possibly part of one hand (don't quote me; I don't remember for sure, but it's basically nothing). Will can do just about nothing for himself: someone has to feed him, bathe him, wipe him, put him to bed, adjust him if he's not comfortable in a chair, brush his teeth--do you get the picture? Pre-accident, Will was an adventurer, a man who lived on the edge and did this and that and never stopped moving--until he did. That Will lived. This Will barely survives--couldn't on his own--and merely exists, but this Will isn't living. And here's where the thinking--and the spoiler--comes in. Will has a date set, and if on that date he still wants to die, he will go to a controversially known facility that helps people take their own lives, circumstances depending--it's assisted suicide. And you have to wonder: why would Will willingly kill himself? He survived the accident, after all. He has family, and maybe a friend or two who's willing to converse with the wheelchair-bound Will. But then you think, and I mean think: how do you live like that? You can't do a damn thing for yourself except breathe and blink and talk and think--the most mundane tasks are no longer possible. Are you living, or are you existing? Can you really blame Will for wanting to go on his terms and choose his last adventure? I'm too afraid of death to go near it, willingly or unwillingly, but I still thought about it, if I was in this situation. A fish in a tank has more freedom than you. How do you live? That, my friends, is the thinker. The gosh damn fucking thinker. 
 Here's another fun fact (and let's get off such a serious topic, shall we?): I kind of hated this book at first, and Me Before You and I were not getting along, and it was making my head hurt a bit, which is never a good thing for a book to do. The problem was the writing. I did not like it all. I couldn't even tell you what, exactly, that problem was. But it was a problem. (Also, the random point-of-view switches were random and a bit jarring, and I'm not sure they were necessary.) Fortunately, I persevered. And eventually--and suddenly--I realized the writing no longer bothered me. (Thank gosh.) Perhaps that's because I became so immersed with the story. I wanted to know what was going to happen and how it all would end, tried to figure out how it could possibly end in a way that wasn't going to hurt me. Maybe the book was notoriously sad but would turn out happy. I reached a point where I wanted no one to bother me and got in one of those moods where I just read and read and read. I didn't want to put it down, but I was also afraid of reaching the end. It's one of Those Books. 
 Louisa is such a fun, bubbly, and quirky character. (I have hopes for the movie based on the various trailers; it seems to stay pretty true.) She lives in this small house with her parents, grandfather, sister, and nephew, and it can be crowded but in a somewhat comfy way. Louisa can be rather cheery about things, but can still have her breaking points, which help to build her up as a character and someone real. She has a boyfriend, but he's stupid and no one likes him. Her family could get a bit frustrating at times, but they were close-knit and had this sort of...essence about them, which I really liked. And then there's Will Traynor. I've already told you about him, but let me tell you About him. He's a paralyzed man in a wheelchair, and Louisa, desperate for a job and inexperienced, gets to be his caretaker. Will is...well, he's in a situation and hates everything about it. He pushes people away, can be standoffish and rude, and could be called an ass. But Louisa is infectious, and like a disease she spreads into Will, and maybe, just maybe, Will might be a little bit less of an ass. 
 Me Before You defies expectations. You go into it expecting something sad, and you'll get that, but you'll also get so much more. Yes, I cried--but not as much as I thought I would. Not very much at all, really. You expect a Lifetime or Hallmark movie but get something much deeper and meaningful. It still feels like a lighter novel--thank gosh--and that's probably in part to Louisa and her personality and atmosphere. But sometimes that lightness gets a little cloudy and you find out that this novel is simply just more. It's one of Those Books.

 I immediately liked the main character, Yelena. She's a strong female lead. She admits that she killed a man and she's not sorry for it. However, she does want to live, so when she's pulled out of the dungeon and offered a job as the royal food taster, she takes it. In return, she agrees to risk dying for Commander of Ixia and to take deadly Butterfly Dust everyday. Fallen in Love is a collection of stories that happened on a Valentine's Day. It includes the Valentine of Shelby and Miles, Roland, Arianne, and Luce and Daniel. To be honest, I had little hopes for this book. I was never that into Luce and Daniel and the other characters. I just liked to read the books because of the story itself. Fallen in Love didn't exactly start after Passion. Miles and Shelby's did. For Arianne, it happened during the medieval time. And for the others, it transpired during the travel. 
 The first short story was of Miles and Shelby's. It started out quite dull, as expected, since they are my least liked characters in the books. After they separated from Daniel in Passion, Miles and Shelby stepped into an Announcer that was supposed to lead them back home, but instead, it led them to another place in the medieval era. I never pegged them as a couple so it surprised me how things between them developed. I thought it was a little too fast, but it also surprised me how I actually ended up liking their story. 
 The second story is Roland's. At first, I thought all the stories would be fluffy, but his is bittersweet. But still, among the four short stories, his is my favorite. The third story is Arianne's. I don't read romance between two female, but strange enough, I also ended up liking her story. Like Roland's, her story is sad and more tragic. She fell in love with a demon who wanted her to join Hell so they wouldn't have to hide their relationship. But Arianne remained loyal to Heaven, and finally chose to follow Daniel. 
 The last is Luce and Daniel's. Although each character has their own Valentine story, all of them happened on a single Valentine's Day. This is the only Valentine's that Daniel and Luce shared and it happened because Shelby, Miles, Roland and Arianne helped to make it happen. All in all, Fallen in Love, despite my initial impression of it, turned out to be a quite a good read. 
 Rating: 3.5 stars!

This review was originally published at Fluttering Butterflies 
 I do so adore the Fallen series by Lauren Kate so I was thrilled to hear of this collection of short stories, Fallen In Love, is being published during the long wait for Rapture and just in time for Valentine's Day! 
 Daniel and Luce's love transcends time and lifetimes, as they have lived countless times and fallen in love in each life - all to end tragically. I'll admit, I wasn't completely sold on the romance between Daniel and Luce from the first book, Fallen. It took me reading the other books in the series - Torment, in which Luce really questions her feelings and relationship with Daniel, and also Passion, in which Luce takes things into her own hands by jumping into the announcers in order to explore her past lives lived loving Daniel - for me to see and believe that this love is real and true. I believe it now and I'm so behind their relationship! I'm absolutely hooked on this series now, I find it incredibly beautiful. 
 And what Fallen In Love does is that it gives us as readers and as fans a tiny glimpse back into the world of Fallen, and into the hearts of some of our favourite characters. And I thought these stories were sweet, sad, heartbreaking and romantic. It was a wonderful stop-gap before Rapture! Plus, it was quite fun, set in a medieval England setting on Valentine's Day before it had become the holiday that it is today. 
 The first of these four connected short stories concerns Miles and Shelby. After reading Passion, I did at first feel a little bit bad about Miles and how he obviously doesn't stand much of a chance with Luce now that she's knows the full extent of Daniel's and her history. But never fear, he looks set to begin a rather adorable new relationship. What I loved the most about this story was the thoughtfulness of the Valentine's Day gifts. Take note lovers! Something personal and meaningful is always going to make for a better result on Valentine's Day. 
 This is quickly followed by two rather sad stories regarding Roland and Arriane. Roland and Arriane are both characters that I'd never really sat up and took notice of. That is, not until now. Oh, Lauren Kate. You break my heart in so many ways. These two stories deal with lost love and thinking of someone else's happiness over your own and about sacrifice and heartbreak. Roland's story made my eyes well up a bit but Arriane's really had me crying. Both were quite beautiful stories of broken love. 
 But I think most people's main reason for picking up Fallen In Love will be for the Daniel and Luce story at the end. It is the only Valentine's Day in all of their long history that they've ever shared. And it is just as sweet and romantic as you'd imagine it to be. 
 This book is perfect for Fallen fans and die-hard romantics!

May Contain Spoilers, if you actually care 
 Earlier this year I gave A Man Named Dave: A Story of Triumph and Forgiveness by Dave Pelzer the title of "Most Unnecessary Book Ever". I think this title needs to be divided into genres, because he still gets it for 'Memoir' but this book, Fallen In Love deserves it for 'YA Paranormal' or whatever you want to call this genre. So, I hereby give Fallen In Love the title of "Most Unnecessary YA Paranormal Book Ever." 
 This book adds nothing to the Fallen series. Nothing. I don't even like the Fallen series that I am in the midst of reading, but this is the book I truly regret wasting my $16.99 on. What a ripoff! I'm not the first person to say it, but Kate's really milking the cash cow on this one. 
 Timeline wise, this book fits in just before the end of Book 3, but I can't work out which life Luce came from before landing here in medieval England (not that it really matters). Shelby, Miles and Roland have all ended up there, too. And despite being told multiple times, DO NOT MESS WITH THE PAST. What do they do? They mess with the past, to give Luce and Daniel a 'Valentine's Day like no other'. But, if you think this means sexytimes, well you're wrong. It just means flowers and swooning and whatnot. 
 As well as that, we get some backstory to Roland and Arianne, and then Shelby and Miles fall in love randomly, despite the fact that all they talk about is Luce and Daniel. Everyone is so obsessed with Luce and Daniel and I frankly don't understand the appeal. 
 You do not need to read this book as part of the Fallen series. If you're reading the series just to read the series, I wouldn't bother with this one unless you too are obsessed with Luce and Daniel and you like their sappy romance and other sappy romances. 
 I was glad to see the introduction of LBGT characters and also liked how emphasis wasn't placed on the fact that they were LBGT (does that apply to angels?), but more on the good vs. evil battle. I don't understand Tess' reasons for siding with Lucifer and I certainly don't agree with the 'you must choose' mentality. It was interesting but I felt like Kate ruined it with the rushed storyline. 
 200 pages of crap is not worth the money I paid for it. Should have made it a cheap novella online or even a free ebook with the purchase of another title, for the diehards who are actually enjoying this series. 
 My series wrap up can be found on my blog, Crash My Book Party, under Series Binge Read.

Finally I'm writing a review for this one. 
 AS TO BE EXPECTED... I LOVED IT! 
 If you know me then you know that I'm a huge Colleen Hoover fan and Confess didn't let me down. 
 Confess is about this girl named Auburn, she moves from Portland to Dallas, she doesn't know what she wants, she needs money and someday she's walking on the street and there's a desperate help sign in this place called "Confess", which is an art studio where people write down their personal confessions and they slip them into a slot outside of the art studio and the artist uses the confessions as inspiration for his paintings and each piece is inspired by a real confession. 
 The idea of the confessions was captivating, and all the confessions in this book were sent to Colleen Hoover by her readers, and the art on this book is breathtaking, SO beautiful. 
 Every time you read a confession it hits you and even more when you get to see the confession with the art, it's AMAZING. 
 The connection between the characters felt so real (Like in every CoHo's books) It was so easy to drawn into the story, since the very first page I couldn't put it down. 
 It was beautiful, breathtaking, heartbreaking, funny, amazing, it was everything. I ended up crying in different parts of the book, let me tell you that I was a completely mess. 
 Colleen Hoover, writes in a way that you think you have figured out the whole book and then BAM!! YOU WERE SO DAMN WRONG! 
 PEOPLE YOU NEED TO READ THIS BOOK!

You know you love an author when you don't even have to read the synopsis of their book to know you're going to read it. Colleen Hoover's books are like that for me, of all her books I've read, she hasn't let me down yet! I am so excited to get my hands on this... 2 days!!!!! 
 Colleen Hoover, you are amazing. This book literally had me thinking about it for two days straight. I started it late last night and unfortunately had to go to bed because of - ugh - work this morning, so I got about 1/4 of the way through it. And, I was pretty frustrated. I had So. Many. Questions. I literally kept the e-book open on my phone all day, when I went to the bathroom at work I snuck in a few pages, when I was driving to my sister's gym tonight and stopped at red lights, I snuck in a few sentences. I was obsessed, possibly stupid, but obsessed. I even talked to my sister post-workout about the book and all the scenarios that were running through my head as to what could have been going on... I will say we had some interesting theories, but some were close! 
 Then I finally got home and was able to read - uninterrupted. And, I can say I don't regret being up at 2:30a.m. when I know the alarm shrieking in a few hours is going to suck, because I finished the book! Tore through it as fast I could - without skipping like a have a tendency to do! And while I was concerned, like SERIOUSLY concerned, there in the middle - I was SO HAPPY with the ending. I knew I could trust Colleen to write the perfect story, why was I doubting?! 
 Auburn and Owen's story is one I will keep with me forever. It's a story of selflessness. A story that shows what it means to love someone more than yourself. 
 There's so much I want to type - so many disjointed thoughts about this book that are getting stuck in my head... but I don't want to give too much away. I read in another's review once that the less you know about Colleen's books going in, the better they are. And, it's so true. It's the pleasure (or torture, you know, same thing) of thinking about the outcome in between the times you get to read that make the stories that much better. 
 Just know this story gave me hope. Hope for Auburn and Owen, hope for their families, hope for people out in the world going through the exact same situations... or ones like it. I can only wish that everyone could find their Auburn or their Owen. Someone to pick you up when you can't. Someone to show you that you're worth it. Someone to love you. 
 I loved this book. And, if you'll excuse me, I think I'm going to go push it on unsuspecting people asap. :)

I hated this book the first time I read it, but when it was chosen for book club I decided to try to give it a second chance and try to be more objective. It didn't work. I still hate it. 
 When I first read it I thought I only hated it because of the way it completely twisted some of my favorite novels from childhood (The Narnia Chronicles) but I realize now it's much more than that. This novel has been described as being "Harry Potter for adults" but that statement couldn't be more wrong. This is Harry Potter for adults who have become completely disillusioned by books about magic. There's nothing even magical about this book - Grossman turns magic into science and takes away everything that's magical about magic. The book feels completely sterile and antiseptic, with no heart or imagination at all; instead of the creativity and color Harry Potter inspires in my imagination, I pictured this whole world dreary and grey. The style and tone of the book made the narration feel toneless, and uninterested, which made it hard for me to care about what was happening or get into the story. I didn't like any of the characters in this novel - not because they were unlikable, but because I simply didn't care about them at all. 
 And I haven't even gotten into the minor things that bugged me, like the fact that the school's calendar is randomly 2 months off from the rest of the world for no apparent reason. I've discussed this book with some other people who defended it based on the fact that the tone is intentional and the author is trying to make a statement on these types of novels, but even if this is the case it just put me off the book entirely. If you're looking for Harry Potter for adults, do not read this book. Check out Jim Butcher's Dresden Files instead.

I'm still not entirely sure how I feel about this book. The structure is unusual in a way that might be flawed, or it might just be different from what I'm used to. There isn't a conventional story arc, but it's not arranged as a series of interludes connected by a device, either. Normally, a story with school at its center will be structured around the school time frame, but this isn't. Sometimes a lot of time passes with the narrative just skimming and skipping over things, then other times we stop and zoom in on things that don't necessarily move the plot or develop the characters, although they aren't really objectionable to read. And then the whole school thing turns out to be not so important, in a way. 
 I think the protagonist is problematic for me. I don't really like Quentin, but then he is an anti-hero and I'm not really supposed to like him. It's more that, while Quentin may be more realistic than a conventional hero, he doesn't feel real to me as a fully developed character. After everything he experiences, I still don't feel like I know him or understand what makes him tick. In some cases, I might say that was the desired effect, or I was just not connecting to that particular character, but in this case I'm afraid it's because the character isn't whole. 
 Overall, I still enjoyed the book to a reasonable extent, and I'm looking forward to seeing how the second book picks up the story and pushes the characters in hopefully new directions. I guess I'm supposed to talk about how the book is and is not like Harry Potter, or how Fillory is or is not like Narnia, but really, that's tiresome. It's refreshing to see the Hogwarts-like situation given such a different treatment, and the Narnia stuff seems like perfectly acceptable and somewhat traditional literary signifying.
Fantastic read. Can not wait to start the next book in the trilogy.
Got halfway through before the Young Adult and "don't think about things that are happening in the book" aspects got too large.

I'm giving up. Not only does this book really have no point behind it but it has stolen so much from other books that I just can't understand how Grossman could do it. First he actually uses some of the same made-up words and ideas from Harry Potter and then the last straw was when I realized that he used the same exact in-between type world as was used in the Magicians Nephew by C.S. Lewis. I mean come on.

Quentin is sort of the lovechild of Harry Potter and Holden Caulfield; this is his magical "coming of age." Q is self-centered, petty, insecure, and awkward...in short, your average teenager. This is a novel of his dreams and fuck ups, both spectacular. I really liked it, tho the pacing was a little off for me, and most of the time you want to strangle the protagonist. I'm not running out to devour book 2, but I'll get to it eventually.

I might change my two stars later when I have calmed down a bit, but good lord this book made me livid! If it was written well, all of the blatantly obvious references to The Secret History and fantasy literature (Harry Potter and Narnia in particular) would have been forgiven as they could be passed as homage or intertextuality. But the writing is so terrible (has anyone heard of an editor?), it came across as blatant freebooting (in print form). 
 A magical land visited by four English children (where only human children can sit on the four thrones)? 
 A wizard's school? 
 A hunt for a white stag? 
 A group of precocious and bored university students drinking themselves to death? 
 Drunken orgies in the woods? 
 A time-turner disguised as a pocket watch? 
 A form of wizard chess? 
 A world-between-the-worlds with ponds to jump into? 
 Seriously - are Donna Tartt and J.K. Rowling getting any royalties from this? 
 And lets not forget the worst line in the book: "Of course it matters, Vix," Quentin said. "It's not like they're all the same." "Vix" was a term of endearment with them, short for vixen, an allusion to their Antarctic interlude, vixen being the word for a female fox.

As other reviewers have said, equal parts Harry Potter, Narnia and Catcher in the Rye -- without the depth of any of them. Intriguing concept and there were moments I wanted to love this, but it's too rushed to get truly invested and that's to say nothing of your childhood hopes and dreams getting crushed by the biggest Eeyore of all protagonists imaginable . I'm not sure what Grossman was gunning for with the oppressive negativity, but his characters' collective lack of wonder, motivation and compassion doomed this book.

I have no earthy idea why this book is or ever was popular. The idea that SyFy bought the rights to the property and has made a television series from it blows my mind. To me this book read like J. K. Rowling's older, 'cooler' brother mansplaining all the ways in which Harry Potter was juvenile drivel. And true to form, by doing so the quibbler missed one of the very coolest things about Harry Potter: good or bad, rich or poor, gifted or average, cool or uncool, all of the students at Hogwarts are just that: students. The great social rift of girls below and boys above is practically ignored. 
 I tried to give The Magicians the benefit of the doubt. I mean, it is written from the POV of a teenage boy. The fact that Quentin's self-absorbed isn't a huge surprise, nor are his more neanderthal views on women. 
 Where I fell off the joy train was during the Antarctic portion of the program. First up, the Russian who runs the concentration camp they call a school is creepy to the point of vulgarity. The whole 'theft of voices' thing boded ill, but it wasn't until the 'hammer and nail' game that Grossman really hacked me off. 
 The scene is set thusly: a dank stone cell, a table and chair, a block of wood, a hammer and nails, and a fiddly spell so oft repeated to suit various conditions as fill the provided book. Our hero is set the task of completing every iteration of this pointless spell that's purpose is simply to allow the caster to drive a nail into a piece of wood with one whack of the hammer without bending said nail or crushing their thumb. The narrative expounds on the conditions covered ad nauseum: different locations, altitudes, weather -- some examples specific, some not. Finally, only three variables remain to be tested: the caster's gender: male, female or 'hermaphrodite.' Naturally, the protagonist balks over the last option like any genderist prig. 
 Obvious irks aside, why exactly are those the final three options? Wouldn't every iteration of the spell have three versions based on the caster's gender? Is it just a given that only a man would find himself having so much trouble driving a nail into a board 'on a tropical island during a snowstorm' that he would have to resort to magic? How does that even make sense? 
 I actually lasted a bit past that. It was when the entire fourth year class was turned into foxes as an excuse for wholesale rape that I gave up. The protagonist describes how the object of his desire's 'eyes roll in terror' as he penetrates her only to 'fog with pleasure' seconds later. (That was written by a true man...with no real sense of spacial relationships.) Our hero describes how uncomfortable things are the next day, wonders if his lady love is still a virgin...and all the other ridiculous garbage anyone with a lick of sense would avoid voicing at all cost. 
 I plan to return my copy to Audible because I just can't justify giving Lev Grossman a single dime.

book_b.title: The Red Tent
book_b.user_review: Such a unique story beautifully written! I snagged this book in a cozy used bookstore while visiting Chicago. I had heard about it prior in regards to it being an empowering story of a girl brought into womanhood. The part that is intriguing is that it is based of the narrative of the bible and the members of Jacob's family, focusing on his only daughter Dinah. You follow Dinah's life story and feel every raw emotion. You know a truly good novel when the author can shatter your heart and you still leave the story reminiscing and sweet on your mind, just as what I experienced reading this novel. A hidden gem, and interested genre! This will remain a favorite.

sample_reviews.review_text: Something in the way this was written made it feel like torture to read. I muddled through, but it felt like really hard work! Fiction should not be such hard work!
lumbering in parts but a fascinating world to be sunk into.
Laborious and boring. I almost finished it, but went into labor with my daughter and never had the time or desire too finish it afterwards.

A beautiful story depicting the lives of some of the women of the Bible. Moving, touching, educational, and believable, we experience the lives, wisdom, and roles of women in Biblical times. I wasn't always pleased with how the One God seemed to fair in this story, but I can't say that the women's point of view was unreasonable. The women were those who likely received little instruction in the following of "the god of Jacob's father", and so may have known little and understood less. And that is depicted in this story, along with the loves, marriage, pregnancies, rites of passage, and customs of Dinah's time.

I wasn't sure about this novel at first but the second half and the ending swept me up in the story. I actually felt pretty emotional by the end and was desperately reading on the train home so that I could see what happened! It's a novel that makes you feel powerful if you're a woman, as cheesy as that may sound. Try it out!

I added The Red Tent to my TBR a long time ago and not remembering why I jumped straight in. From the first page I was hooked. The writing was crisp, vibrant, and engaging. The subject matter at times unforgettable. I found it hard to put down and when I was finished regretting that the end finally came. 
 I found the subject matter fascinating, I had vague recollections from the tale of Jacob. I really liked seeing a modern tale woven in and out of the Old Testament. The message of live, love, sacrifice, and redemption which was present from cover to cover was simply beautiful to read. 
 I do enjoy historical fiction quite a bit so this fell into one of my favorite genres. I could definitely see myself re-reading this again some day. 
 What this book gets right is its message, the writing is beautifully done, and the story is engaging pretty much from beginning to end. 
 What this book gets wrong is some of the medicinal and scenes were not quote right according to what science has been able to document but does not take away from the story. Some things were a step out of time.
Hmmm, I couldn't get past the first chapter. Too much menstruation.
I hated this book. It's supposedly based on one of Jacob's wives from the Bible. It was gruesome. I guess life was like that back then, but it didn't appeal to me.

I found myself constantly putting this book down because it was dull and slow. The story itself was interesting, and embellished, from the Bible. I understand it was a fictionalized account of the lives of women in biblical times, but it was horribly drawn out and rambling. I finally started to enjoy the book about 70 pages from the end (for about 40 pages) but it dropped off again. If it wasn't a book group selection I would have dumped it at about page 50.

I read this book for book club, and wouldn't have bothered to finish it if it weren't for that. I guess you can't really call skimming over all but the first few chapters of the book just prior to book club "finishing" it, but that's what I'll call it. Anyway, I am no biblical scholar, and the author admits that the book is intended to stand on it's own as fiction, but I have enough knowledge of the Bible to know that this author took the basic story and pulled the rug out from under it, so to speak. The author suggests that sex with sheep occurs while tending the flock, that a father has no problem touching his daughter in inappropriate ways, and that premarital sex as teenagers is all part of the daily norm in the lives of these nomads. I just couldn't enjoy the story on any level. 
 I guess that knowing the actual characters role as written in the Old Testament could have worked against me in this case because honestly everyone else in my group seemed to love the story. There was just far too much of the authors imagination in it to make it an enjoyable read for me. 
 So my advice is, if you're familiar with the story as it stands and don't really see the need to invent more drama into an already dramatic story then don't bother reading this book. But that's just my opinion.

reference_book.title: Animal, Vegetable, Miracle: A Year of Food Life
reference_book.review_text: As much as I applaud Barbara Kingsolver for advocating for the local food movement, I can't help but think this book might attribute to the local food movement's negative reputation. Kingsolver doesn't come off as very like-able to the reader. In fact, to me, she comes off as self-indulgent, boring, and quite frankly just strange. If she had created more like-able characters maybe the reader could have connected more to this book. The only thing good that came from this book are the end of the chapter recipes and the general plea to eat local.

book_a.title: Down and Out in Paris and London
book_a.user_review: This book definitely makes sense of why George Orwell ended up writing 1984 and Animal Farm. Super interesting to see where his interest in Communism and Socialism started. I would recommend this book to any history loving nerd or anyone interested in 20th century Europe.

sample_reviews.review_text:
A wonderful read- a treasure trove of observations and characters. Full of reasons to be grateful we live in the modern world but whilst it is a look at a by gone era, it still seems a current and pertinent read. With homelessness soaring in this country since 2010 and people's compassion at an all time low we are not so very far away from returning to the conditions of this time. 
 The book is not all doom and gloom, by any means, though. As well as being hard hitting and concerning it has many moments lightness and fun and for the curtain twitchers, people watchers and gossipers amongst us it is often a joy.
not bad, but not really my thing

Unha xenial descricion do que alguns chaman o "4o mundo". A pobreza, a mendicidade, os traballos miserabeis... Parece incribel que sexa unha parte da vida de Orwell. 
 Calquera que lea este libro lembrarase del cada vez que vexa un "pobre". 
 Creo que o ingles directo de Orwell e perfecto para os que non dominamos totalmente a lingua. 
 Una genial descripcio d'allo que alguns anomenen el "4t mon". La pobresa, els pidolaires, les feines miserables... Sembla increible que sigui una part de la vida d'Orwell. 
 Qualsevol persona que llegeixi aquest llibre se'n recordara cada cop que vegi un "pobre". 
 Crec que l'angles directe d'Orwell es perfecte per als que no dominem totalment la llengua.

Brilliant insight into poverty. As well as being an interesting historical record time it makes lots of points that are still relevant for today. Essential reading for anyone interested in history or politics.
Really enjoyed this one. Read in 2007 I think. Might just read it again sometime.

This often overlooked book is as much of a masterpiece as Orwell's better known work. With often disgusting detail, Orwell lets us know the realities of being totally down and out during the 1930s. And as usual with him, this book carries a very strong social message. And, of course, the writing is beautiful, even when describing very ugly situations,

A few days ago, my dad and I had a conversation what you can call anti-semitic and what you can't . . . we had this conversation when I asked if George Orwell hated Jewish people or not. This question didn't come out of nowhere, in less than 20 pages I had already twice about Jews being disgusting and the worst people in the world, only there to take away from you your money and dignity. 
 I am Jewish, and I am fucking tired of reading about this. My dad - who isn't Jewish - said I couldn't call GO anti-semitic, and I see his point : anti-semitism didn't exist back then, it was a thing to hate Jews . . . but then doesn't it mean I can't call Nazis anti-semitic as well? I know, I can't compare GO to a Nazi, even I know this, but does that also mean you can't call the XXth society misogynist because women didn't know anything else? When can you call something/someone by its name? That's my question. 
 So I'm not calling GO anti-semitic, but I'm saying it as it is : this book is full of hate towards Jewish people. It's full of it, and I can't stand it anymore.

"Op het ogenblik heb ik, geloof ik, alleen nog maar de periferie van de armoede gezien. Maar toch heb ik doordat ik aan de grond heb gezeten enkele dingen geleerd. Ik zal nooit meer denken dat alle zwervers verzopen schurken zijn, noch zal ik dankbaarheid verwachten van een bedelaar als ik hem een penny geef. Evenmin zal ik het voortaan vreemd vinden dat werkloze mannen geen energie meer hebben. Ik zal het Leger des Heils niet steunen, mijn kleren niet naar de lommerd brengen, een strooibiljet niet weigeren aan te nemen en niet lekker gaan eten in een chic restaurant. Dat is een begin." (252)

This book reminded me of a more depressing "Tale of Two Cities." I don't feel too sorry for people who are down on their luck, because usually it's because they didn't work hard enough to prevent it. Maybe that's harsh but it's true. There were points in this story when I just wanted to shake the main character and say, "Stop being so stupid." I guess that means that Orwell wrote a good story because he did a good job conveying all the characters flaws.

Orwell (or his publisher?) has a bizarre/troubling sense of propriety - all profanity has been excised, even when meaning is sacrificed ("The current London adjective, now tacked on to every noun, is ------. N doubt in time ------, like 'bloody,' will find its way into the drawing-room and be replaced by some other word" -p. 177) . A story about an assault on a prostitute, though, gets casually retold to open the book (p. 12-15). 
 A meta-review of Orwell's book & all of the "Down and Out in..." titles/Bette Midler movies it spawned is low-hanging critical fruit. Let's get on this, universe!

book_b.title: A Moveable Feast
book_b.user_review: I loved it but it definitely isn't a novel anyone would love. I would say that you have to have a love for Paris, the 1920's, and Hemingway's writing. That being said, it was a supremely entertaining book. I loved seeing Paris in the 1920's through Hemingway's eyes. He was so immersed in the city and it's artists and writers at that time. Definitely telling my friends to read it!!

sample_reviews.review_text: Considering my disdain for Hemingway's machismo and condescension, I was surprised to enjoy this book so thoroughly. His writing shone with amusing irreverence.

This is the newly restored edition of my all time favorite book. The Preface by Patrick Hemingway and the Introduction by Sean Hemingway provide new perspective on the writing of this book by their father/grandfather and the changes to the original manuscript made by Hemingway's fourth wife Mary. 
 After reading it I can't say that there was much different although I loved the way they included several versions of the same lines to show how his thought process worked when he was writing. It is true that his actual descriptions of Scott Fitzgerald were far more compassionate and positive than what was published based on earlier drafts of his work. 
 To me the most interesting thing is his writing about Hadley. When you remember that this book was written over 30 years after their marriage ended and while he was with his fourth wife, his loving, lovely words about her are almost difficult to bear. Much of this book is really a love letter to her. 
 Such a fascinating writer.
I like Hemingway's fiction but could not get into this.

So why does one read A Moveable Feast? I like Hemingway and I love Paris, so it's a must read, right? A friend said she finished it and still didn't feel like she knew Hemingway; yet, it's a memoir. She's right. He wrote like a journalist even in these short takes on his life in Paris in the early 1920s. But I find it interesting to see what he includes and what he omits. Surely this tells us something about Hemingway. He includes lots of references to how poor they were, but they are always drinking beer and wine in one cafe after another. He talks in several stories about the beautiful women he encounters yet he resists them like a man committed to his wife Hadley, whom we never describes or mentions in a very positive way. He talks about writing at cafe tables, but not much about the craft of writing. Whether you like Hemingway or Paris or neighter, you should read the chapter on Scott Fitzgerald if nothing else. Gatsby may make much more sense.
At least it was short
One of the best books ever. I wasn't lucky enough to live in Paris as a young man but when I did visit this book came with me
The only Hemingway work I could tolerate!

This was an okay read, 
 I enjoyed the first few parts where he talks about writing. For example, he mentions he writes in the morning or in a place where is by himself like a cafe or something; and that once his work is done for the day, he closes his book, and doesn't/didn't think of writing until the next day so he had ideas ready to go. 
 But towards the middle it got boring. He talked too much of Scott as well nearing the end. I just didn't care for some dialogues. 
 I also disliked how he kept looking at women or making certain comments despite having a wife. 
 I lost interest towards the end and skimmed instead and was shocked to read about his affair. 
 I am not a fan of such thing but I don't even hate on the guy because he is no more or because it's just ehh Idk. Nothing comes out of hate from this book because you take your lessons and shut the book. 
 For me what I took away was the writing tip that was mentioned a few times. 
 Other than that, not much.

Hemingway's spare writing style is very evocative and draws you into 1920s Paris and the so-called "Lost Generation." This version includes unedited pieces of sketches Hemingway prepared for the book before he died, some of which he had intended to discard. I found I missed an editor's touch but overall, it's well worth reading.

A very enjoyable surface-level dive into Hemingway and Paris, for true fans of either. This 'memoir' is little snippets, written long after the fact, of Hemingway's time spent poor, hungry, and writing in Paris during the roaring twenties there. 
 It features a cast of characters familiar to any Hemingway/Midnight in Paris fan, most prominently Gertrude Stein, The Fitzgeralds, and more painters. It contains scenes of writing in cafes and walking through the Luxembourg Gardens, as well as a road trip debacle with FScott. 
 Hemingway writes well, as you'd want him to, and brings you into his world - albeit at arm's length in diary-like entries. There are many classic Hemingway aphorisms here. It prepared me nicely for our Paris trip (since much of the locations and feelings remain frozen in time there), but it's not a change-your-life book or fully baked novel. One can tell it was composed of scraps to be published posthumously.

reference_book.title: Difficult Women
reference_book.review_text: Along with the ones dealing with outright rape, almost every story in this collection is filled with violent sex and features female characters who allow or even beg men to sexually hurt, abuse, and degrade them. This is feminism?

book_a.title: Foreplay (The Ivy Chronicles, #1)
book_a.user_review: This was one of my first forays into the NA/erotic romance genre, and I was disappointed. While I don't recall anything particularly offensive about this book, it seems like NA is just an excuse to write about virgins meeting hot bad boys. The plot was pretty lackluster. Even the sex was lackluster, unless nervous virgin scenes turn you on, and personally I don't really find them interesting to read.

sample_reviews.review_text:
PJV Quickie: In Foreplay, Sophie Jordan has taken the bad-boy/good girl trope and given it a nice little twist. It was a quick read and I stayed interested in the story - normally I read by switching between two books at a time but I didn't touch my 2nd book the entire time I was reading Foreplay. 
 Review: 
 Pepper is a 19-year-old college student who has been pining for her best friend's older brother, Hunter, since she was 12 years old. We're talking serious longing, as in - she chose her college because Hunter goes there. When her BFF calls to tell her Hunter has broken up with his girlfriend of two years, Pepper is ecstatic...then petrified: she has absolutely no experience with dating and the other physical aspects that go along with dating. How is she going to catch Hunter's attention and make him see her as a love-interest, and not her kid sister's best friend, if she has no idea what she's doing? Her roommate, who knows about Pepper's obsession with Hunter, has decided they need to get Pepper some experience, so they pick a local bartender with a reputation as a man-whore to give Pepper some experience with the opposite sex. 
 Reese works at the local college bar, Mulvaney's, and is attracted to the cute co-ed who's been flirting with him. When he finds out she's looking for dating experience, he's more than happy to help. What he doesn' t count on is that he genuinely likes her, which makes it that much more difficult to give her "lessons" that she plans to use on another man. 
 ~~~~~~~~~~ 
 Where to start? I am a fan of Ms. Jordan's Young Adult Firelight series, and when I saw she was doing a New Adult series I was thrilled. I was right to be excited; I really, really enjoyed reading Foreplay. 
 I immediately liked Pepper, you get the impression she's book-smart, and maybe street-smart (not by choice), but in spite of, or maybe because of, those things, she's not very experienced in the ways of dating and sex. Because of her bleak childhood, she is trying to ensure a happy, secure future, and she knows that future involves being part of her best friend's 'perfect' family. She's loved Hunter for 7 years, and all she wants is to make him fall in love with her. I was a little bit frustrated on this point, that she wanted Hunter to 'save' her from her past, instead of saving herself, and yes, the author works around it, but still...it bothered me a bit. 
 And Reese, oh Reese! What a great, swoon-worthy hero. He's not your typical (what I feel is typical, anyhow) promiscuous NA hero, he's a genuinely good guy in unfortunate circumstances, trying to do right by his younger brother and a difficult father. (I know I describe him as a man-whore in my recap above; there's a funny thing about that...) 
 I loved reading the relationship between these two - it was backwards, if you will: they started out with the physical stuff and as they got to know each other it got more emotional and complicated. The story had no outside conflict, it was all character driven, and although I found myself frustrated with Pepper at times, her choices were understandable given her history and her idealization of Hunter's family. Even when she started to think maybe Reese could be the right choice for her, once she knew his history she knew he wouldn't be able to give her the 'perfect' life that Hunter could. The scenes between Pepper and Reese later in the book just tore at my heartstrings. 
 There is a big scene near the end that was a little over-dramatic, but the ending left this reader sighing (in a good way!). I did not realize this is a series when I started reading Foreplay, and I am happy to say there is no cliffhanger here. All in all, Foreplay was a engaging read with likable characters and an interesting premise. I've already added the second book in the series, Tease, to my wishlist. 
 Recommendations: 
 Recommended for fans of New Adult, swoony bad-boy heroes, moderate angst, and happy endings.

3.5 stars.. 
 I really enjoyed reading this fast paced NA book.. Pepper was a girl that had been through a lot growing up, she was never the popular, flirty girl... She had everything planned out in her head of how her life was going to be. Until she met Reece and everything changes. It's great to see the character development, how Pepper gets to be more confident and what I really liked about her is that she was really honest. 
 Asides from the fact that I really liked the main character I thought this story was very realistic comparing to others NA books, there was no crazy billionaire control freak( like fifty shades of grey and so many other NA books). 
 Foreplay was a fun and funny book, and I really recommend this book, specially if you like romances! The ending was very predictable, but still good..

The majority of romances are highly predictable. You know that going in of course, and sometimes the story is deep enough or does something a little out of the norm that you don't mind that the ending isn't really a mystery. But this book was frustrating because I felt like I was just plotting along a path I already knew, there was no shock or interest that grabbed me and made me invested in THIS book over any other romance. 
 That being said, the writing was fine and it wasn't a struggle to get through.
I loved Reece, didn't really like Pepper

Odio a la protagonista!!!! 
 Como rayos una inteligente estudiante de psicologia es tan estupida???!!! 
 Uso practicamente al chico y se lo dice, para conseguirse a otro y el chico Reese se enamora de ella. Es una historia con una historia floja, repetitiva y con personajes planos y aburridos. Con los tipicos cliches de chica con pasado traumatico, virgen que desea experimentar con el chico malo. Chico tonto que ss frio, y que es usado pero aun asi se enamora perdidamente. 
 Secundarios tonto de la tipica amiga extrovertida y algo zorra y la tranquila estable. 
 La escritura es ligera, y facil de leer pero peca de no expresar nada.

Review originally posted at Step Into Fiction 
 Actual rating: 4.5 stars 
 This is another one of those books that you finish and ask yourself why you put it off for so long? It's not that I didn't want to read it, it's just that I couldn't find them time. Or more correctly, I wouldn't make the time. It's a problem when you have too many books to read and never enough time, choosing becomes a tougher project that you can imagine. But I wanted something quick, fun and great so I chose this. Best decision I've made in awhile. Not to mention I finished it in one sitting but I fell in love with it. 
 You know when you read a story and in the beginning, you're all for the protagonist and one of the love interests ending up together, like really into it happening but then . . . the more you read, the more you question yourself? This was one of those stories. I really liked the idea of Hunter and Pepper in the beginning but then I was asking myself why would someone want to be with someone who never really noticed her before? Why would you rule out any other guy just because you've had your heart and your head stuck on this one guy for the past seven years? Basically, just why? I liked Reece the moment we met him even before we knew his name. He may appear to be dark, dangerous and mysterious but really, he's a gentleman and you learn that the very first time you meet him. 
 Pepper was tough to love sometimes but when you came across the way she thought, you just had to put yourself in her place. When you father dies at such a young age and your mother abandons you, not to mention the lifestyle she had before abandoning you. You probably have a different outlook on life and especially on how you want your future to look. So while it's hard to understand her way of thinking yourself, putting yourself in her shoes makes it much clearer. She's a good person with a rough past but she's more concerned with building her future and hats off to her for that. 
 I read Sophie Jordan's YA book, Uninvited and knew I wanted to read more of her work. While I've been told to read her other YA series asap, it was this book I wanted to read more. I've been on a New Adult kick and this sounded right up my alley. It was a quick, fun, sexy read. I couldn't help falling in love with all of these characters (sidekicks included) and I can't wait to read about more of them. Thankfully, I don't have long to wait for TEASE and I can't wait to dive in to that. 
 I loved this book something fierce but I'm struggling to put my feelings in to words which explains my semi-short review (if you've read a lot of my reviews, you know I gush and gush and ramble a lot). Don't judge a review on it's length :-P - if you like New Adult, you'll want to read this book. If you're looking to give this genre a chance, start here.

Originally reviewed at Reading the Best of the Best. 
 Currently Listening To: Heart Attack by Demi Lovato 
 If there's anything I will give New Adult, it's the fact that I can always read the book for a good time, quick and easy, light and fun. When I heard that Sophie Jordan was writing a new adult, I was neither surprised nor disappointed. After all, I'm not the biggest fan of NA. But I was a fan of Sophie Jordan's so I had some expectations wit this book. Foreplay, sadly, wasn't the new, fresh NA I was hoping for. Instead, while it was an enjoyable read, it was fairly predicable, with nothing new to add. 
 The Plot 
 Nothing new. As I kept reading Foreplay, I wasn't surprised by anything. Nothing seemed new and fresh and original. For a "genre" that is just getting it's start, is this not a little sad? Sure, I liked the idea that Pepper and Reece weren't originally falling in love and the sexual tension was there to keep me engaged, but again, nothing new. I also wanted a little more with this book. The plot was too fast: Pepper and Reece fell in love too fast, the pace was too fast, there wasn't enough background to really understand either Pepper and Reece. 
 The ending was also way to perfect and cookie cutter. Reece and Pepper were madly in love and all of their baggage and issues were resolved. For example, certain issues in Reece's life were introduced in this book that weren't looked into. It was just a touch on the surface and by the end of the book it was gone completely. 
 The Characters 
 Pepper: I liked Pepper to be honest, more than I thought I would. She was broken and had a tough past but she didn't let it define her. She was also a very smart girl who made some stupid mistakes. But unlike most of the mistakes girls in NA books make, Pepper's were more concurrent to her character. The mistakes weren't life changing but rather mistakes a girl makes when she likes a guy. I smiled and laughed at Pepper but I also loved her. while her characterization could have been stronger, and I think she didn't develop as much as she should have by the end of the book, Pepper was fun to read about. 
 Reece: Okay, I liked Reece. He's my type of guy: tall, dark, handsome and a little bit older. But my biggest issue with Reece was that we never really get to know him. What are his interests? What does he like to do? What are his hobbies? I mean, I didn't want his entire characterization but Reece was basically just the hot, sexy bartender throughout this entire novel. 
 The supporting characters: Georgia and Emerson were my favorites. Not only because I could identify each girl with my friends in real life, they were always there for Pepper. None of the supporting characters were developed enough but they had enough personality to tell them apart. 
 The Writing 
 I'm not sure there's anything new or exciting about this writing. It's really light and quick to read. The diction is really conversational and there aren't any big words to be confused by. Honestly, it's one of the better written books and I've found that it comes with the territory. 
 The Verdict 
 Foreplay was simply a quick, fun read. I was in the mood for something light that would make me smile but I knew I wouldn't get any life changing advice from. While the plot was so much like many of the NA books I've read, I liked Pepper a lot. I think it's really because I can see myself as Pepper. There wasn't enough character development or background and I think the book ended too nicely but what can you do?

Foreplay was my first venture into the New Adult genre. I knew Sophie Jordan would be the perfect author to help make it an enjoyable experience. I'm 100% certain she can't write a book I won't love. 
 Foreplay was a fun read. The chemistry between Pepper and Reece was off the charts. The scenes when he was ill. Oh. My. Goodness. I ate it up. 
 I absolutely adored Pepper's personality. I wasn't sure if the premise, virgin wanting to hook up with hot guy to impress crush, could be pulled off sans cheesiness. Thankfully it was! 
 Reece was everything I want in a love interest. All surly bad boy on the outside, but oozing with sweetness underneath the tough exterior. Oh how I loved him. He has a great story, and I'm so glad I was able to experience it. 
 Sophie Jordan is a romance novel writing goddess. I couldn't put this one down and can't wait for the next.
