 So I told myself this would be the year that I would read 10 stand-alone books. One of those being Amy and Roger's Epic Detour. I also told myself that I would read all of the books Morgan Matson had published. Second Chance Summer is my second read from her and I have to say... I was disappointed with this one. As much as I wanted to like this, I just didn't. 
 Before I get into my review, I want to say something in regards to contemporary books being longer than 400 pages. I like contemporary novels. I really do. Some of my favorite books are contemporaries. Ellen Hopkins is a favorite author of mine. I like the realness of them. Sure I like fantasy, paranormal, and sci-fi, but I like to kick back, relax and enjoy a good contemporary book. But sometimes, and I'll be honest, when I see a contemporary book longer than 400 pages, I get a bit worried about it. 
 Now, I have read contemporary books with more than 400 pages. Examples would be Whisper to Me by Nick Lake, Before I Fall by Lauren Oliver, Made You Up by Francesca Zappia, and others. The reason why I enjoyed them was because there was something happening in them. They have a plot and great characters. I enjoyed every bit of those pages. However, with Second Chance Summer, it didn't have anything. I mean, there was a plot, but to me, it felt like nothing happened. 
 Second Chance Summer is about second chances for Taylor, her friends, and her family. Her father was diagnosed with stage four cancer and he doesn't have that much time left. So Taylor and her family decide to spend one last summer together at their summer house near a lake. Except Taylor doesn't want to go because of something she did five summers ago. She has to confront what she had left behind as well as trying to bond with her family given the amount of time they have. 
 This all sounds good. A family coming together to reminisce on good memories and bond together. Except, that didn't happen as much. It did. But not as much. 
 I'll start off with the only positive thing I have to say about the book. What saved the book from being a 1 star was the dynamic of Taylor's family. Since her father doesn't have much time left, they decide to have a second chance of being a close family. This part I liked. Even though I didn't enjoy the story as much as I wanted to, I did like the bond of the family. It showed the things we take for granted and when life comes and throws a curveball at you, it takes the bond of family and friends to know that you're not alone. The family aspect was the best thing about the book. 
 And the only good thing about it because I did not enjoy the rest of it. 
 On to the things I didn't like about the book. 
 For starters, not much happened. Literally, Morgan could've done away with 100 pages and the book may have been better. For the most part, all we get to see is Taylor's life at the summer house, her job near the beach, and her trying to rebuild her relationship with her friend and an ex-boyfriend. I kid you not, most of this stuff bored me. I had to force myself to read these parts just so I can get to the good stuff. It was just talking and talking and talking and talking and blah blah blah. Just plain boring. 
 Then we have Taylor. She's one of those characters that makes things worse. Like if there's a problem, she makes things worse by running away and not dealing with it. That bothered me a lot. Especially near the end when she did something stupid. 
 The romance is another thing I had an issue with. There was no development between Taylor and Henry. I felt NOTHING for them. NOTHING! 
 Verdict 
 There's a good story along with a good message between the lines. But the rest of it took too much of the plot, hindering my chance of enjoying the book. 
 There was potential for the book to be great. Sadly it wasn't in my opinion. It isn't a bad book by any means, it's just wasn't what I expected. 
 If Morgan had deleted some scenes, then maybe I would've enjoyed it. But it was 450 pages of nothing. Which makes me nervous about reading her next two books. One of them being 500+ pages. I'll read another standalone in the meantime and then start Since You've Been Gone. 
 Thanks for reading my review! 
 -Cesar

My overall thoughts: 
 1. This book pleasantly surprised me as I am not a massive fan of romance novels. We follow the story of a young American girl named Anna who gets sent away to Paris to study, she is torn away from her friends and family and is thrust into a new culture that is so far from her own. Although at first Anna struggles she makes friends at her new school and one in particular takes her fancy; Etienne St Clair, a young man whom Anna can't help but fall for. The only problem is that St Clair has a girlfriend and Anna is tied up in relationships back in America. When feelings begin to arise within them we see the highs and lows of being a teenager in love and how even the most trivial of things can cause your world to come tumbling down. 
 2. This book explores so many different topics that I could not help but fall in love with the story. We see the heartache involved in moving away from home, the torment of young love and the devastating effects that can occur when one steps over the boundaries of a friendship. Perkins writes in such a way that I was reluctant to put the book down! Every chapter left me wanting to read more and more until the very end, the drama that was spun throughout this story really had me hooked! 
 3. The relationships in this novel build at a realistic pace, there isn't any kind of instalove that is commonly found in a lot of YA literature. I enjoyed the fact that Anna couldn't have what she wanted for the majority of the novel and I loved how so many of the circumstances were so true to real life allowing me to imagine these things happening with my own friends. 
 4. One thing that I really enjoyed about this book was the amount of cultural knowledge that was shared during Anna's stay in Paris, although I have never been to Paris and have never really studied it I have always had an interest and this book has definitely sparked that interest up again! 
 5. This was an absolutely fantastic read and I can't wait to get my hands on the next in the series; Lola and the Boy Next Door. 5 out of 5 from me, I would recommend to fan of romance but also to those who find it difficult to get into love stories.

I was on and off the first few chapters of this book (not the books fault) I was in a reading slump and this book was perfect for pulling me out. I related so much to the main character Anna. The story was written so beautifully but I wish I had more! Seriously an amazing contemporary and I highly recommend

Definitely a feel good, easy read book. In the beginning has quite a lot of funny moments and good jokes but towards the end it's loaded with drama and that part was a bit too much. So I'm a bit torn between giving it 3 or 2 stars. Half of this book I absolutely loved but half not that much. 
 In the end I gave it 3 stars because I loved the references it makes on movies and Paris itself. That's something I enjoyed the most in this book:) ... feeling like I was exploring Paris along with main characters.

Anna is feeling angry and anxious when her parents send her to Paris to complete her senior year of high school. Not only is she leaving her family, friends, and a boy that she's "in love" with, she doesn't know anything about Paris and feels lost. 
 Luckily, she is taken under the wing of Meredith, and she introduces Anna to her group of friends. One of her friends just so happens to be the dreamy Etienne St. Clair. Too bad he's taken. 
 ____________ 
 Okay, don't get me wrong; there were parts in this book that I thought were kinda cute, but overall, it was so cliche and people that are saying that this plot is unique need to think a little harder! I guarantee there's hundreds of authors out there that thought "hmm, should I write about a girl who goes to Paris and falls in love with Prince Charming?" and then go eh, that might be too cliche. Which they are so right! I get it, it's the City of Light, Love, whatever, but I'm just surprised I haven't read a book about this sooner. 
 On to the characters. Anna was my least favorite character, hands down. I get that you love this guy, and you want to stab his girlfriend's eyes out, but um, hello? She was here before you were...she seems to have no problem helping him cheat on his girlfriend, which was just kinda gross and I got a little second hand embarrassment. 
 Not only is Anna a boyfriend-stealer, she isn't that great of a friend either, which is disappointing because her friends are really cool, but no, she's too absorbed by a guy that she can't give them the time of day or consider their feelings. 
 Basically, this book felt like Romeo and Juliet for me, but there was a happy ending. Like, it was basically love at first sight and they probably would have died for one another within the first week of being friends. 
 Now that I've talked about the things that irked me about this book, don't let me sway you from reading this. If you like chick lit and romance novels that are love at first sight and are totally predictable from there, go ahead. 
 This book was easy for me to just sit and flip through quickly though, which I guess shows that it wasn't that bad.

reference_book.title: Ready Player One
reference_book.review_text:
Alright, I have so many things to say about this novel. First and foremost, if you are searching for the answer to whether or not you should purchase and read this book: 
 Do you like science fiction? Do you appreciate constant references to other science fiction and fantasy universes (they're tactful, I swear)? Do you have about eight hours to read a book right now (because once you pick it up you are not going to want to put it on pause)? 
 If your answers are yes, yes, and totally, then I would 100% recommend this book. Cline does a fantastic job of building a world and then allowing a story to play out within it. Among the references to Firefly, Star Trek, and just about every other show and movie I've ever watched is a teenage boy's development from someone who hides from reality in his video games to a young man who finds power in both actuality and the virtual world. 
 My personal vibes from it are a bit Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, but that may very well be because that is my co-favorite science fiction book alongside this one. Either way, a fantastic read.

Oh man oh man oh maaaaaan. Now I am a huge science nerd and that probably has significant affect on my appreciation but oh maaaaaan. Ten stars out of five, at least. I watched the movie first, which I do about half of the time, but usually I'm like "this movie is moderately okay, so the book must be pretty good" (as that tends to be the pattern of ratios with that whole thing). 
 When I first watched the movie, I immediately thought it one of my favorite hard science fiction movies (perhaps even movies overall), so obviously I bought the book immediately. Actually, I ordered the book before I had completely finished the movie. Shoutout to Amazon. 
 All in all, I love space and Mark Watney. I always paralleled myself to Hermione Granger before, but I rather think of myself more as Watney now. Smart but also a smartass, and occasionally very difficult to deal with. Biggest difference between us is the magnitude of the word "smart", as the solutions put into use during the novel are honestly #goals. 
 I would highly recommend the book to anyone who finds humor in space puns and copious amount of the cleverest type of cursing. With characters that handle problems in the most unpredictable of predictable ways, it's hard to put down from start to finish. Even if you've watched the movie. And you have Calculus 2 homework to finish. 
 On second note, maybe you should make sure you don't have anything on your immediate calendar before grabbing a copy. You'll want to read it from cover to cover.

sample_reviews.review_text: It was ok at first, but then it went down hill from there

A fast paced thrilling scifi drama that takes a unique look at a postapocalyptic universe where only a devastating plague has wiped out most of the adult population, leaving only children and teenagers as well as senior citizens, those who had the opportunity to be vaccinated. Callie's attempt to get her and her younger brother out of the slums brings her to Destination Prime, a technology that rents out the bodies of teens to thrillseeking seniors. Her first few clients are fine, but then Callie gets wrapped up in an assassination plot and learns more about the terrible plans the government has for their citizens, especially those in poverty. 
 Action-packed and fun, Starters has plenty of twists to keep you guessing.

First off, I hate the cover. Hate it. It has nothing to do with the actual content of the book and though it does catch your attention, it has no meaning. Second, I received this book through Random Buzzers to promote and review. I am not being paid except for the free copy I received. 
 I really liked this book. It's 4.5 stars for me, but rounded down to four simply because I didn't find it as amazing as some of my "most favorite read again and again" books. An average of one book out of every seven I await publication actually are as good as I think they will be. This book was delightfully so. I received it on Friday and tore through it. I would have read it in one sitting, but I had things I had to do over the weekend. 
 A lot of reviews are going around saying that they liked the idea but hated the execution and so on. I like to read a book at face value. I never expect anything to happen and let myself enjoy the ride. I think this contributed very highly to my perception of the story itself. There were good twists, a thrilling mystery, and enough action for me to have a hard time finding a stopping place to pause reading. 
 Callie was highly likable. I didn't adore her, but then do you adore every person you meet? She had pros and cons with more of an emphasis on the pros. Thinking back on my initial impression at the very beginning of the book (street rat, starving, wanting to protect her brother) to her becoming a "donor" she's very different. There's a bit of a void in the character development, but I think that is fairly consistent with the aspects of "donating" your body. Unfortunately, aside from the fellow "renters" Callie interacts with, little character development happens with the initial street rat possible love boy who takes care of her little brother alongside her. I do understand why her little brother and Michael would be lesser characters, but they felt a bit like a block of granite with half a face chiseled out. I hope they'll play a bigger role in the next book, ENDERS, whenever that comes out. 
 The execution of the plot idea was, in my opinion, handled very well. It was plausible (I hate those dystopians that are very vague about what happened to the population on Earth and why because the foundation crumbles under scrutiny) and was actually a piece of the story itself, not as a result of or in addition to. There were many roads this book could have traveled with many plot threads left hanging, but I felt a sense of satisfaction when I came to the end of the book that only comes from that creative balance of closure and no closure. Am I dying to get a hold of the next book right this moment? No, not really. But I do anticipate its publication and will read it when it comes out. 
 If you enjoy dystopians that aren't bogged down with too much emotional distraughtness or complicated jargon that flow fairly consistently, I think you ought to take this book for a spin. You might not be disappointed.

This review originally posted at Hooked on Books 
 Are we all familiar with the awesomeness that is Total Recall? If not go out and rent it. We'll wait ... 
 Ok now that we're all caught up, that excellent movie was based on an even more amazing book called We Will Remember It For You Wholesale by Philip K Dick. That book is filled with awesome and cyber-punky action and Starters by Lissa Price reminded me of it in so many ways. 
 This book is full of action right from the get go. It doesn't hold back - it just throws you right in. I loved it. It's been awhile since I've read a book that's had me right on the edge of my seat, biting my nails, waiting to see what happens next. The cover blurb compares this book to the Hunger Games. This drives me crazy. I don't know why there's this obsession with comparing everything to the Hunger Games when there's a more perfectly suited comparison. If you're looking for a real comparison think more Divergent. Starters has a more urban, action movie feel, rather than the dystopian feel of the Hunger Games. 
 In addition to the action, this was also a really unique story. Has it just been me but has every YA sci-fi/dystopia felt incredibly similar lately? Well thankfully Starters was a breath of fresh air. The story wasn't predictable, and it held my attention from the beginning to end. Best of all I thought I had the big twist at the end all figured out and I was wrong. I know that probably sounds weird but I would much rather be surprised than be able to guess everything that was going to happen. 
 Finally, I adored the main character, Callie. Mostly because she was so completely motivated by her love for her younger brother. Incredibly admirable. But I also loved her because she took action. She refused to let herself be a victim and didn't just let things happen to her. All of that equals a pretty boss young lady in my mind. 
 This is a really fun book and if you're looking for an exciting read that really packs a punch this will be right up your alley. Perfect for fans of Divergent, The Maze Runner, Cory Doctorow, and young (or young at heart) Philip K Dick readers

It's amazing how many fantastic books by debut authors that I have had the honor of reading so far in 2012, and STARTERS is no exception to this honor. I ripped through the pages of this book like one would rip through a super delicious candy bar. It was that good and OH-SO thrilling to read! Starters presents itself as a dystopian novel, but between the covers it is really quite a lot more than that. Starters is a suspenseful thriller, as well as a carefully plotted mystery, that will have your eyes and mouth gaping wide until the very last page... 
 You can read my full review of STARTERS over at Making the Grade.

The plot is simple, at least at some length. We are in the future where, after a bio war only the old people (aka enders) and the teens (aka starters) are alive. The thing is, old people are really old, like 150yo and have all the money and essentially rule the world. 
 The starters have no rights, are poor, really poor and live as outlaws in a world where the old people are evil (most of them anyways). I'm not really sure I buy this, but is not so out of the box I would take off my list (aka The Amazing Apocalypse Theories' List), so it's still on the list. 
 The main character is this starter girl that has a little brother and want to make money to save them from a life in misery. So she finds this clinic called Prime Destinations. The job is easy and you would get the money in your sleep, literally. 
 Starters can't have jobs until they have 19yo, so she would be a donor and would get pay lots of money to (get this) rent her body to enders to get the feeling how to be young again. 
 Body snatcher much? Yep, I think so. But still, very interesting stuff. 
 They have this contract that has all this "don'ts" and if the renters, aka enders, brake the rules they pay like a gadillian of dollars. It looks like bullshit? Yep. Still believable? yep. 
 I'm not gonna say Callie, the starter, had no other choice, she had, but desperate times ask for stupid choices. So she decides to do this crazy stuff and after three rentals she would be free with her payment and a better life. 
 That would be great, but then we wouldn't have a very long story, would we? As you can imagine, the stuff is deeper than it seems. Human rights, sacrifice, priorities and a whole lot of etic discussion fill this book. 
 I like it very much, but I can't say the plot is that perfect. The idea is better than the execution. The action part is really good, but the interaction seems a little robotic. It felt a little cold and flat. Since this is the first book and I know there's a second, I hope this get better. 
 As far as twists and turns, this one is good. I had some moments I was surprised and that's good, but I wish it had more warmth in the writing. 
 All in all is a very good book and I'm certainly gonna read the sequel.

The premise is good and, honestly, could easily provide a thought provoking dystopian novel that the YA audience would be talking about. Unfortunately, it also suffers from the dreaded "tries too hard" that is so common these days. The beginning is slow and plodding but this does pick up as the story moves on. By about midway through the novel almost seems to change completely and it becomes non-stop action packed which will appeal to reluctant readers (but they have to get past the slow part first which most will not do and give up early on). The characters are likeable enough but not particularly engaging...just so-so, not at all memorable. The biggest problem, though, is the pointless middle section of the book where a series of "scenes" just seem to be added for filler. It seems so much like filler that I honestly wondered if this was a short story that the author has attempted to lengthen into novel form for the sake of publication. Overall, I had high expectations for this book and was unfortunately let down by the novel.

Inhalt: Italien, 1453: Alles deutet auf das bevorstehende Ende der Welt hin. Geruchte uber schwarze Magie, Werwolfe und andere mysteriose Erscheinungen ranken sich quer durch das Land. Im Auftrag eines geheimen Ordens macht sich der junge Novize Luca auf, diese ratselhaften Vorkommnisse aufzuklaren. Sein erster Fall fuhrt ihn in ein Kloster, dessen Nonnen unter schrecklichen Visionen leiden und die Wundmale Christi zeigen. Angeklagt wird die hubsche Isobel - einzig Luca glaubt an ihre Unschuld. Doch kann er sie auch beweisen? Die Suche nach der Wahrheit fuhrt ihn tief in den Abgrund der dunkelsten Angste und Geheimnisse des Mittelalters. (Quelle: Verlag) 
 Meine Meinung: Ich war eigentlich nie Fan von historischen Romanen. Wurde man mich nach Buchgenres fragen, die ich nicht lese, ware dieses wahrscheinlich dabei gewesen. In letzter Zeit habe ich jedoch immer wieder mit dem Gedanken gespielt, mal einen Schritt in diese Richtung zu wagen. Als ich dann eine Mail von Fischer bekam, in der mir Order of Darkness angeboten wurden konnte ich nicht nein sagen. Denn das ist der Auftakt einer Jugendreihe im Genre historische Romane aus der Feder von Philippa Gregory, die schon einige Erfahrungen auf diesem Gebiet sammeln konnte. 
 Es ist sehr schwer dieses Buch zu bewerten, denn meine Meinung dazu schwank zwischen den beiden Extremen fand ich gut und fand ich gar nicht gut. Erst einmal konnte mich die Autorin mit diesem Roman eindeutig von dem Genre uberzeugen. Mission erfullt also und ich bin gespannt, weitere historische Romane zu lesen. Ich hatte immer meine Probleme damit, die ganzen Brauche und Denkweisen des Mittelalters in einem Buch zu finden. Besonders, was den Aberglauben und die Religion angeht. Aber genau um diese Dinge geht es hauptsachlich in Order of Darkness und glucklicherweise haben mich diese Dinge beim Lesen nicht gestort. 
 Obwohl es im Klappentext den Anschein hat, als seien auch Fantasy Elemente im Buch enthalten, ist dem nicht so. Die mysteriosen Erscheinungen im Buch fundieren auf dem Aberglauben und werden von den Protagonisten auf eine tolle und uberraschende Weise gelost und diese Auflosung war nie vorhersehbar und konnte mich immer uberraschen. Ich habe das Buch eigentlich sehr gerne gelesen und zusammen mit Philippa Gregorys Schreibstil hat das Lesen wirklich Spass gemacht und war kurzweilig. 
 Soviel zu den positiven Punkten. Ich habe allerdings auch einige kleine Kritikpunkte. Im Klappentext bekommt man den Eindruck als wurde das Buch aus Isobels Sicht erzahlt und als spiele Luca nur eine nebensachliche Rolle. Ich komme sehr gut mit Frauen als Erzahlerinnen klar und war sehr erleichtert, dass dies in meinem ersten historischen Roman auch der Fall sein wurde. Besonders, da die Frau im Mittelalter ja auch eine ganz andere Rolle inne hatte, als heute. Das Buch wird allerdings zu 95% aus Lucas Sicht erzahlt, was mich erst einmal uberrascht hat und dann auch ein wenig gestort hat. Der Schreibstil und wahrscheinlich auch die ziemlich mannliche Sichtweise Lucas haben dann dazu gefuhrt, dass ich zwar mit den Personen mitfuhlen konnte, mich aber leider nicht in sie hineinversetzen konnte. Dazu kommt noch, dass ich Isobel und auch ihre Freundin Ishraq um einiges interessanter fand. 
 Ein weiterer Kritikpunkt ist, dass ich angenommen habe, dass sich das ganze Buch um den Konflikt dreht, der im Klappentext erwahnt wird. Allerdings nimmt dieses Thema nur die erste Halfte des Buches ein, wahrend Luca in der zweiten Halfte zu einem neuen Fall geschickt wird. So erinnert das Buch eher an zwei Kurzgeschichten in einem Buch und hat den Lesefluss zwischendrin auch ein wenig gestort. 
 Bewertung: Philippa Gregory konnte mich trotz einiger Kritikpunkte mit Schicksalstochter fesseln und hat mir das Genre historische Romane erfolgreich naher gebracht. Das Buch war spannend und nicht immer vorhersehbar und man bekommt Lust auf die beiden Fortsetzungen der Reihe. Wegen meinen beiden kleinen Kritikpunkten gebe ich Order of Darkness: Schicksalstochter nur 4 von 5 Fuchschen. 
 Vielen herzlichen Dank an den Fischer Verlag fur das tolle *Rezensionsexemplar.

Despite having an interesting setting the book is unable to get out of the lazy cliches used to catch young readers. In fact it never really takes off and it's filled with them. 
 The protagonists are Luca Vero, a young monk who due to his curiosity, imprudence and luck gets to be part of a secret Catholic order that wants to understand the knowledge the pagan cultures currently have and use to win battles against them (right after the fall of Constantinople) and Isolde of Lucretili, a young woman raised to be an independent owner of his father's lands that finds herself betrayed by his own brother in some pretty silly circumstances. When they meet each other whatever promise the initial setting had to be anything more than a run of the mill light romance setting dies off. And both Luca and Isolde's role is reduced to blushing when talking to each other while their servants Frieze and Ishraq do all the work and solve the uninspiring mysteries (An additional character is just there to remind Luca he has work to do and nothing else). Philippa Gregory uses a couple of pathetic devices to try to work it out. The fact that the kid is on his first couple of missions so we don't get to see any of his special skills and an annotation at the end of the book about how different the medieval mindset was from the one we currently have (we don't see any of this in the book, so it works as an excuse to make the truth-searching missions something very ordinary) 
 At the end of the book she mentions something about being her first actual piece of fiction without characters based on any historical figure. Unfortunately this lack of experience is painfully evident and thanks to the cliches and the lack of anything to look forward to, turns Philippa's effort into borderline rubbish. It doesn't matter if Luca ends up discovering corruption in the Pope's order or if he just helps Isolde's to set things straight with his brother, assuming her style doesn't improve the story will just follow past them while they predictably fall in love with each other like any poor fanfiction.
Solid read, liked the historical details, even if I hate the way women were treated back then.
This book was so bad I didn't even finish it and I was halfway through. Ugh.

book_b.title: Marcelo in the Real World
book_b.user_review:
Marcelo Sandoval is 17 years old. He has been attending a special school due to an unspecified disability that seems to be something like Asperger Syndrome. His plans to spend the summer before his senior year of high school training ponies to work with disabled children are suddenly upended by his father, who wants him to work "in the real world" for the summer - specifically, as a law firm mailroom clerk. Marcelo is an interesting character, but his voice is inconsistent, and the ambiguity of his disorder reads as a way for the author to avoid being constrained by the characteristics of an actual diagnosed condition. Marcelo's parents are often given peculiar-sounding dialog, contributing to the uneven voice. 
 While this book is being marketed as a YA title, it feels more like adult literary fiction. The mild mystery and romance elements are nearly lost in the narrative. Pages of beautifully crafted prose are suddenly interrupted by clunky phrases. Overall, a promising concept that falls flat in the execution. Disappointing.

sample_reviews.review_text: Great book dealing with Asburger's syndrome. This book almost made me move past my own prejudices dealing with they way people speak and act without really thinking about it, and how hard it could be for someone who deals with things so literally, great book.

I have had this book on my to-read list and am so glad I came across it in the library recently. If you liked The Curious Incident of the Nighttime Dog, then I believe you will like this one. It is narrated by Marcelo who is a high-functioning autistic teenager and is pressured by his father to work in the mail room at his father's law firm over the summer. As you read the book, Marcelo's narration changes as he changes which is fascinating to read. Additionally, the mysteries Marcelo uncovers while working at the law firm make this one a page-turner.

I really enjoyed the voice of the main character in this book. It was intriguing to see the world from the narrator's perspective. The author created situations where common questions about the autism spectrum could be answered without making the reader feel less for having those questions or awkward for being curious about the answers. There were parts of the story that didn't really seem to fit. It seemed like the ending tried to very quickly tie everything up into a neat bow when it may have been better if it was left more open ended.
This is a beautiful book about Asberger's (and life). Definitely judge this book by its cover --- slightly subdued, but intense and real.
Becki - I LOVED it. Thank you for recommending this to me!

Marcelo Sandoval hears music no one else can hear--part of the autism-like impairment no doctor has been able to identify--and he's always attended a special school where his differences have been protected. But the summer after his junior year, his father demands that Marcelo work in his law firm's mailroom in order to experience "the real world." There Marcelo meets Jasm...more Marcelo Sandoval hears music no one else can hear--part of the autism-like impairment no doctor has been able to identify--and he's always attended a special school where his differences have been protected. But the summer after his junior year, his father demands that Marcelo work in his law firm's mailroom in order to experience "the real world." There Marcelo meets Jasmine, his beautiful and surprising coworker, and Wendell, the son of another partner in the firm. 
 He learns about competition and jealousy, anger and desire. But it's a picture he finds in a file -- a picture of a girl with half a face -- that truly connects him with the real world: its suffering, its injustice, and what he can do to fight. 
 Reminiscent of "The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time" in the intensity and purity of its voice, this extraordinary novel is a love story, a legal drama, and a celebration of the music each of us hears inside
this book was hard for me to get through, too slow. i dont think i would have finished it if i didnt have the audio and had a better book waiting for me to read.

Marcelo has Autism in the Asperger Spectrum so he's high functioning but still has trouble understanding and living in "the real world" outside his special school. Poised to spend an idyllic summer working with the horses he loves, Marcelo is horrified when his father insists he work at his father's law-firm instead. If Marcelo wants to go back to his special school and avoid spending his senior year at a public high school he has to succeed at fitting into the real world and working at the law firm. When the law firm takes on a high stakes corporate liability case Marcelo is forced to decide between helping an injured stranger, even if it means angering his father, or turning a blind eye so that he doesn't end up in public school. 
 I've seen several people compare this book to "The Curious Incident of the Dog In The Night." I find the comparison lacking in depth. The two are similar only in that their main characters are autistic. Stork's novel has far more depth and resonance for me than the other book ever managed. Months later I can barely remember the plot of the "Curious Incident" but I have a feeling Marcelo will stay with me for a while. 
 Stork brings Marcelo's story to life with precise descriptions, excellent dialogue and characters that feel as real as your closest friend. At times the lessons imparted by the book feel a bit forced but overall it is beautifully written and Marcelo has such a distinctive voice and world view that it's easy to get sucked into the story. This was a fairly fast read but a good one. I can see why the book has been getting so much buzz. It's not perfect but it doesn't have to be. Stork's excellent characterizations carry the book from start to finish.

Really? A four star average rating? Huh. 
 I'm abandoning books left and right lately. I just don't feel like struggling through a story right now. Why do that? There are too many books out there. I gave this one eight chapters and then gave it the axe.

Marcelo attends a private school catering to his autism, aspergers syndrome needs. His structured comfort zone has never been challenged until his father insists he experience "the real world," by working in a law firm over the summer, in an effort to prepare him for life. 
 Marcelo's eyes are opened as he sees for the first time what a troubled world we live in. He is introduced to lust, alcohol, betrayal, deceit, pain, racism, hatred, spite, loneliness, and greed. In "the real world" Marcelo finds his calling and future as he tries to combat the confusing firm he works in. 
 One star sounds so harsh... but I "didn't like" this book. That is not to say that it wasn't a good idea for a story, I just didn't like it. I know that it has received high marks all around by readers, so it's hard for me to go against the crowd. 
 Stark's writing style didn't grab me. The crudeness, swearing, and lack of character development were disappointing. Characters were inconsistent throughout the story, Marcelo included, and the change in voice was distracting. I found myself not liking the story, and not loving the characters. In the end this book was hard to wade through and predictable. 
 For children I would recommend Anything But Typical by Nora Raleigh Baskin. It's cleaner, stronger, and better written. I wouldn't recommend "Marcelo in the Real World" to anyone younger then 17, it's definitely not for kids.

 I read this book for the Unapologetic Romance Readers' New Years 2017 Reading Challenge. For more info about what this is, click here. 
 Can I just take a moment to say that I finished not one, but BOTH of my romance group's monthly picks? As someone who is notoriously bad at buddy/group reads, I take pride in this! #yaass 
 SPARROW was our January pick - I think I was actually the one who suggested it, because I'd gotten it for free from the Kindle Store & was trying to give myself a reason to get to it faster. Mafia romances are not usually my thing...I don't think I've ever read one I liked, and that's usually because "power" is portrayed as "moronic jackass who likes to wave his designer gun around." I don't know much about the mafia, but I'd imagine politics and business dealings are far more effective weapons than a pistol. 
 Troy Brennan is definitely a jackass who enjoys waving his gun around. To be fair, in the beginning of the book, he felt genuine. There was an icy restraint to him that felt authentic and convincing, kind of like Bastien Toussaint from Anne Stuart's Ice series, on steroids. I felt like that subtlety was far more threatening than anything overt. This disappears pretty quickly. Troy wants you to know he's a bad guy, so he's always wearing his gun, always using the f-word, always brandishing that stupid list of his so you know he means business. In the beginning, we see him kill one guy and get a graphic description of how he tortures another guy, and that was genuinely scary but after that, it's adolescent posturing, with Troy bawling out, "SHE BELONGS TO MEEEEEEEE!" to anyone who will listen. 
 But - he's also a CHEATER. 
 When he first gets married to the heroine, Sparrow, he gives her a gift and then gleefully tells her that his mistress picked it out. It's lingerie. When she needs a dress, his mistress sends her one. He sleeps with his mistress in the bedroom he shares with his wife, because he is a CHEATER. 
 He also fetishizes the heroine's virginity in a very weird way. At one point, he implies that her being a virgin makes her taste better after oral sex. The heroine is so afraid that he's going to rape her on their wedding night that she slices her foot and puts the blood "in there" so she can tell him she's on her period. Troy makes her take her underwear off, demanding to see the blood, and then PUTS HIS FINGER IN THERE AND LICKS SOME. Ew. I think that is worse than the tampon scene in FSoG. Even grosser, we find out later that Troy was forced to marry Sparrow by his father to get her inheritance, and knowing that, he kept her a virgin her whole life by threatening anyone he thought was interested. 
 "[He ke]pt you a virgin all this time so he'd be the one to pop your cherry" (246) 
 She was a blank, clean, white sheet for me to scribble on (222). 
 What makes this even more annoying is the fact that Troy has no problem sleeping around. CHEATING aside, he's slept with most of the women in their city, and brags about it. But God forbid his wife cheats on him. He threatens her about this several times, putting her purity on a pedestal. 
 Sparrow isn't much better, personality-wise. She doesn't have a personality, really. All we know about her is that she's a virgin, 5'3", underweight, and very young looking. (I think in the beginning of the story, she describes herself as looking barely legal.) She makes a big point of insulting all the other women in this story, including (especially) Troy's mistress, Cat. But not just Cat. Any sexually mature woman is portrayed as a vile, swooping harpy, whose only mission in life is to titter lasciviously in an attempt to coax men to cheat, usually juxtaposed against good, sweet, PURE Sparrow by means of comparison. Here's how she describes an innocent waitress whose only crime is to check out a man in Sparrow's presence: 
 "A middle-aged waitress with fake boobs and enough makeup to sculpt a small-sized vase brushed past us and eye-licked Brock..." (173) 
 She never appears in the story again, but it's so important that you know what a scheming tramp she is that not one, but two, descriptors are applied to her appearance to make you realize how pathetic she is. 
 I will admit that, bar a few typos, the writing in SPARROW was pretty good. And the beginning of the story showed a lot of promise. In my book group, I initially praised the author for taking the time to actually show - NOT TELL - us that the hero was a bad guy. I think the problem was that the author seemed to want Troy to be this troubled guy, who was so much MORE than an evil, heartless mobster (as that big reveal with Cat towards the end seemed to suggest). I.e. "He's damaged and just needs a hug, etc., etc." But his portrayal fell apart, and he became very immature and unprofessional, and his constant need to posture just made him seem insecure instead of powerful and intimidating. 
 I'm not sure I'd read another book by this author. Even though this is definitely the "best" mafia romance I've read, I still didn't enjoy it. I was tempted to give it a 2* because I felt like the author really did try her best, but I was just too annoyed with the hero and that tacked-on happy ending. A 2* would have felt fake. If you enjoy mafia romances, you'll probably enjoy this one, as it is better written than most. Just be aware that there's CHEATING, for those who are bothered by that trope. 
 1 to 1.5 stars

Sometimes bad books make me angry. Sometimes I feel compelled to make a list of reasons why. 
 If you're fond of this book, don't continue on, because I fully admit that I'm going no holds barred. I'm not taking off my rings. I am not beneath sharpening my nails. I claim the bitter reviewer's right to be nitpicky and overly judgmental. 
 So here we go. 
 Her name is Sparrow. The review could really start and end right there, because what is there left to say? If you're like me, though, and you take perverse joy in outlining someone's ridiculous choices, we can turn to page 14: 
 The sparrow is associated with freedom. At one time, sailors got a tattoo of a sparrow for every five thousand nautical miles they traveled. Sparrows were believed to bring good luck. Sometimes the sailor got his sparrow tattoo even before leaving the docks, hoping it would act as a talisman and help bring him safely home again. 
 You don't say. Sarcasm aside, I do think that's interesting information, but here's a free hint: SYMBOLISM SHOULD NOT BE SO BLATANT. Symbolism's nice, and well-done symbolism is a hallmark of solid writing, but nothing good ever came of shoving it into your readers' faces. Trust them enough to figure it out on their own, and practice weaving it into your narrative in subtle ways lest you end up with this: 
 Sparrow was free to go, to spread her wings and fly. 
 D: 
 You're not free. Not if you're flying away with nowhere to go, and for all the wrong reasons. 
 D: D: 
 "No, not from me," he agreed. "But trust me, lovebird. Even if I let you out of this cage, you'd be flying back in no time." 
 D: D: D: 
 So not only is the symbolism here screaming in your face, it's cheesy enough to be paired with wine. The grand majority of the novel is like this, and I practiced rolling my eyes on every other page. 
 Beyond her name, let's talk about the way Sparrow looks. Because, unfortunately, her physical and emotional characteristics are also a cliche. 
 I am so sick of fire engine red hair and freckles being synonymous with free-spirited characters. Is there no other way to tell me that she's unique? In order to be a genuine person, is it necessary to clarify that she's a tomboy who only has one dress in her closet? In order to assure me that she's humble, is it necessary to remind me that she donates food to charity and is content to serve blueberry pancakes when she's supposedly a master chef? 
 Apparently so. 
 Imagine how many minds would be blown if someone wrote about a brown hair, brown eyed girl who loved wearing boyfriend jeans AND tights, who could be humble and still make mistakes, and whose story didn't revolve around power games with other women and her partner. 
 Sparrow is a TSTL Mary Sue, and I do not understand her appeal. 
 Anyway, the story itself is this: Troy is a dead mob boss's son. He wants to avenge his father's death. He's a fixer. He has a crazy amount of power over what happens in Boston, and most importantly, he's an asshole. Before he died, his father extracted a promise from Troy that he'd marry Sparrow. If he divorced her, she'd get the grand majority of the divorce settlement. So he kidnaps her, basically, and forces her to marry him at the beginning of the novel. 
 Charming, charming man. 
 I love a good reformed asshole story just as anyone else. I enjoy seeing character growth. But, man: Troy is unlikeable. He falls for Sparrow, of course, and, oh god, we need to talk about this scene. 
 So, Sparrow comes from a poor family. Her mom scooted out of the picture when she was super young and she was raised by her drunken but sweet father. She loves cooking. One of her dreams is to work at a fancy restaurant (Troy owns it), and on their first farce of a date, she is given a task to make a complicated dish. If she impresses the chef, she can have the job. Of course she nails it. 
 I am sorry, but you cannot convince me that taking a few culinary classes per week turns you into a master chef. There is no way that Sparrow would be prepared to walk into a high-end, bustling kitchen during prime time dining hours and make something elaborate enough to earn a job on the spot. That is shiny Mary Sue territory. 
 Also, let's talk about the recipe that she's told to make that I Googled and found word for word on the Foot Network's website. It's venison. Venison in June in Boston? Stupid for several reasons: 
 1. Most restaurants intended for the upper echelons of society do not serve deer. I'm not saying they won't, because I checked and some actually do, but it's a stretch from the start. 
 2. You are not going to have fresh venison in Boston in June. It's not legal to kill deer until late fall. Of course there's freezing, but I can't imagine that the best of the best restaurants would settle for anything but fresh. 
 Moving on: of course this impresses Troy. She has spirit! When the chef was sassy, she was sassy right back! He suddenly realizes she has backbone. Unlike all the fake women around him, she is willing to work. SHE is different. Raise your hand if this sounds familiar. 
 Get out of here, super special snowflake Sparrow. 
 Anyway, the plot will progress exactly as you think it will. You will not be shocked. Everything could be cleared up if everyone just got their shit together and had a couple of adult conversations and maintained consistent characterization. 
 There's more, but I'm out of energy. Hating is exhausting. I'm ready to move onto something I actually like. 
 This author has promise, despite all my words. She needs to try again.

Omg this book!!! Seriously. Sparrow was the first book I have read by this author, but I can promise you it will not be the last! 
 Sparrow has everything that I look for in a book. A strong alpha male. An equally strong heroine. And an amazing plot that leaves you guessing, so you can't stop turning the page! 
 Seriously an amazing read and one of my favorite reads this year. If you haven't read it, you are truly missing out!

This is the most refreshing novel I've read in a long time. I LOVED it, a lot! 
 New to me author, meet your new to you newest fan. So impressed with the writing style and the author's ability to weave humorous sarcasm in an otherwise serious story. It worked, and worked well. 
 This will be going down as one of my top 2016 reads. 
 An extra pair of eagle eyes prior to publishing to catch those minor blemishes on this outstanding story would have made it that much sweeter. That aside, I thoroughly enjoyed every page and look forward to reading more from this author.

"I was feeding myself even more lies. Because I told myself I didn't care. While slowly, he crept under my skin. Piercing through layers. Clawing his way deeper into me. And I knew it was only a matter of time before he reached the most dangerous place in my body. 
 My heart."-Sparrow

I bought this book on a whim. I started it yesterday and couldn't put it down. It's dark, gripping, a wee bit angsty, and the banter and feistiness between both Sparrow and Troy is perfect. You do not want to miss out on this book if your a lover or fan of dark mobster reads. 
 Troy is alpha but he's also bad and by bad I mean that he kills people, he breaks the rules, he's selfish and he's not ashamed of it or who he hurts in his path to getting what he wants. He's a complex character that you will love to hate, and hate to love. Sparrow is a fighter, she's making due with what life has thrown her way but instead of lying back and taking the crap that Troy dishes out she stands up to him and fights for herself. 
 In the end the story was amazing, every twist and turn, every fight and every perfectly swoony part were superb. L.J. Shen is a great new author and Im not sure if this is her debut novel or if it's her second but I'm intrigued and I can't wait for more from her.

Can you imagine all of your hopes and dreams flying out the window because of a promise? That's the reality that is facing Sparrow Raynes. Growing up in Boston, Sparrow had glimpses into the seedier side of life. Her father worked for a mafia boss and had quite the drinking problem. Sparrow did her best to stay away from the dark side of growing up in her neighborhood. She had dreams that fueled her towards the future. Then Troy Brennan walked into her life. 
 Known as 'The Fixer', Troy is the son of Cillian Brennan ...the local mafia boss. As the reigning king of the realm, Troy is no stranger to vengeance. Now Troy has asked for Sparrow's hand in marriage. Normally, this would make any girl happy. Sparrow doesn't see it that way. After all, she knows next to nothing about the rugged Troy. 
 Secrets, lies, and deception surround this marriage. Troy didn't plan on having anything to do with his wife. After all - the marriage was honoring a promise to his father. Made years ago without a true understanding of why Cillian had chosen Sparrow to be Troy's wife. Now the vows were made and their life together was about to get more interesting by the moment. Neither knowing what to expect. Troy was about to get more than he bargained for. Sparrow was anything but a typical trophy wife, and she was about to show Troy just how independent she really was. 
 My ...oh my....what an amazing book I just found!! Sparrow is anything but ordinary. This fast paced romance is definitely unpredictable! Revenge is the focal point at the beginning of the story, and it certainly keeps you drawn to the characters. 
 There is no 'insta-love' in this tale. Nope....not a bit. Troy is any but the coddling new husband. He is abrasive, set in his ways, and makes no excuses for his behavior. Sparrow is the complete opposite of a 'doormat'. She is determined to make the most our of her situation without sacrificing who she is deep down. Layers are uncovered surrounding their lives....making for an interesting and seductive relationship!! 
 I couldn't get enough of this book!!! Sparrow is such a great book! It held my attention from cover to cover. It was engaging and entertaining. There was also an element of suspense that surrounded the plot. Seriously - I couldn't get enough! This is the first time I have ever read a book by L.J. Shen, and it will definitely not be the last! Trust me.....take the time to meet Sparrow and Troy....you will thank me later!!

3/5 stars 
 I honestly didn't feel much throughout this story, and therefore I don't really have much to say on the matter. I'm a sucker for a bit of a mobster/mafia romance story, but I felt like this book was lacking in every aspect. 
 Sparrow Raynes was born and bred in Southie, her father having been low ranking muscle for the local gangs. Sparrow had lived a quiet life, she didn't have much of a social live until the notorious son of an Irish mobster, Troy Brennan, tells her they're to be married. 
 This was a hate to love kind of book, with mistresses and cheating playing a key point in the plot. Honestly, I found the whole thing to be rather boring, I didn't feel any emotional connection to the characters or their stories. 
 And the fact that Troy seemed to suddenly grow emotions overnight made me roll my eyes, he went from truly giving zero shits to suddenly head over heel with her? 
 It was 100% better than the first L.J Shen book I read (and hated) Tyed, but it wasn't something that interested me very much. The writing was easy to follow and I found it to be pretty humours at times, but just a little too cliche for my liking.

FANTASTIC!! 
 This book consumed me!! I was so enthralled by their story that I lost sleep!! I just knew love was real between them!! This book had just enough balance to make it absolutely perfect! I hope there's more to their story.

 Where I read books with terrible embarrassing covers, but hope the writing is good. 
 Well... This story really did deserve a better cover! It's not a epic book... the plot is pretty simple... But the cover makes it seem like this is a Porn Without a Plot book. 
 For a sweet insta-love romance this book is great. The couple has chemistry, their banter is fun and the secondaries characters are all funny and adorable. 
 The plot is simple: The girl goes to a tattoo shop and meets the guy. He's attracted to her but comes too strong and ends it up being punched in the face. Next day he finds her playing guitar at a subway. Takes her to dinner, discovers that she's homeless and next thing you know they are living together along with his 4 brothers. He's deaf, she's dyslexic. He didn't speak with anyone in 8 years, but since he can't communicate with her any other way, he begins to speak only with her. This is just something to show the connection between the two, but it was the one thing that didn't sit well with me. He goes more then 8 years without speaking, and then, all of the sudden he's speaking a lot and can control the volume of his voice perfectly so no one hears him? I find this very hard to believe because my friend's brother, who I grew up with, was death and I remember it was very hard for him to talk. It was a daily practice and still is. But maybe it's different for everyone, I don't know. I've never meet anyone else with that problem. 
 Now, the dyslexic thing I buy it because I have a cousin with that problem and her response to the problem is pretty similar to Emily's. 
 But lets go back to the story, shall we? 
 See, Emily ran away from home and people are looking for her, so she can't say anything about herself to Logan. Even her name. Logan won't have sex with her without knowing at least her name. 
 At the beginning the author says she wrote two versions of the book: One with sex and other with less sex (or light sex). I've read the one with sex, I thought that if the sex bothered me (as usually does with erotica) I could always go to the light version. But really the sex was almost inexistent. The sexual tension was very strong. There were a couple of masturbation scenes, a little dirty talk, but only one night of sex. Seriously: One night! At the end! There really was no reason for the light version. The story ends the very next day after they have sex for the first time. 
 I really hated the end of this book. It's almost like a cliffhanger, but not really. There's almost no relationship drama except the fact that he wants to know her and she can't tell him. The book is pretty much all about the sexual tension. Once this is done, you probably can already tell she has to come back home because of the plot. Of course, it's not really a spoiler unless you're purposely oblivious to anything obvious. But (And here's comes the spoiler) there's no one trying to get the other back. Pretty much the same time he figures it out that she's back home, he knows she'll come. 
 And it ends at that: With a promise that everything is gonna be ok...She's gone for a while but she promises that she'll be back. 
 Is this a cliffhanger? I don't know. I don't think I've ever seen a cliffhanger at a HEA. There's a second book, where they have to figure it out how to stay together despite her father and ex-boyfriend. I didn't read the sequel, and probably won't be reading anytime soon. 
 It just feels like they jumped the second act, you know? 
 There's the first act, where you build anticipation, the second act where the drama, the tension the climax, happens. And then the third act, where everything falls into place. But she built anticipation the entire book and then.. BAM! Everything falls into place so fast you have your head spin. There's no drama, no pain, no learning from your mistakes... nothing... 
 I did not see the point to this story.. But it still was fun to read. There are funny scenes, and good characters... I was just very disappointed at the end, or maybe with the middle? I don't know. I just know that something is missing in this story.
Great book but did not like the ending!!

Anti-climactic, sudden ending. The buildup was enjoyable, but the ending was very underwhelming. So many annoying eye-roll moments, unrealistic plot points and magical solutions to unsolvable problems. 
 Kit annoyed the hell out of me, she was such a drama queen/martyr. Ok, you're homeless, you're scared of going home with this guy because you don't know what he expects in return. He hauls you over his shoulder, your response? Well I may as well just hang here like a sack of potatoes because he's deaf and wouldn't hear my protests. I can't argue with such faultless logic. 
 She mentioned that she's been away from home for "so long now" that she couldn't imagine going back? Imagine my surprise when her mother says it's been 6 months...that isn't a "long time" for a 19 year old to have run away for. I also don't get why she didn't just get a job at McDonalds or something and rent somewhere...why this absolute shutdown? Either I go to Juilliard or I'm homeless? There's no middle ground? Also she's a rich kid with her own trust fund etc. why not plan your escape more carefully? Withdraw enough money to keep you afloat, keep in with you in cash, that would still be untraceable to her father, but at least she'd be safe. If she's defiantly trying to prove to her family that she isn't stupid and that she's responsible enough to make her own decisions, this isn't exactly going to help her case. Endangering yourself when you have every opportunity to plan ahead and NOT put your safety at risk is stupid. 
 With the amount of worrying she does about people finding out about her true identity, I thought her dad was in the mafia or something. If her identity was such a secret, how did Paul know she was rich in the first chapter? "not one of us" and all that? 
 Also, Matt has cancer. Second round of chemo, he collapses, the doctor's say it's only a matter of time. But oh! Wait, there's this new magical treatment that can help an end-stage cancer patient and has a super high success rate! What mystical witchcraft is this? It's true, but it's expensive and will cost "hundreds of thousands of dollars". Yeahh..no. Such a hurried "perfect" solution, where nobody actually sacrifices/pays/learns anything screams of an impending deadline set by the publisher. 
 That being said, this is still a perfectly acceptable fluff book. You know the kind, mood boosting light reading material.

book_a.title: The Wind-Up Bird Chronicle
book_a.user_review: A sprawling, at times exhausting, read that I found myself savoring rather than devouring. It's a mysterious novel, at times vague, but meaningfully so. The protagonist's existential struggles to find out the truth of things was effectively wrought. If you like your plot resolutions tidy, though, you might want to skip this one.

sample_reviews.review_text: After slogging through the first 400 pages of this pseudo-philosophical treatise, I still couldn't explain what it was about or bring myself to care about any of the characters. The third "book" did finally pique my interest enough to get me through to the end, but barely. I walked away with no real sense of resolution or even a sense that the lack of resolution was on purpose. The only reason this warrants two stars is because my book club had a fantastic conversation about it. We didn't resolve anything either, but our general inability to describe or agree on any one point was interesting in itself.

The Wind-up Bird Chronicle is a wildly imaginative tale straddling the known and apparent world and a shadow world where strange, malevolent and sometimes inexplicable forces are at work. On its face, the tale concerns a jilted, cuckolded husband whose cat and then his wife disappear. Trying to understand and regain her, he encounters a series of very odd women, some of whom he sleeps with. His attempt to reconnect with his wife is punctuated by long stories of the pre-World War II occupation of Manchuria related in part by one of the strange women and in part by an old soldier of the war. Much of the book is spent in the bottom of a literal well. 
 It is a nonlinear tale, a pastiche of news accounts, real-time narrative, old war stories, letters, and personal histories. A number of disparate themes present themselves throughout: fate, water, birds, baseball, skin, men without faces. None is really tied up in a neat way; unfinished threads hang from this book's pages. While many of the individual war stories would themselves make fine stand alone narratives full of doomed and evil men and driven by strong narrative force, the tale of the main character's search for his wife is far more slack. 
 What drives this slackness is the fact that the main narrator, the husband, is by far and away the least interesting character in the novel. Females full of character and drive and ambition surround and dote on him, but he is completely acted upon rather than acting as an agent himself. He largely obeys their direction. We learn a lot about the sandwiches he prepares and the cigarette varieties he does not smoke. When the going gets tough, he disappears down a well for days to think. I kept hoping he would disappear from the novel and let the more interesting characters have more room on the stage.

I can't keep doing this to myself 
 File this one under a new Goodread tag: books-i-gave-up-reading. 
 I did not hate this novel, but I could not finish this novel. I'll tell you why: 
 My general rule for reading novels is to give it 50 pages. If by that time the novel isn't doing anything for me--the style of writing, the characters, the story development--I'll stop. I mean: *something* the author is doing must make me want to read. Rarely have I put a book down. Rarely is there nothing--style, characters, story--to make me *not* want to read. 
 Well, I gave The Wind-Up Bird Chronicle much much more than 50 pages. But I can't go on. 
 As I've mentioned in other reviews, novelists give themselves away in their novels. It can't be helped; it's part of the creative process. What also can't be helped is that novelists tell you about their novel *within* the novel. With the best writers--in the best novels--this is very subtle. It's almost non-existent, or transparent, because it's so much a fabric of the novel itself. But it's always there. It's always there. 
 And here it is in The Wind-Up Bird Chronicle: Mr. Murakami warns us what kind of novel he's writing on p. 82. It's free form literature. He mentions three "free jazz" musicians on p. 82. Albert Ayler. Ah, I thought. I see where he's going with this, and I'm not liking it. On the next page, p. 83, Mr. Murakami reviews the main portions of the "story," such as it was up to that point, for us. Thank you, I wanted to say, because I don't remember! And don't really care anymore! 
 I plodded on. 
 By page 180 I felt like the narrator when he says to himself: "I had to move my body, to begin working toward some goal." The next page stopped me cold: "I felt as if I had become part of a badly written novel....." 
 I put the book down and thought: I wouldn't say "badly written." I would say "poorly constructed." To this point in the book it was like reading a Bukowski "slice of life" novel; or, watching Andy Warhol's 45-minute epic "Eat". It's idiotic. 
 As a writer and reader, I find nothing of value to continue reading this book. I take that back. I find things of value in how *not* to write. But I can't go on. 
 I'll leave my review of The Wind-Up Bird Chronicle at that and close this book and place it back up on my shelf where it will remain likely unread for the remainder of my days.

I really wanted to like this book, having LOVED THE SH*T out of Ready Player One... but it disappointed. This review pretty much nails it--it's a pale imitation of his own work. http://www.avclub.com/review/ready-pl... 
 The pop culture references felt forced. The characters were flat. And there were major plot holes. (Major pet peeve: over and over, there would be a series of events that was supposed to occur in a length of time that was RIDICULOUSLY short, but very specific--like, the 7 seconds it takes for a drone to self destruct. Why not make it 30 seconds, author man??) 
 The audiobook narration by Wil Wheaton was the sole saving grace.

After reading Ready Player One, I was ready to once again immerse myself in a pop-culture vintage gaming world that only the geek-addled mind of Ernest Cline could possibly cook up. 
 Alas, be careful what you wish for is the phrase of the day as I was left feeling bitter, empty and unsatisfied by the end of Armada. What went wrong? Well... everything. 
 First, the pop culture references were just too much. We get it Cline, you know your stuff, but no mother speaks in incessant Star Wars quotes. No mother can out-geek their incredibly geeky teenage son, because a mother has got other life things to worry about, like a job, and keeping the house in check, and just doing mum stuff. You know, real stuff, that somehow Zack's mother can easily manage in addition to keeping up with the latest pop culture and video gaming trends. But that's not where it ends. Oh no, apparently every single person in the world is a geek guru, a maestro of pop culture, a wizard of obscure movie references. While Zack spews out pop culture references like some sort of geek machine gun, every person he interacts with not only understands, but responds with the same unashamed gusto and level of knowledge normally reserved for those who are so obsessed with particular fandoms that they tend to neglect everything else, including personal hygiene. 
 Not Zack though, and not his friends, or casual bystanders. Strike one. 
 Second, Zack is introduced as a teenage kid with anger issues stemming from the death of his dad at a young age. A solid, if cliched, basis for a character. Then his anger issues just sort of... never come into play again, except for some off-hand reference to them fueling his mad gaming skills and his headstrong attitude. Cline commits this sin again by introducing a character that you think will kindle a lasting rivalry with Zack, only to never mention them again except as a brief one-liner during the weak climax. Cline does this over and over again, like a malfunctioning Chekov's Gun that leaves us with nothing but a vague feeling of dissatisfaction. Strike two. 
 Third, everything else in the book is crap. The characters have less depth than a rain puddle. I've witnessed greater twists and turns watching paint dry. I've felt more sorrow when I stepped on a slug that one time than when particular characters die. I experienced greater satisfaction from a train arriving on time than I did reading the climax and the aftermath. There is nothing in this book that's redeemable, except maybe Zack's music playlist that he ceaselessly reminds us of, over and over again. We get it, it's called Raid the Arcade, it's your dad's, you listen to it when you're gaming, now please for the love of god just shut up. 
 Strike three, four, five, everything. Here's a geek reference for you, Cline: Alt-F4 this book and try again.

This is the first audiobook I've ever listened to and Will Wheaton's narration was amazing. 
 The story however? I didn't enjoy it as much as Ready Player One.

Ernest Cline kind of surprised everyone with the adventurous entertainment of his debut novel, Ready Player One, with its fun video game atmosphere and myriad 80's jokes and references. Sadly, his follow up novel, Armada, has an interesting premise that is plenty entertaining, but just doesn't feel very original. 
 It's a familiar storyline: Zack Lightman lives in a different world to everyone else. He is always daydreaming, obsessed with a number of video games, particular Armada, and continues to wonder about his father who died in a freak accident. His old man left lots of journals and books about the games he played, as well as one specific volume with all his conspiracy theories about video games and how they're really an elaborate cover-up to brainwash everyone about how we are not alone in the universe and one day they'll be coming and we need to be ready for them. 
 Then one day while he's daydreaming in class, he sees a flying saucer outside in the sky in broad daylight. Only it's not your stereotypical flying saucer, it's specifically a ship from the video game he can't get enough of, Armada. As Zack takes a journey down a thought path that is convinced his father was insane with all his crazy conspiracy theories, and now Zack is following in the same footsteps. 
 Then it happens. It turns out a number of the characters and ships and weapons from Armada are in fact completely real. Zack has just been drafted, as one of the game's top players, to fight. Because the evil aliens in the game are also real and have plans to attack and destroy Earth. Also, his dad happens to be alive, working to fight against the aliens, and is currently residing on the moon. 
 Armada would feel like a great original and entertaining novel if it weren't for Orson Scott Card's Ender's Game, about a group of kids who think they're playing video games but are in fact fighting aliens and saving the world. While this book is different, it is too close and similar of a storyline to not set the reader off in anger. 
 Originally written on August 27th, 2015 (c)Alex C. Telander. 
 For more reviews, check out the BookBanter site.

2,5 
 And not much really to say about this one, because everything has been said already and, sadly enough, all the low rates and reviews were pretty accurate. 
 Do I think this novel is really that bad? Well, as you can see based on my rating, that's not the case... and it is, at the same time. How do I explain that? Not that tricky... EXPECTATIONS. Clearly enough, after 'Ready Player One' we all were expecting another gripping imaginative blockbuster best-seller from Cline... the problem is 'Armada' is too much of a blockbuster, and nothing more than that. 
 I can imagine the author wondering what was so special about his first book as to turn it into the big success and even cult novel it turned out to be and trying to repeat the formula. The problem is he didn't get things right. The magic in 'Ready Player One' was in the totally cool 80's atmosphere, capable of relate so intimately with a whole generation. But that happened because of the pop culture references -we all have seen the same movies as kids, all around the world- not because of all the mega geeky gamer references that are just too much in this new novel. So no, it doesn't work and Cline just lost us in the proccess... 
 About the plot and characters... Well, a single word can sum it up: basic. Cliche after cliche, after cliche... the trip can be fun at times and is overall entertaining, but yep, the destination and the ending itself are quite ridiculous, and the word for the whole thing is still disappointing. 
 Blame expectations, Cline... but we'll keep waiting for a great second novel from you... 'Armada'? What's 'Armada'? Oblivion.

When I was little, this was the book I always wanted to read at my grandma and grandpa's house. I think the story appealed to me because in kindergarten, my parents bought a house and we moved from our rental that was being moved to make way for storage buildings. I remember first feeling devastated that our house was not going to be there anymore, so this book was extremely comforting to me. As an adult, I still love the illustrations and the story. This one will always have a place in my heart.

We grabbed this book after finishing our successful love affair of Mike Mulligan. Once we started I realized that I vividly remember the drawings from my childhood. It's a story of a tiny country house, who has a big city grow up around it. Unrealistically a long lost family stumble back upon the house in poor condition and have it moved back out into the country. My husband, child, and I all found the notion that they drove around with the house, waiting to find the perfect location. Nobody cavorts around while hauling a house - even the two year old knows that.
This is one of those books that I loved as a child and was able to rediscover as a parent.
