sample_reviews.review_text: Very interesting read and nice to learn about Seaworlds background. Especially good news recently that they won't be capturing any more whales!

Sorry to the author for the fact that it is taking me so long to finish this book. It is just something that I have been unable to get into and read. I am not sure why, because I want to find out about his dog (a breed that I have had and love). I wish this was more appealing to me, and it has been hard for me to finish. I will try again at another time, and hopefully I will be able to read it all.

Like John Hargrove I was enthralled by the allure of the killer whales the first time I went to Sea World as a child. Unlike Hargrove, my mom never let me pursue my dream to work with them. I thoroughly enjoyed this book because it gave me a glimpse into what could have been my life had a gone down the same path. Hargrove and Blackfish opened my eyes to the lives Sea World's killer whales live and how they essentially prisoners. Like Hargrove I too fell victim to the entertainment branding and never looked the beneath the surface. Reading about Hargrove's experiences with the whales, learning about Sea World and their business, and watching Blackfish really forced me to look beyond the Sea World brand and think about the animals. In 2003, I participated in Sea World's Trainer For A Day program and fell in love with the life Hargrove lives. But, it was a business deal where I paid Sea World to allow me a day close to the animals. I didn't get to see what really goes on. Now, I feel like I've had a glimpse and will not be visiting Sea World again or taking my kids there. Instead, as a result of Blackfish and this book I plan to educate my children about all types of animals in other ways that are less money focused and more focused on animals. 
 I highly recommend this book to anyone who loves Sea World so that they see beyond the brand and really think about what they are contributing money towards.

Just finished a very profound and eye opening book called Beneath the Surface by John Hargrove. He tells the other side to the life of Killer Whales in captivity and their life at Sea World. He used to be a trainer at Sea World until he finally saw the "light" and what was really going on. I never thought about what he discusses in his book at what goes on behind the scenes at Sea World. I blindly went to Sea World as a child many times, enjoying the park and everything else. What an eye opener this book and the documentary, Blackfish was. I will never see Sea World the same way or the way this magnificent animals live and are treated again.

I'm having a difficult time with the book. On one had I did find it interesting to read and to get an insight into the life of these horribly abused creatures (the stars given are entirely for them), on the other hand I found the voice of the author completely intolerable all through the book. The guy worked at these parks in direct contact with the animals for 14 years and it took him that long to realize that they are abused and don't live in acceptable conditions? I don't claim to know a whole lot about Orcas myself, but isn't that entirely obvious? And, while there is no question about the faults within the SeaWorld corporation, they would not exist without people like the author .. you don't get away with blaming the big bad corporation if you are an intrinsic part about it. And whining about how badly you're paid and how dangerous the job is certainly does not excuse anything. My biggest issue was that the author may have realized how wrong the situation was, he still focuses on his relationship with the animals. That's like a pedophile reminiscing about how wonderful his love for the abused child was and how they even returned it. Ugh!

Maybe I missed something here because even though I don't support SeaWorld's business practices and keeping whales in captivity, I found Hargrove to be tedious, at best. 
 I find it extremely hard to fathom how it took him two decades (and not until 2012!) to come to the realisation that keeping whales in captivity might not be all that good. It's all the more surprising given every chapter has Hargrove mentioning his love of the whales, and how everything he ever did was for them, at least once. 
 For someone that apparently read everything that could be found on whales, it's not just a question of how did these thoughts never occur (or occurred so late rather). It's one of how could anyone even begin to think that it might be a good idea. 
 It starts with Hargrove's dream and implicit selfishness that never gets discussed. He was relentless in his pursuit of working at SeaWorld as an orca trainer. There's no doubt that SeaWorld bears the brunt of the blame, and that corporations create often unjust systems that others have to live/survive within. 
 The difference with systems of oppression and its participants compared to this one is that Hargrove always had a choice. He says so himself: there are very few "elite" orca trainers in the world. It's not a job that you accidentally find yourself in or one that you take to pay the bills. You have to want to be part of the system. 
 People can change their minds, of course and maybe Hargrove is a better advocate for ending whale captivity now because of his firsthand experience. There's no denying that he brings a unique perspective from having been part of the captor-machine. But do we really buy into the belief that you need to have been part of the problem before you can solve it though? 
 His point of difference is not enough. Hargrove continually anthropomorphises the whales and does not confront the role that he played in their captivity. His answer to the question "if you knew what you do now then, would you still pursue this career" is evident enough. (Again, how is this question something he had never independently contemplated). Until he acknowledges this, no matter how much of a changed person he is today, his advocacy is shallow. 
 Hargrove discusses why he is an advocate and not an activist. It has little to do with how SeaWorld perceives activists, it's because activists have moral codes and values by which they live, even if they evolve. Advocates can just as easily be(come) lobbyists. 
 (The second star is because, even though I found Hargrove to be unsympathetic, it's an interesting insight.)

After seeing him on The Daily Show I decided to get a hold of a copy of his book as soon as I could. Beneath the Surface is a sad heartbreaking tale of a Sea World trainer who loved his job and loved the animals he worked with till he slowly came to the realization of just how greedy the Sea World Corporation is. The book details just what a trainer goes through from how they become one to the break down and wear and tear on their bodies. The bond between the trainer and the whales are undeniable. My biggest problem with the book is that often he would go off on a tangent and keep branching off from that tangent so it sometimes made it hard to follow where he was going with a chapter. The book is far more in depth than the movie and goes into more details of the attacks, trainers lives, and Johns own experiences. John contributed to the movie Blackfish. 
 Still do to the very interesting subject matter and the fact that I had a hard time putting down the book I give it a 5 out of 5 rating.

An excellent memoir by Hargrove, sharing his life with the orcas and exposing the seedy underbelly of the entertainment industry. Hargrove is understandably biased, as he loves the killer whales like family, and his life with sea mammals makes him a unique voice to read. I think there is certainly more to read on the subject, and more voices like Hargrove's need to be heard in a country where dissenting voices are often silenced. The author's love for his subject is evident, even from his childhood; he's a great example of finding what you love and pursuing it.

As I listened to this book written by a former orca trainer at Sea World, the analogy that kept coming to mind was alien abduction. Humans have taken orcas out of their natural environment by force. They are made to live in cells with others of their species with whom they do not share a language. Several died before the exact requirements for keeping them were figured out. Humans control when they eat, when they play, and when they are bred. Humans separate them from their offspring even though we know orcas have complex matriarchal families. 
 This is a fitting analogy because eventually the author discusses it too. Seen in this light, it is impossible to justify the practice of using whales and dolphins for entertainment. 
 The author started as a true believer in Sea World. From the age of 6 he dedicated his life to becoming an orca trainer. He loved the whales. He believed that some of the whales cared for him too. But he came to realize that no matter how close the relationship between whale and trainer was, at the end of the day he was still their prison guard. It is only natural that an intelligent creature kept under these conditions will try to fight back. 
 The book opens with the detailed account of his attack by a whale. He is clear that the whale chose to let him live. His break with Sea World came after the 2009 and 2010 deaths of trainers. In each instance Sea World's public statements blamed the trainers for making mistakes. After studying the incidents it was clear to him that they did not and that Sea World was lying to hide the fact that this aggression was a result of psychological stress to the whales. 
 He discusses many types of aggression and health problems that result from captivity. One telling story concerns the baby whales. They swim nonstop for several months after birth. This is because in the wild orcas never stop moving. They have to learn to stop and float still in the tiny Sea World pools. 
 Since the animals are not able to released, he discusses options for how to care for the current whales in a more humane way.This review was originally posted on Based On A True Story

I appreciated this book about the atrocities regarding the treatment of "show" killer orca whales at Sea World in Florida, Texas, and San Diego. I appreciated it and found it very informative to have this behind-the-scenes info about how these captive, impressive and enormous creatures are treated. But, I found the writing very "sterile", and maybe this is because I just finished another much more raw, bracing and honest memoir with a lot more personal and emotional info. This one just came off very sterile by contrast, and it felt like it was aimed at the lowest common denominator audience. 
 But, it was interesting and I've never been to Sea World so it was good to get a mental picture of what actually occurs there. The shows sound just astounding--I can't believe all the acrobatics the trainers manage to pull off, riding on the tops of whales and being pushed along and thrown in the air. It sure SOUNDS dangerous. 
 Due to public outcry regarding the documentary "Blackfish", these shows will be discontinued in 2016!

I have been looking forward to reading this book for quite some time, and decided it should be one of my first books of the year. Unfortunately I was gravely disappointed! I love the Salem witch trials: movies, TV shows, books etc., I find it so fascinating. I was hoping this book would be storylike but with historical facts backing it up. At the very least I was wanting a history book telling me about the trials. What the book actually is is a history book with seemingly no order or structure. It skips around from topic to topic, introduces new people almost every page (sometimes they come back again most of the time they don't), and will often start telling you about someone, and then go off on an unrelated tangent, only to resume talking about that person 10 pages later. A history book would have been preferable because it likely would have started at the beginning and gone until the end, and had a few chapters with key people in-between. I tried very hard to like this book but I was not even able to finish it. Each time I thought about reading more DREAD filled me.

it is decent, especially if one is seeking a quick overview of the history of the massachusetts bay colony during the late seventeenth century in the context of the salem witch trials. i found myself both intrigued and bored--oftentimes on the same page--largely because schiff's droll asides are forced to compete with insouciant attempts at paraphrasing the primary (?) sources (they aren't as interesting as she might think).

(other readers have rightfully complained about the lack of a thesis, though i think its absence would have been fine if it were structured differently.)

 "I want to be a legend. Legends never die. Even if they die alone." 
 One..Two..Three...Four..Five... Six. That's right, six books where readers like myself where consumed and captivated by the stunning prose and raw characters of Katy Evans. And in this sixth and final installment of The Real Series, Katy delivers a knockout punch that will forever be cemented in our hearts!! 
 It's a bittersweet feeling to say goodbye to Remy and his crew. It truly has been one REAL journey of ups and down and I loved every raw moment that Ms. Evans took her readers on. And in this final stop, Ms. Evans has gripped her readers for one unforgettable story that will remind us all why LEGENDS are remembered and never forgotten. 
 "He gives me this rebel vibe. Like he'd rather say I'm sorry than may I, and maybe not even the sorry at all. There's a fierce passion in his features and a kindled fire in his eyes." 
 LEGEND was the perfect last installment. Everything about this book was just PERFECT and I LOVED IT HARD. If I thought I couldn't share my love for Remy, I was wrong because Ms. Evans has written another hero who was just as amazing as Remy. Maverick "the Avenger" Cage is the hero who is worthy to take the place of Remington Tate. 
 Maverick Cage has fought his way to the top on his own merits. He truly worked his way to gain the recognition he deserves. He fought for his mother. For his future. For his love and passion of the sport. And for his self-worth. While no one wanted to give Maverick a shot because of his birth father. His father, Scorpion was a fighter, who is synonymous as one of the most dirtiest fighter left a reputation for Maverick that was undesired. While Maverick didn't know his father, he never denied who his birth father was. He didn't want to be known as the son of a fighter. Maverick Cage wanted to be a fighter to be remembered for his own skills. He wanted to be a legend. And every great fighter must be battled tested. And one way to rise to the top is take down the reigning champion. Remington Tate. 
 "He's kissing me. . . . His tongue, dipping inside my mouth. His mouth is possessive; his grip is possessive; he is acting so possessive. My tongue has never given me so much pleasure than when it's stroked, slow and sure, by his tongue." 
 Reese Dumas needed a fresh new start. She needed to go find herself. Find what makes her happy and live the life that she was meant to live. And so when she was hired to be the nanny to her cousin Brooke's son, Reese took this opportunity to get her life in track. And one mission Reese wanted to accomplish was to be a healthy and fit. As part of Tate's team and household, Reese was immediately welcomed and treated like family. She loved taking care of Racer, Brooke and Remy's son. So when Reese was working out, she sort of befriends Maverick at the gym when she helped him out on a bind. 
 "I think of you." He reaches out with his bruised-knuckled right hand and touches my face. All of Maverick Cage's fingers are on my face . "I think of you a lot." He searches my face and his thumb caresses my chin so briefly, but so powerfully, my knees feel like overbaked cake. "I think of kissing you," he says. I feel like he's kissing me now, with his metal eyes. Kissing me and making me fly." 
 Knowing that Reese didn't have to help him out, Maverick was in awe with Reese's genorisity and kind heart. Soon he begins to form a friendship with her. And as they two begin to spend more quality time together, feelings begins to emerge. Soon Reese was embedded in his thoughts and the same could be said of hers as well. A deep friendship was formed and soon a deep sexual and emotional relationship was also formed. 
 "I want you to love me very hard. Because I'm pretty sure I've never loved someone as hard as I love you, Maverick." 
 Maverick was all about delivering the knockout punch to his opponents but what he failed to realized was that Reese Dumas was the girl to bring him to his knees. There was only one thing Maverick Cage was afraid of losing. It was not a title match but it was losing Reese. And as their relationship deepened emotionally, Maverick knew that Reese was his everything. And the same thing could have been said of Reese as she realizes that this feeling that she is feeling is LOVE. And this kind of love can bring anyone down to their knees. 
 The love of Maverick and Reese was tangible and palpable right from the start. I loved how Ms. Evans made their relationship feel so natural. She allowed her characters to really feel the depth of their connections. Nothing was rushed or forced. And so when it was time for Maverick and Reese to be in a committed relationship, readers felt the full grasp of their intense love. It was the kind of love that reminded me of Brooke and Remy. 
 While I can go on and on about how beautiful their relationship is, I loved that this book was still layered with so much depth, meaning and raw emotions. Ms. Evans allowed her readers to be consumed with an honest, raw, and vulnerable tale of a young man discovering his self worth and inner strength. A young man seeing pass all the negativity and demons. A young man discovering why legends are born and made. And for Maverick Cage, he discovered that settling for a life less than the one you are capable of living is not what makes a LEGEND. And for him, his dream to succeed and find a woman worthy of loving is what makes a legend. And sometimes getting to the top is about showing that even a nobody can be remembered. 
 "He's taking me now, deep and powerful. "Am I hurting you?" Maverick Cage. The Avenger. We're a part of each other. No teams, no past, no future. I rasp out, "Only in the best ways." 
 So once again, I just want to say a big thank you to Katy Evans for bringing these beloved and raw characters into our lives. She has truly given her readers a ringside performance that has kept us entertained throughout the six book journey. And throughout this REAL journey, readers like myself had cried, laughed, swooned, loved, and cheered on for their fighter. And if it was Katy's mission to deliver a knockout punch, mission accomplished. So I think it's fitting if I end my review in the words of Rocky Balboa: "How much you can take, and keep moving forward. That's how winning is done. Now, if you know what you're worth, then go out and get what you're worth." And so if you are ready to read a romance that is layered with grit, passion, humility, honesty, and raw emotions then get ready to fall in love with a LEGEND. 
 Review can also be found on Four Chicks Flipping Pages: http://fourchicksflippingpages.weebly...Katy Evans

sample_reviews.review_text: This one failed to grab me and I had to put it down. Too slow to develop and when it got going, nothing interesting was there.
Yep, loved it, and on the strength of this will go back and read the other associated novels. Thanks for a great story, beautifully told.

The third book in the trilogy that began with "Given Day" and "Live by Night" ends with a bang. Joe's back and though he's retired and he can't shake his reputation nor his work. Someone is trying to kill him, or is that just a rumor? Keep your enemies closer and your friends closer. Great way to end the trilogy.

I have to admit that the only book I have read by this author before this one was Shutter Island. I loved that book, so I was looking forward to trying out his latest book, World Gone By. Unfortunately, I think I am in the minority when I say that I didn't like this book. I'm not saying the writing was bad. This author is a talented writer.. But, I didn't know this was part of a series. I wish I had read the first two books to give me some more background on the characters. I kind of felt like I was walking into the middle of a movie. 
 I got about halfway through and stopped. I really didn't like the mobster mentality of the characters. There was a lot of senseless killing all for power and money. That just doesn't appeal to me. I guess it just wasn't what I was expecting. I think fans of this series will love this book. It just wasn't for me.

This book was o.k. Of the three in the "Coughlin" series, I would say this is the weakest. That is not to say it is a poor story.....it's just fairly predictable, which I won't get into or it would spoil the story. If you are looking to read this book without reading the other two in the series, I think that would be a mistake. You could maybe skip the first, "The Given Day", but you need to read "Live by Night" before reading this one, there is back story you will need to get the full effect.

This book was okay. However, when I read it I didn't realise it was the final book in a trilogy, so perhaps if i'd read the others I would have liked it more. 
 I really liked the main character (Joe) and thought he was interesting and well developed. I also enjoyed the general story line, which although didn't grip me with suspense was good enough to keep me turning the pages. 
 What I didn't particular bond with was the supernatural elements - being the same author as Shutter Island, I expected some kind of twisty weirdness, but this felt disjointed and kind of just shoved in there. I feel it took away from the story as opposed to adding to it. Again, perhaps if I'd read the first two books (if they are even in the first two books?) my opinion may be slightly different.

Great gangland novel set in WWII era Florida and Cuba. The third (last?) addition to the Coughlin trilogy that began with The Given Day. 
 I think Lehane returns to his top form in this book. In my opinion his best work was "The Given Day" and this is the closest he's come to that since. 
 LeHane knows how to tell a story, and he knows how to conjure up colorful characters at the drop of a hat. I think I read this in three or four sittings.

I listened to the previous Coughlin books and really like the first one, liked the second and not at all the last. The book dragged. This one should have been a novella and quickly got to the end. I think the ending is a set up for the 4th.

Dennis Lehane sure does know how to tell a story. I didn't get into the story right at the beginning even though my interest was piqued, then I couldn't stop reading! I loved that there were no terrorist, no Islamic, nothing that we are saturated with everyday, just a good old-fashioned gangster story. I only wish I had known there were 2 previous Joe Coughlin books before I read this because, although I will read the first two, it just won't be the same as starting with #1. Joe is a great character and he's not so "in character" that you can be sure of how he will act and react in any given situation. I love him. The story does get a bit intense but thrilling.
Interesting and engaging, I found myself emotionally involved by the end of the story.

 A certain measure of authorial talent is required in order to make the truly depraved not only readable, but enjoyable. In this realm we can gratefully place the Styrons and Steinbecks of the world. Without such talent, however, the work in which this subject matter is contained becomes nothing more than a product of what Nietzsche called bildungsphilister, or cultural philistines; it is this term that applies to author Karin Slaughter, and her work Pretty Girls is, unsurprisingly, nothing more than worthless torture porn. 
 Clumsy and often self-contradictory plotline? Check. Paper-thin characters? Check. Poorly concealed racism? Check. Disgusting and unrelenting scenes of rape and torture, far more than needed even if they were called for in any amount? Check. A protagonist not only unsympathetic, but thoroughly repugnant? Check. A laughable inattention to detail that verges on farce? Check. 
 If I didn't know better, I'd give the author the benefit of the doubt and write off this literary abortion as a cautionary tale, either as an example of how not to write or as a moral lesson against humanity's darker urges. But I can't in good faith do that, because this is a book intended as casual entertainment for, if the author's bestseller status is to be believed, a staggeringly credulous and brutish audience. Do not read this. Moronic torture porn demeans the reader as much as it does the author and publisher.

** spoiler alert ** 
 This book had a lot of twists to it, which I liked, but I had a hard time relating to Claire. I get that the author was trying to convey through Lydia's eyes that Claire usually made things worse and wasn't the brightest person. 
 At the same time though, I was really frustrated by some of the decisions that Claire made. It didn't come off as believable to me and seemed more like a way to make a scene more dramatic than it really needed to be. 
 At the same time, I get you need to do that occasionally. It's the same with horror movies when they run up the stairs instead of out the front door (you wouldn't have a movie otherwise). 
 The overall plot and ending of this just seemed a little over the top for me. Not in general but certain details. 
 SPOILER ALERT: 
 These high end people not only risking themselves being photographed, but thumbs up? 
 Overall, it left me a little aggravated.

Karin Slaughter is a wordsmith of high repute. She draws a visual picture no pen can touch. Unfortunately, in Pretty Girls, her talent turns to the total degradation of women, the horror of complete mutilation in mind and body. One after another, after another. There is no redeeming value to this book, no matter how they peddle it. I feel ashamed that her unique abilities are used for such a purpose.

Well...I am still a bit traumatized by this book so forgive my review. Twenty some years ago, the oldest sister of Claire and Lydia disappeared causing a between the sisters and destroying the family as a whole. The two haven't spoken to each other in decades, that is until Claire's rich husband is murdered. 
 I can't really review this without giving too much away. I both loved and hated this book. The plot was pretty interesting and it certainly was a page turner, but spoiler...way too gory for me. I can only handle so much and this was a little too messed up. I sometimes wonder how authors think of this messed up stuff without having some knowledge of it themselves.... 
 For some reason throughout the book I kept picturing the Rubber Man from American Horror Story Season 1. Once you read the book you will get what I mean. 
 My biggest gripe with this book was all the I guess you can say, internal dialogue. Every time a character was thinking, it was just question after question. It was if the characters are "thinking" in questions just to make sure the reader is thinking the same thing. It just got a little annoying after awhile. 
 Over all, pretty good book. I little too disturbing for me, but if that's your cup of tea, this will be a good one.
I love Slaughter's writing but this is a VERY graphic book.

Questioning my "Friends" who know me well, saw that I was reading this in my Goodreads newsfeed and let me continue. This is about as close to a horror book as I would ever even touch and there was a lot of detail that I wish I hadn't known/read/heard. Removed a star for that for sure... 
 I felt like I was dropped in the middle of a story from time to time, so -1 star for that. 
 But, I wanted to know what happened next and listened to this non stop, so +1 star for that. 
 I also felt like I foresaw a lot of the major plot points before they happened, so -1 star for that. 
 But, there were enough twists and turns to keep me guessing, so +1 star for that. 
 If you're not squeamish and can deal with graphic detail of really bad things happening, give it a read. Had someone given me that warning, I probably would have skipped it because I'm a chicken, but I powered through.

This is the first book I've read by this author. I doubt I will read others. The story jumps back and forth between two sisters, Lydia and Claudia. It's hard to distinguish one from the other. Their personalities are too similar for me to keep them apart in my head. 
 At the three-quarter mark in the book, I look down and can't remember whose mind I'm in. Then I realize that the point of view has switched in the middle of the scene from one sister to the next. No wonder I've lost track of the characters. 
 I'm closing the book and not finishing it.

book_a.user_review: Seriously, nothing happened in this book. I was bored to tears. I keep giving Lisa Kleypas a chance, but she is not the author for me. This will likely be my last Kleypas book.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I can't believe it took me so long to complete a Lisa Kleypas book. 
 Winterborne, the book and the hero, were not what I expected. I expected a story line where Winterborne has to woo Helen. Helen comes across as a delicate flower in Cold-Hearted Rake, but turns into a kick-ass heroine inasmuch as one can be kickass in Victorian England and still be a lady. 
 Nope, Kleyas turns that trope on its head by having Helen go right Winterborne in the first chapter, surprising both hero and readers alike. 
 Here is where I dropped from what was sure to be a four star to a three star and never recovered. 
 I know there are so many reviews that detail plot lines so I'm going to stay away from that. 
 Please don't read unless you really don't mind spoilers. My first issue is Winterborne seduces Helen immediately. There was something uncomfortable with the scene for me. Too clinical? Too sudden? I'm not sure. 
 I did not care for Lady whatsit who came to chaperone, and I despised Helen's natural father and really wanted Winterborne to give him a big smackdown. 
 Winterborne was another surprise as he was such a brooder in the first book and the first chapter of this one. Helen turns him inside out and into a great big teddy bear. I did love how much he adores Helen who is deserving of it. 
 Can't wait for the twins West's story.

My expectations were too high, it seems. My biggest problem probably was the fact that I enjoy slow-burn romance the most of all, but this book starts with our main heroes already basically being in love with each other. I understand that we witnessed the beginning of their relationship in the 1st book of the series, but I wanted that build-up to continue in this one as well. 
 Overall I really liked the main couple together and separately, and I enjoy the series a lot.

Helen and Rhys are interesting. I loved their dynamic in Cold Hearted Rake, but was really...surprised about how this book began. And the gradual build of the book in general. I enjoyed it but found myself wishing circumstances within the book were just a little bit different.
A recipe for breath mints. Yay!

What exactly was the point of this book. 
 Helen and Rhys were my FAVORITE part of Cold Hearted Rake. Their dynamic was unexpected and fascinating. I kept waiting for the story to get back to them and their hurt/comfort, delicate beauty/rough Welchman relationship. I ate it up with a spoon. And then I read that snippet of THEIR book and it was amazing. I was SO PUMPED. 
 Then I got their own book and all of the sparkling chemistry and excitement disappeared immediately following the initial confrontation in his office. All of the nervousness they felt around each other and inexplicable desire just fell completely flat. What followed was 4oo pages of them hanging out. There was no real exploration of a relationship that still had A LOT to work through. They were just like, alright cool, we are getting married at some point. Suddenly Helen could stand up for herself and Rhys wasn't that mean or ruthless anymore. 
 The whole thing with Helen's father never really felt like a real issue, because any tension between her and Rhys disappeared in that first chapter. I didn't buy into any of it. 
 But, it's Kleypas, so it was still an enjoyable read. I just had such incredibly high hopes for this book.
I haven't been crazy about this series so far. But I love Lisa's writing so I will continue to read what she's got!

I'm amazed at how much I loved this book after LOATHING Cold Hearted Rake! I adore Helen and Rhys. They were good people with flaws who obviously loved each other right from the start and the book was just the story of them finding their way to each other. It was lovely and sweet and Rhys may be my new book boyfriend!!

Much better than book 1. The description is kind of misleading. It sounded a bit rapey but it wasn't anything like that all. Helen came to see Rhys and renew their engagement. Rhys didn't think her cousin Devon would approve of their match because Devon was still angry with him, so he thought that the only way they could marry without eloping was if he "compromised" her, which in historical romances means sex with a virgin before marriage. Anyway, Helen agrees to this plan because she wants him so bad, except she wants to wait to have the wedding until she's out of mourning... five months! Rhys is frustrated but he's really quite smitten and he gives in reluctantly. During this time, Helen finds out something about her past that she thinks will be a deal breaker. She's conflicted about telling Rhys because she doesn't want to lose him. Rhys's reaction in the end when he finds out wasn't anything she expected. I loved how the story ended. This book had more funny moments than book 1, and the secondary characters, especially the bratty twins and charming cousin West, were all very lively. I liked the way the twins didn't judge but were totally on Helen's side. The villain was dispatched pretty easily, but I didn't really care. I was a little impatient with how long Helen held onto her secret, but was rewarded in the end. All the suspense and tension completely paid off. Even Devon and Kathleen were much more likable this time around. The audiobook narration was pretty good, though Lady Berwick's voice reminded me a bit too much of Maggie Smith's character in Downton Abbey (I forgot her name). Pandora's story, book 3, release date is Feb 2017... long wait. Hopefully, it'll live up to or exceed expectations.

I am a little bit of a romance novel snob. I like them but I am hesitant to admit it in public specially because there are so many trashy bad ones. Let me shout it out today, I love this romance novel, Marrying Winterborne. A welsh magnate, Winterborne is a self made man who lack for nothing other than a title. Here enters Lady Helen Ravenel, a soft delicate beauty who can provide the status he lack but ... he actually falls in love with her but ... she has a secret. Rhys Winterborne is deliciously attractive as the love interest and Lady Helen proves to have a little bit of spunk. This novel has quite a few spicy sex scenes but I really enjoyed the characters and the plot. I am so excited that there is a third one coming out.

It was sweet, but damn if these male leads aren't disgustingly perfect. Murr I'm a rake this, murr I'm a bastard that, but in the end they're perfectly cuddly bears. Christ, it gets irritating. Manic pixie dream boys, the lot of them. Especially with this series. It's not bad, but I think I've had enough of these perfect men. I suppose I'm a bit bitter about it, seeing as how I'm currently single and not available, so this is why I rated it with just okay. Well written, nice story, interesting plot. I'm just not feeling it right now.

Once I started this book, I couldn't put it down. There was a beautifully painful familiarity with the topic (weird writer girl trying to survive a lonely first year in college) that kept gutting me as the story unfolded. I loved the way the chapters were interspersed with snippets of Snow and Baz's stories (both canon and fanfic) and that the romance was realistic and cathartic at the same time. This is one of my top books for the year for sure.

I loved this story and how it was told. I felt that the characters were believable in their flaws and the issues they dealt with were realistic and portrayed authentically. For me, it was interesting because 10 years ago I would have related to Wren, heck I was Wren my freshman year, and now I relate a whole lot more to Cath. I've become more introverted, I'm completely comfortable in my nerdiness (though I'm not to her extreme) and am perfectly content with staying in all the time. It made me reflect on how much I have changed, for good and bad over the last decade. I'm not sure that was really a goal of Rainbow when she wrote this but it was an added take away for an otherwise very enjoyable story.

Dit is een heel leuk boek om te lezen! Een leuk verhaal, niet echt voorspelbaar en mooi geschreven. 
 Waarom geen 4-5 sterren? Ik vond de angsten van Cath wel herkenbaar, maar soms vond ik het een beetje overdreven. Op het einde vond ik de kusscenes met Levi ook een beetje too much. En het fangirl-gedeelte vond ik wel leuk in het verhaal, maar soms begreep ik het gewoon niet zo goed. 
 Al bij al, een leuk verhaal om tussendoor te lezen, ik heb genoten!

This review was originally posted at https://natysbookshelf.wordpress.com/ 
 I enjoyed this book since chapter 1. I have to say, however, that I am quite biased towards it - my boyfriend and I met in a US University, I have a history with fanfiction writing (I used to be admin of the fanfiction section on an anime website! Much nerding? Yep.) and have social anxiety myself. So a lot of the book just felt like - yes, exactly, someone gets it! 
 The story is rather character-driven, which means for a lot of the time it doesn't feel like much happens. There is lots of character development, which I really liked to read! The relationship between Cath and Wren felt very well portrayed, I love a good story with sisterly relationships! I've read a few reviews complaining that Cath's social anxiety protrayed fanfic readers in a bad stereotype, but I honestly didn't see it that way at all. I found her anxiety very easy to relate to, and although her social ineptitude felt frustrating at times, it never felt unrealistic. I really loved Levi's character and Wren's. In my opinion, only Reagan was left not quite as complex as the other characters, I wish her story had been more explored. 
 I didn't quite understand how the parts of the Simon Snow story added before new chapters did much for anything... I figured it could possibly give a prelude to what the chapter ahead was going to be about, but I never kept them in my mind while reading the chapter quite enough to tell. Also, I felt like there were many loose ends! I had to go to the FAQ to have one or two questions answered, but definitely not all! 
 It's also important to point out that, while the name of the book, the synopsis and some blurb about it point to it being a book about fanfiction and fandom, it's not. It's the story of Cath, who happens to be a fanfic writer. As much as fanfic is a big part of the book, it's not the main story, and you don't get to see lots of fandom. 
 I loved seeing the writing process of Cath and how difficult it could get, or how easy. I loved writing a while ago, and I had the same situation with fiction writing when it wasn't fantasy... it just didn't feel right. And world building is so damn hard, I admire so much authors who can pull it off. 
 Fangirl made me literally happy while reading it, and transported me right back to college years, and to falling in love. I am absolutely sure I will read this more times, and I look so much forward to reading Carry On! 
 Veredict: You will enjoy this book if you like YA and romance, I smiled a lot through the book, especially the first third. If you love fanfiction, this might resonate a lot with you, but don't expect to see lots of fandom. A very cute summer read!

I was so excited to read this book as I still think back on Eleanor and Park and smile really big however this one just didn't quite do anything for me. All the components were there for a story I love, great characters with background info that made me want to know more - a sweet, budding romance that I was totally "rooting for" - even the fan fiction back story (although a bit much for my taste) had a purpose and helped me understand the main characters better...I was hoping it would all come together in the end and develop into something that I could adore and remember fondly but when I got to the last page I just felt sort of irritated that I came all this way on a journey that didn't take me anywhere at all. Truly wish I had liked it more.

This has been one of my favorite books in a long time. It had a feel like season one of Felicity with a touch of Greek. Cath reminded me a lot of myself during my first year of living in the dorms. 
 This book may not resonate with others like it did me. Apart from seeing parts of my life in Cath's, she's also a writer, which has made me want to work on my half finished manuscripts. 
 The story felt real, with the characters growing during the year, but not such absurd amounts of change that you question the reliability of the narrator. 
 The most surprising part of the book for me was that I found myself beginning to become invested in the Simon Snow series. I would be very interested in seeing Rowell write that whole story for us. 
 The ending wasn't perfect, I feel like it really needed 2 more chapters just to tie things up...but just because the school year is over, that doesn't mean that all loose ends in your life are going to get tied up. 
 This is one book that I highly recommend to everyone.

oh how i wish i could be a writer like cath..seriously! 
 the characters were charming and i loved cath, she had her faults but she was so... real. levi was the cutest and i loved her dad. 
 there's really nothing to complain about i guess and i have to say... i get the whole fanfiction stuff. i had times where i also read a lot of them (harry potter helloooo) 
 oh and i have to say... i would love to read the simon snow series haha

Fangirl by Rainbow Rowell is set in Nebraska. Twins Cath and Wren are heading to college only Wren has decided she wants to branch out and insists on rooming with someone new, rather than Cath. Cath ends up sharing with Reagan and through her she meets Levi. Instead of socialising and going to class, Cath prefers to stay in her room writing fan-fiction. 
 I really expected to love this, but I didn't. There were moments and characters I really liked but the main character and some of the language really bothered me. 
 Cath is well known in the fan fiction world and Wren used to be, too. Wren has moved on and wants to experience real life, Cath wishes she could join the fantasy world that she writes about. She's socially awkward and judgemental, and this judgeyness becomes worse when she and Reagan become friends as they enjoy sitting in the cafeteria judging people based on their looks. We all do this to some degree, but Cath really took it to another level. Basically she's an introvert and that's not an excuse to hate on everyone around you. I can understand not wanting to do what everyone else is doing, I can understand enjoying being online more than participating in real life activities, but I would not want to be her friend. 
 Cath is dealing with her dad's health and her sister's distance, so at times I did feel for her. I also liked the tricky sisterly relationship between Wren and Cath, it felt very realistic. 
 Levi almost made up for Cath, he was really sweet and put up with her frostiness. I don't think there are many people who would stay interested in a person that was constantly talking down to them, so he must be one heck of a good guy. 
 Vegan reference: Wren starts the Skinny Bitch diet (it's a book focused on eating vegan). 
 Ableist language: this book is absolutely littered with words like retard, spaz, moron, lame, dumb, crazy etc I started making a note of page numbers and finally gave up. If I had an ebook I would have done a count of each word to add here - it was frustrating and unnecessary. 
 Thanks to St Martin's Press for my review copy.

This and other reviews can be found at wovenwithwords. 
 The Gist 
 Should I even do these gist things anymore? I feel like it's the same as the plot, but maybe I'm wrong. Anyhow, so - the summary is self-explanatory. I was a huge Harry Potter keep back when it was like the hugest thing since penicillin. I mean, I still love the books and I appreciated that it seemed like she was making Harry Potter into Simon Snow, but there was a reference to Harry Potter verbatim and I was so confused. The book is divided into regular chapters, but each begins with an excerpt from the Simon Snow series or from Cath's FanFixx fanfiction. Between the passages, you have a fresh-out-of-high-school girl who's socially inept and the complete opposite of her twin sister - Wren. She has to deal with the ramifications of choosing to follow Wren to college and having a roommate who seems to have a string of guys coming in and out of their dorm. Obviously, the most significant is Levi who actually surprised me the most. 
 I'm on a roll for realistic fiction novels lately and I have to say that I was blase about reading 'Fangirl' as I knew that everyone really liked it and I tend to see a book before I hear and see the commotion over it. Commotion sort of turns books off for me. But the idea of sitting in a cafe all day in a bookstore is too good of an opportunity to pass up reading a stand alone book like this. Plus, Kristen dumped it on my table and was all, READ! 
 So I did and I liked it. 
 Cover Art 
 The cover I have to admit is one of those adorable covers that you really can't hate. I love that it's drawn and you can obviously tell this is a book about a fangirl (duh XD). I also like that Levi is on the cover - the way that the text makes him sound, it just reminds me of one of those alien guys from that movie, 'Knowing' with Nicholas Cage. I know that's like the most horrible thing ever, but whenever I started thinking Levi wasn't that hot, I'd look at the cover and be all...yes, I like. Plus, Rowell's descriptions of Levi improved - at least I'd like to think so. :) 
 Plot 
 Uuuuh, hmm. What is the plot? I think it was simple and straight-forward. You have a girl going to college for the first time and has to deal with the separation from her twin sister who she's self-identified since they were in the womb. The protagonist, Cath - she is terrible at socializing. And throughout the book, she starts to compensate and develop some self-worth which I did appreciate. I think that Rowell did a good enough job in that aspect, but I felt as if she added unnecessary plot points and didn't even expand on the points she should have. I was thoroughly annoyed with the 'mother' conflict and I disliked how open-ended it was. But maybe that had something to do with how antagonizing Cath was towards her and how insufferable and bitchy the mother was. I don't know. But I wanted to know and see more and I was left unsatisfied. The other part I was bothered by was how quickly Cath's who Fiction-Writing class predicament was swept under the rug. Not that Rowell didn't touch on it, but it seemed like such an integral part of the book and of Cath's character that there should have been more. There were all these scenes where Cath and her professor, Professor Piper talk about writing and what it means. But in the end, it's not addressed very well. As someone who wants to be a writer and for others who identity with the internal struggle of writer, I just...I needed more. 
 I mean how do you go from something this meaningful and seemingly necessary to the book to have it brushed aside? 
 "Why do we write fiction?" Professor Piper asked. 
 Cath looked down at her notebook. 
 To disappear. 
 There were some really poignant moments that I felt hit home. The fear to write. The fear of rejection or criticism. And the fear to create something that you never thought you could pull off. Writing is like jumping into the depths of something unknown. 
 "You said something last time that I've been thinking about--you said that you didn't want to build your own world." 
 Cath looked up. "Yes. Exactly. I don't have brave new worlds inside of me begging to get out. I don't want to start from nothing like that." 
 "But Cath--most writers don't. Most of us aren't Gemma T. Leslie." She waved a hand around the office. "We write about the worlds we already know." 
 I appreciate Rowell's attempt at trying to characterize a fangirl, but I definitely found it stereotypical. I mean, there are great parts where Cath really gets into it and it's special - like when she begins to read her fanfiction to Levi. The idea of fandom is to enjoy some kind of genuine art (whether it's painting, building carburetors, writing, or making pies) with others. And to open others to it and spread the awesomeness. But for the majority of the time, you have Cath being socially awkward, obsessing over things that I admit that I obsess over (like having the need to establish GOOD content if you're one of those people) too. Rowell paints a picture of a character that I do identify with. I like staying home and scrolling Tumblr and creating stuff for my fandoms. But that's not everything. I like seeing my friends and going out. I don't want to be harsh about it because there are moments where I definitely feel like Rowell captures what fangirling is - but then there are other times where she takes it a little too far. 
 The plot was distracting when it came to all the other elements Rowell added to the story. I just wanted to read about Cath and her friends and her family and her college life. Instead, I found at least 1/4 of the book with too many unnecessary passages of Simon Snow. 
 Characterization 
 My favorite character was Levi. Yes, my favorite characters tend to be the blokes of the stories - I don't know. I guess a lot of authors have difficulty with developing a female character that is likable, but to each her/his own. It's just my opinion and I'm sure that a lot of people love Cath and identify with her. I just have to say that I really loved Levi and how he was a genuinely good guy. 
 I also have to admit that there were slight moments where I feel like he was bordering on being a Gary Sue. It was more so after the last third of the book that I felt like he was too good, too perfect - but I still loved him as was. But there was a moment about him that pissed me off, which I'm sure everyone knows what I'm talking about. And then it leads to the scene at the hospital with Cath that makes me want to shoot him in the face with an arrow. XD However, I love how easy going he is - how Cath characterizes him as a man who likes to make people happy because then it just makes him want to make his loved ones happy, too. He's just such a good guy. Eugh. I don't know what to say. 
 OH, and I loved how much he encouraged Cath. He pushed her to do things that she was giving up on and I think he would have done Cath's dad proud. There are so many scenes in the book that I want to reference, but I'll keep it to a minimum. :) 
 "...Are you rooting for me?" 
 Cath shook her head, and this time it just meant that she was confused. "What do you mean?" 
 "I mean..." Levi leaned forward, hands still fisted in his pockets. "I mean, I spent four months trying to kiss you and the last six weeks trying to figure out how I managed to fuck everything up. All I want now is to make it right, to make you see how sorry I am and why you should give me another chance. And I just want to know--are you rooting for me? Are you hoping I pull this off?" 
 To be quite frank, I don't know if I really loved any of the other characters. They were nice. Cath was nice. Reagan was nice. Wren was nice. But all of them irritated me and made me roll my eyes at times. I hated how Cath was just so incapable of doing certain things and just avoided them like they wouldn't come back to bite her in the ass. Reagan made me want to throttle her because she could be so petty, especially when she's talking to Cath about setting ground rules with Levi. She's not particularly prominent throughout the book which I didn't really care if she was, but I did appreciate how she deniably cared about Cath. The scene where she takes her down to the cafe gave me the chuckles. And Wren, bejeezus - Wren just made me want to wring her neck. I mean..She was so obnoxious until the accident and then she had a sudden turnaround and I was just so..whatever to. By the end, I did like her more than when I started the book. 
 I wanted to kill Nick. If anyone ever did to me what he did to Cath...I would not have brushed it off like she did. I would have made him out of the fool that he was and left him in the ashes of his own humiliation. And done it publicly. Yes. I was so ready for him to just be one of those nice guys who Cath has to choose from and I'm just like...eugh - you library jerk. 
 I liked Cath. She was funny and sweet and annoying and eugh. I know I've said that she's this strange character that I don't know whether I really like her as a moving character of the book or if she's just there as a tool for Rowell to use to express something and make it meaningful. I think she's really ballsy and she surprises me. I mean, seriously: 
 "No," she said. "No. I don't want to be distracted. I want to touch you back." 
 Levi's chest rose steeply, just as she set both hands on his flannel shirt. 
 His eyes were wide. "Okay..." 
 Cath focused on her fingertips. Feeling the flannel, feeling it slide against the T-shirt he wore underneath--feeling Levi underneath that, the ridges of muscle and bone. His heart beat in the palm of Cath's hand, right there, like her fingers could close around it. 
 "I really like you," Levi whispered. 
 She nodded and spread out her fingers. "I really like you, too." 
 Gotta say, I was proud of that girl. 
 I think a lot of people loved Mr. Avery. I know I did - especially during some witty sass between him and Cath: 
 "I still wish you'd get a dog," she said. 
 "I'd never remember to feed it." 
 "Maybe we could train it to feed you." 
 That says a lot about Mr. Avery's character and I really loved him. 
 I am awful and I always forget if parents have first names addressed in the book. So for now, I will call him Mr. Avery until I can find out his first name. Chances are I will be too lazy to change this in the future. So yes, I thought he was a good daddy. Not my favorites of daddies in the world of literature, but nonetheless - so good-hearted and caring about his daughters. I felt so awful for him at times and I liked that Rowell didn't go into this part too much. You can understand that a lot of it is going on while Cath and Wren are away at school and you can feel that he's not doing well at home all alone. It was sad to think about and I wanted to just give him his own taco truck. 
 Oh, and Grrrrravioli. 
 Writing 
 There was nothing wrong with the writing. When it came down to it, I believe Rowell did a good job addressing what she wanted to write about. I was definitely distracted by the way that she found it necessary to put so much from Simon Snow into the book. I was happy with the short excerpts at the beginning of each chapter but when the text took up 2, 3, 4 pages, I found myself skipping the pages and not getting too invested in what was happening in the realm of Simon Snow. If Rowell wanted me to get into the fandom of SS, it was not very successful. 
 The dialogue was witty and funny and I appreciated the humor. Conversations were sassy and snappy. I love when characters can achieve that. I suppose it is overdone in novels, but it's just so good to read, y'know? 
 "I still can't believe you work at Starbucks," she said. 
 "What's wrong with Starbucks?" 
 "It's a big, faceless corporation." 
 He raised a good-natured brow. "So far, they've let me keep my face." 
 Don't get me wrong - I easily find this cheesy just as I find it cute. But come on, how can you not smile an chuckle? 
 Also, I think the first kiss scene was terribly adorable. 
 Cath's eyes were half closed, and so were Levi's--and his lips only looked small from afar, she realized, because of their doll-like pucker. They were perfectly big, really, now that she had a good look at them. Perfectly something. 
 He nudged his nose against hers, and their mouths fell sleepily together, already soft and open. 
 When Cath's eyes closed, her eyelids stuck. She wanted to open them. She wanted to get a better look at Levi's too-dark eyebrows, she wanted to admire his crazy, vampire hairline--she had a feeling this was never going to happen again and that it might even ruin what was left of her life, so she wanted to open her eyes and bear some witness. 
 But she was so tired. 
 And his mouth was so soft. 
 And nobody had ever kissed Cath like this before. 
 Oh, and the emergency dance party? Oh my gosh - I never knew I needed a moment like that. See, there are some beautiful gold moments. 
 Levi stood in front of Cath, his face serious (for once) (seriously, for once) and his head deliberately bobbing up and down. "So," he said loudly. "Emergency dance party." 
 Cath nodded. 
 And nodded. And nodded. 
 Levi nodded back. 
 And then Cath started laughing and rolled her eyes away from him, moving her hips from side to side. Just barely. 
 And then her shoulders. 
 And then she was dancing again. Tighter than before--her knees and elbows almost locking--but dancing. 
 When she looked back at Levi, he was dancing, too. Exactly the way she would have imagined him dancing if she'd ever tried. 
 It was a nicely written book. No doubt.

I normally don't pick up a YA contemporary. Nothing against the genre, but sometimes, you get to a certain age where you just can't sympathize with a character anymore, for many many reasons. 
 But in saying that, I'm glad I decided to read this. I'd have to say that the ending was a little anti climactic. But the whole story wasn't exactly leading to a climactic ending. It was just a story, and a beautiful one at that. 
 One thing about YA is that sometimes the dialogue is too unreal. Like an 18-year-old would never think of saying that. Maybe that's just me. But Fangirl made me believe and it made me root for the characters. "I am rooting for you" Geez! Just typing that gives me the feels!!

WELCOME TO THE WORLD OF DISASTER! (*clapping hands*) 
 the fact that I gave both books 2 stars shows I didn't hate them entirely. 
 so, let's stars this review, shall we? 
 when reading the many reviews of one star before(!) reading the book you think you're going into a battlefield- good girl, bad violent boy and another completely abusive relationship. 
 I'm sorry to say, THAT'S NOT ENTIRELY TRUE. 
 Both Travis and Abby are seriously fucked up, more then someone their age should be. and even though one might claim they've been through alot, they're more fucked up then what they should be. yet, qfter you'll read both books you'll realize something- They are perfect for each other, because they are fucked up to the very same degree. 
 I know many people thought that the end result would be that someday Travis would hit or kill Abby or someone else, because he's a violent bastard. But, after seeing many abusive relationship and marriage go wrong in the past year I can say that he won't, he loves her and he won't hurt her even though he tends to be violent. 
 Now, that doesn't make him any less creepy with walking in on her while she showers, watching her while she sleeps or dress up, going through her stuff, being possesive, forcing her to sleep in the same bed as him, getting angry and drunk and then having a loud three-some and once done going to sleep next to her still stinky only because he heard her saying that she won't date him cause they're not good for each other, oh and crushing her date with someone. 
 Also, though the writer probably didn't intend to do so, Travis comes across as a lousy lover. 
 I have more problems with Travis- he inkes her name on his wrist (though it's only her nickname), and play pissing contest with some other guy just to prove to himself that he is still important to her. he loves her but he doesn't listen nor understand that taking someone's suggestion to make loads of money is gonna hurt her and cost him losing her, not until she leaves him. 
 Basucally- he's so afraid of screwing up that he keeps on screwing up until Abby runs out of patience. he thinks that saying he's fucking damn sorry would get her back. 
 when he realize that ain't gonna happen, that sorry doesn't fix everything he accept it and starts to change. he tries his best to let her go, and eventually he realize she's important to him- enough to consider her before his needs and desires, enough to finally speak to her and SPEAK of how he feels finally. of being true that he's insecure and would probably screw up but he'll try his damnest not to, that they should speak. 
 suddenly he doesn't try to posses her as much as making her understand that she's his. and that's where it's finally good. 
 Now, Mcguire took a violent guy made him physically attractive and mentally smart, thus, making sure the reader would be attracted to him just like Abby is, so when he does all those jerk things the reader would understand why Abby sticks around and why she's patient. 
 now Abby, sometimes she acts like a grown up and sometimes like a child. she's supposed to be 19 but feels more like 15 most of the time. they all do, it's supposed to be college but most of tje time it came across as highschool. 
 Abby is not afraid of Travis, she stands up to him when she sees fit, she screws up plenty on her own by trying to be someone she's not instead of accepting herself. thus trying to fight her attraction to Travis. Travis and Abby are really alike in their core. 
 what did drive me crazy was how many times Travis screwed up people would tell Abby she needs to be patient and accept it, until that one time that's too much and then even her best friend understands that that's it. 
 the things I loved: 
 shepley and america- they were good side characters. I loved them, their interaction and relationship. 
 Travis's family. they were fantastic. 
 also, Mcguire is right with part of her messege- sometimes you meet a person and it's just it. 
 What I'm afraid of- that young girls that would read this story wouldn't understand the differenc between Travis and abusive male and end up with some abusive guy thinking they tamed them some Maddox. that would be disastrous!!! 
 Travis is a bad boy in many ways, and quite on the dangerous side. He won't be tamed unless he wanted to. the kind of girl that would tame such a guy is too rare, I think it's better that young girls won't try, so they won't end up with some abusive jerk that would hit them and abuse them emotionally and phisically. 
 because, abusive males are charming, full of confidence and insecure deep down in them (just like Travis), but they'll try to isolate the girl from her supporting network of friends and familly, making her completely dependent on him, they'll try to hurt her 
 self-confidence and merge her identity with his. until she'll think of how he would react to something she did before she did it, losing herself and her will. being completely affected by his moodswings, he'll blame her for most things that went wrong, and if he was successfull she'd blame herself. he'd hurt her and then apologise, then he'll try to make it up to her until next time- creating a destructive and neverending cycle. 
 so yes, some points in the story were borderline to this kind of attitude, but in the end when you look closely you see it wasn't- Travis never tried to cut Abby from her support, he didn't blame her for every screwup, he apologised and tried his best to change (and did change), he accepted the fact that she's a person of her own- and she never let him forget that- and he tries to encourage her. 
 so, just be careful, ok?

I have made a resolution not to search for books on goodreads anymore, because inevitably, the ones with higher ratings are ones that are liked by Bella-Edward fans, who write in their reviews "YAAAA!!!!!!!!!!!! HEART LOVE HEART LOVE ." 
 This book has a very cliched and boring premise: Good girl intrigues bad boy; bad boy tricks good girl into "hangin'" with him, bad boy falls in love with her. 
 However, I thought to myself that such a cliched storyline could not POSSIBLY have garnered such a high rating if it weren't special, right? Plus, that cover is pretty awesome -- I'm thinking to myself, Is the butterfly trapped in the jar representative of the characters in the book? Symbolic of societal issues? 
 Answer: I didn't get far enough into the book to find out. Basically, I didn't get even as far as the "good girl intrigues bad boy." What happens in the beginning of the book is that this good girl is somehow always pulled by her friend America to events, including an underground fight ring. The first fight she attends has the main guy "Travis Mad Dog Maddox" as a combatant. He does nickname her some really weird, random nickname, Pigeon, for no reason at all. I mean, does she look like a bird b/c she's skinny? Does she tilt her head to one side when she's thinking? Does she have beady black eyes and poop on statues? NOTHING is revealed as to this mystery. 
 Moving past that, let's discuss how such a "good girl" would be friends with America, who's hanging out with what I'm assuming to be kind of shady characters (um, such as a combatant in an underground fight ring?)? We're also led to believe at some point that Travis has aced his literature class. Also, the first time the main girl (I can't even remember her name) is tricked into eating with Travis is totally nonsensical -- granted, she made a promise to Travis to go to his dorm, but she went with America and her boyfriend. Granted, she did not have dinner, but how is she in any way obligated to go on what turns out to be a date with Travis??? Please, can we just call her the way I see it? A big giant hypocritical LOSER?? 
 The book is incredibly lame. Let's assume that Travis is the hottest stud in the world, sprays himself regularly with Axe cologne so that women are undressing around him and fall at his feet. I went to a high school with 2400 people, and there were TONS of hot guys everywhere. Seriously, we had some male models at my school (I realize not everyone has hot people at their school, but I really did. My yearbook looked like an Abercrombie advertisement), and no matter how hot or studly these guys were, I NEVER saw any girl (or two girls at the same time openly vying or) gaping after Travis Maddox in the fashion described in this book. I mean, we're assuming that alcohol isn't openly consumed on the school campus, right? 
 So, either every girl is drunk (and maybe doing drugs as well, hallucinogens, probably), or Travis Maddox is actually an alien sent to infiltrate and impregnate the human race, one college girl at a time. Which would make for a far more interesting book, if you ask me.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I love everything about this really dysfunctional friendship/relationship between Abby & Travis. He was the bad boy on campus who could have anyone and she was new in town trying to escape her past. At first she was sending him all kind of signals just making him even crazier about her. He just reminded her of everything she was trying to run from and thought that maybe someone like Parker would be a better fit for her new life. I slowly came to like their back and forth antics between each other. I loved the family time at the Maddox's house. At the end of the book I just wanted to get more on the fire's aftermath. I know that their are other books that follows (probably) behind this one. So hopefully they'll fill in the puzzle to tie everything together. It's a good read and I recommend it :).

Wow!! There were so many feelings and emotions as I read this book that it was just amazing. While I put this as a romance book, it was not your typical sweet and mushy romance at all. It was rough at times, pulled at the heartstrings, made you mad, sad, and happy. There were times I wanted to close my eyes because I could not believe what was happening and then there were other times I couldn't turn the pages fast enough. I read this book in one day. 
 I don't really know what to say other than it was just amazing! I liked all of the characters from Abby and her supposed naivety, to Travis and his rough and toughness, their friends America and Shepley, and even Abby's roommate Kara. There was Travis' family of brothers and Abby's dad. This book portrays very well that families are not perfect, maybe a little dysfunctional or a lot dysfunctional, but that we are all seeking something better. 
 I also enjoyed the college setting. Having not actually attended college as a dorm student and living away from home, I really enjoyed the talk about the underground, the parties, the cafeteria, etc. I could picture the campus and excitement of college life. 
 If you are looking for something to shake your world and take your time away from laundry, cooking, and other responsibilities, you should read this book. Just beware that you will be hooked within the first few pages.
